elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点关注 HPV16 衍生的 E5 和 E6 在宫颈癌发生中的生物学功能,并探索针对这些癌基因的基因沉默策略的治疗应用。核心问题是通过基因沉默方法靶向E5和E6是否可以有效预防或治疗HPV相关的宫颈癌。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述是对针对 HPV16 E5 和 E6 的基因沉默方法的临床前研究的叙述性综合。它不报告系统搜索方法、数据库或荟萃分析。证据来自 E5 和 E6 的生物学机制、它们在致癌作用中的作用以及实验模型中基因沉默干预的结果。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该综述得出的结论是,E5 和 E6 对于 HPV 介导的癌变至关重要,其中 E5 调节生长因子信号传导并促进细胞存活,而 E6 主要通过降解 p53 驱动恶性转化。基因沉默技术,例如 siRNA 和基于 CRISPR/Cas 的系统,在抑制 E5 和 E6 表达、恢复肿瘤抑制功能以及增强癌细胞对常规疗法的敏感性方面显示出巨大的潜力。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该综述强调了将临床前研究结果转化为临床应用的挑战,包括需要对基因沉默策略的长期安全性和有效性进行更多研究。它还指出,缺乏关于这些方法对不同人群的影响的数据,以及需要进一步探索其体内机制。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述建议,未来的研究应优先开发针对HPV16 E5和E6的安全有效的基因沉默疗法,重点是临床试验和长期安全性评估。它还强调了扩大研究范围以纳入不同患者群体并探索这些策略与现有 治疗 相结合的潜力的重要性。

full_text: Background and objectiveAdults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are screened for cervical cancer at substantially lower rates than adults without disabilities. Communication differences, sensory sensitivities, and difficulty tolerating speculum-based examination all contribute. Deferred screening is frequently recorded as patient refusal rather than as an unmet need for adapted care. Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing on self-collected vaginal specimens is now recognized as an acceptable screening option, but published implementation strategies for this population are limited. The objective of this study was to evaluate respondent-reported acceptability, tolerability, and level of assistance required for a nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model in an interdisciplinary primary care clinic serving adults with IDD.MethodsWe conducted a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) at University of Florida Health Jacksonville. Vaginal specimens for HPV testing were collected in the clinic by the patient under nurse guidance, with hands-on assistance from a trained program nurse or a caregiver as needed. The model also included structured pre-visit planning, an animated patient education video, and caregiver engagement. A structured post-visit survey administered in REDCap assessed the level and appropriateness of assistance, patient tolerance, observable distress, acceptability, and support for future use. The survey was designed as a caregiver proxy instrument and was completed directly by the patient where able; outcomes are therefore described as respondent-reported, with proxy and direct responses distinguished explicitly. Results are reported as n (%). Recruitment is ongoing toward a planned enrollment of 30, and these are preliminary findings.ResultsOf 23 patients identified as eligible, 18 (78.3%) were offered the pathway. Among those offered, 14 (77.8%) completed collection, and four (22.2%) declined; zero (0%) attempted collection without completing it. Uptake was 14 of 23 (60.9%) among those identified as eligible. All 14 specimens (100%) returned negative high-risk HPV results. Complete survey data were available for 13 of the 14 completed collections. Among these 13 encounters, tolerance was rated very good in 11 (84.6%) and good in two (15.4%), with zero (0%) rated fair, poor, or very poor; no distress was observed in 12 (92.3%) and mild distress in one (7.7%), with zero (0%) moderate or severe. All 13 encounters with available assistance data (100%) required hands-on assistance, provided by the nurse in nine (69.2%) and by a caregiver in four (30.8%); zero (0%) were completed unaided or with verbal coaching alone, and zero (0%) were unable to be completed despite assistance. All 13 respondents (100%) judged the level of assistance appropriate, rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, and would support offering it again.ConclusionsA nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model was well tolerated and highly acceptable to respondents in an academic primary care clinic for adults with IDD. Every encounter with available assistance data required hands-on assistance, indicating that nursing support is integral to the model rather than incidental. Clinic efficiency, physician time, and scalability were not measured and remain hypotheses for future evaluation. Recruitment continues. Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis was a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study evaluating the feasibility and acceptability of an adapted cervical cancer screening workflow offered as part of routine clinical care. It was conducted at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) at University of Florida Health Jacksonville, an interdisciplinary primary care medical home led by a physician medical director, operationalized by a registered nurse (RN) program coordinator, and delivered by advanced practice providers, physicians, and nursing staff in close partnership with caregivers. The program was established in 2013 and serves approximately 350 adults with IDD, many of whom are nonverbal or minimally verbal and have significant sensory sensitivities and anxiety related to clinical examination. Approximately 40% of the program population are women, and approximately 80% of those fall within the 25- to 64-year screening age range, giving an estimated 110 potentially eligible patients. These are program-level estimates rather than counts from a verified screening registry. Data were collected between February 3, 2026 and August 25, 2026. Recruitment is ongoing.Participants and eligibilityPatients were eligible if they were adults aged 25-64 years receiving care at the PAIDD clinic, had a diagnosis of intellectual and/or developmental disability, had a cervix, were due for cervical cancer screening per clinic practice, and if a caregiver was available and willing to complete a proxy survey. full_text_sections.abstract: Background and objectiveAdults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are screened for cervical cancer at substantially lower rates than adults without disabilities. Communication differences, sensory sensitivities, and difficulty tolerating speculum-based examination all contribute. Deferred screening is frequently recorded as patient refusal rather than as an unmet need for adapted care. Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing on self-collected vaginal specimens is now recognized as an acceptable screening option, but published implementation strategies for this population are limited. The objective of this study was to evaluate respondent-reported acceptability, tolerability, and level of assistance required for a nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model in an interdisciplinary primary care clinic serving adults with IDD.MethodsWe conducted a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) at University of Florida Health Jacksonville. Vaginal specimens for HPV testing were collected in the clinic by the patient under nurse guidance, with hands-on assistance from a trained program nurse or a caregiver as needed. The model also included structured pre-visit planning, an animated patient education video, and caregiver engagement. A structured post-visit survey administered in REDCap assessed the level and appropriateness of assistance, patient tolerance, observable distress, acceptability, and support for future use. The survey was designed as a caregiver proxy instrument and was completed directly by the patient where able; outcomes are therefore described as respondent-reported, with proxy and direct responses distinguished explicitly. Results are reported as n (%). Recruitment is ongoing toward a planned enrollment of 30, and these are preliminary findings.ResultsOf 23 patients identified as eligible, 18 (78.3%) were offered the pathway. Among those offered, 14 (77.8%) completed collection, and four (22.2%) declined; zero (0%) attempted collection without completing it. Uptake was 14 of 23 (60.9%) among those identified as eligible. All 14 specimens (100%) returned negative high-risk HPV results. Complete survey data were available for 13 of the 14 completed collections. Among these 13 encounters, tolerance was rated very good in 11 (84.6%) and good in two (15.4%), with zero (0%) rated fair, poor, or very poor; no distress was observed in 12 (92.3%) and mild distress in one (7.7%), with zero (0%) moderate or severe. All 13 encounters with available assistance data (100%) required hands-on assistance, provided by the nurse in nine (69.2%) and by a caregiver in four (30.8%); zero (0%) were completed unaided or with verbal coaching alone, and zero (0%) were unable to be completed despite assistance. All 13 respondents (100%) judged the level of assistance appropriate, rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, and would support offering it again.ConclusionsA nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model was well tolerated and highly acceptable to respondents in an academic primary care clinic for adults with IDD. Every encounter with available assistance data required hands-on assistance, indicating that nursing support is integral to the model rather than incidental. Clinic efficiency, physician time, and scalability were not measured and remain hypotheses for future evaluation. Recruitment continues.

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis work demonstrates that a nurse-assisted workflow can be used to deliver HPV cervical cancer screening on a self-collected vaginal specimen to adults with IDD in routine primary care. Self-collected HPV screening is now recognized in national guidance as an acceptable option for average-risk individuals, but its implementation in populations with significant sensory, cognitive, and behavioral barriers remains limited. This report describes a pragmatic implementation strategy rather than a novel diagnostic or technological intervention.A key feature of the approach is the integration of nursing staff into the screening workflow to support patient preparation and specimen collection. Caregiver involvement supports communication, patient comfort, and completion of screening within a single encounter, which is relevant in a population for whom additional visits carry transportation, scheduling, and anxiety burdens.Among patients offered the pathway, 14 of 18 (77.8%) completed collection, no attempt that began was left unfinished, and no patient proved unable to complete collection despite assistance. Four patients (22.2% of those offered) declined. Declination is reported here as a legitimate outcome of a model built on assent rather than as a failure of the workflow. These proportions describe completion among patients offered a specific pathway at a clinic encounter and are not comparable with population-level cervical cancer screening coverage estimates, which use different denominators, timeframes, and ascertainment methods; no such comparison is drawn here.The most consequential finding is that no encounter with available assistance data was completed unaided or with verbal coaching alone. All 13 such encounters required hands-on assistance, from the nurse in nine (69.2%) and from a caregiver in four (30.8%). Self-collection in this population is therefore better understood as nurse-assisted collection: the term describes who holds the swab less than it describes a procedure that removes the speculum, the stirrups, and the clinician-directed examination while retaining hands-on support. This distinction matters for anyone planning to replicate the model, because a clinic that budgets for unassisted self-collection will not be able to deliver it. It also means that the accuracy literature on self-collected specimens [9] bears on the specimen type used here rather than on the staffing model.Acceptability was uniform among respondents. Every respondent rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, judged the assistance provided appropriate, and would support offering it again, and tolerance was rated good or very good in every encounter with survey data. Observable distress was rare and mild where present, with no encounter requiring the procedure to be stopped. In a population where speculum examination is frequently deferred or performed under sedation, a screening pathway that no respondent found unacceptable is a substantive result even in a small cohort.The model requires no additional equipment or capital investment beyond the collection kit and aligns with existing preventive care reimbursement structures, which suggests it may be transferable to other primary care settings, including academic clinics, federally qualified health centers, and community practices. Clinic efficiency, physician time, staffing cost, and screening uptake at the clinic level were not measured in this study; however, the scalability of the model therefore remains a hypothesis rather than a finding. The requirement for hands-on nursing assistance in every encounter with available data is itself a resource implication that any replicating site would need to plan for.The animated education video is a low-cost component that is independently transferable. Accessible preparation materials address a barrier that procedural adaptation alone does not, since informed assent requires that the patient understand what the procedure involves. The video is publicly available and can be adopted by other clinics without cost, although its independent contribution was not evaluated in this study.The approach supports more inclusive, sensory-informed care for patients who may otherwise be unable to tolerate or complete speculum-based examination. It emphasizes structured assent, caregiver partnership, and minimization of distress, consistent with principles of patient-centered and disability-affirming care.LimitationsThis evaluation has several limitations. It was conducted at a single academic site with an established interdisciplinary IDD program, and the findings may not generalize to settings without comparable nursing capacity or caregiver engagement. The sample was small, with 14 completed collections against a planned enrollment of 30, and surveys were completed at the end of the encounter, which may favor positive reporting. One respondent recorded the encounter but did not submit the experience items, so those outcomes describe 13 of the 14 completed collections (92.9%); because the survey dataset is anonymous by design, the missing outcomes could not be recovered from the clinical record, and that encounter may have differed from those reported. The uniformly positive ratings should also be read with the setting in mind: respondents were reporting on a service delivered by a team they know, in a program they have chosen to remain with, which is a context that discourages criticism. The survey instrument was investigator-developed and was not formally validated or pilot-tested, so its measurement properties are unknown. Experience was reported largely by caregivers acting as proxies rather than by patients directly, a limitation in a population whose own preferences are underrepresented in the literature, although three respondents were patients reporting on their own experience. There was no comparison group and no pre-intervention acceptability measure, so the results describe acceptability of the adapted approach rather than improvement relative to usual care. Clinic-level screening uptake data were still being collected at the time of this report, so effectiveness cannot yet be assessed. No high-risk HPV infections were detected in this cohort, so the downstream pathway for managing an abnormal result, including speculum-based evaluation or anesthesia-assisted follow-up, was not tested in practice.The HPV assay used here is a laboratory-developed test rather than an assay cleared by the FDA for primary cervical cancer screening. It detects 13 high-risk genotypes and does not include HPV 66, which is covered by some FDA-approved primary screening assays. Pooled accuracy of HPV testing on self-collected specimens is lower than on clinician-collected specimens overall, with the difference concentrated in signal amplification rather than PCR-based assays [9]. The assay used here is PCR-based, but clinics replicating this model should confirm that their laboratory has validated its assay for self-collected vaginal specimens. Clinically, the approach does not eliminate the need for speculum-based evaluation when HPV results are abnormal, and some patients may still require anesthesia-assisted procedures for follow-up. Because the recommended repeat interval following a negative self-collected result is three years rather than five, the reduction in lifetime procedural burden relative to clinician-collected primary HPV testing is smaller than the avoidance of a single speculum examination might suggest [5]. Individuals with HIV infection or immunocompromising conditions may have impaired viral clearance and are not ideal candidates for HPV-only screening pathways. Patients with prior high-grade cervical disease or in utero DES exposure likewise require alternative screening strategies.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsCervical cancer screening disparities among adults with IDD are driven substantially by modifiable system-level barriers rather than by patient refusal. A nurse-assisted model of self-collected HPV screening was feasible within an existing interdisciplinary primary care clinic and was well received: 14 of 18 patients offered the pathway (77.8%) completed collection, tolerance was rated good or very good in all 13 encounters (100%) with complete survey data, observable distress was rare and mild, and all 13 respondents (100%) judged the process acceptable and would support offering it again. Every encounter with available assistance data required hands-on assistance, which should be planned for rather than treated as an exception, and the model is therefore more accurately described as nurse-assisted self-collection. Whether the model improves clinic efficiency, preserves physician time, or is scalable beyond this setting was not measured and remains to be tested. Recruitment toward the planned enrollment of 30 is continuing, and final results will be reported on completion. Further work should evaluate screening uptake before and after implementation, downstream clinical outcomes, patient-reported rather than proxy-reported experience, and sustainability across diverse care settings.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionInclusive cervical cancer screening is a critical health equity issue. Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are substantially under-screened for cervical cancer. A population-based study comparing women with and without IDD found significantly lower participation in cervical screening among women with IDD, leading the authors to question whether screening programs are delivered equitably to this population [1]. This disparity is multifactorial and reflects both patient-level and system-level barriers. Traditional speculum-based pelvic examination may be intolerable or distressing for some individuals with IDD. Deferred screening is then often mischaracterized as patient refusal rather than as a need for adapted care approaches. A prior review examined barriers to pelvic examination for cervical cancer screening in women with cerebral palsy, a group that overlaps substantially with the population served by this clinic [2].Multiple patient-level and structural barriers contribute to this gap, including sensory sensitivities, communication differences, mobility limitations, anxiety related to pelvic examination, and limited availability of clinician time and training to support adapted screening workflows in primary care settings. A systematic review of cancer screening behavior among people with intellectual disabilities identified barriers and facilitators operating at the patient, caregiver, and health system levels, indicating that screening uptake in this population is shaped by modifiable factors rather than by patient preference alone [3].In practice, options offered to patients who cannot tolerate speculum examination have included modified examination technique, sedation or anesthesia in selected cases, and greater caregiver involvement. Each is resource-intensive, and none is easily scalable in routine primary care.Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing on a self-collected vaginal specimen offers an alternative pathway, and current guidance distinguishes it from clinician-collected primary HPV testing. The American Cancer Society recommends that individuals with a cervix begin cervical cancer screening at age 25 years and continue through age 65 years, with primary HPV testing on a clinician-collected cervical specimen every five years as the preferred strategy [4]. In a 2026 update, the American Cancer Society concluded that clinician-collected cervical specimens remain preferred, but that self-collected vaginal specimens are acceptable for cervical cancer screening in average-risk individuals aged 25-65 years, with repeat testing recommended at three years rather than five years following a negative self-collected result [5]. The World Health Organization recommends HPV DNA detection as the primary screening method for the general population of women and, as a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence, suggests that HPV DNA testing may be performed on either a provider-collected or a self-collected sample [6]. A US Preventive Services Task Force draft recommendation statement addressing patient-collected high-risk HPV screening was posted for public comment on December 10, 2024; that draft has not been finalized and does not represent a current Task Force recommendation [7]. Published implementation experience describing how self-collected HPV screening can be operationalized for patients with significant sensory, cognitive, and behavioral barriers remains limited.The aim of this work was to evaluate respondent-reported acceptability and tolerability of a clinic-based, nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model for patients with IDD within an academic primary care setting and to characterize the level of assistance required to complete collection.Portions of this work were previously presented as a plenary presentation at the Society of General Internal Medicine Southern Regional Meeting (Inclusive Cervical Cancer Screening: Nurse-Led, Self-Administered Swab Model for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities, 2026, New Orleans, LA, USA) and as a poster at the Down Syndrome Medical Interest Group-USA (DSMIG-USA) Annual Symposium (Implementing Nurse- and Caregiver-Supported Self-Collected HPV Screening in Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities, 2026, Orlando, FL, USA).

title_original: Respondent-Reported Acceptability and Tolerability of a Nurse-Assisted, Self-Collected Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Cervical Cancer Screening Model in Adults With Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities: A Preliminary Report

analysis.research_question_and_background: Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are screened for cervical cancer at substantially lower rates than adults without disabilities. The study aimed to evaluate the acceptability and tolerability of a nurse-assisted, self-collected HPV cervical cancer screening model in this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This was a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study conducted at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) clinic at University of Florida Health Jacksonville. Recruitment is ongoing toward a planned enrollment of 30, and these are preliminary findings. Of 23 patients identified as eligible, 18 (78.3%) were offered the pathway.
analysis.methods: The study used a structured post-visit survey completed at the end of the encounter. Data were collected between February 3, 2026 and August 25, 2026. The HPV Type-Detect 4.0 multiplex real-time PCR assay was used to identify and distinguish 13 high-risk HPV genotypes. The model included structured pre-visit planning, an animated patient education video, and caregiver engagement.
analysis.main_results: Of 23 patients identified as eligible, 14 (60.9%) completed collection. All 13 respondents (100%) judged the level of assistance appropriate, rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, and would support offering it again. No patients met criteria for alternative screening strategies.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that the nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model was well tolerated and highly acceptable to respondents in an academic primary care clinic for adults with IDD. This is a novel approach to addressing screening barriers in this population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that this model could improve cervical cancer screening rates among adults with IDD, potentially enhancing early detection and prevention efforts. They inform the development of more accessible and patient-centered screening strategies for this vulnerable group.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Given the pilot design and small sample, no inferential testing was performed, and no comparison group was used. The evidence is therefore limited in scope and strength, with a moderate confidence assessment due to the preliminary nature of the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the acceptability and tolerability of a nurse-assisted, self-collected HPV cervical cancer screening model in adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD). The research aimed to address the lower screening rates observed in this population. Conducted at the Program for Adults with IDD at University of Florida Health Jacksonville, the study involved 23 eligible patients, with 14 completing the screening process. All respondents found the model acceptable and appropriate, highlighting its potential for improving screening access. However, the study's small sample size and lack of a comparison group limit the strength of the evidence, suggesting a moderate confidence level. The findings inform the development of more inclusive and accessible screening strategies for adults with IDD, emphasizing the importance of caregiver involvement and tailored approaches.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 患有智力和发育障碍 (IDD) 的成年人接受 宫颈癌 筛查的比率远低于无残疾的成年人。该研究旨在评估护士协助、自行采集的 HPV 宫颈癌 筛查模型在该人群中的可接受性和耐受性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这是一项前瞻性、单中心、最低风险观察性研究,在佛罗里达大学健康中心杰克逊维尔分校的智力和发育障碍成人项目 (PAIDD) 诊所进行。招募工作正在进行中,计划招募 30 人,这些只是初步调查结果。在 23 名被确定符合资格的患者中,有 18 名 (78.3%) 获得了该途径。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用了在访问结束时完成的结构化访问后调查。数据收集于2026年2月3日至2026年8月25日之间。使用HPV Type-Detect 4.0多重实时PCR检测来识别和区分13种高危型HPV基因型。该模型包括结构化的就诊前规划、动画患者教育视频和护理人员参与。
elements_zh.main_results: 在 23 名被确定符合条件的患者中,14 名 (60.9%) 完成了收集。所有 13 名受访者 (100%) 均认为援助水平适当,认为流程可接受或非常可接受,并支持再次提供援助。没有患者符合替代筛查策略的标准。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将研究结果解读为,护士协助的自我收集 HPV 筛查模型对于 IDD 成人学术初级保健诊所的受访者具有良好的耐受性和高度可接受性。这是解决该人群筛查障碍的一种新颖方法。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,该模型可以提高 IDD 成人的 宫颈癌 筛查率,从而有可能加强早期发现和预防工作。它们为这一弱势群体制定更容易获得和以患者为中心的筛查策略提供了信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 鉴于试点设计和小样本,没有进行推理测试,也没有使用对照组。因此,证据的范围和强度有限,由于研究结果的初步性质,可信度评估适中。

full_text: IntroductionThis retrospective, single-center study aims to analyze the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection in women undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China.MethodsA total of 13,492 females, 18–85 years, undergoing HPV testing at the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou, China, were recruited. Cervical cast-off cells were collected for HPV testing by low-density gene chip and flow hybridization technology using HPV typing test kit. A total of 27 kinds of HPV types were detected using this method, including 17 kinds of high-risk HPV (HR-HPV) and 10 kinds of low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV).ResultsThe overall HPV infection rate was 16.86% (2,275/13,492), with 12.59% (1,699/13,492) females detected as single HPV-type infection and 4.27% (576/13492) females detected as multiple HPV-type infection. Among all 27 detected HPV types, HPV52 exhibited the highest prevalence (3.58%, 483/13,492), followed by HPV53 (1.76%, 237/13,492) and HPV81 (1.71%, 231/13,492). The most common HPV coinfection pattern was HPV52 + HPV53 (12/2,275). Overall HPV prevalence showed a “two-peak” age-related distribution, with the first peak in the ≤29-year age group (19.69%) and the second peak in the ≥60-year age group (24.45%), respectively. It decreased in the 40- to 49-year age group (13.64%). The prevalence of single/multiple HPV and HR-HPV/LR-HPV infection also exhibited age-related trends similar to those described above. Binary logistic regression analysis revealed a non-linear relationship between HPV prevalence and age (p < 0.05).ConclusionOur study revealed the basic genotype- and age-specific distribution of HPV infection among females attending the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou. These results emphasized that the specific population should strengthen regular HPV surveillance and improve awareness of vaccination, especially for the highly prevalent HPV types (HPV52,53,51). In addition, our findings provide valuable insights for the measurement of HPV prevention interventions. 2Materials and methods2.1Ethics statementThe study involving humans was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhangzhou Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University (Ethics approval number: 2026LWB202) on 4 June 2026. The study was conducted in accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. Written informed consent for participants was not required from the participants or the participants’ legal guardians/next of kin because this is a retrospective study, and all the participants’ results were retrospectively collected.2.2Study design and populationsInitially, a total of 23,650 participants with HPV testing data were retrospectively retrieved from the laboratory information system (LIS) at Zhangzhou Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University, from January 2025 to August 2025. Participants who underwent HPV testing at the health examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou were included (n = 13,492). Meanwhile, the participants attending other clinics in this hospital, including gynecology, urology, and obstetrics, were excluded (n = 10,029). We excluded male participants (n = 129). Duplicate records were checked using unique participant IDs. Among the 13,492 included participants, no duplicate subjects were observed. In addition, no cases with incomplete data were observed. Therefore, the number of final included participants was 13,492, aged 18–85 years. The participant selection flow diagram is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Participants’ selection flow diagram.Flowchart illustrating participant selection: from 23,650 initial participants, 10,029 attending other departments and 129 males were excluded, leaving 13,492. No samples were excluded due to incomplete data or duplication, resulting in 13,492 final included participants.2.3HPV genotypingTo collect the cervical cast-off cells, a vaginal dilator was used to expose the cervix. Cervical mucus was removed with a cotton swab. The cervical brush was placed at the cervical opening and gently rotated clockwise for 3–5 times. The cervical brush was slowly removed and placed into a sample tube containing cell preservation solution. The brush head was left in the sample tube, and the bottle cap was tightened. The sample tubes were labeled with number and date and then transported to the laboratory for immediate DNA extraction or stored at 2–8 °C for no more than 2 weeks.To extract the HPV DNA, 0.5–1.0 mL of cell preservation solution containing cervical cast-off cells was centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 1 min, and the supernatant was discarded. Then HPV DNA was extracted using cell lysis buffer (Kaipu Biotechnology, China, Catalog: 20150019) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Then, 1 μL of extracted DNA sample was served as a template for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification and flow-through hybridization technology using the HPV typing test kit (PCR + Membrane Hybridization Method) (Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Catalog: 20143402188) and nucleic acid molecule rapid hybridization instrument (HHM-2, Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd.) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines.This testing method used PCR to amplify HPV DNA. The PCR products were then applied to a low-density gene chip, and flow-hybridization technology was used to detect hybridization between the amplified products and type-specific probe membranes; thereby, a total of 27 different HPV genotypes were detected.According to the HPV classification framework of IARC, HPV types were classified into group 1 (carcinogenic to humans), group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans), group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), and group 3 (non-oncogenic HPV or uncertain oncogenic significance). In this study, the HPV types of IARC Group 1/2A/2B were classified as HR-HPV. Meanwhile, the HPV types of IARC Group 3 were classified as low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV). Here, we detected 17 HR-HPV types (HPV16, HPV18, HPV26, HPV31, HPV33, HPV35, HPV39, HPV45, HPV51, HPV52, HPV53, HPV56, HPV58, HPV59, HPV66, HPV68, HPV82) and 10 LR-HPV types (HPV6, HPV11, HPV40, HPV42, HPV43, HPV44, HPV55, HPV61, HPV81, HPV83) using HPV kit.2.4Quality control and judgment criteria(1) Limit of detection (LOD): The kit’s LOD is no higher than 5,000 copies per reaction.(2) Specificity: The detection results of HPV negative standard samples should all be negative. In addition, the detection results of HPV-positive standard samples or HR-HPV samples should not exhibit any cross-reactions. The cross-reactivity rate in the detection of LR-HPV samples should be less than 10%.(3) Quality control: Plasmid clones containing HPV DNA were used as the positive control samples. DNase-free H2O was used as the negative control sample. Each membrane has a biotin control point to detect the reaction between alkaline phosphatase and its substrate. In addition, the membrane contains an internal control point, which serves as an inner quality control template for DNA. If the internal control point is positive, the results are reliable.(4) Judgment criteria: This reagent is a qualitative detection reagent. The positive test result is a clear and visible blue-purple dot. Based on the arrangement of various HPV probes on the membrane strip, the HPV type can be determined by the positive point. If the internal control point and biotin point are positive while the other points are negative, the test result is judged negative. If one or more HPV genotyping points are positive, the sample is judged as single- or multiple HPV positive.Single genotype infection was defined as the infection of one HPV genotype among the 27 HPV types mentioned above; multiple infection is defined as the infection of ≥2 positive HPV types among the 27 HPV types mentioned above.2.5Statistical analysisStatistical analysis was performed using SPSS software 26.0 (IBM Corp., NY, USA). The prevalence of age-specific or HPV type-specific infection was reported with Wilson score 95% confidence intervals (CI). Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated by comparing the HPV prevalence across different age groups with ≥60-year age group as reference; 95% confidence intervals for ORs were calculated by Woolf’s logit method. Chi-square or Fisher’s exact test was applied for the comparison of prevalence in different age groups with ≥60-year age group. For comparison between multiple age groups, p-value was adjusted using Bonferroni method; p < 0.05/10 = 0.005 was considered statistically significant.Logistic regression analysis was performed with age and age squared (age2) as continuous variables to evaluate non-linear (quadratic) associations between the prevalence of HPV infection and age. HPV infection status (positive or negative) was included as the dependent variable, whereas age and age squared were included as independent variables. We included HPV infection status, age, and its quadratic term (age2) in the binary logistic regression model. Statistical significance of the quadratic term was set at a p-value of < 0.05.GraphPad Prism 10 (Boston, MA, USA) was used for data visualization, and frequencies were used to calculate HPV types. The predicted logistic plot of logistic regression was produced by GraphPad Prism 10; a p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 2.2Study design and populationsInitially, a total of 23,650 participants with HPV testing data were retrospectively retrieved from the laboratory information system (LIS) at Zhangzhou Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University, from January 2025 to August 2025. Participants who underwent HPV testing at the health examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou were included (n = 13,492). Duplicate records were checked using unique participant IDs. Among the 13,492 included participants, no duplicate subjects were observed. In addition, no cases with incomplete data were observed. The participant selection flow diagram is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Participants’ selection flow diagram.Flowchart illustrating participant selection: from 23,650 initial participants, 10,029 attending other departments and 129 males were excluded, leaving 13,492. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn this study, we investigated the age- and genotype-specific HPV prevalence among females attending the physical examination center at a hospital in Zhangzhou City, Fujian Province, China. Our research identified the predominant HPV types in Zhangzhou and the age-related distribution of HPV prevalence among all participants. Our research provides baseline HPV prevalence data in Zhangzhou, which contributes to the formulation of HPV preventive measures and emphasizes the importance of HPV surveillance, especially for the age groups with high HPV prevalence.Our data revealed that the overall HPV prevalence in Zhangzhou is 16.86%, which was similar to the overall HPV prevalence in Beijing (17.28%) (8) and the nation-wide research among Chinese women (17.70%) (6). The overall prevalence in our study was significantly lower than that reported in Fujian Province in 2017 (38.3%) (7) and higher than that reported in Zhejiang Province (15.29%) (9). These significant discrepancies may partly reflect the increasing HPV vaccination coverage and the improvement of social HPV-preventive awareness in Fujian Province in recent years. Other potential explanations for the discrepancies should also be considered, including discrepancies in study populations, sampling strategies, age-group distribution, laboratory detection assays, study time windows, cervical screening-seeking behaviors, and additional epidemiological determinants. However, vaccination status and other epidemiological factors were not available for individual participants in this study. Therefore, this hypothesis needs further investigation in the future. These observations suggest that HPV infection remains a public health challenge in some regions of China. In addition, regional disparities in HPV prevalence across China highlight the importance of effective public health measures for the prevention of HPV infection.We observed that the predominant HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City were HPV52, HPV53, HPV51, HPV58, and HPV39, respectively. A previous study in Fujian Province reported that HPV16 (8.5%), HPV52 (7.9%), HPV58 (6.2%), and HPV53 (3.5%) accounted for over 60% of all HPV-positive cases (7). Another study in Zhejiang Province demonstrated that HPV-16, HPV-52, HPV-58, and HPV-18 were the predominant HPV types (9). In addition, HPV-52, HPV-16, and HPV-58 were predominant types in Guangzhou (10). Based on these studies, we found that the prevalence of HPV16 and HPV18 was comparatively low in Zhangzhou, which was inconsistent with the findings from other geographical regions of China. Therefore, these results indicate that HPV genotype distribution differs significantly across geographical regions, which may be attributable to regional differences in economic conditions or HPV vaccination programs.In China, the licensed 9-valent HPV vaccines provide predominant protection against the most prevalent HR-HPV genotypes, including HPV16, 18, 6, 11, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 (11, 12). In this study, we observed that the most prevalent HPV type, HPV-52, has been included in the licensed vaccine in China. However, other prevalent HR-HPV types, including HPV53 and HPV51, were not included in the licensed vaccines in China. In addition, the included types HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 6, and 11 exhibited relatively low prevalence in Zhangzhou. These findings reflect only the genotype diversity of local individual HPV infection characteristics and do not indicate the inadequacy or ineffectiveness of the currently available HPV vaccine in China. Therefore, additional local HPV vaccination data need to be collected to further clarify the protective effectiveness of current HPV vaccines against HPV infection in Zhangzhou. In conclusion, these findings underscore the need to consider the relationship between the currently available HPV vaccine and the currently prevalent HPV types. Furthermore, it provides valuable insights for the development of next-generation HPV vaccines.In our study, we observed that the ≥60-year age group exhibited the highest HPV prevalence, implying that HPV infection still posed a substantial disease burden among older adult females. The females in the ≤29-year age group also showed an elevated HPV prevalence. Therefore, the HPV prevalence among females in Zhangzhou City seemed to exhibit a “two-peak” age-related distribution. Furthermore, logistic regression analysis also revealed a non-linear association between age and HPV infection. These observations were similar to previous research in Zhejiang Province and nation-wide research in China (6, 9). However, the correlation between age and infection rate was only limited to speculation, as a few factors, such as sexual activity (13), changing sexual partners, immune weakening, and vaccine coverage, may influence HPV infection (14–17), have not been taken into account in our research. In conclusion, our data underscore the need for regular HPV screening and surveillance among young and older adult females in Zhangzhou.Our research still has the following limitations: (1) We only provided basic and limited information about the study population, including age and testing results. Other important population characteristics, including marital status, residence/urban–rural status, previous cervical cancer screening, HPV vaccination status, and history of cervical lesions, may significantly influence HPV infection. Therefore, more detailed information about the study population needs to be collected. (2) The participants in this study are hospital-based, which may differ substantially from the general population. Therefore, our findings may not be applicable to the general population. (3) Our research is a single-center retrospective study. Therefore, these findings may not be generalized to a wider population in Zhangzhou. (4) Cytological and histopathological findings related to cervical lesions and clinical follow-up data were unavailable. Consequently, we could not identify CIN1/CIN2/CIN3 or invasive cervical cancer cases, and could not establish associations between specific HPV genotypes and cervical cancer based on the current data. The conclusions are limited to HPV prevalence and genotype distribution.In conclusion, this research investigated the prevalence and genotype distribution of HPV infection in females attending the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou City, China. A non-linear distribution was observed between HPV prevalence and age, with older adult females (≥60 years old) exhibiting the highest HPV infection rate. In addition, HPV52, 53, and 51 were the highly prevalent HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City. Our results implied that HR-HPV infection still poses a substantial disease burden among older adult females in Zhangzhou City and revealed the prevalent HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City. This study emphasized the importance of HPV infection surveillance, especially among older adult females, and provided valuable insights into the preventive measures targeting predominant HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionCervical cancer ranks as the fourth most prevalent cancer among females across the world, contributing an estimated 660,000 newly diagnosed cases and 350,000 disease-related mortalities globally in 2022 (1). Cervical cancer ranked sixth in mortality among all female malignancies in China in 2022, with an estimated 150,700 new cervical cancer cases and 55,700 related deaths (2). Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) has been identified as a risk factor for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer. The World Health Organization proposed a 90–70–90 global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer by 2030, which is to achieve HPV vaccination rates of ≥90% in women before the age of 15, efficient screening coverage rates of ≥70% in women before the age of 35 and 45, and treatment rates of ≥90% for diagnosed cervical lesions (3).Over 200 types of HPV have been identified. According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) Working Group HPV classification framework, 12 HPV types, including HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59, have been classified as carcinogenic (IARC Group 1) to humans, other eight HPV types in this high-risk clade, including 26, 53, 66, 67, 68, 70, 73, and 82, were classified as probable/possible carcinogenic (IARC Group 2A and IARC Group 2B). In addition, HPV types 6, 11, 40, 42, 43, 44, 54, 61, 72, 81, and 89 were classified as non-oncogenic (IARC Group 3). Currently, the HPV vaccine is still the most effective strategy to prevent HPV infection and cervical cancer. In addition, routine HPV screening, especially HR-HPV screening, is strongly recommended, which can contribute to the prevention of cervical cancer (4, 5).Previously, a nationwide study in China revealed that the overall HPV prevalence of Chinese females was at a relatively high level (17.70%), with high- and low-risk types being 13.12 and 4.58%, respectively (6). Several studies have demonstrated that HPV prevalence among women and the distribution of predominant HPV genotypes exhibit distinct geographical disparities and genotypic diversity. A study in Fujian Province demonstrated that HR-HPV infections were mainly attributed to HPV16, HPV52, HPV58, and HPV53 types (7). Zhangzhou City is located in southeastern China, Fujian Province. However, the prevalence and infection patterns of HPV among females in Zhangzhou City have not been reported yet. Therefore, it is necessary to obtain the local baseline data of HPV prevalence in Zhangzhou City, which will contribute to the prevention of HPV infection and the implementation of the HPV vaccination program.In this study, we aim to investigate the local genotype-specific prevalence of HPV infection and analyze the age-related trends of HPV infection among females undergoing HPV testing in a physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou City. 2.1Ethics statementThe study involving humans was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhangzhou Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University (Ethics approval number: 2026LWB202) on 4 June 2026. The study was conducted in accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. Written informed consent for participants was not required from the participants or the participants’ legal guardians/next of kin because this is a retrospective study, and all the participants’ results were retrospectively collected. 2.3HPV genotypingTo collect the cervical cast-off cells, a vaginal dilator was used to expose the cervix. Cervical mucus was removed with a cotton swab. The cervical brush was placed at the cervical opening and gently rotated clockwise for 3–5 times. The cervical brush was slowly removed and placed into a sample tube containing cell preservation solution. The brush head was left in the sample tube, and the bottle cap was tightened. The sample tubes were labeled with number and date and then transported to the laboratory for immediate DNA extraction or stored at 2–8 °C for no more than 2 weeks.To extract the HPV DNA, 0.5–1.0 mL of cell preservation solution containing cervical cast-off cells was centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 1 min, and the supernatant was discarded. Then HPV DNA was extracted using cell lysis buffer (Kaipu Biotechnology, China, Catalog: 20150019) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Then, 1 μL of extracted DNA sample was served as a template for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification and flow-through hybridization technology using the HPV typing test kit (PCR + Membrane Hybridization Method) (Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Catalog: 20143402188) and nucleic acid molecule rapid hybridization instrument (HHM-2, Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd.) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines.This testing method used PCR to amplify HPV DNA. The PCR products were then applied to a low-density gene chip, and flow-hybridization technology was used to detect hybridization between the amplified products and type-specific probe membranes; thereby, a total of 27 different HPV genotypes were detected.According to the HPV classification framework of IARC, HPV types were classified into group 1 (carcinogenic to humans), group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans), group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), and group 3 (non-oncogenic HPV or uncertain oncogenic significance). In this study, the HPV types of IARC Group 1/2A/2B were classified as HR-HPV. Meanwhile, the HPV types of IARC Group 3 were classified as low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV). Here, we detected 17 HR-HPV types (HPV16, HPV18, HPV26, HPV31, HPV33, HPV35, HPV39, HPV45, HPV51, HPV52, HPV53, HPV56, HPV58, HPV59, HPV66, HPV68, HPV82) and 10 LR-HPV types (HPV6, HPV11, HPV40, HPV42, HPV43, HPV44, HPV55, HPV61, HPV81, HPV83) using HPV kit. 2.4Quality control and judgment criteria(1) Limit of detection (LOD): The kit’s LOD is no higher than 5,000 copies per reaction.(2) Specificity: The detection results of HPV negative standard samples should all be negative. In addition, the detection results of HPV-positive standard samples or HR-HPV samples should not exhibit any cross-reactions. The cross-reactivity rate in the detection of LR-HPV samples should be less than 10%.(3) Quality control: Plasmid clones containing HPV DNA were used as the positive control samples. DNase-free H2O was used as the negative control sample. Each membrane has a biotin control point to detect the reaction between alkaline phosphatase and its substrate. In addition, the membrane contains an internal control point, which serves as an inner quality control template for DNA. If the internal control point is positive, the results are reliable.(4) Judgment criteria: This reagent is a qualitative detection reagent. The positive test result is a clear and visible blue-purple dot. Based on the arrangement of various HPV probes on the membrane strip, the HPV type can be determined by the positive point. If the internal control point and biotin point are positive while the other points are negative, the test result is judged negative. If one or more HPV genotyping points are positive, the sample is judged as single- or multiple HPV positive.Single genotype infection was defined as the infection of one HPV genotype among the 27 HPV types mentioned above; multiple infection is defined as the infection of ≥2 positive HPV types among the 27 HPV types mentioned above. 2.5Statistical analysisStatistical analysis was performed using SPSS software 26.0 (IBM Corp., NY, USA). The prevalence of age-specific or HPV type-specific infection was reported with Wilson score 95% confidence intervals (CI). Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated by comparing the HPV prevalence across different age groups with ≥60-year age group as reference; 95% confidence intervals for ORs were calculated by Woolf’s logit method. title_original: Prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus infection among women undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China: a retrospective study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection among women undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China, to provide insights into the epidemiological patterns of HPV in this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective, single-center study was conducted at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China, involving 13,492 females aged 18–85 years who underwent HPV testing. Male participants were excluded, leaving 13,492 females in the study population.
analysis.methods: DNA samples were extracted and used as templates for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification, followed by flow-through hybridization technology using an HPV typing test kit. Logistic regression analysis was performed with age and age squared as continuous variables to assess non-linear associations between HPV prevalence and age. The Bonferroni method was used to adjust p-values for multiple comparisons.
analysis.main_results: The overall HPV infection rate was 16.86% (2,275/13,492), with 12.59% (1,699/13,492) being single-type infections and 4.27% (576/13,492) being multiple-type infections. HPV52 had the highest prevalence at 3.58% (483/13,492), followed by HPV53 (1.76%) and HPV81 (1.71%). The prevalence showed a "two-peak" age-related distribution, with peaks in the ≤29-year and ≥60-year age groups, and a decrease in the 40- to 49-year age group.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study revealed the age-specific and genotype-specific distribution of HPV infection in females attending a hospital in Zhangzhou, highlighting the need for targeted surveillance and awareness of vaccination for highly prevalent HPV types.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform public health strategies for HPV surveillance and vaccination programs, particularly emphasizing the importance of monitoring and managing the most prevalent HPV types in this population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its single-center design and retrospective nature, which may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational approach and potential for confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective study analyzed the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection among 13,492 females aged 18–85 years undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China. The overall HPV infection rate was 16.86%, with HPV52 being the most prevalent type. The prevalence showed a "two-peak" age-related distribution, peaking in the ≤29-year and ≥60-year age groups, and decreasing in the 40–49-year age group. The study also identified common co-infection patterns, such as HPV52 + HPV53. These findings highlight the need for targeted HPV surveillance and vaccination efforts, especially for the most prevalent types. The study's limitations include its single-center design and retrospective nature, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational approach and potential for confounding factors.

title: Expression of concern-Effect of Brazil's national human papillomavirus vaccination programme on the incidence of cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 in women aged 20-24 years: a population-based study.
abstract: In October 2025, The Lancet Global Health published a population-based study to estimate the effect of Brazil’s national human papillomavirus vaccination programme on the incidence of cervical cancer,1 by Thiago Cerqueira-Silva and colleagues. On July 15, 2026, the corresponding author alerted us to some coding errors that affected several numerical values in the findings—some substantially. In view of the extent of these errors, we now issue an Expression of Concern while working with the authors to correct the record, including further review of the revised paper.

analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该审查基于 2025 年 10 月发表在《柳叶刀全球健康》上的一项基于人群的研究。该研究的目的是评估 疫苗接种 计划对指定结果的影响。通讯作者发现了影响研究结果中数值的编码错误,导致发布了一份关注表。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该研究旨在评估巴西HPV 发病率项目在减少发病率和宫颈上皮内瘤变3级方面的有效性。但由于编码错误,研究结果不可靠,该论文正在进一步审查中。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该研究的结果受到影响多个数值的重大编码错误的影响,引发了人们对结果准确性和可靠性的担忧。这些错误需要重新评估数据以及从中得出的结论。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 研究中的错误凸显了仔细的数据验证和报告结果的透明度的必要性。需要进一步的研究和审查来准确评估 HPV 疫苗接种 计划对 宫颈癌 和宫颈上皮内瘤变 3 级 发病率 的影响。

full_text: Most existing studies focusing on human papillomavirus (HPV)-microbiota interactions are confined to the cervicovaginal tract, while mucosal microecological crosstalk at oral, anorectal and penile sites remains insufficiently summarized. This mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of current sequencing and epidemiological evidence regarding potential bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and site-specific mucosal microbiota across extra-cervicovaginal niches in both males and females. Oral HPV reshapes microbial composition in a sex-, race- and population-dependent manner; periodontal dysbiosis, high-risk HPV and Candida albicans jointly form a tripartite oncogenic axis that may contribute to oral squamous cell carcinoma, and periodontal inflammation independently elevates oral HPV susceptibility. Among men who have sex with men, pro-inflammatory anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis and Sneathia accumulate in anorectal HPV-related lesions, and concurrent HIV or sexually transmitted bacterial co-infections worsen mucosal dysbiosis and viral persistence. On penile skin, Corynebacterium is associated with a lower prevalence of HPV, whereas anaerobe-dominant community state types increase high-risk HPV risk, with HIV-induced baseline dysbiosis masking HPV-specific penile microbial signatures. Collectively, tissue-specific mucosal dysbiosis may represent an important co-factor linked to persistent HPV infection and subsequent malignant transformation. This review offsets long-standing sex-related and anatomical research bias, clarifies multi-site host-virus-microbe mechanisms, and provides theoretical support for developing microbiota-based biomarkers and microecological interventions to prevent non-cervical HPV-associated malignancies. 6ConclusionThis mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of observed associations and potential bidirectional interactions between HPV and mucosal microbiota in oral, anorectal and penile niches beyond cervicovaginal tissues. Site-specific microbial dysbiosis is associated with impaired mucosal immunity and may facilitate persistent HPV colonization and may contribute to oncogenic progression; meanwhile HPV infection can reshape local microbial composition. Distinct protective and pathogenic bacterial taxa are identified across three anatomical sites. Nevertheless, the supporting evidence is far more robust for the oral cavity, whereas evidence from anorectal and penile mucosa is limited and heterogeneous. Therefore, a uniform mechanistic model for all three anatomical sites cannot be assumed. Future longitudinal cohorts and functional experiments are required to clarify causal mechanisms and develop microecology-based preventive strategies for extragenital HPV-related malignancies. 1IntroductionHuman Papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection globally, with the most sexually active men and women estimated to have been infected with genital HPV at least once during their lifetime (Bruni et al., 2023). HPV can be transmitted in many ways through different abrasions, with sexual intercourse, when the newborn passes through an infected genital tract, and from a variety of self-inoculation positions (Erickson et al., 2013; Muzio et al., 2021). HPVs are capable of infecting multiple human anatomical niches including the skin, vagina, cervix, oral cavity and gut. Distinct dominant high-abundance HPV genotypes are enriched at separate body sites, exhibiting prominent tissue-specific tropism (Ma et al., 2014).The mechanisms underlying persistent HPV infection remain incompletely elucidated, with mucosal microbial dysbiosis emerging as an important contributing factor. Studies have shown that microbial imbalance is associated with sustained HPV inflammation and may contribute to the initiation and progression of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) (Song et al., 2020; Lebeau et al., 2022). Certain bacterial metabolites can activate epithelial inflammasomes, amplify inflammatory cascades, and potentiate the activity of HPV oncoproteins, thereby reinforcing persistent viral infection (Song et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). Each individual harbors a unique microbial fingerprint. Organ-specific microbiotas regulate host immunity and mucosal physiological functions (Kilian et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2022).Extensive research has delineated the complicated interplay between cervicovaginal microbiota and HPV, confirming its pivotal role in cervical carcinogenesis (Usyk et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2024; Oyedokun et al., 2026). However, bidirectional crosstalk between HPV and mucosal flora at oral, anorectal and penile sites remains insufficiently characterized, and few reviews have provided a summary of these extra-cervicovaginal microbial niches. This narrative mini-review integrates available evidence for extra-cervicovaginal mucosal niches in both sexes to mitigate the historical cervix-centered research bias (Table 1). (2026) MSM, men who have sex with men; hr-HPV, high risk HPV; lr-HPV, low risk HPV; CST, Community State Type.*MOUTH study, The Men and Women Offering Understanding of Throat HPV study. 2Oral mucosal microbiota and HPV infectionThe mouth is the second largest and diverse microbiota niche after the gut, harboring over 700 species of bacteria (Muzio et al., 2021; Benjamin et al., 2023). The overall prevalence of oral HPV among healthy general populations ranged from 0.67% to 11.89%, and infection rates were higher in males than females (Maltseva et al., 2025). Chronic inflammation linked to the oral microbiome may induce abnormal immune responses and interfere with the clearance of oral HPV infection, which could potentially contribute to carcinogenesis (Tezal, 2012). HPV infection is a significant risk factor for oropharyngeal cancer (McQuillan et al., 2017). Approximately 70% of oropharyngeal cancer are associated with oral HPV infection (D'Souza et al., 2007; Marur et al., 2010; Joseph and D'Souza, 2012). The oral microbiome can also cause periodontal diseases, which are risk factors for both oral HPV infection and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (Feng et al., 2024). Observational data suggest that members of the oral microbiota may interact with HPV by modifying its pathogenicity or bacterial community behavior (Ghannoum et al., 2010; Muzio et al., 2021).2.1HPV–oral microbiota interactions in general populationsTwo independent population-based oral microbiome studies reported sex-specific microbial alterations correlated with oral HPV infection (Feng et al., 2024; Maidment et al., 2025). One cohort found depleted Streptococcus salivarius and S. parasanguinis in low-risk HPV-positive males, while HPV-positive females showed lower Shannon α-diversity and distinct oral β-diversity (Maidment et al., 2025). Large-scale NHANES cross-sectional data (n=5496) further confirmed that reduced oral microbial α-diversity and unique community profiles were only significantly associated with high-risk oral HPV among males, a sex-based discrepancy consistent with men’s higher susceptibility to HPV-related head and neck malignancies (Park et al., 2022; Gaeta et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024).Another cross-sectional study analyzing more than 5000 oral-rinse specimens reported higher relative abundance of Veillonellaceae and reduced Gemella among HPV-positive individuals. Notably, Gemella was enriched in HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer, indicating that Gemella overgrowth arises in late tumor-related dysbiosis rather than during early-stage HPV infection (Byrd et al., 2026).Study has confirmed that oral HPV infection reshapes overall oral microbial community β-diversity and distinguished taxonomic features differing by HPV status (Zhang et al., 2022). HPV carriers show enriched Actinomycetaceae, Prevotellaceae, Veillonellaceae and Campylobacteraceae, whereas Gemellaceae decline and Bacteroidetes rise in infected individuals (Zhang et al., 2022). Two mechanistic pathways may explain this association. First, periodontopathic Prevotella and Actinomyces sustain mucosal inflammation and barrier damage to boost HPV entry, echoing epidemiological ties between periodontal disease and HPV-associated head and neck cancer (Tezal et al., 2012; Bui et al., 2013; Cekici et al., 2014; Larsen, 2017). Second, HPV-positive oral microbiota displays impaired xenobiotic degradation of naphthalene, styrene and chloroalkanes; accumulated toxins induce oxidative DNA damage and activate ATM kinase to support HPV replication. Pathogenic Campylobacter further releases genotoxins to trigger genomic instability. In summary, metabolically disrupted oral dysbiosis may represent a co-factor associated with increased risks of oral HPV acquisition and persistent infection.It is reported that oral HPV does not induce distinct oral microbial taxa or ecotypes, but colonizes pre-existing oral ecosystems with coordinated virulence networks (Chambuso et al., 2026). HPV-positive specimens were enriched in periodontal anaerobes favoring viral persistence and oncogenic synergism, with HPV persistence dependent on rearranged functional modules for adhesion, invasion and immune crosstalk rather than elevated total microbial virulence (Chambuso et al., 2026). Such viral-microbe interactions differ drastically from the hypoxic, immune-suppressed microenvironment of HPV-driven malignancies.2.2HPV–oral microbiota interactions in special populationsA sequencing analysis among 63 HIV-negative tumor-free MSM demonstrated hrHPV-associated oral microbial shifts only among HIV-negative participants; suggesting that pre-existing HIV-driven oral dysbiosis may mask hrHPV-specific microbial signatures (Escobar-Marcillo et al., 2025). HIV-stratified hrHPV subgroups carried distinct pathogenic bacteria: periodontopathic Parvimonas in HIV-negative subjects and pro-inflammatory Bulleidia in HIV-infected counterparts, alongside hrHPV-linked perturbations in carbohydrate metabolism and virulence protease pathways (Escobar-Marcillo et al., 2025). This work indicates pre-existing oral dysbiosis driven by HIV masks microbial signatures of hrHPV, and hrHPV further disturbs mucosal microecology by expanding pathogenic taxa.Higher oral microbial richness among oral-HPV-positive pregnant women was reported, with elevated relative abundance of Selenomonas, Megasphaera and TM7-related taxa (Tuominen et al., 2018a). Nevertheless, such findings are constrained by the small sample size and exclusive recruitment of pregnant subjects, which limits the generalizability of these conclusions to broader human populations. Separately, infant oral microbiota data from the same group showed oral HPV positivity altered bacterial profiles at genus and family levels without changing overall α-diversity (Tuominen et al., 2018b). HPV carriers and virus-free infants exhibited divergent oral bacterial structures: Veillonella dispar prevailed in HPV-negative infants, while Ureaplasma and Propionibacterium accumulated in HPV-positive ones. As a core infant oral genus, Veillonella predicts elevated caries risk later in life (Könönen et al., 1999; Jiang et al., 2016; Mashima et al., 2017). Early HPV exposure disrupts oral commensal balance, chronically impairing mucosal immunity and predisposing individuals to subsequent oral lesions.Stratified subgroup analyses identified distinct HPV profiles and oral microbial dysbiosis among head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) subtypes (Chan et al., 2022). Non-oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) exhibited high HPV prevalence alongside mild microbial disturbance. title_original: Beyond cervicovaginal limitations: potential bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and mucosal microbiota from oral, anorectal and penile sites — a mini-review

analysis.scope_and_question: This mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of current sequencing and epidemiological evidence regarding potential bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and site-specific mucosal microbiota across extra-cervicovaginal niches in both males and females.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Elucidating the correlation between extra-cervicovaginal microbiomes and HPV infection will further clarify mucosal HPV susceptibility and relevant host-microbe-viral interactions. The overall prevalence of oral HPV among healthy general populations ranged from 0.67% to 11.89%, and infection rates were higher in males than females (Maltseva et al., 2025).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Observational data suggest that members of the oral microbiota may interact with HPV by modifying its pathogenicity or bacterial community behavior (Ghannoum et al., 2010; Muzio et al., 2021). Large-scale NHANES cross-sectional data (n=5496) further confirmed that reduced oral microbial α-diversity and unique community profiles were only significantly associated with high-risk oral HPV among males, a sex-based discrepancy consistent with men’s higher susceptibility to HPV-related head and neck malignancies (Park et al., 2022; Gaeta et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024). It is reported that oral HPV does not induce distinct oral microbial taxa or ecotypes, but colonizes pre-existing oral ecosystems with coordinated virulence networks (Chambuso et al., 2026).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Such findings are constrained by the small sample size and exclusive recruitment of pregnant subjects, which limits the generalizability of these conclusions to broader human populations. Another cross-sectional study analyzing more than 5000 oral-rinse specimens reported higher relative abundance of Veillonellaceae and reduced Gemella among HPV-positive individuals.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The work indicates pre-existing oral dysbiosis driven by HIV masks microbial signatures of hrHPV, and hrHPV further disturbs mucosal microecology by expanding pathogenic taxa. Higher oral microbial richness among oral-HPV-positive pregnant women was reported, with elevated relative abundance of Selenomonas, Megasphaera and TM7-related taxa (Tuominen et al., 2018a). Separately, infant oral microbiota data from the same group showed oral HPV positivity altered bacterial profiles at genus and family levels without changing overall α-diversity (Tuominen et al., 2018b).

analysis.summary_en: This mini-review explores the bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and mucosal microbiota in non-cervicovaginal sites such as oral, anorectal, and penile regions. It synthesizes evidence from multiple studies, highlighting sex-specific differences in oral microbiota associated with HPV infection, particularly in males. The review also discusses the impact of HIV-driven oral dysbiosis on HPV-specific microbial signatures and the role of microbiota in HPV persistence and pathogenicity. However, the findings are limited by small sample sizes and restricted populations, such as pregnant women and HIV-negative men. The review emphasizes the need for further research to understand these interactions across diverse populations and their implications for HPV-related diseases.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 这篇小型综述对当前测序和流行病学证据进行了叙述性综合,涉及男性和女性宫颈阴道外生态位中 HPV 感染与特定位点粘膜微生物群之间潜在的双向相互作用。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 阐明宫颈阴道外微生物群与 HPV 感染之间的相关性将进一步阐明粘膜 HPV 易感性和相关的 宿主-微生物-病毒相互作用。健康普通人群口腔HPV总体患病率范围为0.67%至11.89%,男性感染率高于女性(Maltseva et al.,2025)。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 观察数据表明,口腔微生物群的成员可能通过改变 HPV 的致病性或细菌群落行为来与 HPV 相互作用(Ghannoum 等,2010;Muzio 等,2021)。大规模 NHANES 横断面数据 (n=5496) 进一步证实,口腔微生物 α 多样性减少和独特的群落特征仅与男性中的高危口腔 HPV 显着相关,这种基于性别的差异与男性对 HPV 相关头颈恶性肿瘤的易感性较高一致(Park 等人,2022 年;Gaeta 等人,2023 年;Feng 等人,2024)。据报道,口腔 HPV 不会诱导独特的口腔微生物分类群或生态型,而是通过协调的毒力网络定殖预先存在的口腔生态系统(Chambuso 等人,2026)。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 这些发现受到样本量小和仅招募怀孕受试者的限制,这限制了这些结论对更广泛人群的普遍适用性。另一项横断面研究分析了 5000 多个口腔冲洗样本,报告显示 HPV 阳性个体中韦荣菌科的相对丰度较高,双粒菌减少。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 这项工作表明,由 HIV 驱动的先前存在的口腔生态失调掩盖了 hrHPV 的微生物特征,而 hrHPV 通过扩大致病类群进一步扰乱粘膜微生态。据报道,口腔 HPV 阳性孕妇的口腔微生物丰富度较高,其中硒单胞菌属、巨球菌属和 TM7 相关类群的相对丰度较高(Tuominen 等人,2018a)。另外,来自同一组的婴儿口腔微生物群数据显示,口腔 HPV 阳性改变了属和科水平的细菌谱,但没有改变整体 α 多样性(Tuominen 等人,2018b)。
