full_text: AbstractIntroductionThe cervicovaginal microbiome is a proposed modifier of HPV-associated cervical disease, yet its relationship with viral type heterogeneity, cytological grade, and community state type (CST) remains incompletely understood.MethodsThis cross-sectional study characterized cervicovaginal microbiome composition and functional potential across HPV infection status, viral type categories (No HPV, HPV High Risk, HPV16, HPV18, HPV Other), cervical cytological grades, and CSTs in 311 non-pregnant women using whole-genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing, integrated diversity analyses, MaAsLin2 differential abundance testing, and HUMAnN 3.0 functional pathway profiling.ResultsHPV-positive samples showed increased bacterial species richness, and a reciprocal Lactobacillus-to-Gardnerella dominance shift compared to HPV-negative samples. HPV Other showed the highest bacterial species richness and distinct taxonomic and predicted functional associations, including higher inferred abundance of siderophore- and lipopolysaccharide-biosynthesis pathways; however, overall species-level community composition did not differ significantly across HPV type groups. CST I and CST II exhibited compositional stability regardless of HPV status, while CST IV showed pronounced Lactobacillus depletion in HPV-positive women. LSIL was associated with lower Fannyhessea vaginae and Alloscardovia omnicolens abundance and higher Phocaeicola vulgatus abundance relative to NILM.DiscussionThese findings indicate that oncogenic potential and dysbiosis severity are not aligned, and that CST type modifies HPV–microbiome interactions.Keywords: cervical dysbiosis, cervicovaginal microbiome, community state type, human papillomavirus, shotgun metagenomics 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study design and populationThis cross-sectional study was conducted at the National Research Center for Mother and Child Health, a tertiary academic medical center in Astana, Kazakhstan. Non-pregnant women aged 18–46 years with regular menstrual cycles and an intact cervix were recruited from the outpatient gynecology clinic. Participants were excluded for major chronic or immunocompromising conditions, acute inflammation, recent antibiotic/probiotic/immunosuppressive therapy, smoking, intrauterine device use, prior HPV vaccination, or recent invasive gynecological procedures. Samples with incomplete metadata, insufficient sequencing data, or missing CST classification were excluded from the relevant analyses. A subset of the HPV-negative, NILM (normal cytology) participants characterized here (n = 92) was previously reported as a dedicated multi-kingdom baseline cohort in Rakhmankulova et al. (2026), which used the same BioProject accession (PRJNA1337009) to describe bacterial, viral, fungal, and archaeal community structure in HPV-negative women prior to HPV-positive comparison. The present study extends those baseline findings by incorporating HPV-positive comparator groups (HPV16, HPV18, HPV Other, HPV High Risk), cervical cytological grade stratification, and CST-based differential abundance and functional pathway analyses not covered in the earlier report.2.2.Sample collection, DNA extraction and sequencingCervical samples were stored at −80 °C until processing. Total genomic DNA was extracted using the ZymoBIOMICS DNA Miniprep Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Sterile nuclease-free water was included as a negative extraction control, and the ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard was used as a positive control. DNA samples were required to contain at least 1.0 μg total DNA, with good integrity and no visible impurities. DNA concentration was measured using a microplate reader with a broad-range DNA assay, and DNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis.Raw paired-end sequencing reads were processed using fastp for adapter trimming and quality filtering. Read pairs were discarded when adapter contamination was detected, when more than 5 bp contained ambiguous nucleotides, or when more than 40% of bases were of low quality. Sliding-window trimming was performed using a 4-bp window and a Q15 threshold. The mean numbers of raw and clean reads were 48.5 million and 47.9 million reads per sample, respectively. Mean Q20/Q30 values were 98.2%/93.8% for raw reads and 99.0%/95.3% for clean reads.Human-read depletion was performed by alignment against the human GRCh38 reference genome using Bowtie2 v2.4.4. In the original pipeline, read pairs failing concordant alignment to the human reference were retained using the --un-conc-gz option while preserving paired-read structure for downstream metagenomic classification. Residual host content after depletion was evaluated using Kraken2 v2.1.3. On average, 92.1% of reads in the Bowtie2-retained fraction were subsequently classified as Homo sapiens, indicating substantial residual host sequence after this permissive depletion step. Approximately 7.9% of reads in the retained fraction were not classified as human and comprised microbial and unclassified reads available for downstream taxonomic classification.Taxonomic classification was performed using Kraken2 v2.1.3 against the PlusPFP Kraken2/Bracken database. Bracken v3.0 was subsequently used to refine genus- and species-level abundance estimates. Functional profiling was performed using HUMAnN 3.0 with UniRef90 protein annotations and MetaCyc pathway reconstruction. No predefined minimum non-host sequencing-depth threshold was applied in the original pipeline. Because effective bacterial sequencing depth varied substantially among samples, classified bacterial depth was quantified directly from the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken bacterial count table and was explicitly evaluated in subsequent depth-corrected and sensitivity analyses. Classified bacterial sequencing depth was defined as the total number of reads assigned to the bacterial domain (d:Bacteria) in the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken count table.2.3.GroupingsSamples were analyzed according to four main clinical and microbiome grouping variables: HPV status, HPV type group, cytology/histology grade, and bacterial community state type (CST). HPV status was assessed using the RealBest DNA HPV High Carcinogenic Risk Genotype real-time PCR kit (Cat. No. C8899; Vector-Best), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The assay detects the following high-risk HPV genotypes: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59. A sample was considered positive when at least one HPV genotype produced a cycle-threshold value of Ct ≤35. Samples without detection of any target genotype were classified as negative for the high-risk HPV types included in the assay. Whole-genome shotgun sequencing data were also screened for HPV sequences to identify genotypes not included in the PCR panel. The standard Reference sequence databases were used. Samples positive by either PCR or WGS were classified as HPV-positive. For descriptive analyses, HPV16 and HPV18 were retained as separate categories, other oncogenic genotypes were classified as HPV High Risk, and detected genotypes outside the predefined high-risk list were classified as HPV Other. The HPV Other group comprised samples in which WGS screening identified only genotypes classified as low-risk or non-carcinogenic by IARC (HPV6b, 7, 11, 26, 30, 32, 34, 53, 54, 71, 85, 90, 144, 156, and 166). A small number of HPV Other samples additionally showed trace-level WGS reads mapping to the high-risk genotypes HPV16, HPV31, or HPV35; because these reads represented less than 5% of the relative HPV sequence abundance within the sample, well below the threshold used to call a genotype present, these samples were retained in the HPV Other group rather than reclassified as HPV16, HPV High Risk, or HPV-positive for the corresponding high-risk type. Cytology/histology grade was categorized as NILM, ASC-US, LSIL, and ASC-H. CSTs were assigned manually from species-level relative abundance profiles following the five-community framework of Ravel et al. (2011). The dominant taxon was defined as the CST-associated bacterial species with the highest relative abundance within each sample. Samples were classified as CST I, CST II, CST III, or CST V when Lactobacillus crispatus, L. gasseri, L. iners, or L. jensenii, respectively, showed the highest relative abundance. Samples lacking dominance by these Lactobacillus species and characterized by predominance of anaerobic bacteria were assigned to CST IV. No fixed abundance threshold was used.2.4.Statistical and bioinformatic analysisBacterial alpha- and beta-diversity analyses were performed using species-level bacterial relative-abundance features only. Observed richness was defined as the number of detected bacterial species per sample; Shannon diversity and Pielou evenness were calculated from the same species-level matrix.Samples with zero total microbial abundance were excluded before diversity analysis. Because alpha-diversity and pathway-abundance measures were not assumed to follow a normal distribution, non-parametric tests were used for group comparisons. Differences across more than two groups were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis test, whereas two-group and stratified HPV-positive versus HPV-negative comparisons were assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test.Beta diversity was calculated using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and visualized by principal coordinates analysis. Differences in overall community composition were tested using PERMANOVA with 999 permutations. Pseudo-F statistics, permutation p-values, and pseudo-R2 values were reported, with R2 interpreted as the proportion of total variation in the distance matrix attributable to the grouping variable. PERMDISP with 999 permutations was performed to assess homogeneity of within-group multivariate dispersion and to determine whether PERMANOVA findings could be influenced by differences in dispersion rather than group-centroid separation.Because observed richness is sensitive to sequencing depth, we performed a depth-corrected sensitivity analysis using exact rarefaction of terminal species-level bacterial counts. Species counts summed exactly to total classified bacterial counts for each sample. All 311 samples were rarefied without replacement to 357,456 bacterial reads per sample, corresponding to the minimum classified bacterial depth. Rarefaction was repeated independently 100 times to assess sensitivity to stochastic subsampling. We additionally evaluated the association of observed richness with HPV status using linear regression adjusted for log10-transformed classified bacterial depth.Species-level differential abundance was evaluated using MaAsLin2 in R. Two abundance datasets were used according to the primary predictor. CST-associated analyses were performed using a taxonomically collapsed species table to reduce artificial inflation from strain- and isolate-level labels. Assignments corresponding to Gardnerella vaginalis strains and reference isolates were aggregated into a single G. vaginalis feature, whereas the remaining unresolved Gardnerella assignments were combined as Gardnerella unspecified. Strain-like Lactobacillus assignments were aggregated to the corresponding species-level labels. HPV type group- and cytological grade-associated analyses were performed using the uncollapsed species table to retain finer species-, strain-, and isolate-level resolution. Taxon names were standardized for formatting, and only exact duplicate labels generated by formatting standardization were aggregated. No biological consolidation of Gardnerella, Lactobacillus, or other taxa was applied in the HPV type group and Grade models. Predefined implausible assignments, including Clostridium tetani, were excluded from both datasets. Taxon filtering was performed independently for the collapsed and uncollapsed datasets after matching participants with complete model covariates. Taxa were retained when detected in at least 10% of samples and when their mean relative abundance was at least 0.05%. Samples with zero total bacterial abundance or incomplete model covariates were excluded from the corresponding analysis. Because the input tables contained relative-abundance percentages, no additional normalization was applied within MaAsLin2. Relative abundances were log-transformed, and linear models were fitted without predictor standardization. Each model included HPV type group, CST group, cytological grade, age, number of deliveries, bacterial sequencing depth, and marital status as fixed effects. Age and number of deliveries were entered as mean-centered continuous covariates. Bacterial sequencing depth was calculated from the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken bacterial count table, transformed as log10(depth + 1), and mean-centered. Marital status was modelled as a categorical variable comprising married, not married, and divorced/widowed categories. No HPV, CST I, NILM, and married status were used as the respective reference categories. Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied, and q-values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. MaAsLin2 coefficients represent the direction and magnitude of association with log-transformed relative abundance relative to the relevant reference category while holding the remaining model variables constant. For visualization, up to six species with the lowest adjusted q-values for each primary predictor were displayed as boxplots. The boxplots show raw relative-abundance distributions, whereas the reported coefficients and q-values were obtained from the adjusted models. Coefficient heatmaps included all significant taxa up to a maximum of 50 features. Heatmap colors represent unscaled MaAsLin2 coefficients; rows were hierarchically clustered, whereas comparison columns were retained in predefined order.To evaluate the robustness of differential-abundance results, MaAsLin2 analyses were additionally repeated after exclusion of samples below the 25th percentile of classified bacterial depth (3,108,006 reads). This retained 226 of 302 complete-case participants. The same feature matrices and model specifications as in the primary analyses were used, and taxa were not re-filtered after exclusion so that removal of low-depth samples was the only analytical change.Categorical variables were compared using Pearson’s chi-squared test when expected cell counts were adequate. Fisher’s exact test was used for sparse contingency tables. For larger-than-2 × 2 tables where exact computation was impractical, Fisher’s exact test with Monte Carlo simulation was applied.An additional exploratory HPV-positive versus HPV-negative taxonomic comparison was performed using Welch’s two-sample t-test, which does not assume equal group variances, together with Cohen’s d as a standardized effect-size measure. Before differential testing, the same predefined taxonomic exclusion filter used in the main bacterial analyses was applied to remove implausible environmental, animal-associated, and likely misclassified assignments at both genus and species levels. full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Clinical and demographic characteristics of the study populationA total of 311 non-pregnant women were included in the study. Of these, 148 (47.6%) were HPV-positive and 163 (52.4%) were HPV-negative. By HPV type group, 163 participants (52.4%) had no HPV infection, 64 (20.6%) were classified as HPV High Risk, 43 (13.8%) as HPV16, 34 (10.9%) as HPV Other (low-risk types), and 7 (2.3%) as HPV18. The mean age of participants was 34.5 ± 6.3 years and differed significantly across HPV type groups (p = 0.002), with HPV16 (31.4 ± 5.3 years) and HPV18 (30.4 ± 6.1 years) groups being younger compared to No HPV (35.3 ± 6.1 years) and HPV Other (35.3 ± 6.7 years) groups. Body mass index (mean 23.5 ± 4.3 kg/m2) and age at menarche (mean 13.4 ± 1.4 years) did not differ significantly across groups (p = 0.41 and p = 0.35, respectively). Because the HPV18 group comprised only 7 participants (2.3% of the cohort), demographic and clinical contrasts involving this group, including the younger age and lower parity noted above, are based on a small subgroup and should be regarded as descriptive and exploratory rather than definitive. Cytological grade distribution differed significantly across HPV type groups (p < 0.001). Overall, NILM was the most prevalent grade (142 women, 45.7%), followed by LSIL (79, 25.4%), ASC-US (73, 23.5%), and ASC-H (10, 3.2%). Among No HPV participants, NILM predominated (61.3%), whereas LSIL was the most common grade in HPV High Risk (43.8%) and HPV16 (55.8%) groups. The HPV Other group showed the highest proportion of NILM (67.6%). ASC-H was most prevalent in the HPV16 group (11.6%) and was rare in No HPV (0.6%). Community state type (CST) distribution did not differ significantly across HPV type groups (p = 0.074). CST IV was the most common overall (140 participants, 45.0%), followed by CST III (70, 22.5%), CST I (67, 21.5%), CST II (25, 8.0%), and CST V (9, 2.9%). The HPV Other and HPV16 groups had the highest proportions of CST IV (61.8% and 62.8%, respectively), while CST I was most prevalent in HPV High Risk (26.6%).Regarding demographic and reproductive characteristics, the majority of participants identified as Kazakh (91.3%), with no significant difference in ethnicity across groups (p = 0.93). Most participants held a bachelor’s degree (69.8%), and educational level did not differ across HPV groups (p = 0.52). Marital status differed significantly (p = 0.008): married women comprised 65.6% of the total cohort and were most prevalent in the No HPV group (74.8%), while the proportions of unmarried and divorced/widowed women were higher among HPV-positive groups, particularly HPV18 (57.1% unmarried) and HPV Other (26.5% unmarried). The mean number of deliveries differed significantly across groups (p = 0.005), being lowest in the HPV18 group (0.5 ± 0.8) and highest in the No HPV group (1.9 ± 1.4). Mean cycle length also differed modestly across groups (p = 0.025), with HPV Other showing the longest mean cycle (34.3 ± 18.8 days) compared with HPV High Risk (28.8 ± 2.1 days). Menstrual cycle regularity (92.6% regular overall), menstrual phase at sampling, and days since last menstrual period did not differ significantly across groups (p = 0.69, p = 0.89, and p = 0.98, respectively). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionIn this study, we characterized cervicovaginal microbiome composition and predicted functional potential in relation to HPV status, HPV type group, cytological grade, and community state type. The HPV-negative NILM subset of the present cohort overlaps with the multi-kingdom baseline cohort described in Rakhmankulova et al. (2026); the CST distribution and Lactobacillus-dominance patterns observed here for HPV-negative women are consistent with that earlier report, supporting the internal consistency of CST assignment across the two analyses and reinforcing the present study’s characterization of HPV-positive comparator groups against this baseline. HPV-positive samples showed increased bacterial species richness, whereas Shannon diversity and Pielou evenness were not significantly different between HPV-positive and HPV-negative groups. HPV-positive samples were also enriched in phylogenetically diverse anaerobic taxa and depleted in several health-associated bacterial lineages. These findings are consistent with previous studies reporting Lactobacillus depletion and enrichment of anaerobic bacteria in HPV-positive women (Lee et al., 2013; Brotman et al., 2014; Audirac-Chalifour et al., 2016; Łaniewski et al., 2018). At the genus level, the lower relative abundance of Lactobacillus and higher abundance of Gardnerella were consistent with a shift toward a dysbiosis-associated community profile. This pattern is also consistent with meta-analyses linking bacterial vaginosis and Lactobacillus-depleted communities with HPV infection (Gillet et al., 2011; Brusselaers et al., 2019). However, the direction and mechanistic basis of this association remains debated. Dysbiosis may facilitate HPV persistence through altered mucosal immunity and reduced colonization resistance, whereas HPV-associated epithelial or inflammatory changes may themselves disrupt microbiome homeostasis (Aldunate et al., 2015; Mitra et al., 2015; Hearps et al., 2017; Shannon et al., 2017). Species-level Bray-Curtis community composition did not differ significantly by HPV status, suggesting that the principal HPV-associated diversity signal was an increase in the number of detected species rather than broad restructuring of overall community composition.HPV Other showed the highest observed species richness, but species-level Bray-Curtis differences across HPV type groups did not reach statistical significance. This pattern differed from the expectation that greater oncogenic risk would necessarily correspond to greater microbiome alteration. However, HPV Other comprised a heterogeneous collection of genotypes, and the observed differences may reflect genotype composition, infection duration, age, reproductive characteristics, behavioral factors, or baseline microbial ecology. In the final covariate-adjusted model, HPV type group was associated with only four species. Suicoccus acidiformans and Globicatella sp. PHS GS PNBC 21–1553 were associated with HPV Other, whereas Enterococcus faecalis and Alloscardovia omnicolens were associated with HPV High Risk. The narrower set of significant taxa after adjustment suggests that some variation observed in preliminary analyses was explained by CST, grade, age, number of deliveries, sequencing depth, or marital status. Because several of these species were abundant only in subsets of participants, they should not be interpreted as stable HPV-specific biomarkers without external validation. The cross-sectional design cannot determine whether bacterial differences preceded HPV acquisition, followed infection, or reflected common underlying determinants.Shotgun metagenomic functional profiling further suggested that HPV type-specific microbiome differences extended beyond taxonomic composition to differences in predicted microbial functional capacity. The HPV Other group showed higher inferred abundance of pathways annotated to siderophore-group nonribosomal peptide biosynthesis, drug metabolism involving other enzymes, lipoic acid metabolism, lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, porphyrin metabolism, glycan degradation, streptomycin biosynthesis, flavonoid biosynthesis, and stilbenoid-related pathways. These findings indicate differences in the genetic potential for secondary-metabolite biosynthesis, lipid-associated processes, and complex carbohydrate degradation; however, they do not demonstrate that these pathways were transcriptionally active or that the corresponding metabolites were produced in vivo. Some pathways were relatively higher in HPV-negative samples, although their biological interpretation in the cervicovaginal microbiome remains uncertain. The pathway patterns were broadly consistent with the higher species richness and the taxonomic patterns observed in the HPV Other group, but they do not establish that these communities were metabolically more active or that the predicted products influenced HPV persistence or epithelial function. Metatranscriptomic and metabolomic validation will be required to determine whether these predicted pathways are expressed and whether their products are biologically relevant in vivo.High-risk HPV-mediated carcinogenesis is primarily driven by viral oncogene activity, which may help explain why oncogenic HPV types were not necessarily associated with the most pronounced microbiome disruption (Zur Hausen, 2002; Doorbar et al., 2012). Conversely, the association of HPV Other with higher species richness and selected taxonomic/functional patterns may reflect differences in viral persistence, host susceptibility, or local ecological conditions rather than greater transforming potential. This pattern may reflect distinct ecological strategies: high-risk HPV types may be adapted to establish persistent infection in health-associated microbiomes where intact colonization resistance would otherwise facilitate viral clearance (Hearps et al., 2017), whereas one possibility is that different HPV categories may be associated with distinct local ecological contexts with compromised colonization resistance and altered local immunity (Molijn et al., 2005; Godoy-Vitorino et al., 2018). Alternatively, dysbiosis may impair immune-mediated clearance of low-risk types that would otherwise be rapidly eliminated, allowing their persistence without malignant transformation. This interpretation is biologically plausible because anaerobe-rich cervicovaginal communities have been associated with altered cytokine and interferon responses that may influence viral persistence across HPV types (Torcia, 2019; Mitra et al., 2020), which could theoretically facilitate viral persistence across HPV types regardless of oncogenic potential. The differing patterns observed for HPV16 and HPV18 further suggest that microbiome associations may vary among individual oncogenic genotypes (Anahtar et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2015). However, the HPV18 group included only seven participants, and its apparent microbiome pattern may therefore be strongly influenced by individual observations and should be interpreted as exploratory. Few studies have directly compared taxonomic and predicted functional profiles across HPV risk categories, because most previous investigations have focused on HPV-positive versus HPV-negative comparisons. Such binary comparisons may obscure heterogeneity among HPV genotypes and risk groups (Piyathilake et al., 2016; Mitra et al., 2017; Usyk et al., 2020), potentially obscuring important heterogeneity in HPV-microbiome associations. Rather than dysbiosis uniformly driving progression, our data suggest that HPV types differ in their associated microbiome states and metabolic activities.CST-stratified analysis indicated that HPV-associated microbiome differences depended on the baseline community state. CST I and CST II remained predominantly Lactobacillus-dominated regardless of HPV status, suggesting greater ecological stability of these community configurations (Boris and Barbés, 2000; Tachedjian et al., 2017…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsThis study demonstrates that HPV infection, HPV type group, cytological grade, and community state type are associated with distinct cervicovaginal microbiome patterns. HPV-positive women showed greater bacterial species richness and shifts in dominant bacterial taxa, whereas Shannon diversity, Pielou evenness, and overall species-level Bray–Curtis composition did not differ significantly by HPV status. CST analyses confirmed the expected separation between Lactobacillus-dominant and anaerobe-rich communities. Predicted functional differences were also observed across HPV groups, but these findings represent microbial potential rather than measured activity. Overall, the results support a complex relationship between HPV and the cervicovaginal microbiome, while the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality or disease progression.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionHuman papillomavirus (HPV) infection remains the primary etiological factor in cervical carcinogenesis, with high-risk HPV types responsible for virtually all cervical cancer cases worldwide (Walboomers et al., 1999; Okunade, 2020). However, the transition from transient HPV infection to persistent infection and subsequent progression to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive carcinoma occurs in only a fraction of infected individuals, suggesting that host factors beyond viral oncogenicity play critical roles in disease pathogenesis (Schiffman and Wentzensen, 2013). The cervicovaginal microbiome has emerged as a potential modifier of HPV-associated disease risk, with accumulating evidence indicating that bacterial community composition influences viral persistence, immune responses, and epithelial transformation (Mitra et al., 2016; Kyrgiou et al., 2017; Łaniewski et al., 2020).The cervicovaginal microbiome exhibits distinct community state types (CSTs), primarily classified by dominant Lactobacillus species or absence thereof (Ravel et al., 2011). Lactobacillus-dominant communities, particularly those dominated by L. crispatus (CST I), are associated with vaginal health through production of lactic acid, hydrogen peroxide, and bacteriocins that maintain acidic pH and inhibit pathogen colonization (O’Hanlon et al., 2013; Petrova et al., 2015; Amabebe and Anumba, 2018). Conversely, polymicrobial communities depleted of Lactobacillus and enriched in anaerobic bacteria (CST IV), characteristic of bacterial vaginosis, associate with increased susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections, including HPV, and adverse reproductive outcomes (Ma et al., 2012; Borgdorff et al., 2014). However, the specific interactions between HPV infection, viral type heterogeneity, cervical cytological changes, and microbiome composition remain incompletely characterized.Important knowledge gaps remain regarding whether HPV–microbiome associations differ by viral type group, whether different HPV categories are associated with distinct bacterial profiles, and how cervicovaginal microbiome composition differs across cytological grades. Furthermore, the context-dependency of HPV-microbiome interactions across different baseline CST configurations requires systematic investigation. Previous studies have yielded conflicting results regarding Lactobacillus depletion in HPV-positive women, with some reporting significant associations while others found minimal differences, potentially reflecting heterogeneity in HPV types, cytological grades, or CST distributions (Di Paola et al., 2017; Tamarelle et al., 2019; Norenhag et al., 2020).The present study addresses these gaps through comprehensive characterization of cervicovaginal microbiome composition across HPV status, HPV type categories (including separate analysis of low-risk HPV Other, high-risk HPV types, HPV16, and HPV18), cervical cytological grades (NILM, ASC-US, ASC-H, LSIL), and baseline CST types. We employed whole-genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing, combined with alpha and beta diversity analyses, differential abundance testing, and functional pathway profiling, to characterize HPV type-specific microbiome signatures, identify grade-associated bacterial markers, and determine CST-dependent responses to HPV infection. 2.2.Sample collection, DNA extraction and sequencingCervical samples were stored at −80 °C until processing. Total genomic DNA was extracted using the ZymoBIOMICS DNA Miniprep Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Sterile nuclease-free water was included as a negative extraction control, and the ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard was used as a positive control. DNA samples were required to contain at least 1.0 μg total DNA, with good integrity and no visible impurities. DNA concentration was measured using a microplate reader with a broad-range DNA assay, and DNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis.Raw paired-end sequencing reads were processed using fastp for adapter trimming and quality filtering. Read pairs were discarded when adapter contamination was detected, when more than 5 bp contained ambiguous nucleotides, or when more than 40% of bases were of low quality. Sliding-window trimming was performed using a 4-bp window and a Q15 threshold. The mean numbers of raw and clean reads were 48.5 million and 47.9 million reads per sample, respectively. Mean Q20/Q30 values were 98.2%/93.8% for raw reads and 99.0%/95.3% for clean reads.Human-read depletion was performed by alignment against the human GRCh38 reference genome using Bowtie2 v2.4.4. In the original pipeline, read pairs failing concordant alignment to the human reference were retained using the --un-conc-gz option while preserving paired-read structure for downstream metagenomic classification. Residual host content after depletion was evaluated using Kraken2 v2.1.3. On average, 92.1% of reads in the Bowtie2-retained fraction were subsequently classified as Homo sapiens, indicating substantial residual host sequence after this permissive depletion step. Approximately 7.9% of reads in the retained fraction were not classified as human and comprised microbial and unclassified reads available for downstream taxonomic classification.Taxonomic classification was performed using Kraken2 v2.1.3 against the PlusPFP Kraken2/Bracken database. Bracken v3.0 was subsequently used to refine genus- and species-level abundance estimates. Functional profiling was performed using HUMAnN 3.0 with UniRef90 protein annotations and MetaCyc pathway reconstruction. No predefined minimum non-host sequencing-depth threshold was applied in the original pipeline. Because effective bacterial sequencing depth varied substantially among samples, classified bacterial depth was quantified directly from the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken bacterial count table and was explicitly evaluated in subsequent depth-corrected and sensitivity analyses. Classified bacterial sequencing depth was defined as the total number of reads assigned to the bacterial domain (d:Bacteria) in the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken count table. 2.3.GroupingsSamples were analyzed according to four main clinical and microbiome grouping variables: HPV status, HPV type group, cytology/histology grade, and bacterial community state type (CST). HPV status was assessed using the RealBest DNA HPV High Carcinogenic Risk Genotype real-time PCR kit (Cat. No. C8899; Vector-Best), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The assay detects the following high-risk HPV genotypes: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59. A sample was considered positive when at least one HPV genotype produced a cycle-threshold value of Ct ≤35. Samples without detection of any target genotype were classified as negative for the high-risk HPV types included in the assay. Whole-genome shotgun sequencing data were also screened for HPV sequences to identify genotypes not included in the PCR panel. The standard Reference sequence databases were used. Samples positive by either PCR or WGS were classified as HPV-positive. For descriptive analyses, HPV16 and HPV18 were retained as separate categories, other oncogenic genotypes were classified as HPV High Risk, and detected genotypes outside the predefined high-risk list were classified as HPV Other. The HPV Other group comprised samples in which WGS screening identified only genotypes classified as low-risk or non-carcinogenic by IARC (HPV6b, 7, 11, 26, 30, 32, 34, 53, 54, 71, 85, 90, 144, 156, and 166). A small number of HPV Other samples additionally showed trace-level WGS reads mapping to the high-risk genotypes HPV16, HPV31, or HPV35; because these reads represented less than 5% of the relative HPV sequence abundance within the sample, well below the threshold used to call a genotype present, these samples were retained in the HPV Other group rather than reclassified as HPV16, HPV High Risk, or HPV-positive for the correspo…

title_original: Cervicovaginal microbiome alterations across HPV infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between the cervicovaginal microbiome and HPV infection, particularly focusing on how viral type heterogeneity, cytological grade, and community state type (CST) might influence microbial composition.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional study was conducted at the National Research Center for Mother and Child Health in Astana, Kazakhstan, involving 311 non-pregnant women. The participants were analyzed based on HPV infection status, viral type categories, cervical cytological grades, and CSTs.
analysis.methods: The study used whole-genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing, integrated diversity analyses, MaAsLin2 differential abundance testing, and HUMAnN 3.0 functional pathway profiling. Sequencing data were processed using fastp for adapter trimming and quality filtering, and taxonomic classification was performed using Kraken2 v2.1.3 against the PlusPFP Kraken2/Bracken database. Depth-corrected sensitivity analyses and linear regression were also conducted to assess richness and its association with HPV status.
analysis.main_results: HPV-positive samples showed increased bacterial species richness and a reciprocal Lactobacillus-to-Gardnerella dominance shift compared to HPV-negative samples. HPV Other samples had the highest bacterial species richness and distinct taxonomic and functional associations, including higher inferred abundance of siderophore- and lipopolysaccharide-biosynthesis pathways. CST IV exhibited pronounced Lactobacillus depletion in HPV-positive women.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that oncogenic potential and dysbiosis severity are not aligned, and that CST type modifies HPV–microbiome interactions, highlighting the complex relationship between microbiome composition and HPV infection outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights into the role of the cervicovaginal microbiome in HPV infection dynamics, which could inform future studies on microbiome-based interventions for HPV-associated diseases and improve risk assessment strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study excluded samples with incomplete metadata or insufficient sequencing data, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate, as the findings are based on cross-sectional data and adjusted models, but the analysis of microbiome composition and its associations with HPV types is well-supported.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the relationship between the cervicovaginal microbiome and HPV infection, focusing on how viral type heterogeneity, cytological grade, and community state type (CST) might influence microbial composition. Conducted at a tertiary medical center in Kazakhstan, the cross-sectional analysis included 311 non-pregnant women. Whole-genome shotgun sequencing and metagenomic tools were used to assess microbiome diversity and function. Results showed that HPV-positive samples had increased bacterial richness and a shift in Lactobacillus-to-Gardnerella dominance, with HPV Other samples displaying distinct taxonomic and functional profiles. CST IV was associated with Lactobacillus depletion in HPV-positive women. The authors suggest that CST modifies HPV–microbiome interactions, indicating a complex relationship between microbiome composition and HPV infection outcomes. The study's findings are moderate in strength due to cross-sectional design and exclusion criteria, but they offer valuable insights for future research on microbiome-based interventions and risk assessment for HPV-associated diseases.

elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用了全 基因组 鸟枪法宏基因组测序、综合多样性分析、MaAsLin2 差异丰度测试和 HUMAnN 3.0 功能通路分析。使用 fastp 处理测序数据以进行接头修剪和质量过滤,并使用 Kraken2 v2.1.3 针对 PlusPFP Kraken2/Bracken 数据库进行分类学分类。还进行了深度校正敏感性分析和线性回归来评估丰富度及其与 HPV 状态的关联。
elements_zh.main_results: 与 HPV 阴性样本相比,HPV 阳性样本显示细菌种类丰富度增加,并且乳杆菌向加德纳菌的优势相互转变。HPV 其他样本具有最高的细菌物种丰富度和独特的分类学和功能关联,包括推断的铁载体和脂多糖生物合成途径丰度更高。CST IV 在 HPV 阳性女性中表现出明显的乳酸菌消耗。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,致癌潜力和生态失调的严重程度并不一致,并且 CST 类型改变了 HPV 与微生物组的相互作用,凸显了微生物组组成和 HPV 感染结果之间的复杂关系。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为了解宫颈阴道微生物组在 HPV 感染动态中的作用提供了见解,这可以为未来基于微生物组干预 HPV 相关疾病的研究提供信息,并改进风险评估策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究排除了元数据不完整或测序数据不足的样本,这可能会限制普遍性。证据是中等的,因为研究结果基于横截面数据和调整模型,但微生物组组成及其与 HPV 类型的关联的分析得到了充分支持。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between the cervicovaginal microbiome and HPV infection, particularly focusing on how viral type heterogeneity, cytological grade, and community state type (CST) might influence microbial composition.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional study was conducted at the National Research Center for Mother and Child Health in Astana, Kazakhstan, involving 311 non-pregnant women. The participants were analyzed based on HPV infection status, viral type categories, cervical cytological grades, and CSTs.
analysis_en.methods: The study used whole-genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing, integrated diversity analyses, MaAsLin2 differential abundance testing, and HUMAnN 3.0 functional pathway profiling. Sequencing data were processed using fastp for adapter trimming and quality filtering, and taxonomic classification was performed using Kraken2 v2.1.3 against the PlusPFP Kraken2/Bracken database. Depth-corrected sensitivity analyses and linear regression were also conducted to assess richness and its association with HPV status.
analysis_en.main_results: HPV-positive samples showed increased bacterial species richness and a reciprocal Lactobacillus-to-Gardnerella dominance shift compared to HPV-negative samples. HPV Other samples had the highest bacterial species richness and distinct taxonomic and functional associations, including higher inferred abundance of siderophore- and lipopolysaccharide-biosynthesis pathways. CST IV exhibited pronounced Lactobacillus depletion in HPV-positive women.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that oncogenic potential and dysbiosis severity are not aligned, and that CST type modifies HPV–microbiome interactions, highlighting the complex relationship between microbiome composition and HPV infection outcomes.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights into the role of the cervicovaginal microbiome in HPV infection dynamics, which could inform future studies on microbiome-based interventions for HPV-associated diseases and improve risk assessment strategies.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study excluded samples with incomplete metadata or insufficient sequencing data, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate, as the findings are based on cross-sectional data and adjusted models, but the analysis of microbiome composition and its associations with HPV types is well-supported.

full_text: Abstract Based on the transmission mechanism of HPV, this paper establishes a dynamic model that includes sexual and non-sexual transmission. First, the threshold \(R_{0} \) of the model is obtained using the next-generation matrix method. It is found that when \(R_{0} < 1 \), the disease-free equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable, while when \(R_{0} > 1 \), the endemic equilibrium exists. Subsequently, numerical simulations verify that vaccination strategies targeting susceptible populations are more effective than input measures for vaccinated populations. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis is conducted on threshold \(R_{0} \), and the corresponding optimal control problem is considered. It is found that when implementing a single measure, sexual contact control is the most effective, followed by non-sexual contact control. In addition, vaccination measures should not be ignored. Data availability This research does not involve real data. No data were used, and no new data were created. title_original: Optimal control of human papillomavirus transmission models integrating sexual and non-sexual routes

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to establish a dynamic model of human papillomavirus (HPV) transmission that integrates both sexual and non-sexual routes to better understand and control its spread.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study employed a mathematical modeling approach to simulate HPV transmission dynamics, focusing on the stability of disease-free and endemic equilibria under varying conditions.
analysis.methods: The model used the next-generation matrix method to calculate the threshold $R_0$, and sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate the impact of different control measures on the model's outcomes.
analysis.main_results: The model demonstrated that when $R_0 < 1$, the disease-free equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable, and when $R_0 > 1$, an endemic equilibrium exists. Numerical simulations showed that vaccination strategies targeting susceptible populations are more effective than input measures for vaccinated populations.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that controlling sexual contact is the most effective single measure, followed by non-sexual contact control, and emphasized the importance of vaccination measures in HPV transmission management.

full_text: ABSTRACTHuman papillomavirus (HPV) infection contributes to rising incidence of HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer (OPC). After the U.S. expanded HPV vaccination to adults aged 27–45 y in 2018, COVID-19 caused preventive visits and routine immunizations to plunge. We analyzed 2019 and 2022 NHIS data among adults aged 27–45 (2019 n = 8,745; 2022 n = 7,303). The primary outcome was ever HPV vaccination (≥1 dose), regardless of age at first vaccination. We estimated age-adjusted, survey-weighted coverage and used multivariable logistic regression to estimate adjusted odds of vaccination by sociodemographic characteristics; secondary 2022 analyses assessed initiation between ages 27 and 45. Ever HPV vaccine uptake increased from 15.1% in 2019 to 20.7% in 2022 (difference 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.03–7.07). In both years, lower odds were observed with increasing age, men, non-Hispanic Asian adults, individuals with lower educational attainment, and those without a usual place for care. By 2022, lower income-to-poverty ratios and lack of insurance were associated with reduced odds, whereas LGB+ and unmarried adults had higher odds, and adults in the Northeast had higher odds than those in the South. Only 1.43% (95% CI, 1.07–1.80) initiated vaccination between ages 27 and 45 in 2022. Initiation was more common among females, LGB+ and non-Hispanic Asian adults, and unmarried adults, and less common among those with lower education and no usual place for care. The increase in lifetime HPV vaccine coverage likely reflects childhood and adolescent vaccination rather than initiation at ages 27–45, which remained uncommon, and persistent inequities highlight missed opportunities for equitable OPC prevention.KEYWORDS: Human papillomavirus, vaccination, oropharyngeal cancer, HPV vaccine Materials and methodsStudy sampleThis study is a cross-sectional, secondary data analysis of the 2019 and the 2022 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) datasets, available from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).14 The NHIS is a cross-sectional survey administered every year by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), designed to collect health data from a nationally representative sample of the non-institutionalized U.S. population. The survey used a stratified, clustered, and multistage sampling design to ensure representativeness across the diverse demographic and geographic groups.15 The interview comprised the core and supplemental questionnaires, encompassing demographic characteristics, health status (including mental health), and healthcare services. This study analyzed publicly available, de-identified NHIS public-use data files made available by the CDC/NCHS. All potentially identifiable information has been removed from these files. Accordingly, no ethics committee approval or additional informed consent was required for this secondary analysis.In the current study, we analyzed two independent cross-sectional samples: 8745 adults aged 27–45 y from the 2019 NHIS database, and 7303 participants in the same age group from the 2022 NHIS database, all of whom had complete data on HPV vaccine uptake status and had important sociodemographic data available. The smaller 2022 analytic sample reflects the independent annual NHIS sample size and application of the same age restriction and complete-case inclusion criteria used for both survey years; no additional exclusion criterion was applied uniquely to the 2022 sample. Analyses were limited to those aged 27–45 y at the time of survey. Responses such as refused, don’t know, and not ascertained were recoded as missing data for all variables and excluded from the study.MeasuresSociodemographic data and HPV vaccination status were self-reported. The primary outcome was self-reported ever receipt of ≥1 HPV vaccine dose, based on the NHIS item: “HPV is the Human Papillomavirus. Have you ever received an HPV shot or vaccine?” Respondents were classified as ever vaccinated if they answered “yes,” regardless of age at first vaccination. The primary outcome captures lifetime HPV vaccine receipt among respondents aged 27–45 y at the time of survey and does not necessarily indicate vaccination initiated after age 27 or after the 2018 policy change. For descriptive analyses, age at first HPV vaccination was categorized as 9–12, 13–18, 19–26, and 27–45 y, and survey-weighted estimates were calculated for 2019 and 2022. Analyses focused primarily on adults aged 27–45 y, with younger age groups included for context.In a secondary analysis using 2022 data, we used age at first HPV vaccination to identify respondents whose first HPV dose occurred between ages 27 and 45. These respondents were classified as mid-adult initiators and were compared with respondents who reported never receiving HPV vaccination. Respondents whose first HPV vaccination occurred before age 27 were excluded from this secondary initiation analysis. The analogous 2019 mid-adult initiation model was not estimated because only 16 respondents reported first HPV vaccination between ages 27 and 45. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTHuman papillomavirus (HPV) infection contributes to rising incidence of HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer (OPC). After the U.S. expanded HPV vaccination to adults aged 27–45 y in 2018, COVID-19 caused preventive visits and routine immunizations to plunge. We analyzed 2019 and 2022 NHIS data among adults aged 27–45 (2019 n = 8,745; 2022 n = 7,303). The primary outcome was ever HPV vaccination (≥1 dose), regardless of age at first vaccination. We estimated age-adjusted, survey-weighted coverage and used multivariable logistic regression to estimate adjusted odds of vaccination by sociodemographic characteristics; secondary 2022 analyses assessed initiation between ages 27 and 45. Ever HPV vaccine uptake increased from 15.1% in 2019 to 20.7% in 2022 (difference 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.03–7.07). In both years, lower odds were observed with increasing age, men, non-Hispanic Asian adults, individuals with lower educational attainment, and those without a usual place for care. By 2022, lower income-to-poverty ratios and lack of insurance were associated with reduced odds, whereas LGB+ and unmarried adults had higher odds, and adults in the Northeast had higher odds than those in the South. Only 1.43% (95% CI, 1.07–1.80) initiated vaccination between ages 27 and 45 in 2022. Initiation was more common among females, LGB+ and non-Hispanic Asian adults, and unmarried adults, and less common among those with lower education and no usual place for care. The increase in lifetime HPV vaccine coverage likely reflects childhood and adolescent vaccination rather than initiation at ages 27–45, which remained uncommon, and persistent inequities highlight missed opportunities for equitable OPC prevention.KEYWORDS: Human papillomavirus, vaccination, oropharyngeal cancer, HPV vaccine
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsStudy sampleThis study is a cross-sectional, secondary data analysis of the 2019 and the 2022 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) datasets, available from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).14 The NHIS is a cross-sectional survey administered every year by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), designed to collect health data from a nationally representative sample of the non-institutionalized U.S. population. The survey used a stratified, clustered, and multistage sampling design to ensure representativeness across the diverse demographic and geographic groups.15 The interview comprised the core and supplemental questionnaires, encompassing demographic characteristics, health status (including mental health), and healthcare services. This study analyzed publicly available, de-identified NHIS public-use data files made available by the CDC/NCHS. All potentially identifiable information has been removed from these files. Accordingly, no ethics committee approval or additional informed consent was required for this secondary analysis.In the current study, we analyzed two independent cross-sectional samples: 8745 adults aged 27–45 y from the 2019 NHIS database, and 7303 participants in the same age group from the 2022 NHIS database, all of whom had complete data on HPV vaccine uptake status and had important sociodemographic data available. The smaller 2022 analytic sample reflects the independent annual NHIS sample size and application of the same age restriction and complete-case inclusion criteria used for both survey years; no additional exclusion criterion was applied uniquely to the 2022 sample. Analyses were limited to those aged 27–45 y at the time of survey. Responses such as refused, don’t know, and not ascertained were recoded as missing data for all variables and excluded from the study.MeasuresSociodemographic data and HPV vaccination status were self-reported. The primary outcome was self-reported ever receipt of ≥1 HPV vaccine dose, based on the NHIS item: “HPV is the Human Papillomavirus. Have you ever received an HPV shot or vaccine?” Respondents were classified as ever vaccinated if they answered “yes,” regardless of age at first vaccination. The primary outcome captures lifetime HPV vaccine receipt among respondents aged 27–45 y at the time of survey and does not necessarily indicate vaccination initiated after age 27 or after the 2018 policy change. For descriptive analyses, age at first HPV vaccination was categorized as 9–12, 13–18, 19–26, and 27–45 y, and survey-weighted estimates were calculated for 2019 and 2022. Analyses focused primarily on adults aged 27–45 y, with younger age groups included for context.In a secondary analysis using 2022 data, we used age at first HPV vaccination to identify respondents whose first HPV dose occurred between ages 27 and 45. These respondents were classified as mid-adult initiators and were compared with respondents who reported never receiving HPV vaccination. Respondents whose first HPV vaccination occurred before age 27 were excluded from this secondary initiation analysis. The analogous 2019 mid-adult initiation model was not estimated because only 16 respondents reported first HPV vaccination between ages 27 and 45. The sociodemographic information included the respondents’ age (continuous variable), sex (male, female), sexual orientation (heterosexual, LGB+ including lesbian, gay, bisexual, and other sexual orientation), race and ethnicity (Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, Non-Hispanic Asian, Hispanic, and Non-Hispanic Other which includes American Indian and Alaska Native, other single not included in the questionnaire, and multiple races), marital status (married/partnered, not married), highest level of education (college graduate including professional school degrees, master’s degree and doctoral degree, some college such as associate degree in occupational, technical, and vocational and academic program, high school graduate, less than high school), ratio of family income to poverty (ITP < 1, 1 ≤ ITP < 2, 2 ≤ ITP < 4, ITP ≥ 4), insurance status (yes, no), having a usual place for healthcare (yes, no), general health (excellent, very good, good, poor/fair), and geographic region of residence (Northeast, Midwest, West, South).Statistical analysisAge-adjusted and survey-weighted HPV vaccine uptake prevalence was estimated for both years of 2019 and 2022. The HPV vaccine uptake prevalence in each sociodemographic group was also tested between these two years using Chi-square tests. The odds of HPV vaccine uptake (receipt of ≥1 vaccine dose) were estimated based on sociodemographic factors using weighted multivariable logistic regression models. All analyses were performed with survey package in R (version 4.4.0) to incorporate sampling weights and adjust for the complex survey design. Statistical significance was tested at a significance level of P < .05. For 2022, we also estimated the prevalence of mid-adult initiation (first receipt between 27–45) and fit a separate multivariable logistic regression model for mid-adult initiator as defined above. Analogous age-at-initiation analyses were not performed for 2019 because of the small number of respondents initiating vaccination in this age range in that early post-policy period.

In both years, individuals with a high school education (2019 = 0.61 [0.49–0.76]; 2022 = 0.55 [0.43–0.69]) or some college (2019 = 0.80 [0.68–0.96]; 2022 = 0.67 [0.56–0.81]) had significantly lower odds of HPV vaccine uptake compared to those with a college degree or higher. However, less than high school education was only statistically significantly associated with 64% lower odds of uptake in 2022 (0.36 [0.23–0.54]), and not in 2019 (0.72 [0.50–1.03]). Similarly, individuals without a usual place for care had lower odds of vaccination in both years (2019 = 0.73 [0.57–0.93]; 2022 = 0.62 [0.50–0.77]). Some associations with ever HPV vaccine receipt were statistically significant in 2019 but not in 2022, while others were statistically significant in 2022 but not in 2019. In 2022, LGB+ individuals had significantly higher odds of HPV vaccine uptake than heterosexual individuals (1.32, [1.03–1.70]), a contrast to 2019 where the difference was not statistically significant. Similarly, unmarried adults were more likely to be vaccinated in 2022 (1.25 [1.07–1.45]), while no significant difference by marital status was observed in 2019. In 2019, income and insurance were not associated with HPV vaccine uptake. In 2022, adults in all income-to-poverty categories below 4 had lower odds of receiving the HPV vaccine than those with a ratio ≥ 4 (ITP < 1: aOR = 0.65 [0.48–0.89]; 1 ≤ ITP < 2: aOR = 0.76 [0.61–0.95]; 2 ≤ ITP < 4: aOR = 0.76 [0.64–0.92]), as did those without insurance (aOR = 0.73 [0.56–0.95]). Regional trends also shifted. In 2019, individuals in the West had significantly higher odds of vaccination compared to those in the South (1.54, [1.27–1.86]). However, in 2022, those in the Northeast had significantly higher odds of vaccine uptake than those in the South (1.27 [1.02–1.59]). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn these nationally representative NHIS samples, self-reported ever receipt of ≥1 HPV vaccine dose among adults aged 27–45 y increased from 15.1% in 2019 to 20.7% in 2022. This finding should be interpreted as a change in lifetime HPV vaccination history among adults in this age range, not as a direct estimate of vaccination newly initiated under the 2019 ACIP shared clinical decision-making recommendation. Because the primary measure did not distinguish age at first vaccination in both survey years, the observed increase may reflect a combination of mid-adult initiation, vaccination received before age 27 among cohorts aging into the 27–45 y age range, and secular changes in vaccine access and awareness. Consistent with this interpretation, the 2022 age-at-first-dose analysis showed that only 1.43% of adults aged 27–45 initiated HPV vaccination between ages 27 and 45. Even with this low level of mid-adult initiation, the findings identify persistent inequities in HPV vaccine receipt by sex, age, education, usual source of care, insurance, and income. Given that approximately 78% of U.S. adolescents now receive at least one HPV vaccine dose, increasingly vaccinated cohorts aging into the 27–45 y population should raise observed coverage in this age group over the coming decade, while adolescent vaccination is expected to have a greater population-level impact on OPC prevention than vaccination initiated in mid-adulthood because it more often occurs before HPV exposure.16The observed increase in HPV vaccine coverage among adults aged 27–45 y is particularly relevant because OPSCC has overtaken cervical cancer as the most common HPV-associated malignancy in the U.S.6 Annual OPSCC incidence now exceeds 18,000 cases – nearly three-quarters in men – and almost all tumors harbor high-risk HPV16.17 Unlike cervical cancer, OPSCC lacks a universal screening test that can intercept precancerous lesions, so vaccination could be the only line of defense against future disease. Modeling studies suggest that even modest mid-adult vaccination gains could avert thousands of future OPSCC cases and spare patients the swallowing, speech, and quality-of-life burdens of chemoradiation.18 Evaluating how disruptions in preventive care access, vaccine delivery, clinic operations, and healthcare utilization during 2019 to 2022 advanced – or hindered – progress toward this prevention goal is thus critical for realizing the full benefit of the 2018 age-expansion policy.Similar to our study, Suk et al.13 documented a post-policy uptick in vaccination using commercial claims through 2020, but the present study extends those observations to uninsured and publicly insured populations that claims data miss. Likewise, cross-sectional NHIS analyses reported low, unequal uptake in 2019 but did not assess temporal change.11 By pairing two NHIS waves, we charted both progress and emerging inequities, providing a temporal view of mid-adult HPV vaccine behavior during a period of historic disruption.The COVID-19 pandemic is more than a convenient time marker – it fundamentally reshaped the context in which vaccination decisions were made. Preventive visits plunged, routine immunizations fell by double-digits, and public-health resources pivoted toward SARS-CoV-2.10 Clinic closures and stay-at-home orders posed new logistical hurdles, especially for communities already facing access barriers. Simultaneously, mass layoffs undermined employer-sponsored coverage19 just as the out-of-pocket cost of a 9-valent series can exceed $500,20 particularly in non-Medicaid-expansion states. The insurance and income gradients that emerged in 2022 align with evidence that economic shocks translated into missed preventive services for under-insured adults. Perceptions of vaccination also shifted. Media attention to mRNA technology raised awareness and expanded pharmacy-based infrastructure, yet misinformation and vaccine fatigue spilled over to non-COVID products, including HPV.21,22 Surveys from 2021–2023 show a correlation between COVID-19 vaccine skepticism and reluctance toward HPV vaccination,23 suggesting that attitudinal barriers compounded the material ones we observed.Shared decision-making for HPV vaccine uptake was also fundamentally altered by Telehealth, which rose from ≈1% of primary care encounters in 2019 to more than a quarter at the 2020 peak.24 Counseling can occur virtually, but vaccine administration cannot, creating an extra step that may be prohibitive for patients without paid leave or reliable transportation.25 This two-step hurdle likely contributed to the widening socioeconomic gaps in vaccination.Policy innovations introduced from 2019 to 2022 – federal authority for pharmacists to vaccinate adults, streamlined standing orders, and extended pharmacy hours – offer a path forward.26,27 Pilot studies already show higher completion rates when at least one dose is delivered in a pharmacy,28 and our findings point to the populations that could benefit most: uninsured adults, those with lower incomes, and men, who historically under-utilize preventive visits. Institutionalizing these advances while countering cost and misinformation is essential if the U.S. is to realize the OPSCC prevention potential of the 2018 age-expansion policy.In short, the 2019 to 2022 timeframe contained a major disruptive event that exposed vulnerabilities in adult HPV vaccine access and served as a catalyst for innovations that could mitigate them. Interpreting our data through this lens underscores the urgency of expanded vaccination exposure, while simultaneously addressing the economic and informational fallout that deepened inequities. Failure to do so risks locking in the uneven recovery we observed and forfeiting the equitable cancer-prevention potential of the HPV age-expansion policy. Even with a modest increase in HPV coverage, nearly four out of five adults aged 27–45 remained unvaccinated in 2022, which raises concerns about missed opportunities for cancer prevention. Continued monitoring of coverage patterns in this age group will help identify at-risk subgroups and guide interventions to support equitable access and informed decision-making, consistent with the shared clinical decision-making framework.This study should be interpreted in light of several limitations. First, analyses were based on cross-sectional NHIS data, which precludes any inference about temporal or causal relationships. Second, HPV vaccination status was determined by self-report, which may be subject to recall or social desirability bias. Third, the NHIS measure captures whether respondents had ever received an HPV vaccine but does not distinguish between partial vs. complete vaccination series, limiting inferences about the degree of protection against HPV-related cancers. Additionally, the primary outcome captured ever receipt of HPV vaccination and therefore could not distinguish vaccination initiated during mid-adulthood from vaccination received earlier in adolescence or young adulthood. Comparisons between 2019 and 2022 may reflect cohort replacement, secular trends, and pandemic-era healthcare access changes rather than the direct effect of the 2019 ACIP shared clinical decision-making recommendation. The 2022 secondary analysis used age at first vaccination to identify mid-adult initiation, but an analogous adjusted analysis for 2019 was not feasible because of the small number of respondents who initiated vaccination between ages 27 and 45. Finally, NHIS does not include detailed information on provider recommendation, sexual history, prior HPV exposure, perceived risk of new HPV infection, or reasons for accepting or declining vaccination, all of which are central to shared clinical decision-making.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsBetween 2019 and 2022, self-reported ever receipt of ≥1 HPV vaccine dose among U.S. adults aged 27–45 y increased from 15.1% to 20.7%, while first vaccination between ages 27 and 45 remained uncommon in 2022. Increasing age within the 27–45 y range, male sex, non-Hispanic Asian race/ethnicity, lower education, lower income, lack of insurance, and no usual source of care were associated with lower odds of ever HPV vaccine receipt; however, these primary-outcome findings should not be interpreted as predictors of mid-adult initiation. Yet, persistent, parallel inequities in lifetime vaccine receipt and mid-adult initiation highlight the need for more equitable counseling and vaccine delivery under shared clinical decision-making. Given the burden of HPV-associated OPSCC, particularly among men, improving access to evidence-based vaccination counseling remains an important prevention priority. Closing these gaps will require sustained, equity-focused efforts to bring vaccination within reach of the populations most at risk.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionOropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) has become one of the most rapidly rising human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated malignancies in the United States (U.S.), a trend driven almost entirely by persistent infection with high-risk HPV types.1,2 This burden falls disproportionately on men, who remain less likely to be vaccinated against HPV and who account for the majority of new OPSCC cases.3,4 Prophylactic HPV vaccination prior to initial infection prevents HPV infection from progressing to malignant transformation and thus represents a critical cancer-prevention strategy.5,6 Recognizing this, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2018 expanded the indication for 9-valent HPV vaccination to adults aged 27–45 y – a change later endorsed by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) through a shared decision-making recommendation7,8 – and, in June 2020, further updated the label to explicitly include the prevention of oropharyngeal and other HPV-associated head and neck cancers.9 These policy changes support the potential relevance of HPV vaccination to OPC prevention, particularly for adults who may benefit under shared clinical decision-making. However, because HPV vaccines are prophylactic and expected benefit is greatest before HPV exposure, vaccination initiated in adulthood should be interpreted as a selected prevention opportunity rather than as a direct substitute for adolescent vaccination.The COVID-19 pandemic commenced soon after this guideline change, shuttering clinics, diverting public-health resources, and causing steep declines in routine adult immunizations.10 These disruptions, coupled with widespread job loss and insurance instability, threatened to stall HPV vaccine uptake precisely when access had broadened. Early studies, confined to commercially insured populations or National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) snapshots, showed modest mid-adult coverage (~15%) and pronounced demographic disparities, but did not capture pandemic-era dynamics or the uninsured.11–13 Whether the ACIP guideline translated into sustained, equitable gains – or was a missed opportunity to mitigate future OPSCC burden given the circumstances of the 2019 to 2022 timeframe – remains unknown.To fill this gap, we used nationally representative NHIS data from 2019 and 2022 to quantify changes in self-reported ever receipt of ≥1 HPV vaccine dose among adults aged 27–45 y and to examine how sociodemographic predictors of vaccine receipt changed during this period. Because ever vaccination may include doses received before age 27, we also conducted a secondary 2022 analysis of first HPV vaccination between ages 27 and 45. We interpret these findings in the context of ACIP shared clinical decision-making, pandemic-era healthcare disruptions, cohort replacement from earlier adolescent and young-adult vaccination recommendations, and the potential relevance of HPV vaccination to OPC prevention. Study sampleThis study is a cross-sectional, secondary data analysis of the 2019 and the 2022 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) datasets, available from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).14 The NHIS is a cross-sectional survey administered every year by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), designed to collect health data from a nationally representative sample of the non-institutionalized U.S. population. The survey used a stratified, clustered, and multistage sampling design to ensure representativeness across the diverse demographic and geographic groups.15 The interview comprised the core and supplemental questionnaires, encompassing demographic characteristics, health status (including mental health), and healthcare services. This study analyzed publicly available, de-identified NHIS public-use data files made available by the CDC/NCHS. All potentially identifiable information has been removed from these files. Accordingly, no ethics committee approval or additional informed consent was required for this secondary analysis.In the current study, we analyzed two independent cross-sectional samples: 8745 adults aged 27–45 y from the 2019 NHIS database, and 7303 participants in the same age group from the 2022 NHIS database, all of whom had complete data on HPV vaccine uptake status and had important sociodemographic data available. The smaller 2022 analytic sample reflects the independent annual NHIS sample size and application of the same age restriction and complete-case inclusion criteria used for both survey years; no additional exclusion criterion was applied uniquely to the 2022 sample. Analyses were limited to those aged 27–45 y at the time of survey. Responses such as refused, don’t know, and not ascertained were recoded as missing data for all variables and excluded from the study. MeasuresSociodemographic data and HPV vaccination status were self-reported. The primary outcome was self-reported ever receipt of ≥1 HPV vaccine dose, based on the NHIS item: “HPV is the Human Papillomavirus. Have you ever received an HPV shot or vaccine?” Respondents were classified as ever vaccinated if they answered “yes,” regardless of age at first vaccination. The primary outcome captures lifetime HPV vaccine receipt among respondents aged 27–45 y at the time of survey and does not necessarily indicate vaccination initiated after age 27 or after the 2018 policy change. For descriptive analyses, age at first HPV vaccination was categorized as 9–12, 13–18, 19–26, and 27–45 y, and survey-weighted estimates were calculated for 2019 and 2022. Analyses focused primarily on adults aged 27–45 y, with younger age groups included for context.In a secondary analysis using 2022 data, we used age at first HPV vaccination to identify respondents whose first HPV dose occurred between ages 27 and 45. These respondents were classified as mid-adult initiators and were compared with respondents who reported never receiving HPV vaccination. Respondents whose first HPV vaccination occurred before age 27 were excluded from this secondary initiation analysis. The analogous 2019 mid-adult initiation model was not estimated because only 16 respondents reported first HPV vaccination between ages 27 and 45. The sociodemographic information included the respondents’ age (continuous variable), sex (male, female), sexual orientation (heterosexual, LGB+ including lesbian, gay, bisexual, and other sexual orientation), race and ethnicity (Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, Non-Hispanic Asian, Hispanic, and Non-Hispanic Other which includes American Indian and Alaska Native, other single not included in the questionnaire, and multiple races), marital status (married/partnered, not married), highest level of education (college graduate including professional school degrees, master’s degree and doctoral degree, some college such as associate degree in occupational, technical, and vocational and academic program, high school graduate, less than high school), ratio of family income to poverty (ITP < 1, 1 ≤ ITP < 2, 2 ≤ ITP < 4, ITP ≥ 4), insurance status (yes, no), having a usual place for healthcare (yes, no), general health (excellent, very good, good, poor/fair), and geographic region of residence (Northeast, Midwest, West, South). Statistical analysisAge-adjusted and survey-weighted HPV vaccine uptake prevalence was estimated for both years of 2019 and 2022. The HPV vaccine uptake prevalence in each sociodemographic group was also tested between these two years using Chi-square tests. The odds of HPV vaccine uptake (receipt of ≥1 vaccine dose) were estimated based on sociodemographic factors using weighted multivariable logistic regression models. All analyses were performed with survey package in R (version 4.4.0) to incorporate sampling weights and adjust for the complex survey design.
