full_text: IntroductionDespite the availability of a safe and effective Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, uptake remains inconsistent across the United States (U.S.), with marked differences in vaccination coverage across states. This descriptive exploratory study examined key informant perspectives on HPV vaccination promotion across policy-engaged jurisdictions in the U.S. in the post-COVID-19 era.MethodsSemi-structured interviews were conducted with nine key informants across six U.S. jurisdictions. Classification of the interviews was based on those with existing HPV vaccine school-entry requirements or those jurisdictions with recent school-entry policy considerations. Using inductive thematic analysis, we synthesized key informant perspectives and organized themes using analytical dimensions informed by the socio-ecological model.ResultsFindings highlight the importance of provider education, school-entry requirements, cancer prevention messaging, trusted messengers, culturally tailored outreach, and cross-sector partnerships as important components of HPV vaccine promotion. Barriers such as vaccine misinformation and increased hesitancy following the COVID-19 pandemic were also discussed.DiscussionThese insights can inform targeted, context-specific strategies to improve HPV vaccination rates and reduce cancer disparities. 2MethodsWe selected 12 U.S. jurisdictions, categorized into three groups based on their HPV vaccination policy context and comparable sociodemographic compositions. These included (1) jurisdictions with existing HPV vaccine requirements (Rhode Island, District of Columbia, Virginia, and Puerto Rico), (2) those that had recently considered adopting such requirements (Maryland, California, New York, and Massachusetts), and (3) comparable jurisdictions that had not considered requirements (Oklahoma, Mississippi, Iowa, and New Hampshire). For each jurisdiction, we identified between four to eight potential key informants (KI), resulting in a total pool of 69 individuals. Potential key informants were identified through online searches of state and jurisdictional health department websites, immunization programs and coalition webpages, and professional medical association websites. This pool represented potential key informants identified to be invited to participate in the study rather than a predetermined target sample size. These informants represented a range of roles, including immunization program managers, health department directors, representatives from pediatric and family physician associations, and state legislators. Inclusion criteria required participants to be at least 21 years old, have at least 3 years of experience in health or vaccination policy, and have knowledge on HPV vaccination strategies.Recruitment was conducted via email with up to two follow-up reminders, directing potential participants to a REDCap screening survey. Eligible respondents were redirected to the informed consent form and asked to indicate their interview availability. Between May and August 2024, 12 individuals initiated the screening survey, 10 completed it, and nine met the eligibility criteria. Thus, the final sample reflects the eligible participants who completed recruitment and enrollment during the study period. Although the original sampling frame was developed to support comparisons across jurisdictions with different HPV vaccination policy contexts, a small final sample (n = 9) was recruited and did not yield participants from jurisdictions without HPV school-entry policy consideration. As a result, the final analysis was not designed to formerly compare jurisdictions with and without policy activity. Instead, the study was reframed as a descriptive exploratory thematic synthesis of key informant perspectives from jurisdictions with existing (n = 7) or recently considered HPV school-entry requirements (n = 2), offering valuable insights into common and divergent factors shaping HPV vaccination strategies. In this study, the term “multilevel” refers to the analytical organization of participants’ perspectives across provider/organizations, community, and policy/contextual dimensions informed by the socio-ecological model, rather than to sampling participants from each ecological level.While the original intent was to compare perspectives across specific jurisdictions with varying policy environments, confidentiality concerns limited the ability to attribute findings to individual jurisdictions. To protect the identities of key informants, many of whom hold unique roles within their jurisdictions at the time of the interviews, state-level identifiers were excluded from all published materials. Because recruitment yielded only nine eligible participants, data saturation was not reached; therefore, the themes identified should be interpreted as exploratory and should not be considered as exhaustive representation of key informant perspectives across HPV vaccination policy contexts.The semi-structured interview guide was developed using the study aims and existing HPV vaccination literature and is provided as Supplementary material 1. Questions focused on three primary domains: (1) the current HPV vaccination context within the jurisdiction, including ongoing vaccination promotion strategies; (2) perceived barriers and facilitators affecting HPV vaccination efforts; and (3) the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on HPV vaccination promotion and implementation activities. All interviews were conducted virtually via Microsoft Teams and lasted 45 to 90 min. Research team members rotated across moderator, co-moderator, and technical support/note-taking roles. A designated note-taker documented relevant observations and contextual information during each interview. Interviews were audio-recorded with participant consent and transcribed verbatim for analysis.An initial codebook was developed through a close review of the transcripts while remaining informed by the broad domains explored in the interview guide. The codebook was refined iteratively as new concepts emerged from the data. Verbatim transcripts were uploaded to Dedoose, where the research team applied codes to relevant excerpts and organized coded data for thematic analysis using an inductive, iterative approach. Following the consensus-based team-coding model approach outlined by Guest and colleagues (14), three trained researchers independently coded each transcript and met regularly to compare coding decisions and reach consensus. Coding discrepancies were resolved through discussion until agreement was reached.After coding was completed, themes were organized and interpreted using analytical dimensions informed by the socio-ecological framework proposed by Ryan et al. (8), adapted from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) model (15). Thus, while theme generation was data-driven, the socio-ecological framework provided a structure for presenting and interpreting the findings. An overview of the study recruitment, data collection, and qualitative analysis workflow is presented in Figure 1. The protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Puerto Rico Comprehensive Cancer Center (#2023-04-98).Figure 1Study recruitment, data collection, and qualitative workflow.Flowchart outlining sampling, recruitment, data collection, and analysis steps for a qualitative study: jurisdiction selection, key informant identification, recruitment, sample eligibility, interview data collection, verbatim transcription, iterative thematic coding, and final theme development with post-COVID-19 context consideration. 3ResultsNine key informants were recruited, representing public health professionals (n = 6), health educators (n = 2), and an epidemiologist (n = 1), from six jurisdictions: Puerto Rico, Virginia, District of Columbia, New York, Rhode Island, and California. Participants were 89% female, and 55.6% had five to 10 years of experience in HPV vaccination strategies. Seven out of the nine key informants were from jurisdictions with an HPV vaccine school-entry requirement.To organize key informants’ perspectives identified in the interviews, findings were grouped into three analytical dimensions informed by the socio-ecological model: (1) provider and organizational factors, (2) community factors, and (3) policy and contextual factors. A fourth section describes the post-COVID-19 vaccine climate as a cross-cutting context influencing these dimensions. Table 1 provides representative excerpts supporting each theme identified within the provider/organizational, community, policy/contextual, and post-COVID-19 dimensions. Quotations are presented using anonymized key-informant identifiers to protect participant confidentiality.Table 1Analytic dimensions, themes, and representative key-informant excerpts related to HPV vaccination strategies, barriers, and facilitators (n = 9).Analytic dimensionThemeExcerptProvider and organizational factorsHealth provider recommendation“That cooperation from the doctor is vital, because it’s the person the parent has contact with, the one the parent trusts, right? So having them as allies is always necessary.” - KI #3Shift in promotional message“[...] Using that cancer prevention angle, because the way that HPV vaccination was introduced, it was more of a, I’m not going to say promiscuity angle, but parents may have felt that “oh, if my child gets this vaccine that may give them permission to engage in sexual activity. So, that was really not the way to introduce that vaccine. So, we are looking at it and trying to change that perception by looking at it from a cancer prevention angle. And that, I think, has been really helpful.”–KI #7Start vaccination at age nine“[.] A lot of effort has been put into educating about the strategy of starting the HPV vaccination series at ages 9 or 10. And I think that’s been effective because we certainly see over time that more and more providers, even though it’s still a slim minority, but more and more providers are adopting that strategy.”–KI #10Educational material“But I do feel like this is an effective strategy, you know, even if it’s successful in pointing parents in the direction of more information. You know, I’ve had some really great calls with parents who called in and were on guard about, like, “why am I being told to give my seventh grader an HPV vaccine?” and through talking with them, it’s not that they have drastically changed their mind. They’re just open to listening, which, in my view, that’s a success, right? So, I find that [educational materials] can facilitate additional discussions.”–KI #8Dilution of HPV-specific messaging“We do back to school campaigns, but we do not really specifically call out HPV vaccine. We just say, you know, it’s back to school, make sure your kid is up to date with all their vaccines so that they can be healthy and stay in school [.] one wonders how effective those messages can be when they are really general like that, but I do not think that they are not effective. I just do not know if they are as effective as maybe some of the more personalized efforts that we do.”–KI #16Community factorsAddress HPV vaccine myths/misinformation“[A parent] had heard that the vaccine is supposedly related to infertility, when that has been disproven a lot of times, so I think we definitely have to continue making an effort to continue focusing this vaccine on cancer prevention, but also to work on all the myths that surround it.”–KI #11Community engagement and outreach strategies“I think always keep in mind trusted messengers. I think that’s really important in terms of getting your message across effectively to communities and understanding that those messengers or those trusted messengers are different in different communities across the state.”–KI #10Misinformation/misconceptions“You know that people do not know the boy should get it, that we are still dealing with, in questions around the vaccine causing infertility. And I’m like, did not we deal with all of this? Like, when the vaccine first came out. So, I think it’s just reiterating that message.”–KI #16Groups against HPV vaccination“I cannot think of, off the top of my head, any organizations, but I know they do exist. So, I would say general, you know, anti-vaxx groups would be against this particular vaccine. [.] I do believe that spreading of misinformation hinders our efforts because anti-vaxxers are very vocal. They’re very loud. They have the ability to really get information out, get the attention of people because they are loud. They’re a mighty group.”–KI #7Groups in favor of HPV vaccination“[Collaborators] are good, not just for this vaccine, for all vaccines. Medical schools too. Since COVID, medical and public health schools have also become a bit more active and more vocal in helping, promoting, and maintaining the general concept of vaccination, again, not just the HPV vaccine–all vaccines.”–KI #12Institutional support“Our huge convener of community partners is our immunization coalition. And when you see the number of partners that participate in that coalition, it’s really reassuring because it reminds you that there’s just a diversity, there’s a diverse number of professionals in different fields who are advocating for immunizations in general, including HPV. So, yes, I would say that we are very well supported by our community-based organizations.”–KI #8Policy and contextual factorsPolitical facilitators“Another thing with the HPV vaccine being a school-required vaccine, it makes it immensely accessible, you know, especially given how expensive it is. So, you know, under and uninsured adolescents are able to go to a VFC provider and they are able to get that shot.”–KI #8Political barriers“In the legislature, there are groups now that were not present before, and they are definitely anti-vaccine. They are conservative, and within their philosophy, they try to present their objection to the use of that type of vaccine based on their beliefs.”–KI #3Cultural facilitators“We do not really have a huge anti-vax movement up here. So, people for the most, I mean, not to say we do not have them. We definitely have a few, very vocal, frequent fliers. But it’s not nearly at the level of some of my other colleagues have to deal with.”–KI #16Cultural barriers“Some of the common themes, which I think I’ve heard from partners who are in similar spaces as I am, it’s the transmission- the fact that parents feel that it’s an inappropriate vaccine for an 11-year-old, and because of the fact that you cannot catch it in school.”–KI #8Access to health services“[.] If you have coverage, if you do not have coverage, that greatly affects whether people have access to the vaccine.”–KI #3Mandate opposition“I think we have a strong movement in a lot of jurisdictions in our state, but you know, almost exclusively rural areas of the state, not wanting to see government interference in their day-to-day lives, including health decisions, health recommendations.”–KI #10HPV vaccine policy perception“I would say the majority are in interest. I think, you have those that, you know, strongly support vaccinations, then you have those that support vaccinations, but do not agree with there being maybe policies, laws, requirements for vaccines. full_text_sections.abstract: IntroductionDespite the availability of a safe and effective Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, uptake remains inconsistent across the United States (U.S.), with marked differences in vaccination coverage across states. This descriptive exploratory study examined key informant perspectives on HPV vaccination promotion across policy-engaged jurisdictions in the U.S. in the post-COVID-19 era.MethodsSemi-structured interviews were conducted with nine key informants across six U.S. jurisdictions. Classification of the interviews was based on those with existing HPV vaccine school-entry requirements or those jurisdictions with recent school-entry policy considerations. Using inductive thematic analysis, we synthesized key informant perspectives and organized themes using analytical dimensions informed by the socio-ecological model.ResultsFindings highlight the importance of provider education, school-entry requirements, cancer prevention messaging, trusted messengers, culturally tailored outreach, and cross-sector partnerships as important components of HPV vaccine promotion. Barriers such as vaccine misinformation and increased hesitancy following the COVID-19 pandemic were also discussed.DiscussionThese insights can inform targeted, context-specific strategies to improve HPV vaccination rates and reduce cancer disparities.
full_text_sections.methods: 2MethodsWe selected 12 U.S. jurisdictions, categorized into three groups based on their HPV vaccination policy context and comparable sociodemographic compositions. These included (1) jurisdictions with existing HPV vaccine requirements (Rhode Island, District of Columbia, Virginia, and Puerto Rico), (2) those that had recently considered adopting such requirements (Maryland, California, New York, and Massachusetts), and (3) comparable jurisdictions that had not considered requirements (Oklahoma, Mississippi, Iowa, and New Hampshire). For each jurisdiction, we identified between four to eight potential key informants (KI), resulting in a total pool of 69 individuals. Potential key informants were identified through online searches of state and jurisdictional health department websites, immunization programs and coalition webpages, and professional medical association websites. This pool represented potential key informants identified to be invited to participate in the study rather than a predetermined target sample size. These informants represented a range of roles, including immunization program managers, health department directors, representatives from pediatric and family physician associations, and state legislators. Inclusion criteria required participants to be at least 21 years old, have at least 3 years of experience in health or vaccination policy, and have knowledge on HPV vaccination strategies.Recruitment was conducted via email with up to two follow-up reminders, directing potential participants to a REDCap screening survey. Eligible respondents were redirected to the informed consent form and asked to indicate their interview availability. Between May and August 2024, 12 individuals initiated the screening survey, 10 completed it, and nine met the eligibility criteria. Thus, the final sample reflects the eligible participants who completed recruitment and enrollment during the study period. Although the original sampling frame was developed to support comparisons across jurisdictions with different HPV vaccination policy contexts, a small final sample (n = 9) was recruited and did not yield participants from jurisdictions without HPV school-entry policy consideration. As a result, the final analysis was not designed to formerly compare jurisdictions with and without policy activity. Instead, the study was reframed as a descriptive exploratory thematic synthesis of key informant perspectives from jurisdictions with existing (n = 7) or recently considered HPV school-entry requirements (n = 2), offering valuable insights into common and divergent factors shaping HPV vaccination strategies. In this study, the term “multilevel” refers to the analytical organization of participants’ perspectives across provider/organizations, community, and policy/contextual dimensions informed by the socio-ecological model, rather than to sampling participants from each ecological level.While the original intent was to compare perspectives across specific jurisdictions with varying policy environments, confidentiality concerns limited the ability to attribute findings to individual jurisdictions. To protect the identities of key informants, many of whom hold unique roles within their jurisdictions at the time of the interviews, state-level identifiers were excluded from all published materials. Because recruitment yielded only nine eligible participants, data saturation was not reached; therefore, the themes identified should be interpreted as exploratory and should not be considered as exhaustive representation of key informant perspectives across HPV vaccination policy contexts.The semi-structured interview guide was developed using the study aims and existing HPV vaccination literature and is provided as Supplementary material 1. Questions focused on three primary domains: (1) the current HPV vaccination context within the jurisdiction, including ongoing vaccination promotion strategies; (2) perceived barriers and facilitators affecting HPV vaccination efforts; and (3) the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on HPV vaccination promotion and implementation activities. All interviews were conducted virtually via Microsoft Teams and lasted 45 to 90 min. Research team members rotated across moderator, co-moderator, and technical support/note-taking roles. A designated note-taker documented relevant observations and contextual information during each interview. Interviews were audio-recorded with participant consent and transcribed verbatim for analysis.An initial codebook was developed through a close review of the transcripts while remaining informed by the broad domains explored in the interview guide. The codebook was refined iteratively as new concepts emerged from the data. Verbatim transcripts were uploaded to Dedoose, where the research team applied codes to relevant excerpts and organized coded data for thematic analysis using an inductive, iterative approach. Following the consensus-based team-coding model approach outlined by Guest and colleagues (14), three trained researchers independently coded each transcript and met regularly to compare coding decisions and reach consensus. Coding discrepancies were resolved through discussion until agreement was reached.After coding was completed, themes were organized and interpreted using analytical dimensions informed by the socio-ecological framework proposed by Ryan et al. (8), adapted from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) model (15). Thus, while theme generation was data-driven, the socio-ecological framework provided a structure for presenting and interpreting the findings. An overview of the study recruitment, data collection, and qualitative analysis workflow is presented in Figure 1. The protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Puerto Rico Comprehensive Cancer Center (#2023-04-98).Figure 1Study recruitment, data collection, and qualitative workflow.Flowchart outlining sampling, recruitment, data collection, and analysis steps for a qualitative study: jurisdiction selection, key informant identification, recruitment, sample eligibility, interview data collection, verbatim transcription, iterative thematic coding, and final theme development with post-COVID-19 context consideration.
full_text_sections.results: 3ResultsNine key informants were recruited, representing public health professionals (n = 6), health educators (n = 2), and an epidemiologist (n = 1), from six jurisdictions: Puerto Rico, Virginia, District of Columbia, New York, Rhode Island, and California. Participants were 89% female, and 55.6% had five to 10 years of experience in HPV vaccination strategies. Seven out of the nine key informants were from jurisdictions with an HPV vaccine school-entry requirement.To organize key informants’ perspectives identified in the interviews, findings were grouped into three analytical dimensions informed by the socio-ecological model: (1) provider and organizational factors, (2) community factors, and (3) policy and contextual factors. A fourth section describes the post-COVID-19 vaccine climate as a cross-cutting context influencing these dimensions. Table 1 provides representative excerpts supporting each theme identified within the provider/organizational, community, policy/contextual, and post-COVID-19 dimensions. Quotations are presented using anonymized key-informant identifiers to protect participant confidentiality.Table 1Analytic dimensions, themes, and representative key-informant excerpts related to HPV vaccination strategies, barriers, and facilitators (n = 9).Analytic dimensionThemeExcerptProvider and organizational factorsHealth provider recommendation“That cooperation from the doctor is vital, because it’s the person the parent has contact with, the one the parent trusts, right? So having them as allies is always necessary.” - KI #3Shift in promotional message“[...] Using that cancer prevention angle, because the way that HPV vaccination was introduced, it was more of a, I’m not going to say promiscuity angle, but parents may have felt that “oh, if my child gets this vaccine that may give them permission to engage in sexual activity. So, that was really not the way to introduce that vaccine. So, we are looking at it and trying to change that perception by looking at it from a cancer prevention angle. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis descriptive exploratory study identified multilevel factors shaping HPV vaccination promotion strategies across U.S. jurisdictions with existing or recently considered HPV school-entry requirements. At the provider and organizational level, findings were consistent with prior research where provider recommendation (16–21), provider education to recommend the vaccine (16–20) and reframing HPV vaccination as cancer prevention (16, 18–20) emerged as important strategies for vaccine uptake and promotion. Key informants repeatedly described clinicians as trusted sources of vaccine information for parents, and, therefore, strengthening the provider role remains one of the most effective strategies for improving coverage. Provider education could be a foundational strategy because it prepares clinicians not only to understand the vaccine, but also to recommend it confidently, communicate its importance to parents, and address HPV vaccine myths or misinformation during clinical encounters. Taken together with prior research, these key informant perspectives suggest that provider recommendation may function as a bridge between health system strategies and parent-level acceptance, particularly when HPV vaccination is framed as routine cancer prevention rather than STI prevention.At the community level, key informants identified misinformation as an important barrier to HPV vaccine promotion. They also emphasized trusted messengers and culturally tailored communication as strategies for addressing vaccine concerns within communities. Although informational factors are not a distinct level in the socio-ecological model, they operated as a cross-cutting feature of the vaccination environment in this study. Participants’ descriptions of misinformation, including its amplification through social media, are consistent with previous studies (18–23). Their accounts suggest that misinformation should be understood as part of a broader environment shaped by anti-vaccine messaging, circulating myths, and the communication channels through which parents encounter vaccine-related information. These findings underscore the importance of culturally tailored educational strategies, trusted community messengers, and enhanced provider training to address parental concerns described by key informants in ways that are locally credible and responsive to the specific narratives circulating within communities.Key informants also emphasized cross-sector collaboration, including partnerships with immunization coalitions, community-based organizations, academic institutions, medical associations, and parent advocacy groups, consistent with previous research (16, 18, 20). These collaborations may expand the reach of vaccination efforts while supporting culturally appropriate outreach and responses to misinformation.At the policy and contextual level, school-entry vaccination requirements were also identified as powerful structural drivers of uptake, with participants reporting that these requirements normalized HPV vaccination, improved access, and even persuaded hesitant parents. These findings are consistent with prior research demonstrating that school-entry HPV vaccination policies, particularly when combined with other strategies (24), improve uptake (17, 25).Moreover, qualitative studies have shown that the absence of school entry requirements has emerged as a key barrier to HPV vaccination (18, 20, 26). Consistent with prior literature, key informants described structural barriers, such as inconsistent insurance coverage, limited provider supply (16, 18, 20, 24, 27) and cultural concerns about sexual behaviors (18, 20, 21, 26), as factors they perceived to influence HPV vaccination decisions. Expanding the number of providers enrolled in the Vaccines for Children (VFC) program may help address barriers in access to the HPV vaccine by ensuring consistent vaccine availability and reduce financial obstacles (16, 20, 27).Although formal comparisons across policy contexts were not possible, participants from jurisdictions without school-entry requirements emphasized non-mandate strategies such as early vaccination and educational outreach. Their accounts also suggested that resistance was often directed toward mandates rather than the HPV vaccine itself, reflecting broader concerns about government involvement in health decisions. Consistent with McKeithen et al. (27), these findings suggest that the effectiveness of school-entry requirements may depend on careful policy design that reflects local context, as these policies may either be too weak to change behavior or too controversial to be successfully implemented.Participants described how the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted routine preventive care, redirected health system attention towards COVID-19 and other respiratory vaccines, and intensified vaccine fatigue, skepticism, and distrust, affecting both service delivery and the broader information environment in which HPV vaccination messages were received. As a result, post-COVID-19 HPV vaccination strategies may need to address not only missed routine vaccination opportunities, but also broader shifts in vaccine confidence and public trust.This study has several limitations. Although a qualitative study, the small sample size and absence of key informants from jurisdictions without HPV school-entry policy consideration limit the breadth of the findings and preclude formal comparisons across policy contexts. The final sample may also reflect greater interest or engagement with HPV vaccination among those who participated. Nevertheless, the inclusion of key informants from six jurisdictions provided information-rick perspectives on vaccination strategies, barriers, facilitators, and post-COVID-19 challenges. Findings should therefore be interpreted as preliminary and exploratory rather than representative of all U.S. jurisdictions.Several steps were taken to strengthen the dependability and transparency of the findings. Research team members completed shared training in interview guide development, qualitative interviewing, codebook development, and thematic analysis, and conducted practice interviews before data collection. During analysis, the team used a subjective agreement approach to assess intercoder agreement, consistent with Guest et al. (14). The team also maintained an audit trail documenting who was involved in each stage of the research process, including moderation, co-moderation, note-taking, transcription, coding, and analysis. These procedures helped reduce individual coder bias and strengthen the credibility of the thematic interpretation.Future research should build on these exploratory findings through comparative studies that intentionally recruit jurisdictions with and without HPV school-entry requirements, as well as jurisdictions with no recent policy consideration. Mixed method designs that integrate key informant perspectives with HPV vaccination coverage data could help assess how perceived barriers and facilitators align with measurable vaccination outcomes. Future studies could also examine how post-COVID-19 vaccine confidence, routine vaccination patterns, and policy attitudes evolve over time.In conclusion, this study provides exploratory qualitative insights into HPV vaccination promotion across six U.S. jurisdictions with existing or recently considered HPV school-entry requirements. The findings highlight the importance of tailoring HPV vaccination strategies to local policy, organizational, and community contexts, particularly in an environment shaped by misinformation, mandate opposition, access barriers, and changing vaccine confidence. While findings are not generalizable to all jurisdictions, especially those without prior HPV school-entry policy consideration, they offer key informant insights that may help guide future research and context-specific strategies to strengthen HPV vaccination promotion and reduce HPV-related canc…
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionHPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the U.S. and a leading cause of cervical and other HPV-related cancers (1). Over 49 million people in the U.S. are affected by HPV, which causes about 90% of cervical cancer cases (2). Despite the availability of an FDA-approved HPV vaccine, vaccination completion rates significantly vary by state, ranging from 39.1 to 79.8% among adolescents, leaving many vulnerable to this infection and contributing to cancer health disparities (3).Hoss et al. (4) carried out an analysis of U.S. state statutes and regulations related to HPV vaccination. This cross-sectional study identified diverse legal strategies across 34 jurisdictions and the District of Columbia (DC), including mandates, public awareness campaigns, education initiatives, and strategic planning requirements in health department programs. As of May 2024, only DC, Virginia, Rhode Island, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico require HPV vaccination for school attendance, with varying exemption policies (5, 6). Other states promote HPV vaccination through provider recommendations and educational efforts embedded in school curricula. These jurisdictional differences suggest that vaccination strategies are shaped not only by the availability of evidence-based interventions, but also by the policy, institutional, and socio-cultural contexts in which those interventions are implemented.The socio-ecological model is a useful framework for understanding HPV vaccination because uptake is influenced by factors operating across multiple levels, including individual and interpersonal (e.g., family beliefs), organizational (e.g., provider recommendation practices, health system capacity, and provider education), community (e.g., trust and misinformation), and policy-level (e.g., vaccine requirements and insurance) factors (7–9). Understanding the multilevel factors that shape vaccination efforts is essential for guiding effective public health strategies and policy development. Beyond documenting state-level laws and interventions, there remains a need to examine how stakeholders understand the barriers, facilitators, and real-world implementation conditions that influence HPV vaccination strategies across jurisdictions.Despite extensive research on HPV vaccination uptake and school-entry policies, limited qualitative evidence describes how organizational, community and policy-level barriers and facilitators shape decisional process regarding HPV vaccination strategies across U.S. jurisdictions with existing or recently considered HPV school-entry requirements (8, 10). This gap is especially relevant in the current vaccination climate, where pandemic-related disruptions to routine vaccination, vaccine fatigue, and increased skepticism may have compounded existing barriers to HPV vaccine promotion (11–13). Given the limited evidence on how stakeholders perceive these interacting factors across policy-engaged jurisdictions, and how national level qualitative data can help inform future strategies, a descriptive exploratory qualitative approach was appropriate. This study addresses this gap through key informant interviews conducted across multiple U.S. jurisdictions with existing HPV vaccine requirements or those that had recently considered adopting such requirements to identify context-specific factors influencing HPV vaccination strategies and uptake, including how stakeholders perceive the continuing influence of the COVID-19 pandemic on HPV vaccination efforts. 3.1Provider and organizational factors shaping HPV vaccinationVarious effective strategies to improve HPV vaccination rates were reported by key informants. Notably, healthcare provider recommendation and training providers to recommend the vaccine to parents of eligible children were stressed as crucial in boosting HPV vaccination, with participants stating that parents typically trust them. They also emphasized the importance of reframing HPV vaccination from sexually transmitted infection (STI) prevention to cancer prevention. One key informant noted that early HPV vaccine rollout was negatively impacted by concerns of sexual promiscuity, but shifting the messaging to cancer prevention has been very helpful. Overall, participants perceived that normalizing the vaccine as a routine health behavior could improve parental acceptance. Providers should be equipped not only with accurate information about the vaccine, but also with the communication skills needed to explain why HPV vaccination is important, recommend it confidently to parents, and respond to common myths and misinformation. In this sense, provider education is a good starting point in improving the quality and consistency of provider recommendation.Other effective strategies that were reported included starting HPV vaccination at age 9 and providing culturally tailored educational materials, such as factsheets, to help initiate conversations between parents and providers. Key informants were hesitant to signal any one vaccination strategy as ineffective. They mainly expressed that HPV vaccination promotion tends to get diluted among other vaccines in their vaccination campaigns, as there are not as many efforts for the HPV vaccine alone. This suggests that general vaccination campaigns may be perceived as less useful for HPV vaccine promotion when they do not directly address HPV-specific concerns, such as cancer prevention or misinformation. 3.2Community factors shaping HPV vaccinationKey informants also reported the importance of using trusted community messengers and culturally tailored outreach to promote the HPV vaccine. One participant emphasized the need for linguistically and culturally appropriate outreach, taking into consideration how different communities within their same jurisdiction require different trusted messengers and approaches. Some verbalized that it is important to work with community-based organizations, religious leaders, and local advocates to build trust and combat hesitancy.Misinformation about the HPV vaccine emerged as a common barrier for promotion efforts. Key informants shared similar concerns about prevalent myths, such as the belief that the vaccine causes infertility or that it is intended only for females. They pointed to social media as an amplifier of these myths by anti-vaccine groups that “recycle the same arguments,” which leads parents to repeatedly “catch wind of the same myths.” Participants’ accounts suggest that misinformation operated within a broader informational and socio-political environment shaped by social media, anti-vaccine messaging, cultural concerns about adolescent sexuality, religious objections, and resistance to government involvement in health decisions. In this context, trusted messengers and culturally tailored outreach can help respond to misinformation and myths in ways that are community specific. These findings also connect to the provider and organizational dimension, as participants described provider education as an opportunity to address misinformation during parent-provider interactions and reinforce HPV vaccination as cancer prevention.Key informants consistently highlighted institutional support as an important facilitator of HPV vaccine promotion. This support included immunization coalitions, community-based organizations, academic institutions, medical associations, and parent-led advocacy organizations that helped sustain and coordinate vaccination efforts. full_text: BackgroundGestational cervical cancer is rare, with an incidence of 1.4–4.6 per 100,000 pregnancies. Managing locally advanced cervical cancer in the second trimester is challenging, requiring a balance between maternal oncological safety and fetal viability. No standardized protocol exists for stage IB3 cervical cancer diagnosed at 21 weeks of gestation.Case presentationA 27-year-old primigravida at 21 weeks of gestation was diagnosed with stage IB3 cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Initial SCC was 60.15 ng/mL, and MRI was suspicious for stage IIB disease. The patient had no routine prenatal care, and placenta previa on ultrasound contributed to misdiagnosis and delayed recognition. Following multidisciplinary team consultation, she received four cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (nab-paclitaxel 400 mg + cisplatin 140 mg per cycle). Serial SCC showed initial response, a plateau with mild elevation after the third cycle, and a modest decline after the fourth (29.33 ng/mL). At 36 weeks, after dexamethasone for fetal lung maturation, concurrent cesarean section and radical surgery (hysterectomy, lymphadenectomy, ovarian transposition) were performed. A live female neonate (2095g, Apgar 10/10) was delivered. Pathology confirmed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with intermediate stromal invasion (>1/3 and <2/3) and perineural invasion, without lymphovascular invasion or nodal metastasis. Adjuvant pelvic radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin and vaginal brachytherapy was given. At last follow-up (June 2026), SCC remained normal with no recurrence, and the child showed normal development.ConclusionSequential multimodal therapy—NACT, delayed radical surgery at 36 weeks, and adjuvant chemoradiotherapy—is feasible for stage IB3 cervical cancer in the second trimester. Serial SCC monitoring is a useful biomarker for guiding treatment decisions. This case highlights pitfalls including diagnostic delay, radiological overstaging, and false-negative TCT, emphasizing the need for thorough examination and high suspicion in pregnant patients with atypical bleeding. 2.1Patient informationA 27-year-old primigravida presented to Hebei General Hospital on June 19, 2022, with a 3-month history of irregular vaginal bleeding at 21 + 2 weeks of gestation. The patient had no prior regular prenatal examination. Early gestational ultrasound indicated placenta previa, and the vaginal bleeding was initially attributed to placental abnormality. Conservative management with bed rest and oral progesterone was administered, yet bleeding symptoms persisted without improvement. 4Patient's perspectiveThe patient reported significant psychological distress after being diagnosed with cervical cancer at 21 weeks of gestation, mainly stemming from dual concerns regarding maternal tumor prognosis and fetal developmental safety. She was particularly anxious about the potential adverse effects of prenatal chemotherapy on the fetus. Professional MDT counseling on the safety and standardized application of second-trimester platinum-based chemotherapy effectively relieved her psychological anxiety and strengthened her confidence in completing systematic treatment and continuing pregnancy.During the NACT cycle, the patient only experienced mild, clinically manageable fatigue and nausea without severe chemotherapy-related adverse events. She highly recognized the value of multidisciplinary collaborative management, which enabled her to successfully complete four cycles of standardized chemotherapy and safely prolong pregnancy to 36 weeks of gestation.At the 4-year follow-up, the patient had completely recovered without any long-term treatment-related complications, and her quality of life returned to the normal level. The healthy physical and intellectual development of her daughter provided her with great psychological reassurance. She voluntarily consented to share her diagnosis and treatment experience, aiming to provide practical reference and emotional encouragement for other pregnant women facing gestational cervical cancer diagnosis. 2.4Postoperative pathological findingsPostoperative pathological examination confirmed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with cervical wall stromal invasion depth between 1/3 and 2/3, accompanied by perineural invasion (Figure 3B). The tumor measured approximately 4 × 5 × 6 cm on pathological examination of the surgical specimen. Pathological assessment demonstrated a partial response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, with a tumor regression grade of 2 (CRS 2), characterized by partial regression with fibrotic changes, though residual viable tumor remained readily identifiable. No lymphovascular invasion or tumor thrombus was observed, and all surgical resection margins were tumor-negative. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed the squamous phenotype of the tumor, with diffuse positivity for P16, P40, and P63, scattered P53 positivity, and a Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 60%. A total of 15 regional lymph nodes were examined, and no pelvic or para-aortic lymph node metastasis was identified. These representative pathological images confirm the treatment response and placental findings. 3DiscussionWe report a well-documented case of stage IB3 cervical cancer with a delayed diagnosis at 21 weeks of gestation, successfully treated with sequential NACT, delayed radical surgery, and risk-stratified adjuvant chemoradiotherapy, with favorable 4-year maternal and neonatal prognostic outcomes. Five key clinical insights and one study limitation are summarized and discussed below.3.1Diagnostic delay from misattribution to placenta previaThe patient experienced a diagnostic delay due to the initial misattribution of vaginal bleeding to placenta previa. The absence of routine prenatal screening and inconclusive ultrasound findings obscured the underlying cervical malignancy. Clinically, gestational vaginal bleeding is preferentially attributed to obstetric etiologies, and clinicians often hesitate to perform speculum examination and colposcopy during pregnancy due to gestational safety concerns, further delaying the diagnosis of gestational cervical cancer (4). This case reinforces that placental lesions do not exclude concurrent cervical malignancy. For pregnant patients with persistent irregular vaginal bleeding, routine cervical speculum examination is mandatory to rule out malignant lesions, rather than empirically attributing symptoms to obstetric factors. Lack of prenatal cervical screening is an independent risk factor for delayed diagnosis of gestational cervical cancer.3.2False-negative TCT: an inherent diagnostic pitfall in gestational cervical cancerNotably, the patient presented with an 8 cm bulky exophytic cervical tumor, whereas the preoperative TCT result was completely negative, fully reflecting the inherent limitations of cervical cytological screening in pregnant populations. The false-negative rate of cervical cytology screening ranges from 2% to 50% in different clinical populations (5). Physiological gestational changes, including cervical congestion, hormone-induced reactive cellular changes, excessive cervical mucus secretion, and incomplete exposure of the cervical transformation zone, significantly reduce the sampling accuracy of abnormal cells and contribute to false-negative cytological results (6). Retrospective data have confirmed that pregnant patients with cervical cancer and negative initial cytology results have significantly longer diagnostic intervals and are more likely to be diagnosed at advanced tumor stages (5). Consistent with current ASCCP guidelines, HPV 16 positivity prompted timely colposcopic biopsy and corrected the misleading TCT result (7). This case strongly demonstrates that HPV genotyping and clinical pelvic examination are more reliable than isolated TCT cytology for high-risk screening of gestational cervical lesions, and biopsy verification should be performed for clinically suspected cervical masses regardless of negative cytological findings.3.3Staging discordance: MRI overstaging vs. clinical and pathological stagingPreoperative pelvic MRI was suspicious for parametrial invasion (stage IIB), while systematic preoperative rectovaginal palpation revealed no parametrial nodules or sclerosis, leading to a clinical stage IB3 diagnosis. Postoperative pathological examination finally confirmed negative parametrial tissues without invasive lesions. The staging discordance between imaging and clinical pathology is multifactorial. On the one hand, gestational physiological changes, including pelvic hypervascularity, cervical edema, and pelvic ligamentous laxity, easily mimic parametrial invasive signs on MRI, resulting in imaging overstaging (8). On the other hand, NACT may have eradicated microscopic parametrial lesions that could not be detected by clinical examination or imaging before treatment.Existing literature reports that the overall consistency between MRI and clinical staging of cervical cancer is only approximately 63%, with a considerable false-positive rate in parametrial invasion evaluation (9). For pregnant patients with suspicious MRI parametrial invasion but negative clinical examination findings, imaging results should not be the sole basis for abandoning surgical treatment. The MDT strategy of administering NACT to stabilize tumor progression and delaying radical surgery until fetal maturity effectively avoids overtreatment while preserving the opportunity for radical resection. Negative surgical margins and long-term disease-free survival provide supporting evidence for the feasibility and safety of this individualized staging and treatment pathway.3.4SCC dynamics guide chemotherapy termination and surgical timingSerial SCC monitoring provided objective, real-time biomarkers for tumor response assessment and individualized treatment decision-making throughout therapy. The tumor presented obvious chemosensitivity in the first two NACT cycles, with the SCC level declining steadily from 60.15 ng/mL to 34.74 ng/mL. After a third cycle, the rate of decline slowed, with SCC level changing from 34.74 ng/mL to 37.48 ng/mL. A fourth cycle was administered, after which the SCC level decreased to 29.33 ng/mL. The total tumor marker reduction rate from baseline reached only 51%, remaining below the 60% threshold predictive of a favorable pathological response as reported in previous studies (10). Crucially, even after four cycles, the SCC value remained markedly elevated at approximately 20 times the upper normal limit, suggesting that continued chemotherapy was unlikely to achieve a complete response.Notably, although the SCC reduction after four cycles (51%) fell short of the 60% threshold, the final pathological assessment demonstrated a partial response (tumor regression grade CRS 2) with negative margins and no nodal metastasis. This apparent discordance may reflect that the 60% threshold was derived from non-pregnant populations, and pregnancy-associated physiological changes—including increased plasma volume and altered drug distribution—may affect SCC clearance kinetics independently of true tumor response. This observation underscores that SCC dynamics should be interpreted as one component of a multimodal assessment, integrated with imaging and clinical findings.In this case, dynamic SCC monitoring provided supportive information for tumor response assessment, complementing imaging findings and clinical evaluation. While MRI findings were confounded by gestational physiological changes, SCC trends offered additional data points that informed the MDT's decision-making (11). We acknowledge that this observation is derived from a single case and should not be interpreted as establishing SCC as a definitive surrogate marker for imaging, nor as a standalone criterion for treatment decisions in this population.The MDT's decision to terminate chemotherapy at 36 weeks was based on a combination of factors rather than SCC trajectory alone. First, at 36 weeks of gestation, fetal lung maturity had been achieved, and the neonatal benefits of reaching this milestone were well established. Second, although the SCC level continued to decline after the fourth cycle, the rate of reduction had markedly slowed (21.7% after cycle 4, compared with 22.9% and 25.1% after cycles 1 and 2). Third, the absolute SCC value remained markedly elevated at approximately 20 times the upper normal limit. Given these factors—fetal maturity, the slowing rate of biochemical response, and the persistently high SCC level—the MDT decided that the risks of further delaying definitive surgery outweighed the potential benefits of continued chemotherapy. This decision achieved an optimal balance between oncological control and fetal safety: late preterm delivery at 36 weeks significantly reduces neonatal mortality and morbidity compared with earlier gestational termination (12), while timely radical surgery avoids further tumor progression. The favorable 4-year disease-free survival supports the soundness of this decision, though we acknowledge that it was individualized to this patient's circumstances.3.5Multimodal therapy rationale and long-term prognostic valueThe one-stage combination of cesarean section and radical hysterectomy avoids the physical trauma and tumor progression risk of secondary surgery, and enables immediate postoperative pathological risk stratification to guide subsequent adjuvant therapy. Intraoperative bilateral ovarian transposition effectively preserves maternal ovarian endocrine function and prevents irreversible ovarian failure caused by pelvic radiotherapy in young patients (13).Perineural invasion (PNI) has been reported as a potential adverse prognostic factor in cervical cancer. Some studies have shown that PNI may be associated with established intermediate-risk factors, including tumor size, deep stromal invasion, and lymphovascular space invasion, as well as with high-risk factors such as lymph node metastasis (14, 15). In addition, PNI has been reported to be associated with overall survival and disease-free survival in early-stage cervical cancer in several studies (16, 17). A review has also suggested that PNI status might be considered in the decision-making process for adjuvant therapy (18). In one published series, the presence of PNI was correlated with conventional indications for adjuvant therapy (odds ratio 12.0, P = 0.003), and 92% of PNI-positive patients in that series received postoperative radiation therapy or concurrent chemoradiotherapy (14).In the present case, the patient already met the Sedlis criteria based on intermediate-risk factors (middle-third stromal invasion and initial tumor size of 8 cm). The presence of PNI was considered by the MDT as an additional factor that might increase the cumulative recurrence risk. After thorough discussion with the patient, adjuvant concurrent chemoradiotherapy was administered to optimize local control and reduce recurrence risk. The patient tolerated the regimen well without dose-limiting toxicity and achieved 4-year disease-free survival, suggesting that this individualized treatment approach was feasible in this case.This case adds to the limited literature on multimodal management of stage IB cervical cancer during pregnancy, with a treatment trajectory similar to that reported in a recent stage IB2 case (19). The patient completed all adjuvant treatments smoothly without severe adverse reactions and achieved 4-year sustained disease-free survival. For the neonate, accumulating clinical evidence confirms that platinum-based chemotherapy administered after the first trimester does not increase the risks of congenital malformation, physical dysplasia, or neurodevelopmental impairment in offspring (20). The normal physical and intellectual development of the child at 4-year follow-up further supports the safety of second-trimester platinum-based NACT for fetal prognosis.3.6Study limitationsThis study is a single-center, single-case report with inherent limitations. The treatment strategy was formulated based on individual patient conditions, MDT consensus, and the patient's fertility intention, which may not be directly generalizable to all patients with gestational stage IB3 cervical cancer. In addition, although 4-year follow-up confirmed favorable maternal and neonatal outcomes, longer-term follow-up is still required to verify the durable oncological prognosis and long-term developmental safety of the offspring. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundGestational cervical cancer is rare, with an incidence of 1.4–4.6 per 100,000 pregnancies. Managing locally advanced cervical cancer in the second trimester is challenging, requiring a balance between maternal oncological safety and fetal viability. No standardized protocol exists for stage IB3 cervical cancer diagnosed at 21 weeks of gestation.Case presentationA 27-year-old primigravida at 21 weeks of gestation was diagnosed with stage IB3 cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Initial SCC was 60.15 ng/mL, and MRI was suspicious for stage IIB disease. The patient had no routine prenatal care, and placenta previa on ultrasound contributed to misdiagnosis and delayed recognition. Following multidisciplinary team consultation, she received four cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (nab-paclitaxel 400 mg + cisplatin 140 mg per cycle). Serial SCC showed initial response, a plateau with mild elevation after the third cycle, and a modest decline after the fourth (29.33 ng/mL). At 36 weeks, after dexamethasone for fetal lung maturation, concurrent cesarean section and radical surgery (hysterectomy, lymphadenectomy, ovarian transposition) were performed. A live female neonate (2095g, Apgar 10/10) was delivered. Pathology confirmed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with intermediate stromal invasion (>1/3 and <2/3) and perineural invasion, without lymphovascular invasion or nodal metastasis. Adjuvant pelvic radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin and vaginal brachytherapy was given. At last follow-up (June 2026), SCC remained normal with no recurrence, and the child showed normal development.ConclusionSequential multimodal therapy—NACT, delayed radical surgery at 36 weeks, and adjuvant chemoradiotherapy—is feasible for stage IB3 cervical cancer in the second trimester. Serial SCC monitoring is a useful biomarker for guiding treatment decisions. This case highlights pitfalls including diagnostic delay, radiological overstaging, and false-negative TCT, emphasizing the need for thorough examination and high suspicion in pregnant patients with atypical bleeding.

full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionCervical cancer represents one of the most common malignant tumors complicating pregnancy, with a reported incidence of 1.4–4.6 per 100,000 pregnancies (1). In recent years, delayed childbearing and the younger onset of cervical malignancy have increased the overlapping prevalence of pregnancy and cervical cancer. However, the clinical management of locally advanced cervical cancer diagnosed in the second trimester remains controversial, and standardized treatment guidelines for gestational stage IB3 cervical cancer are currently unavailable (2).Current clinical strategies depend on comprehensive evaluation of pathological features, clinical tumor staging, fetal gestational maturity, and maternal fertility intention. For stage IB3 cervical cancer (tumor diameter >4 cm) diagnosed after 14 weeks of gestation, platinum-based NACT is the primary conservative approach to inhibit tumor progression while allowing sufficient time for fetal maturation (3). Nevertheless, the optimal timing of delivery and definitive radical surgery, the necessity and regimen of adjuvant therapy, and long-term maternal and neonatal prognostic outcomes require further clinical validation.Herein, we report a rare case of stage IB3 cervical squamous cell carcinoma with a delayed diagnosis at 21 weeks of gestation, managed with a standardized multimodal sequential treatment strategy including NACT, delayed combined cesarean-radical surgery at 36 weeks, and risk-adapted adjuvant chemoradiotherapy. We focus on dynamic SCC biomarker-guided treatment adjustment, MDT-based individualized decision-making, and 4-year long-term follow-up outcomes, aiming to supplement clinical evidence for the standardized management of gestational locally advanced cervical cancer. 2Case report2.1Patient informationA 27-year-old primigravida presented to Hebei General Hospital on June 19, 2022, with a 3-month history of irregular vaginal bleeding at 21 + 2 weeks of gestation. The patient had no prior regular prenatal examination. Early gestational ultrasound indicated placenta previa, and the vaginal bleeding was initially attributed to placental abnormality. Conservative management with bed rest and oral progesterone was administered, yet bleeding symptoms persisted without improvement.2.2Diagnostic workupPelvic examination revealed loss of normal cervical architecture with an approximately 8 × 6 cm cauliflower-like exophytic mass that was firm and bled easily on contact. Rectovaginal examination showed an enlarged cervix (approximately 8 cm in diameter) with soft parametrial tissues and no palpable nodules.Cervical cytology (Thinprep Cytologic Test, TCT) showed no intraepithelial lesions or malignant cells, but high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) testing was positive for HPV 16. The baseline serum SCC level was markedly elevated at 60.15 ng/mL on June 20, 2022.Colposcopy-guided cervical biopsy was performed on June 21, 2022, which confirmed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. Pelvic MRI conducted on June 25, 2022, demonstrated a bulky cervical mass measuring approximately 70 × 38 × 64 mm and was suspicious for stage IIB disease (Figure 2A). Systemic imaging evaluation excluded distant metastasis.Combining clinical manifestations, imaging features, and pathological results, the final clinical diagnosis was gestational cervical squamous cell carcinoma, stage IB3, at 21 weeks of gestation.2.3Therapeutic interventionGiven the patient's strong desire to continue the pregnancy, a multidisciplinary team (MDT) conference was conducted. The team comprised specialists from gynecologic oncology, obstetrics, medical oncology, reproductive genetics, neonatology, and radiology, who collaboratively formulated an individualized treatment protocol.The MDT faced a critical dilemma: initiating chemotherapy could potentially jeopardize fetal safety, while delaying definitive treatment until fetal maturity risked maternal oncological progression. After extensive deliberation, the consensus strategy was defined as: preoperative NACT with regular fetal ultrasound monitoring, followed by delayed combined cesarean section and radical surgery after fetal lung maturation.The patient received four consecutive cycles of NACT with nab-paclitaxel (400 mg) plus cisplatin (140 mg) at gestational ages of 22 + 3, 25 + 5, 28 + 5, and 32 + 5 weeks, respectively. Based on the patient's body surface area of 1.56 m2, this flat dosing corresponded to approximately 256 mg/m2 for nab-paclitaxel and 90 mg/m2 for cisplatin per cycle. The nab-paclitaxel dose was consistent with the standard neoadjuvant regimen for cervical cancer (260 mg/m2). The cisplatin dose of 90 mg/m2 fell within the high-dose range (80–120 mg/m2) as defined in the cisplatin package insert, which was selected by the MDT based on the patient's good performance status and favorable organ function, with the aim of maximizing the cytoreductive effect prior to definitive surgery. The patient tolerated the regimen well without dose-limiting toxicity. The choice of nab-paclitaxel over conventional paclitaxel was based on its albumin-bound formulation, which eliminates the need for corticosteroid and antihistamine premedication, reduces solvent-related toxicity, and may offer more predictable tumor delivery—advantages particularly relevant in the gestational setting where minimizing unnecessary medication exposure is desirable. The choice of cisplatin over carboplatin was based on its established efficacy in neoadjuvant and concurrent chemoradiotherapy settings for cervical cancer. Serial dynamic SCC levels were recorded as follows: baseline 60.15 ng/mL; 46.36 ng/mL (22.9% reduction) after the first cycle; 34.74 ng/mL (25.1% reduction) after the second cycle; 37.48 ng/mL (7.9% elevation) after the third cycle; and 29.33 ng/mL (21.7% reduction) after the fourth cycle (Figure 1). The interval between the third and fourth cycles was extended to 4 weeks instead of the scheduled 3 weeks due to the patient experiencing grade 2 neutropenia, which required an additional week for hematologic recovery. Pelvic MRI reexamination confirmed significant shrinkage of the cervical mass after sequential chemotherapy, consistent with biochemical response trends (Figure 2B).Figure 1Treatment timeline and SCC dynamics. Serial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI images at three key time points: (A) initial diagnosis (June 2022) showing a bulky cervical tumor with suspected parametrial invasion (arrow), measuring approximately 70 × 38 × 64 mm; (B) post-NACT (September 2022) showing significant tumor shrinkage, measuring approximately 49 × 30 × 64 mm; (C) post-adjuvant therapy (January 2023) showing complete elimination of residual lesions without recurrence.Panel A shows a sagittal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI of the pelvis at initial diagnosis, with an arrow indicating a bulky cervical tumor with suspected parametrial invasion. Panel B shows a sagittal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, with an arrow indicating significant tumor shrinkage. Panel C shows a sagittal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI after adjuvant therapy, demonstrating complete elimination of the residual cervical lesion without recurrence. full_text: BackgroundOcular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) is relatively common, but the cases complicated by fungal infection are quite rare. This study reviewed a rare case of OSSN complicated by Alternaria alternata infection.Case presentationA 59-year-old male patient presented with a one-month history of foreign body sensation and photophobia in the left eye. Diagnostic and evaluative procedures, including a series of pathogenic microorganism staining microscopy and culture, in vivo confocal microscopy, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and histopathological examination, were performed to assess the condition of the cornea, conjunctiva, and sclera. The patient received topical and systemic medication to control infection. Subsequently, he underwent surgical intervention for the left eye consisting of excision of the corneal and conjunctival lesions, cryotherapy, corneoscleral collagen cross-linking, and conjunctival autograft transplantation. Fungal culture of the conjunctival lesion tissue confirmed that the pathogen was Alternaria alternata (AA). Histopathological examination revealed ocular surface squamous neoplasia. The diseases were successfully controlled.ConclusionTo our knowledge, this is the first case report of OSSN with Alternaria alternata infection. Microbiological culture remains the gold standard for diagnosing ocular infectious diseases. For this patient, the combined treatment achieved favorable local clinical control. This highlights the importance of combining multiple treatment methods when dealing with such cases. DiscussionIn this study, the lesion of OSSN was located at the nasal corneal limbus and conjunctiva, which is consistent with the pathogenesis of OSSN. The epithelial recesses at the limbus of the cornea in the most UV-radiated nasal area are densely distributed, and there are a large number of basal epithelial stem cells. These may be the precursor cells of OSSN (8). Regarding the occurrence of OSSN in the inflammatory ocular surface environment, the available literature is extremely limited. Chronic inflammation caused by microbial infections, autoimmune diseases, and environmental irritants may be predisposing factors for atypical epithelial hyperplasia. The literature has reported that patients with atopic keratoconjunctivitis developed OSSN after treatment with cyclosporine (9). Chronic inflammation may have affected the homeostasis of the limbal basal epithelial stem cells, thereby initiating compensatory hyperplasia. Abnormally proliferating DNA-damaged basal epithelial stem cells develop into atypical hyperplasia (5). The occurrence of OSSN may also damage the defense mechanism of the ocular surface, thereby increasing the risk of opportunistic fungal infections on the ocular surface. AA is increasingly recognized as an opportunistic pathogen in individuals with normal immune function, especially among agricultural workers (7). Given that the patient was engaged in agricultural labor, ocular surface fungal infection was considered the primary differential diagnosis during the initial clinical assessment. At present, the exact causal relationship cannot be determined. However, in the eyes with chronic inflammation, OSSN may be overlooked, and clinicians need to be vigilant about the occurrence of OSSN.The clinical symptoms and signs of ocular surface inflammation and OSSN lack obvious specificity. Further diagnosis requires the use of laboratory tests and auxiliary detection methods. The precise identification of pathogens is a multi-step process. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundOcular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) is relatively common, but the cases complicated by fungal infection are quite rare. This study reviewed a rare case of OSSN complicated by Alternaria alternata infection.Case presentationA 59-year-old male patient presented with a one-month history of foreign body sensation and photophobia in the left eye. Diagnostic and evaluative procedures, including a series of pathogenic microorganism staining microscopy and culture, in vivo confocal microscopy, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and histopathological examination, were performed to assess the condition of the cornea, conjunctiva, and sclera. The patient received topical and systemic medication to control infection. Subsequently, he underwent surgical intervention for the left eye consisting of excision of the corneal and conjunctival lesions, cryotherapy, corneoscleral collagen cross-linking, and conjunctival autograft transplantation. Fungal culture of the conjunctival lesion tissue confirmed that the pathogen was Alternaria alternata (AA). Histopathological examination revealed ocular surface squamous neoplasia. The diseases were successfully controlled.ConclusionTo our knowledge, this is the first case report of OSSN with Alternaria alternata infection. Microbiological culture remains the gold standard for diagnosing ocular infectious diseases. For this patient, the combined treatment achieved favorable local clinical control. This highlights the importance of combining multiple treatment methods when dealing with such cases.

full_text: Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide, with approximately 30–40% of patients experiencing recurrence after definitive chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced disease. The concept of minimal residual disease (MRD)—the persistence of viable tumor clones after curative-intent treatment that escape conventional radiographic and clinical detection—has transformed surveillance and treatment paradigms in hematological malignancies and, increasingly, in solid tumors. In cervical cancer, the near-universal association with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) provides a unique molecular handle for MRD detection: circulating tumor HPV DNA (ctHPV DNA) released into the bloodstream by residual tumor cells. Here, we review three interconnected dimensions of MRD in cervical cancer. First, we examine the biological basis of tumor persistence after chemoradiotherapy, encompassing HPV integration-driven genomic instability, immune evasion within the irradiated tumor microenvironment, and clonal repopulation kinetics. Second, we synthesize the rapidly maturing evidence for ctHPV DNA-guided post-treatment surveillance, from digital PCR and next-generation sequencing-based detection platforms to prospective clinical validation studies demonstrating that detectable ctHPV DNA after chemoradiotherapy independently predicts recurrence with lead times of 3–6 months before radiographic progression. Third, we evaluate emerging recurrence-directed intervention strategies, including MRD-stratified treatment intensification (immune checkpoint inhibition and therapeutic HPV vaccination), adoptive cell therapy, and how integrating ctHPV DNA dynamics with immunotherapeutic approaches may define a new framework for personalized post-treatment management in this molecularly tractable malignancy. 5DiscussionThe evidence synthesized in this review supports the central thesis that MRD in cervical cancer is a biologically tractable and clinically consequential phenomenon whose detection and therapeutic targeting are now within reach. However, several cross-cutting themes emerge from our analysis that merit extended discussion: the relationship between assay sensitivity and clinical utility, the interpretation of ctHPV DNA dynamics across heterogeneous treatment modalities, the biological determinants of treatment responsiveness in the MRD setting, and the translational challenges that must be overcome to realize MRD-guided management in routine clinical practice.5.1Sensitivity–specificity trade-offs and the clinical significance of ultra-low ctHPV DNAOne of the most important unresolved questions in the field concerns the clinical significance of ctHPV DNA detected at concentrations below the LoD of ddPCR (~0.1–0.5 copies/mL) but within the reach of ultrasensitive NGS-based assays (~0.02 copies/mL). In the Han et al. study, three patients with ctHPV DNA detectable exclusively by HPV-seq subsequently recurred, suggesting that ultra-sensitive detection captures clinically relevant residual disease (12). However, the broader natural history of ultra-low-level ctHPV DNA—whether it invariably progresses to clinical recurrence, can be spontaneously cleared by host immunity, or can enter long-term dormancy—remains unknown. This question has direct clinical implications: if a substantial proportion of patients with ultra-low ctHPV DNA would never develop clinical recurrence, then deploying assays with maximal sensitivity will generate false-positive molecular results that provoke unnecessary intervention and anxiety, eroding the clinical utility of MRD testing.The colorectal cancer ctDNA literature offers instructive parallels. In the DYNAMIC trial, patients with stage II colon cancer and detectable postoperative ctDNA who received adjuvant chemotherapy had superior outcomes compared with those who did not, establishing the clinical validity of ctDNA-guided treatment decision-making (51). Checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) are most effective when pre-existing tumor-reactive T cells are present but functionally impaired by PD-1/PD-L1 signaling; therapeutic HPV vaccines are most effective when HPV-specific T-cell precursors exist but have not been sufficiently expanded; and adoptive cell therapy bypasses the requirement for endogenous immunity altogether by providing a bolus of ex vivo-expanded effector cells.Currently, no clinically validated biomarker exists to guide the choice among these immunological modalities in the MRD setting. Do patients with persistent ctHPV DNA harbor defects in HPV-specific T-cell immunity that could be corrected by vaccination or checkpoint blockade? Pre-analytical standards for blood collection, plasma processing, and DNA extraction should be harmonized across clinical laboratories, ideally through a consensus guideline analogous to those developed for mutation-based ctDNA testing in lung and colorectal cancer (70). Point-of-care ctHPV DNA detection platforms would be transformative for global access but remain to be developed. Similarly, the development of affordable MRD-directed strategies—off-patent small-molecule immunomodulators, therapeutic vaccines based on widely accessible nucleic acid platforms, or repurposed generic drugs—should be prioritized alongside the evaluation of premium-priced biologics to ensure that advances in MRD management do not widen existing disparities in cervical cancer outcomes.5.6Limitations of this reviewSeveral limitations of this review should be acknowledged. The concept of minimal residual disease (MRD)—the persistence of viable tumor clones after curative-intent treatment that escape conventional radiographic and clinical detection—has transformed surveillance and treatment paradigms in hematological malignancies and, increasingly, in solid tumors. In cervical cancer, the near-universal association with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) provides a unique molecular handle for MRD detection: circulating tumor HPV DNA (ctHPV DNA) released into the bloodstream by residual tumor cells. Here, we review three interconnected dimensions of MRD in cervical cancer. First, we examine the biological basis of tumor persistence after chemoradiotherapy, encompassing HPV integration-driven genomic instability, immune evasion within the irradiated tumor microenvironment, and clonal repopulation kinetics. Third, we evaluate emerging recurrence-directed intervention strategies, including MRD-stratified treatment intensification (immune checkpoint inhibition and therapeutic HPV vaccination), adoptive cell therapy, and how integrating ctHPV DNA dynamics with immunotherapeutic approaches may define a new framework for personalized post-treatment management in this molecularly tractable malignancy.
