full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionCervical cancer is the fourth most common malignancy in women globally, with approximately 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths annually (1). Although prophylactic HPV vaccination and organized screening programs have substantially reduced incidence in high-income countries, the burden remains disproportionately high in low- and middle-income settings, where most patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease (1, 2). For patients with locally advanced cervical cancer (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stages IB2–IVA), definitive cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy (CRT) with brachytherapy remains the standard of care, achieving 5-year overall survival rates of approximately 65–75% (3, 4). However, recurrence rates remain stubbornly elevated at 30–40%, with the majority of relapses occurring within the first two to three years after treatment (3, 5).The central clinical challenge in post-treatment cervical cancer management is the inability of current surveillance modalities—physical examination, cytology, and cross-sectional imaging—to distinguish patients who are cured from those who harbor residual disease that will eventually manifest as clinical recurrence. Post-treatment imaging with fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) at 3 months after CRT demonstrates a complete metabolic response in the majority of patients, yet a substantial fraction of these radiographically “disease-free” patients subsequently relapse (6). This diagnostic gap reflects the presence of minimal residual disease: viable tumor cells that persist below the detection threshold of conventional modalities and are capable of driving late recurrence through clonal repopulation.The near-universal etiological association between cervical cancer and high-risk HPV infection—with HPV16 and HPV18 accounting for approximately 70% of cases—creates a distinctive opportunity for liquid biopsy-based MRD surveillance (7–9). Unlike most solid tumors, in which MRD detection requires tracking patient-specific somatic mutations through tumor-informed sequencing panels, HPV-driven cervical cancers harbor a universally expressed viral oncogenic driver whose DNA can be detected in the circulation. The viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins are obligate drivers of the malignant phenotype; their continued expression is required for tumor cell survival, and the integrated or episomal viral DNA that encodes them is released into the bloodstream upon tumor cell death or turnover (10, 11). Detection of circulating tumor HPV DNA (ctHPV DNA) thus provides a direct, tumor-specific molecular marker of residual disease burden that is both biologically rational and technically tractable.Over the past five years, a convergence of technological advances—ultrasensitive digital PCR assays with limits of detection below 0.1 copies per milliliter, HPV-agnostic next-generation sequencing panels, and standardized plasma collection protocols—has propelled ctHPV DNA from a promising research biomarker to a clinically validated tool for post-treatment surveillance (12–16). Prospective studies have now demonstrated that persistent ctHPV DNA positivity after CRT is independently associated with markedly inferior progression-free survival, that ctHPV DNA clearance kinetics predict treatment response, and that molecular detection of residual disease precedes radiographic recurrence by a median of 3–6 months (12, 15, 16). These data have generated intense interest in whether ctHPV DNA-guided risk stratification can enable a paradigm of recurrence-directed intervention: treating molecular relapse before it becomes clinically evident, rather than waiting for radiographic progression.In this review, we provide a comprehensive synthesis of the biological, technological, and clinical dimensions of MRD in cervical cancer. We first examine the molecular mechanisms by which cervical cancer cells evade definitive chemoradiotherapy and establish persistent residual disease (Section 2). We then evaluate the evidence supporting ctHPV DNA as a liquid biopsy biomarker for post-treatment surveillance, including assay performance characteristics, optimal sampling schedules, and clinical validation data (Section 3). Next, we critically appraise emerging strategies for recurrence-directed intervention, from MRD-stratified intensification of standard therapy to ctHPV DNA-guided deployment of immunotherapy, therapeutic vaccination, and adoptive cell therapy (Section 4). In the Discussion (Section 5), we synthesize cross-cutting themes, address knowledge gaps and trial design considerations, and situate MRD in cervical cancer within the broader liquid biopsy and immunotherapy landscape. We conclude by outlining a unifying framework and the translational roadmap required to realize MRD-guided precision surveillance in cervical cancer. 2Biological basis of minimal residual disease after chemoradiotherapy2.1HPV integration, viral oncogene addiction, and clonal persistenceHPV integration into the host genome is a pivotal molecular event in cervical carcinogenesis that also shapes the biology of residual disease after treatment. In the normal viral life cycle, HPV exists as an extrachromosomal episome within the nucleus of infected basal epithelial cells, with viral gene expression tightly coupled to host cell differentiation (17). Integration—which occurs in >80% of invasive cervical cancers—disrupts the viral E1/E2 open reading frame, releasing the E6 and E7 oncogenes from E2-mediated transcriptional repression and enabling their constitutive, high-level expression (17, 18). This integration event is stochastic with respect to host genomic location but recurrently targets fragile sites and transcriptionally active regions, resulting in copy-number alterations, structural rearrangements, and focal amplifications at integration loci (19).The oncogenic consequences of integration extend beyond E6/E7 dysregulation. Integration sites are frequently enriched near cancer-relevant genes, and the process can generate HPV–host fusion transcripts with oncogenic potential (18). Furthermore, integration stabilizes the malignant phenotype: once integrated, the viral oncogenes become permanent residents of the cancer genome, transmitted to daughter cells through mitosis. This genomic fixation of the viral driver has two critical implications for MRD biology. First, residual tumor cells that survive chemoradiotherapy continue to depend on E6/E7 expression for proliferation and survival—a state of “viral oncogene addiction” that renders them persistently vulnerable to HPV-directed therapies (11, 20). Second, the integrated viral DNA serves as a stable, clone-specific molecular barcode: ctHPV DNA detected in plasma after treatment is necessarily derived from tumor cells and not from normal tissues or lytic viral infection, because integrated HPV DNA is not a feature of productive viral replication (16).The clonal architecture of residual disease after chemoradiotherapy remains incompletely characterized. Chemoradiotherapy imposes a profound selective bottleneck: radiation induces double-strand DNA breaks, while cisplatin generates intra- and interstrand crosslinks, both preferentially affecting proliferating cells (21). However, tumor cell subpopulations with intrinsic or acquired resistance—conferred by hypoxia, enhanced DNA damage repair capacity, cancer stem cell-like properties, or quiescence—can survive this bottleneck and serve as the reservoir for subsequent recurrence (22). In cervical cancer specifically, hypoxia is a well-established adverse prognostic factor that reduces radiosensitivity through multiple mechanisms, including stabilization of HIF-1α, metabolic reprogramming toward glycolysis, and selection of apoptosis-resistant clones (23). full_text: AbstractObjectiveThis study aims to investigate the associations of menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive characteristics with early-onset cervical cancer among women aged ≤35 years.MethodsA hospital-based, individually matched case–control study was conducted at West China Second University Hospital from January 2022 to December 2024. A total of 300 women aged ≤35 years and with histologically confirmed cervical cancer were individually matched 1:1 to 300 screening controls within 0.5 years of age and 7 days of recruitment. Menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive histories accrued up to 90 days before the index data were collected through standardized interviews and medical record reviews. Separate exposure-specific conditional logistic regression models stratified by matched pair were adjusted for prespecified sociodemographic, behavioral, screening-related, infection-related, and current high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) covariates. The model samples ranged from 189 to 277 matched pairs. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed effect modification.ResultsIn the fully adjusted model, menstrual period duration was associated with early-onset cervical cancer, with evidence of nonlinearity (P for nonlinearity <0.001). Each 1-year increase in age at first pregnancy was associated with lower odds (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.717; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.561–0.917). Higher odds were associated with greater gravidity (aOR per pregnancy, 2.959; 95% CI, 1.734–5.050), greater parity (aOR per birth, 3.667; 95% CI, 1.886–7.133), and more induced abortions (aOR per event, 2.672; 95% CI, 1.236–5.773). Longer total breastfeeding duration was inversely associated (aOR per 12 months, 0.189; 95% CI, 0.064–0.560), whereas longer cumulative combined oral contraceptive use was positively associated (aOR per 12 months, 1.335; 95% CI, 1.062–1.678). Age at menarche, menstrual cycle irregularity, ever breastfeeding, categorical combined oral contraceptive status, and other contraceptive methods were not statistically significant after full adjustment. No interaction remained statistically significant after false discovery rate correction.ConclusionsSelected menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive characteristics were associated with early-onset cervical cancer after adjustment for measured confounders and current hrHPV status.Keywords: associated factors, case-control study, cervical cancer, menstruation, reproductive history 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study designThis hospital-based, individually matched case–control study evaluated associations between menstrual and reproductive factors and early-onset cervical cancer among women aged ≤35 years. The study was conducted at West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, from January 2022 to December 2024. The analytic sample comprised 300 individually matched case–control pairs. HPV-positive/NILM controls underwent repeat screening 6–18 months after the index date, with colposcopy and biopsy performed when clinically indicated; control eligibility required no diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher or cervical cancer during follow-up. Both cases and controls were excluded if they were pregnant at the time of enrollment, had severe psychiatric disorders that would impair their ability to provide reliable information, or had incomplete medical records or missing data regarding menstrual and reproductive history. Core menstrual and reproductive variables were required for both members of each pair and were cross-checked between medical records and standardized interviews conducted by trained nurses. Menstrual exposures included age at menarche in completed years, average cycle length and menstrual period duration in days, menstrual flow assessed with a standardized pictorial blood loss assessment chart and categorized as light, normal, or heavy, and cycle regularity during the 12 months before the exposure cutoff (19). Cycle variation of less than 7 days was classified as regular.Reproductive variables included ever pregnancy, age at first pregnancy, gravidity, parity, spontaneous abortions, medication-induced abortions, and surgical abortions. Medication-induced and surgical abortions were summed for the induced-abortion measure, whereas spontaneous and induced abortions were analyzed separately. Cumulative duration was recorded in months. Copper intrauterine devices, levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems, injectable contraceptives, contraceptive implants, and barrier methods were recorded separately. Sexual behavior variables included age at first sexual intercourse, lifetime number of sexual partners, number of new partners during the previous 12 months, and high-risk behavior in partners. Smoking was classified as never, former, or current, and passive smoking was recorded separately. Assay-specific results were harmonized as current hrHPV-positive or hrHPV-negative. Genotype-specific analyses were restricted to HPV16 and HPV18; HPV52 and HPV58 were not included. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectiveThis study aims to investigate the associations of menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive characteristics with early-onset cervical cancer among women aged ≤35 years.MethodsA hospital-based, individually matched case–control study was conducted at West China Second University Hospital from January 2022 to December 2024. A total of 300 women aged ≤35 years and with histologically confirmed cervical cancer were individually matched 1:1 to 300 screening controls within 0.5 years of age and 7 days of recruitment. Menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive histories accrued up to 90 days before the index data were collected through standardized interviews and medical record reviews. Separate exposure-specific conditional logistic regression models stratified by matched pair were adjusted for prespecified sociodemographic, behavioral, screening-related, infection-related, and current high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) covariates. The model samples ranged from 189 to 277 matched pairs. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed effect modification.ResultsIn the fully adjusted model, menstrual period duration was associated with early-onset cervical cancer, with evidence of nonlinearity (P for nonlinearity <0.001). Each 1-year increase in age at first pregnancy was associated with lower odds (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.717; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.561–0.917). Higher odds were associated with greater gravidity (aOR per pregnancy, 2.959; 95% CI, 1.734–5.050), greater parity (aOR per birth, 3.667; 95% CI, 1.886–7.133), and more induced abortions (aOR per event, 2.672; 95% CI, 1.236–5.773). Longer total breastfeeding duration was inversely associated (aOR per 12 months, 0.189; 95% CI, 0.064–0.560), whereas longer cumulative combined oral contraceptive use was positively associated (aOR per 12 months, 1.335; 95% CI, 1.062–1.678). Age at menarche, menstrual cycle irregularity, ever breastfeeding, categorical combined oral contraceptive status, and other contraceptive methods were not statistically significant after full adjustment. No interaction remained statistically significant after false discovery rate correction.ConclusionsSelected menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive characteristics were associated with early-onset cervical cancer after adjustment for measured confounders and current hrHPV status.Keywords: associated factors, case-control study, cervical cancer, menstruation, reproductive history

full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study provides evidence that menstrual and reproductive factors were associated with the odds of early-onset cervical cancer among women aged ≤35 years. In exposure-specific conditional logistic regression models, menstrual period duration showed a nonlinear association, while younger age at first pregnancy, greater gravidity and parity, more induced abortions, shorter total breastfeeding duration, and longer cumulative combined oral contraceptive use remained associated with early-onset cervical cancer after prespecified adjustment, including adjustment for measured current hrHPV status. These estimates represent associations rather than causal effects, and the category-specific estimates for menstrual period duration were imprecise. The associations identified warrant discussion regarding their biological and epidemiological context, while their clinical implications remain exploratory.This study demonstrated that cervical cancer cases had an earlier age at menarche and a higher proportion of menstrual irregularity compared to controls. However, neither age at menarche nor menstrual cycle irregularity remained statistically significant in the fully adjusted analysis. Therefore, the observed between-group differences should not be interpreted as independent associations with early-onset cervical cancer. Earlier menarche and menstrual irregularity have nevertheless been associated with cervical cancer or related outcomes in previous studies. A Chinese epidemiological investigation reported that earlier age at menarche is associated with increased cervical cancer risk (25). Li et al. (26) reported that younger age at menarche was associated with increased risk of cervical cancer recurrence. Okyere et al. (27) conducted a study based on Demographic and Health Survey evidence, revealing that earlier menarche was associated with lower cervical cancer screening uptake. Although this finding was not directly related to cervical cancer incidence, it indicates that the relationship between the timing of menarche and cervical-cancer-related outcomes may also involve differences in health behavior and screening participation. Earlier physiological maturation has also been proposed as a potential marker of earlier sexual activity and longer cumulative opportunity for HPV exposure, although these factors were not directly evaluated in the present study. Furthermore, Varghese et al. (13) investigated the US inpatient database and found that women diagnosed with menstrual disorders had significantly higher odds ratios for cervical cancer diagnosis (OR = 1.582). A cross-sectional study conducted among Ethiopian women also revealed that women with a history of irregular menstruation had twice the risk of being diagnosed with cervical precancerous lesions compared to controls (adjusted OR = 2.29) (28). Differences in study populations, menstrual variable definitions, outcomes, and adjustment strategies may contribute to the inconsistency across studies. In the present analysis, menstrual period duration, rather than age at menarche or cycle irregularity, was associated with early-onset cervical cancer. Nevertheless, this relationship was nonlinear, and the individual categorical estimates were imprecise. Menstrual cycle length also showed evidence of nonlinearity without a statistically significant overall association. Thus, constant per-day effects may not adequately characterize the relationships between menstrual characteristics and early-onset cervical cancer.Regarding reproductive factors, this study demonstrated that the early-onset cervical cancer group exhibited earlier age at first pregnancy and higher numbers of G, P, and A compared to controls. In the adjusted conditional logistic regression analyses, a younger age at first pregnancy and greater gravidity and parity were associated with higher odds of early-onset cervical cancer. These findings are consistent with a previous meta-analysis showing that women with first pregnancy at age 20 or older had a 41% reduced risk of cervical cancer compared to those with first pregnancy before age 20 (29). Another meta-analysis also revealed that gravidity has positive correlation with occurrence of cervical cancer (30). One proposed explanation is that delayed childbearing allows additional time for cervical epithelial maturation, whereas pregnancy-related hormonal and immunological changes may affect cervical susceptibility to persistent HPV infection and neoplastic progression (31, 32). Early pregnancy may reflect early sexual activity, pregnancy-related immunosuppression, or prolonged HPV exposure during vulnerable cervical development (10). Multiple pregnancies and abortions may contribute to cervical trauma, inflammation, and hormonal fluctuations that facilitate malignant transformation (33).The present analysis further distinguished spontaneous from induced abortions because these events may have different determinants and confounding structures. A higher number of induced abortions remained associated with early-onset cervical cancer, whereas the estimate for spontaneous abortions was borderline and was less stable in sensitivity analyses. These findings should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that abortion itself causes cervical cancer. In addition, because gravidity, parity, abortion history, age at first pregnancy, and breastfeeding are closely related reproductive characteristics, each exposure was evaluated in a separate conditional logistic regression model. The resulting estimates describe exposure-specific associations and should not be interpreted as effects that are mutually independent of all other reproductive variables.Among women for whom breastfeeding duration was applicable, a longer total breastfeeding duration was associated with lower odds of early-onset cervical cancer, whereas ever having breastfed was not statistically significant. A cohort study conducted among Korean women demonstrated that women with cumulative breastfeeding duration ≥36 months had the lowest cervical cancer risk (16). Compared to the ≥36 months group, women who breastfed for 13–36 months had a 54% increased risk of cervical cancer (OR = 1.54; 95% CI 1.12–2.11), suggesting that prolonged breastfeeding duration may be associated with reduced cervical cancer risk (16). Possible explanations proposed in previous research include lactational amenorrhea, changes in cumulative hormonal exposure, and breastfeeding-related immunological effects. However, another study has suggested that elevated prolactin levels may be a risk factor for cervical cancer (34), indicating that the relationship between prolactin, breastfeeding, and cervical carcinogenesis may be complex and potentially dependent on exposure duration and timing.The contraceptive analyses showed different patterns according to the specific exposure measure. Categorical combined oral contraceptive use status was not significantly associated with early-onset cervical cancer, whereas longer cumulative combined oral contraceptive use was associated with higher odds of the disease. Currently used oral contraceptives primarily contain estrogen and progestin as active components. The relationship between oral contraceptive use and cervical cancer has been previously established, with relative risks of approximately 1.1 for use less than 5 years, increasing to 1.6 for 5–9 years, and reaching 2.2 for ≥10 years of use (35). More recent epidemiological evidence has also supported the importance of contraceptive formulation and duration when evaluating hormonal contraceptive exposure (36). A potential biological explanation for the association between oral contraceptive use and cervical cancer may involve interactions among estrogen, progestin, and hormone receptors in cervical tissue, thereby affecting the natural history of HPV infection (37). full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsThis individually matched case–control study found that selected menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive characteristics were associated with the odds of early-onset cervical cancer among women aged ≤35 years after prespecified adjustment. The observed associations were exposure specific, showed different levels of statistical robustness, and did not establish causality or statistically significant effect modification across the examined subgroups. Further prospective studies with detailed longitudinal HPV and reproductive exposure assessment are needed before these characteristics can have any role beyond etiological research.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionCervical cancer remains a significant global health burden, ranking as the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide (1). In 2022, the global age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) and age-standardized mortality rate (ASMR) were 14.12 and 7.08 per 100,000 women, respectively (1). The overall incidence of cervical cancer has declined in many high-income countries, coinciding with the implementation of cervical screening and human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programs (2, 3). However, cervical cancer occurring in younger women remains clinically important because its diagnosis and treatment may coincide with key reproductive years (1, 4–7).Early-onset cervical cancer may have clinicopathological characteristics that differ from those observed in older women. Young women have shown differences in histological subtype, tumor differentiation, stage, and lymph node involvement across observational studies, although the findings have not been uniform (5, 6, 8, 9). Moreover, the diagnosis of early-onset cervical cancer has implications for fertility preservation, reproductive health, and long-term quality of life (5–7). Therefore, focusing on women aged ≤35 years may help clarify factors associated with cervical cancer in this age group. While persistent high-risk HPV (hrHPV) infection is the central etiological factor in cervical carcinogenesis, epidemiological evidence suggests that hormonal and reproductive characteristics may also be associated with cervical cancer, particularly among younger women (10–12). Menstrual characteristics may reflect variation in reproductive and hormonal exposures. A previous database study reported an association between menstrual irregularities and cervical cancer diagnosis (13). Menstrual hygiene practices have also been examined in relation to cervical precancer and cervical cancer, although the available evidence remains limited (13, 14). Similarly, reproductive factors such as parity, breastfeeding history, and contraceptive use have been associated with cervical cancer in observational studies, although the reported associations have varied (10, 11, 15–17).Previous studies investigating menstrual and reproductive factors in cervical cancer have predominantly focused on mixed-age populations or older women, with limited data specifically addressing women aged ≤35 years. Therefore, this study conducted an individually matched hospital-based case–control study to evaluate the association between menstrual, reproductive, and contraceptive characteristics and early-onset cervical cancer in Chinese women aged ≤35 years. This study aimed to estimate adjusted associations while accounting for prespecified sociodemographic, behavioral, screening-related, infection-related, and current hrHPV covariates. 2.3.Data collection and variable definitionsData were collected using face-to-face interviews, medical record reviews, and standardized questionnaires.Standardized interviews were administered by trained nurses at recruitment, except for a subset of cases interviewed within 5 days after histologic diagnosis; diagnosis-awareness status at interview was recorded. Only information occurring on or before the exposure cutoff date was included in exposure definitions. Interview data were cross-checked against source records and routine clinical documentation.Demographic and prespecified covariate data included age at the index date, body mass index (BMI), education, occupation classified according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations, household income, residence type, cervical screening frequency during the previous 5 years, HPV vaccination, sexual history, smoking, and chlamydial infection history. Menstrual exposures included age at menarche in completed years, average cycle length and menstrual period duration in days, menstrual flow assessed with a standardized pictorial blood loss assessment chart and categorized as light, normal, or heavy, and cycle regularity during the 12 months before the exposure cutoff (19). Cycle variation of less than 7 days was classified as regular.Reproductive variables included ever pregnancy, age at first pregnancy, gravidity, parity, spontaneous abortions, medication-induced abortions, and surgical abortions. Medication-induced and surgical abortions were summed for the induced-abortion measure, whereas spontaneous and induced abortions were analyzed separately. Breastfeeding variables comprised ever breastfeeding and cumulative duration in months among women with at least one birth. Contraceptive exposures distinguished combined oral contraceptives from progestin-only pills; combined oral contraceptive status was classified as never, current, discontinued within 12 months, or discontinued more than 12 months previously. Cumulative duration was recorded in months. Copper intrauterine devices, levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems, injectable contraceptives, contraceptive implants, and barrier methods were recorded separately. Sexual behavior variables included age at first sexual intercourse, lifetime number of sexual partners, number of new partners during the previous 12 months, and high-risk behavior in partners. Smoking was classified as never, former, or current, and passive smoking was recorded separately. Laboratory and clinical records also provided chlamydial infection history, human immunodeficiency virus status, pathology review, and tissue HPV confirmation when available. Current hrHPV-negative cases were further characterized by histologic type, pathology review status, tissue HPV confirmation, and mode of detection. Current hrHPV-positive/NILM controls were characterized by repeat screening, colposcopy, biopsy, and final follow-up status. HPV16 and HPV18 results were summarized by histologic type among cases. 2.4.HPV assessmentHigh-risk HPV status was based on the result closest to the index date, obtained from clinician-collected cervical exfoliated cells from 21 days before through 7 days after the index date. Testing used the Cobas 4800 HPV DNA, Hybribio 14-type high-risk HPV DNA, or Sansure 15-type high-risk HPV DNA assay. Assay-specific results were harmonized as current hrHPV-positive or hrHPV-negative. Genotype-specific analyses were restricted to HPV16 and HPV18; HPV52 and HPV58 were not included. Persistent high-risk HPV was defined as positive results on two tests at least 6 months apart when a prior result was available (20). Model 2 estimated associations without HPV adjustment, and model 3 included current hrHPV status as a prespecified infection-related covariate based on its established role in cervical carcinogenesis. 2.5.Subgroup and sensitivity analysesExploratory subgroup analyses were specified for five characteristics. The subgroups were defined as follows (1): educational level (primary education or below vs. secondary education and above), (2) occupation type (manual labor vs. professional/managerial and clerical/service combined), (3) age at first sexual intercourse (≤18 years vs. >18 years), (4) smoking status (never smokers vs. ever smokers including former and current smokers), and (5) HPV infection status (positive vs. negative). The examined exposures were age at menarche, irregular menstrual cycles, spontaneous abortions, induced abortions, and cumulative combined oral contraceptive use. For each exposure and subgroup factor, a conditional logistic model included the exposure, subgroup indicator, and exposure-by-subgroup interaction, together with the model 3 covariates; the subgroup main-effect term represented that factor when it was also among the model 3 covariates. Subgroup-specific estimates were obtained as linear combinations, and interaction was evaluated using a likelihood-ratio test. Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across the 25 interaction tests. Age at menarche, menstrual cycle irregularity, ever breastfeeding, categorical combined oral contraceptive status, and other contraceptive methods were not statistically significant after full adjustment. The study was conducted at West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, from January 2022 to December 2024. full_text: AbstractBackgroundTo investigate factors associated with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection and residual or recurrent disease in patients with high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) following loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP).MethodsA total of 903 patients with pathologically confirmed HSIL who underwent LEEP between January 2021 and May 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. HR-HPV genotyping and cervical cytology were performed before and after surgery, and residual or recurrent HSIL was assessed by colposcopy during follow-up. Generalized estimating equation (GEE) logistic regression accounted for within-patient clustering of genotype-specific HPV observations. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with HR-HPV persistence, and Firth's penalized logistic regression evaluated factors associated with residual or recurrent HSIL.ResultsPersistent HR-HPV infection rates were 23.3%, 19.0%, and 17.5% at 6, 12, and 18 months after LEEP, respectively. GEE analysis showed significant differences in type-specific persistence among the α5/6, α7, and α9 species (P = 0.024), with higher persistence in α5/6 than α7 (27.1% vs. 14.0%; OR = 2.30, 95% CI, 1.09–4.85; adjusted P = 0.024), but no significant differences between α5/6 and α9 or between α7 and α9. Multiple HR-HPV infections (OR = 2.76, 95% CI, 1.96–3.89; P < 0.001) and menopausal status (OR = 2.06, 95% CI, 1.18–3.66; P = 0.011), and positive endocervical margins (OR = 2.54, 95% CI, 1.48–4.32; P = 0.007) were associated with HR-HPV persistence. During follow-up, 32 patients (3.5%) developed residual or recurrent HSIL (21 residual, 11 recurrent). Firth's penalized regression identified persistent type-specific HR-HPV infection (OR = 21.88, 95% CI, 8.25–72.76; P < 0.001), number of involved cervical quadrants (P = 0.025), endocervical involvement (P = 0.006), and surgical margin status (P < 0.001) as independently associated with residual or recurrent HSIL.Conclusionsα5/6 species showed a higher type-specific HR-HPV persistence than α7 but not α9 following LEEP. Multiple HR-HPV infections, menopausal status, and positive endocervical margins were associated with HR-HPV persistence. Persistent type-specific HR-HPV infection, multiple involved cervical quadrants, endocervical involvement, and positive surgical margins were independent predictors of residual or recurrent HSIL. Multicenter studies are warranted to validate integrating margin status with HPV genotyping for postoperative risk stratification.Keywords: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, human papillomavirus species, loop electrosurgical excision procedure, risk factors 2.Methods2.1.Study population and inclusion criteriaA total of 903 patients with histologically confirmed HSIL (e.g., cervical CIN2, CIN3, and carcinoma in situ) who underwent LEEP at the Department of Cervical Pathology, International Peace Maternity and Child Health Hospital, between January 2021 and May 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. Inclusion criteria (1): Availability of HR-HPV genotyping results both before and after LEEP (2); Postoperative follow-up of at least 18 months with a minimum of two completed follow-up visits; (3) Complete clinical and follow-up data. Exclusion criteria: (1) Incomplete clinical data or loss to follow-up; (2) Receipt of adjuvant treatment for HSIL, such as hysterectomy or photodynamic therapy; (3) Prior cervical treatment, current pregnancy, or postpartum status within 8 weeks; (4) History of cervical cancer or other malignant tumors of the female genital tract; (5) History of pelvic radiotherapy or systemic chemotherapy; (6) Presence of autoimmune or systemic diseases or use of immunosuppressive medications. This study was approved by the Medical Research Ethics Committee of the International Peace Maternity and Child Health Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University (No. GKLW-A-2025-120-01).2.2.Specimen collection and HPV genotypingHR-HPV genotyping was performed using the Sansure® Human Papillomavirus DNA Diagnostic Kit (PCR Fluorescence Probing) (Sansure Biotech Inc.), which detects 15 high-risk HPV genotypes (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 53, 56, 58, 59, 66, and 68). This assay has previously demonstrated high reproducibility and analytical reliability (13). Based on phylogenetic classification and genetic relatedness of papillomaviruses (12), HR-HPV genotypes in this study were categorized into three species groups: α5/6 (HPV types 51, 53, 56, and 66), α7 (HPV types 18, 39, 45, 59, and 68), and α9 (HPV types 16, 31, 33, 35, 52, and 58). Cervical cytology results were reported according to the Bethesda System and categorized as: no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM), atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), atypical glandular cells (AGC), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H), and HSIL.2.3.Colposcopic examinationColposcopic examination was performed when confirmatory test results were abnormal. Suspicious cervical lesions were biopsied based on colposcopic findings after application of acetic acid and Lugol's iodine staining. All colposcopic examinations were performed by eight experienced colposcopists at our center.2.4.Surgical procedureAfter obtaining informed consent, patients underwent cervical LEEP 3–7 days after the end of menstruation. The cervix was exposed with a vaginal speculum, and the lesion margins were delineated with Lugol's iodine solution. LEEP was performed using a VIO® 300 S electrosurgical system (Erbe Elektromedizin GmbH, Tübingen, Germany) in AutoCut mode at an output power of 40–50 W. Loop electrodes (10, 15, or 20 mm in diameter) or triangular electrodes (10 × 15 or 15 × 20 mm) of appropriate size were selected based on the lesion extent and cervical transformation zone (CTZ) type. The electrode was placed 3–5 mm beyond the visible lesion margin, and the entire CTZ together with the lesion was excised en bloc using a single, smooth, continuous pass. Piecemeal excision was performed when the lesion was too extensive to permit complete en-bloc resection.For type I or II CTZs, the cone height was maintained at 10–15 mm, with a glandular excision depth of ≥5 mm. For patients with type III CTZ, lesions extending into the endocervical canal, or postmenopausal patients, a top-hat endocervical resection was performed after the primary ectocervical excision. A smaller-diameter loop electrode was used to remove suspicious or potentially involved deep endocervical tissue. This separate endocervical specimen was distinctly labeled and submitted for independent histopathological assessment.No cauterization was applied to the margins of the ex-vivo surgical specimen, and routine extensive coagulation of the entire wound surface was avoided. All hemostatic procedures were limited to the in-situ cervical crater. Focal spot coagulation for sites of active bleeding was performed using a 5 mm monopolar ball-tip electrode at an output power of 30–40 W. All surgical procedures were performed by experienced gynecological specialists.2.5.Follow-up protocol and evaluation criteriaCervical cytology was performed at 3 months after LEEP, whereas HR-HPV genotyping and cervical cytology cotesting were performed at 6 months after LEEP. Thereafter, follow-up evaluations were performed every 6 months, with a minimum follow-up duration of 18 months. Follow-up assessments included cervical cytology, HR-HPV genotyping, and colposcopy with biopsy when clinically indicated. Type-specific persistent HR-HPV infection was defined as the detection of at least one identical HPV genotype at both the preoperative assessment and the 6-month postoperative HPV assessment, indicating persistence of the same genotype across the two consecutive HPV assessments. HPV clearance was defined as the complete absence of all HPV genotypes detected preoperatively at the 6-month postoperative HPV assessment. For the analysis of type-specific HR-HPV persistence, each detected HPV genotype was considered an observation, while within-patient correlation among multiple genotype observations was accounted for using GEE models. Postoperative residual disease was defined as biopsy-confirmed HSIL detected within 6 months after cervical conization. Postoperative recurrence was defined as the reappearance of pathologically confirmed HSIL more than 6 months after surgery, following initially negative cytology and HPV test results or normal biopsy findings within the first 6 months after the procedure.2.6.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using RStudio Desktop (Posit Software, PBC, Boston, MA, USA). Continuous variables were presented as the median with interquartile range [P50 (P25, P75)], while categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages [n (%)]. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to assess normality; non-normally distributed continuous variables were compared using the rank-sum test, and categorical variables using the chi-square test.Because individual patients could harbor multiple HPV genotypes, genotype-specific HPV observations within the same patient were correlated. Generalized estimating equation (GEE) logistic regression models with a logit link were therefore used, with the outpatient registration number as the clustering variable. GEE models were used to compare multiple infection rates and type-specific HR-HPV persistence rates across HPV phylogenetic species. Results were expressed as estimated rates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and pairwise comparisons were performed with Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons. Variables with a P value < 0.05 in univariable analyses were included in a multivariable logistic regression model to identify independent associated factors for persistent HR-HPV infection. For the analysis of factors associated with residual or recurrent HSIL, candidate variables were initially selected from univariable analyses using a P value < 0.05. Potential collinearity among candidate variables was assessed using Cramer's V. Given the limited number of outcome events (32 cases) and the sparse categorical data, Firth's penalized logistic regression was used to reduce small-sample bias and mitigate separation. Backward elimination was used to obtain the final model. Results were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% CIs.All statistical tests were two-sided, and a P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant unless otherwise specified for multiplicity-adjusted comparisons. 3.1.Patient characteristicsA total of 903 patients were included in this study. The baseline clinical characteristics of the cohort are summarized in Table 1. The median age was 41 years, with an interquartile range (IQR, 25th-75th percentile) of 35–50 years. Most patients were premenopausal (688/903, 76.2%). Abnormal cervical cytology was observed in 556 patients (61.6%). Postoperative pathological examination revealed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 (CIN2) in 464 patients (51.4%), CIN3 in 435 patients (48.2%), and carcinoma in situ (CIS) in 4 patients (0.4%). Regarding HR-HPV infection status, 623 patients (69.0%) had single-type HR-HPV infection, 206 (22.8%) had infection with two HR-HPV genotypes, and 74 (8.2%) had infection with three or more genotypes. The HR-HPV persistence rates at 6, 12, and 18 months after surgery were 23.3% (210/903), 19.0% (172/903), and 17.5% (158/903), respectively. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractBackgroundTo investigate factors associated with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection and residual or recurrent disease in patients with high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) following loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP).MethodsA total of 903 patients with pathologically confirmed HSIL who underwent LEEP between January 2021 and May 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. HR-HPV genotyping and cervical cytology were performed before and after surgery, and residual or recurrent HSIL was assessed by colposcopy during follow-up. Generalized estimating equation (GEE) logistic regression accounted for within-patient clustering of genotype-specific HPV observations. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with HR-HPV persistence, and Firth's penalized logistic regression evaluated factors associated with residual or recurrent HSIL.ResultsPersistent HR-HPV infection rates were 23.3%, 19.0%, and 17.5% at 6, 12, and 18 months after LEEP, respectively. GEE analysis showed significant differences in type-specific persistence among the α5/6, α7, and α9 species (P = 0.024), with higher persistence in α5/6 than α7 (27.1% vs. 14.0%; OR = 2.30, 95% CI, 1.09–4.85; adjusted P = 0.024), but no significant differences between α5/6 and α9 or between α7 and α9. Multiple HR-HPV infections (OR = 2.76, 95% CI, 1.96–3.89; P < 0.001) and menopausal status (OR = 2.06, 95% CI, 1.18–3.66; P = 0.011), and positive endocervical margins (OR = 2.54, 95% CI, 1.48–4.32; P = 0.007) were associated with HR-HPV persistence. During follow-up, 32 patients (3.5%) developed residual or recurrent HSIL (21 residual, 11 recurrent). Firth's penalized regression identified persistent type-specific HR-HPV infection (OR = 21.88, 95% CI, 8.25–72.76; P < 0.001), number of involved cervical quadrants (P = 0.025), endocervical involvement (P = 0.006), and surgical margin status (P < 0.001) as independently associated with residual or recurrent HSIL.Conclusionsα5/6 species showed a higher type-specific HR-HPV persistence than α7 but not α9 following LEEP. Multiple HR-HPV infections, menopausal status, and positive endocervical margins were associated with HR-HPV persistence. Persistent type-specific HR-HPV infection, multiple involved cervical quadrants, endocervical involvement, and positive surgical margins were independent predictors of residual or recurrent HSIL. Multicenter studies are warranted to validate integrating margin status with HPV genotyping for postoperative risk stratification.Keywords: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, human papillomavirus species, loop electrosurgical excision procedure, risk factors
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Methods2.1.Study population and inclusion criteriaA total of 903 patients with histologically confirmed HSIL (e.g., cervical CIN2, CIN3, and carcinoma in situ) who underwent LEEP at the Department of Cervical Pathology, International Peace Maternity and Child Health Hospital, between January 2021 and May 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. Inclusion criteria (1): Availability of HR-HPV genotyping results both before and after LEEP (2); Postoperative follow-up of at least 18 months with a minimum of two completed follow-up visits; (3) Complete clinical and follow-up data. Exclusion criteria: (1) Incomplete clinical data or loss to follow-up; (2) Receipt of adjuvant treatment for HSIL, such as hysterectomy or photodynamic therapy; (3) Prior cervical treatment, current pregnancy, or postpartum status within 8 weeks; (4) History of cervical cancer or other malignant tumors of the female genital tract; (5) History of pelvic radiotherapy or systemic chemotherapy; (6) Presence of autoimmune or systemic diseases or use of immunosuppressive medications. This study was approved by the Medical Research Ethics Committee of the International Peace Maternity and Child Health Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University (No. GKLW-A-2025-120-01).2.2.Specimen collection and HPV genotypingHR-HPV genotyping was performed using the Sansure® Human Papillomavirus DNA Diagnostic Kit (PCR Fluorescence Probing) (Sansure Biotech Inc.), which detects 15 high-risk HPV genotypes (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 53, 56, 58, 59, 66, and 68). This assay has previously demonstrated high reproducibility and analytical reliability (13). Based on phylogenetic classification and genetic relatedness of papillomaviruses (12), HR-HPV genotypes in this study were categorized into three species groups: α5/6 (HPV types 51, 53, 56, and 66), α7 (HPV types 18, 39, 45, 59, and 68), and α9 (HPV types 16, 31, 33, 35, 52, and 58). Cervical cytology results were reported according to the Bethesda System and categorized as: no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM), atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), atypical glandular cells (AGC), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H), and HSIL.2.3.Colposcopic examinationColposcopic examination was performed when confirmatory test results were abnormal. Suspicious cervical lesions were biopsied based on colposcopic findings after application of acetic acid and Lugol's iodine staining. All colposcopic examinations were performed by eight experienced colposcopists at our center.2.4.Surgical procedureAfter obtaining informed consent, patients underwent cervical LEEP 3–7 days after the end of menstruation. The cervix was exposed with a vaginal speculum, and the lesion margins were delineated with Lugol's iodine solution. LEEP was performed using a VIO® 300 S electrosurgical system (Erbe Elektromedizin GmbH, Tübingen, Germany) in AutoCut mode at an output power of 40–50 W. Loop electrodes (10, 15, or 20 mm in diameter) or triangular electrodes (10 × 15 or 15 × 20 mm) of appropriate size were selected based on the lesion extent and cervical transformation zone (CTZ) type. The electrode was placed 3–5 mm beyond the visible lesion margin, and the entire CTZ together with the lesion was excised en bloc using a single, smooth, continuous pass. Piecemeal excision was performed when the lesion was too extensive to permit complete en-bloc resection.For type I or II CTZs, the cone height was maintained at 10–15 mm, with a glandular excision depth of ≥5 mm. For patients with type III CTZ, lesions extending into the endocervical canal, or postmenopausal patients, a top-hat endocervical resection was performed after the primary ectocervical excision. A smaller-diameter loop electrode was used to remove suspicious or potentially involved deep endocervical tissue. This separate endocervical specimen was distinctly labeled and submitted for independent histopathological assessment.No cauterization was applied to the margins of the ex-vivo surgical specimen, and routine extensive coagulation of the entire wound surface was avoided. All hemostatic procedures were limited to the in-situ cervical crater. Focal spot coagulation for sites of active bleeding was performed using a 5 mm monopolar ball-tip electrode at an output power of 30–40 W. All surgical procedures were performed by experienced gynecological specialists.2.5.Follow-up protocol and evaluation criteriaCervical cytology was performed at 3 months after LEEP, whereas HR-HPV genotyping and cervical cytology cotesting were performed at 6 months after LEEP. Thereafter, follow-up evaluations were performed every 6 months, with a minimum follow-up duration of 18 months. Follow-up assessments included cervical cytology, HR-HPV genotyping, and colposcopy with biopsy when clinically indicated. Type-specific persistent HR-HPV infection was defined as the detection of at least one identical HPV genotype at both the preoperative assessment and the 6-month postoperative HPV assessment, indicating persistence of the same genotype across the two consecutive HPV assessments. HPV clearance was defined as the complete absence of all HPV genotypes detected preoperatively at the 6-month postoperative HPV assessment. For the analysis of type-specific HR-HPV persistence, each detected HPV genotype was considered an observation, while within-patient correlation among multiple genotype observations was accounted for using GEE models. Postoperative residual disease was defined as biopsy-confirmed HSIL detected within 6 months after cervical conization. Postoperative recurrence was defined as the reappearance of pathologically confirmed HSIL more than 6 months after surgery, following initially negative cytology and HPV test results or normal biopsy findings within the first 6 months after the procedure.2.6.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using RStudio Desktop (Posit Software, PBC, Boston, MA, USA). Continuous variables were presented as the median with interquartile range [P50 (P25, P75)], while categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages [n (%)]. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to assess normality; non-normally distributed continuous variables were compared using the rank-sum test, and categorical variables using the chi-square test.Because individual patients could harbor multiple HPV genotypes, genotype-specific HPV observations within the same patient were correlated. Generalized estimating equation (GEE) logistic regression models with a logit link were therefore used, with the outpatient registration number as the clustering variable. GEE models were used to compare multiple infection rates and type-specific HR-HPV persistence rates across HPV phylogenetic species. Results were expressed as estimated rates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and pairwise comparisons were performed with Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons. Variables with a P value < 0.05 in univariable analyses were included in a multivariable logistic regression model to identify independent associated factors for persistent HR-HPV infection. For the analysis of factors associated with residual or recurrent HSIL, candidate variables were initially selected from univariable analyses using a P value < 0.05. Potential collinearity among candidate variables was assessed using Cramer's V. Given the limited number of outcome events (32 cases) and the sparse categorical data, Firth's penalized logistic regression was used to reduce small-sample bias and mitigate separation. Backward elimination was used to obtain the final model. Results were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% CIs.All statistical tests were two-sided, and a P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant unless otherwise specified for multiplicity-adjusted comparisons. 3.1.Patient characteristicsA total of 903 patien…

full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study examined the independent associated factors associated with HR-HPV persistence and residual or recurrent HSIL after LEEP. Our findings provide additional evidence to support risk-stratified postoperative management and contribute to optimizing strategies for the secondary prevention of cervical cancer.4.1.Characteristics and clinical implications of HR-HPV persistenceIn the present study, HR-HPV clearance rates at 6, 12, and 18 months after LEEP were 76.7%, 81.0%, and 82.5%, respectively. Although these rates were slightly lower than those reported in previous studies (3, 14), the overall temporal pattern of postoperative HPV clearance was generally consistent. The discrepancy may be attributable to differences in patient inclusion criteria, such as surgical margin status and treatment modalities, as well as variations in follow-up intervals across studies. Our findings indicate that more than two-thirds of patients achieved HR-HPV clearance within 6 months after surgery. Moreover, the first postoperative year appears to represent a critical period for viral clearance, with relatively few additional clearance events observed after 12 months. These results highlight the importance of close surveillance during the early postoperative period while also highlighting the necessity of continued long-term follow-up.Previous studies have reported considerable variability in persistence rates among different HR-HPV genotypes (7, 15–17). Gosvig CF et al. found that HPV α5/6 species were more likely to persist than α9 species (18). In our analysis, α5/6 species showed the highest GEE-estimated type-specific persistence rate and a significantly higher persistence rate than α7, whereas the difference between α5/6 and α9 was not statistically significant. This discrepancy may reflect differences in study populations, HPV detection methods, follow-up timing, sample size, and statistical approaches. Importantly, our analysis accounted for within-patient clustering among multiple HPV genotype observations using GEE models, which may have affected the precision of the between-species comparisons. The higher numerical persistence rate observed for α5/6 in our study may represent a potential difference in persistence across phylogenetic groups, but the evidence was insufficient to conclude that α5/6 has a significantly higher persistence propensity than α9. In contrast, HPV18 exhibited the lowest persistence rate (4.4%) among all detected genotypes. These findings are consistent with previous reports (18) and may reflect inherent biological differences among HPV phylogenetic groups (19, 20). Although α5/6 species have relatively low prevalence in the general population, they may possess stronger immune evasion capabilities and enhanced adhesion to cervical epithelial cells, thereby facilitating postoperative viral persistence. Conversely, α7 species, particularly HPV18, may induce stronger host immune responses due to greater immunogenicity, resulting in more efficient viral clearance (21).Furthermore, the multiple infection rate was significantly lower in the α9 group than in the α7 and α5/6 groups, which is consistent with earlier studies (16). Although α9 genotypes demonstrate moderate persistence and relatively low rates of multiple infection, their high prevalence and strong carcinogenic potential warrant continued prioritization during postoperative surveillance. In contrast, while α5/6 genotypes exhibit a higher likelihood of persistence, their oncogenic potential may be lower than that of α7 and α9 species, suggesting that some infections within this group may represent solely bystanders (18).HPV53, which belongs to the α5/6 species, was fully genotyped in this study. It showed a high co-infection rate (81.8% pre-LEEP) and a postoperative persistence rate of 36.4%, which is consistent with the general behavior of this phylogenetic group. A previous study has suggested that HPV53 exhibits relatively weak oncogenic potential and is more commonly associated with mild low-grade cervical lesions and slow disease progression, and it is generally considered a genotype with limited independent contribution to HSIL development (22). The clinical significance of isolated persistent HPV53 infection requires further investigation.4.2.Risk factors for postoperative HR-HPV persistence and residual or recurrence HSILIn this study, 23.3% (210/903) of patients developed postoperative HR-HPV persistence. Multiple HR-HPV infection was identified as a significant independent risk factor for postoperative persistence, associated with 2.76-fold higher odds compared with single-type infection (OR = 2.76, 95% CI, 1.96–3.89). This finding is consistent with previous studies (8, 16, 23, 24). Multiple HR-HPV infections may increase the likelihood of immune evasion, impair host immune responses, and ultimately reduce viral clearance efficiency (25). The relationship between multiple HR-HPV infections and residual or recurrent disease remains controversial. Some studies have reported that multiple HR-HPV infections are associated with a modest but significant increase in the risk of postoperative HSIL residual or recurrence, suggesting that they may serve as a potential prognostic indicator of unfavorable outcomes after treatment for high-grade cervical lesions (16, 24). In contrast, other studies propose that multiple HR-HPV infections largely represent random co-infections, with each HPV type independently contributing to cervical lesion development through cumulative rather than synergistic effects (26). The latter interpretation is consistent with our findings, which indicate that multiple HPV infections were associated with HR-HPV persistence but not with HSIL residual or recurrence. These inconsistencies across studies may be attributable to differences in sample size, population characteristics, and follow-up duration, highlighting the need for further validation in larger prospective cohorts.Previous studies and meta-analyses have confirmed that postoperative persistence of the same HR-HPV genotype is the strongest predictor of residual or recurrent HSIL, whereas newly acquired HR-HPV infections post-surgery carry almost no risk of recurrence (6, 20, 27). In our study, 87.5% (28/32) of residual or recurrent HSIL exhibited persistence of the same HR-HPV genotype before and after surgery. Firth's penalized logistic regression further identified postoperative type-specific HR-HPV persistence as an independent risk factor for residual or recurrent HSIL, corroborating previous findings (17, 28–31).Positive surgical margins have been widely recognized as important risk factors for postoperative HPV persistence and lesion residual or recurrence (7, 9, 15, 18). However, relatively few studies have conducted detailed analyses distinguishing among endocervical, ectocervical, and basal margin involvement. In the present study, positive endocervical margins were identified as a strong independent predictor of postoperative HR-HPV persistence (OR = 2.54). Positive endocervical margins indicate possible presence of residual lesions deep within the endocervical canal, which may contribute to persistent HR-HPV infection.Xiao et al. found that positive endocervical and basal surgical margins were strong predictors of residual disease (32). Meta-analyses (33, 34) confirmed that positive surgical margins significantly increase the risks of residual or recurrent HSIL after LEEP. However, margin pathology has low sensitivity for predicting recurrence, and sole reliance on margin status tends to miss high-risk patients. Accordingly, surgical margins are not recommended as an isolated prognostic biomarker, and postoperative risk stratification for HSIL guided by HR-HPV genotyping is preferred in clinical practice. A major limitation of these meta-analyses is the absence of complete HPV genotyping data in nearly all incorporated primary studies, which precluded differentiation bet…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionThis study systematically evaluated the factors associated with HR-HPV persistence and HSIL residual or recurrence after LEEP. Preoperative multiple HR-HPV infection, menopausal status, and positive endocervical margins were associated with postoperative HPV persistence, while persistent type-specific HPV infection, involvement of multiple cervical quadrants, endocervical involvement, and surgical margin positivity were associated with residual or recurrent HSIL. Although α5/6 showed a higher persistence rate than α7, its persistence did not differ significantly from that of α9. Given the high prevalence and oncogenic potential of α9, continued postoperative surveillance remains important. These findings support the potential utility of HPV persistence together with pathological features, particularly lesion extent and surgical margin status, in postoperative risk assessment. Further prospective multicenter studies are needed to confirm these associations and determine their value for individualized postoperative surveillance.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionCervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a precancerous condition caused by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV). Without timely intervention, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) carry a substantially increased risk of progression to invasive cervical cancer (1). The loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) is widely used to remove dysplastic cervical tissue and effectively prevent progression to invasive disease. However, although LEEP eliminates the visible lesion, it does not necessarily eradicate the underlying viral infection (2, 3). Clinical follow-up studies have shown that approximately 5%–25% of patients develop residual or recurrent disease after LEEP, with persistent postoperative HR-HPV infection identified as the strongest predictor of recurrence (4, 5). In particular, patients with type-specific persistent HR-HPV infection may have up to a 30-fold higher risk of disease recurrence (6). Therefore, accurately identifying patients at high risk for persistent HR-HPV infection after surgery is of considerable clinical importance for optimizing individualized postoperative surveillance and improving the effectiveness of secondary cervical cancer prevention.Previous studies have explored factors associated with postoperative HR-HPV persistence and residual or recurrent CIN. Potential risk factors reported include patient age, HR-HPV genotype, viral load, surgical margin status, higher pathological grade, endocervical glandular involvement, and host immune status (7–10). HR-HPV comprises a diverse group of genotypes that can be categorized into phylogenetic species groups, such as α5/6, α7, and α9, based on evolutionary relationships and genetic similarity (11). These phylogenetic groups differ substantially in their biological characteristics, including oncogenic potential and mechanisms of immune evasion (11, 12). Such genotype-specific differences may influence postoperative viral clearance and, consequently, clinical outcomes. However, existing clinical evidence remains limited, particularly with respect to large-scale studies evaluating HR-HPV persistence patterns in the Chinese population.Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the characteristics of HR-HPV persistence and to identify independent associated factors for residual or recurrent HSIL after LEEP. The findings are intended to provide an evidence-based foundation for risk stratification and to support the development of more precise postoperative management strategies for patients with HSIL in the Chinese population. 2.1.Study population and inclusion criteriaA total of 903 patients with histologically confirmed HSIL (e.g., cervical CIN2, CIN3, and carcinoma in situ) who underwent LEEP at the Department of Cervical Pathology, International Peace Maternity and Child Health Hospital, between January 2021 and May 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. Inclusion criteria (1): Availability of HR-HPV genotyping results both before and after LEEP (2); Postoperative follow-up of at least 18 months with a minimum of two completed follow-up visits; (3) Complete clinical and follow-up data. Exclusion criteria: (1) Incomplete clinical data or loss to follow-up; (2) Receipt of adjuvant treatment for HSIL, such as hysterectomy or photodynamic therapy; (3) Prior cervical treatment, current pregnancy, or postpartum status within 8 weeks; (4) History of cervical cancer or other malignant tumors of the female genital tract; (5) History of pelvic radiotherapy or systemic chemotherapy; (6) Presence of autoimmune or systemic diseases or use of immunosuppressive medications.
