full_text: SUMMARYOBJECTIVE:The aim of this study was to evaluate the predictive value of systemic inflammation markers for abnormal cervical screening results and high-grade cervical lesions in women participating in a human papillomavirus- and cytology-based screening program, thereby determining colposcopy indications more accurately to reduce unnecessary colposcopy requests and prevent overtreatment.METHODS:A total of 2,758 women who underwent cervical cancer screening between 2020 and 2025 were included in this retrospective cross-sectional study. Abnormal screening results were defined as abnormal cytology (≥Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance [ASC-US]) and/or high-risk human papillomavirus positivity. Hematological parameters measured within 1 month prior to screening were used to calculate neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and systemic immune-inflammation index. Continuous variables were evaluated using nonparametric tests, and the independent predictors of abnormal screening results and high-grade lesions were identified using logistic regression models.RESULTS:Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and systemic immune-inflammation index values were significantly higher in the abnormal smear groups and in human papillomavirus -positive patients (all p<0.001). Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio displayed the highest diagnostic performance for high-grade lesions (area under the curve=0.871; cutoff value >4.41, sensitivity 66.7%, specificity 99.2%), followed by systemic immune-inflammation index (area under the curve=0.847), while platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio showed lower specificity (area under the curve=0.741).CONCLUSION:In conclusion, our findings suggest that inflammatory markers are associated with abnormal cervical screening results. To determine the significance and clinical utility of serum inflammatory markers, multicenter clinical trials involving larger patient cohorts are needed.KEYWORDS: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, Human papillomavirus, Papanicolaou test, Inflammation METHODSStudy design and settingThis study was designed and reported in accordance with the STROBE Statement. It was conducted as a single-center, retrospective descriptive study at the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology of a tertiary care university hospital in Istanbul, Türkiye.Study population and sampling strategyThe study population consisted of women who presented to our outpatient clinic, had a complete blood count within 1 month, and underwent cervical cytology screening between January 1, 2020, and January 1, 2025. During the study period, a total of 2,758 pap smear tests and blood tests were performed. All women aged 21–65 years who were not pregnant, had no history of treatment for cervical lesions, had a pap smear and/or HPV testing and a blood test within the defined period, and had complete medical records were included. Patients under 21 or over 65 years of age, those with organ failure, people with an active infection or malignant neoplastic diseases, those who had been treated with antibiotics before testing, those taking medication impacting inflammatory markers, and pregnant women were excluded. A total of 82 cases were excluded due to not meeting the inclusion criteria and/or having incomplete data.Research questionsThe study aimed to evaluate effective alternative biomarkers for predicting cervical lesions and to assess their impact on clinical processes in determining the requirement for colposcopy.Data collection and variablesData were retrospectively obtained from the hospital’s Electronic Health Record (EHR) system. The following variables were recorded: age, parity, pap smear and HPV test results, PLR, NLR, and SII values based on the complete blood count results. All data were anonymized before analysis.Definition of exposure and outcome measuresExposure variables were defined as hematological inflammation parameters, including NLR, PLR, and SII, derived from complete blood count measurements obtained within 1 month preceding cervical cancer screening.NLR=neutrophil count/lymphocyte countPLR=platelet count/lymphocyte countSII=(platelet × neutrophil)/lymphocyteWe defined the primary outcome as the presence of an abnormal cervical screening result. Abnormal cytology (≥ASC-US) and/or high-risk HPV positivity were considered to constitute this outcome. Secondary outcomes consisted of the presence of high-grade cytological abnormalities (≥HSIL), evaluation of the relationship between inflammatory indicators and the presence of HPV, and investigation of the performance of hematological inflammation indices in the prediction of abnormal screening results.Follow-upNo follow-up was conducted because of the study’s retrospective design.Handling of missing dataCases with incomplete or missing data were excluded from the study.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 27. Quantitative variables were expressed as mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum, while qualitative variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. The Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test was used to compare qualitative data, and p<0.01 was considered statistically significant.Ethical considerationsEthical approval was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee (Approval No: 5163; Date: November 11, 2025). The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the ethical standards of the country of origin. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Study design and settingThis study was designed and reported in accordance with the STROBE Statement. It was conducted as a single-center, retrospective descriptive study at the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology of a tertiary care university hospital in Istanbul, Türkiye. RESULTSA total of 2,758 patients were included in the study. Continuous variables deviated from a normal distribution, as expected given the large sample size (Shapiro-Wilk, p<0.001), and were reported as medians (IQR); categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages.The median age of the study population was 37 [30–42] years, and 61.2% of the women (n=1,689) were multiparous. Based on the smear results, 66.8% of patients (n=1,841) had benign cytology, 18.2% (n=503) were ASC-US, and 11.3% (n=312) were LSIL. High-grade lesions (ASC-H, HSIL, AGC, AIS, and SCC/AdenoCa) accounted for 3.7% (n=102) of all cases. HPV positivity was observed in 20.8% of patients (n=573), and the most common subtype was HPV 16 (7.7%) (Table 1).Table 1Demographic, clinical, and laboratory characteristics of the study population.Variablen/median (IQR)%/(min–max)Shapiro-Wilk p-valueDemographic characteristicsNumber of patients2,758––Age (years)37 (30–42)21–53<0.001Parity—nulliparous1,06938.8–Parity—multiparous1,68961.2–Hematological parametersNLR2.04 (1.61–2.53)0.30–15.72<0.001PLR125.9 (101.4–156.9)32.4–1,200.0<0.001SII (neutrophil × platelet/lymphocyte)554.1 (414.1–741.6)88.3–7,104.0<0.001Smear resultsBenign1,84166.8–ASC-US50318.2–LSIL31211.3–ASC-H401.5–HSIL (CIN2–3)481.7–AGC/AIS/SCC–adenocarcinoma140.5–Continuous variables are presented as median (IQR, Q1–Q3). All continuous variables showed non-normal distribution (Shapiro-Wilk p<0.001). Categorical variables are expressed as n (%). IQR: interquartile range; NLR: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; PLR: platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio; SII: systemic immune-inflammation index (neutrophil × platelet/lymphocyte); LSIL: low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; ASC-H: atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL; HSIL: high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; CIN2–3: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grades 2–3; AGC: atypical glandular cells; AIS: adenocarcinoma in situ; SCC: squamous cell carcinoma; ASC-US: atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance.NLR, PLR, and SII values were significantly increased in line with cytological grade and were higher in groups with abnormal smear results compared to benign cases (all p<0.001). These markers were also elevated in HPV-positive patients, who had a significantly lower mean age. HPV positivity varied significantly among pap smear groups [χ 2 (7)=873.17, p<0.001]; this rate increased with the severity of cytology, rising from 5.2% in benign cases to 49.9% in ASC-US, 72.9% in HSIL, and 100% in high-grade lesions.Spearman’s correlation analysis revealed moderate-to-strong positive correlations for NLR with smear results, colposcopy findings, and HPV positivity (r=0.514–0.665; all p<0.001). For SII, similar but weaker associations were found (r=0.425–0.554). PLR exhibited weak correlations (r=0.261–0.329). Age showed weak and negative correlations with NLR and SII (Table 2).Table 2Correlation of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and systemic immune-inflammation index with clinical variables.MarkerAge r (p)Smear result r (p)Colposcopy r (p)HPV positivity r (p)NLR-0.048 (0.011)* 0.514 (<0.001)*** 0.572 (<0.001)*** 0.665 (<0.001)*** PLR-0.034 (0.078) ns0.261 (<0.001)*** 0.277 (<0.001)*** 0.329 (<0.001)*** SII-0.038 (0.048)* 0.425 (<0.001)*** 0.477 (<0.001)*** 0.554 (<0.001)*** Spearman correlation analysis.*p<0.05***p<0.001; ns: not significant. NLR: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; PLR: platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio; SII: systemic immune-inflammation index.In univariate analysis, NLR, PLR, SII, and HPV positivity proved to be significant predictors of each outcome (all p<0.001). In multivariate analysis, however, the significance of PLR was reduced. While NLR (OR 3.627) and HPV positivity (OR 1.755) were independent predictors of abnormal smear results, NLR (OR 2.245), SII (OR 1.439), and HPV positivity (OR 1.957) independently predicted advanced lesions (all p<0.001).The ROC analysis indicated that NLR demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance in identifying high-grade lesions (AUC=0.871); the optimal cutoff value was >4.41 (sensitivity 66.7%, specificity 99.2%). SII also demonstrated acceptable performance (AUC=0.847), whereas PLR showed lower accuracy (AUC=0.741). Since the cutoff values were obtained from the same dataset, external validation is required (Table 3).Table 3ROC analysis of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and systemic immune-inflammation index for the diagnosis of high-grade cervical lesions.MarkerAUC (95%CI)Optimal cut-offSensitivity (%)Specificity (%)PPV (%)NPV (%)NLR0.871 (0.827–0.916)>4.4166.799.276.498.7SII0.847 (0.800–0.895)>818.6574.583.114.598.8PLR0.741 (0.685–0.797)>133.9481.458.87.198.8Optimal cutoff values were determined using the Youden index. AUC confidence intervals were calculated by the DeLong method. An AUC >0.80 was considered to indicate good discriminatory performance. PPV: positive predictive value; NPV: negative predictive value; NLR: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; PLR: platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio; SII: systemic immune-inflammation index; CI: confidence interval; AUC: area under the curve DISCUSSIONThis study reveals that systemic inflammatory markers show a statistically significant correlation with the severity of cervical cytopathology and HPV positivity in a large screening cohort. Our key finding demonstrates a progressive increase in these markers as cervical lesions progress from benign to high grade. Specifically, the NLR emerged as the strongest independently predictive marker for high-grade lesions (HSIL+), with a remarkable specificity of 99.2% at a cutoff value of 4.41.The linear progression of HPV positivity—ranging from 5.2% in the benign group to 100% in high-grade lesions—highlights the critical role HPV performs in the development of cervical cancer. This tendency is consistent with the established understanding that high-risk HPV types promote a chronic inflammatory environment prone to neoplastic transformation 14 . Our results suggest that this inflammation is not limited to the local area, but appears to be systemic, as indicated by elevated hematological indices. The strong correlation between HPV positivity and NLR (r=0.665) suggests that the systemic inflammatory response is linked to viral load or the persistence of high-risk HPV subtypes. This situation is consistent with recent findings regarding the complementary role of HPV status in cytological smear reporting 15 . Additionally, in a study carried out by Tóth et al. involving 395 patients, the NLR was observed to be significantly associated with HPV DNA positivity and p16 expression; the NLR was found to be higher in HPV-positive patients. But its diagnostic performance remained moderate (AUC≈0.61) 16 .In a 2024 study by Qin and Zhang evaluating 324 participants, it was found that although NLR, PLR, and SII levels were significantly higher in patients with cervical lesions, the predictive power of these markers alone was restricted, and their AUC values were relatively low, which indicates that the clinical utility of these markers as triage biomarkers is limited. Compared with other studies, our study achieved an AUC of 0.871 for NLR, which is statistically significantly higher than previously reported values in the literature, including the AUC of 0.569 reported by Qin and Zhang 17 . This inconsistency may be related to our larger sample size (n=2,758) and the inclusion of a wider range of cytological abnormalities in the study.Atlıhan et al. noted that although both NLR and PLR levels tended to increase with the severity of CIN, only NLR showed a statistically significant association, whereas PLR was not an independent predictor 18 . The lower specificity of the PLR may be attributed to the fact that platelet count is influenced by multiple factors. Consequently, the NLR appears to be a more reliable biomarker for cervical lesions. While the PLR was found to be meaningful in the univariate analysis, it likely became insignificant after adjustment due to multicollinearity with the NLR and SII. In contrast, NLR was a significant independent predictor in all models; this confirms its clinical value as a simpler and more reliable parameter compared to PLR or SII.Our findings have significant clinical value. Given the NLR’s high specificity (99.2%) at a cutoff >4.41, this indicator can serve as a meaningful “diagnostic verification” tool in triage procedures. In situations where resources are limited or as a supplement to primary HPV/cytology screening, the NLR can help determine which patients should be referred for colposcopy, potentially reducing unnecessary procedures while ensuring that high-risk patients receive prompt treatment. The availability and cost-effectiveness of complete blood counts enhance the feasibility of incorporating these markers into routine clinical practice 19 .Despite the strengths of this study, certain limitations must also be considered. First, the retrospective nature of this study complicates the identification of a definitive causal relationship between systemic inflammation and the progression of cervical lesions. The small sample sizes in rare high-risk groups (AGC, AIS, SCC/adenocarcinoma) limit the generalizability of the findings. Also, although we have determined optimal threshold values, they were derived from the same data set; therefore, an external validation study in independent cohorts is required to verify their diagnostic performance 17 . CONCLUSIONIn conclusion, markers of systemic inflammation are associated with abnormal cervical screening results, but their clinical utility varies. Among these, NLR appears to be a reliable independent predictor of abnormal cytology and high-grade lesions, while PLR lost its significance after adjusting for covariates, and SII did not demonstrate superior performance. While these findings suggest that inflammation may play a role in cervical carcinogenesis and HPV persistence, they indicate that NLR is the most practical biomarker. Given their limited discriminatory ability, however, these markers should be considered complementary rather than primary screening tools. Future multicenter prospective studies are needed to validate these findings. INTRODUCTIONCervical cancer is a type of malignant tumor affecting the female reproductive system; it is the most common gynecological cancer in developing countries and accounts for the fourth most common type of cancer worldwide 1 Global Cancer Statistics (GLOBOCAN 2022) data indicate that 662,301 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2022, and an estimated 348,874 died from the disease 2 . As cancer screening programs have become more widely available, it is known that the rate of diagnosed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) has increased. In contrast, the incidence of advanced-stage cancer has decreased 3 . Early detection plays an important role in the prevention and treatment of cervical cancer 4 . During clinical practice, women who receive abnormal screening results should be evaluated with a colposcopy and biopsy to detect precancerous lesions and cervical cancer 5 .Human papillomavirus infection is a major risk factor associated with the development of cancer and can potentially lead to CIN. This infection is relatively common and affects approximately 90% of people during their lifetime, potentially leading to serious health issues. There are more than 200 genotypes of HPV. While the majority of them are not associated with complications and resolve spontaneously, some types are considered high-risk and can lead to cancer 6,7 .In recent studies, the potential value of hematological markers in the early diagnosis and prognosis of cancers has been recognized. It is considered that inflammatory parameters such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) are correlated with tumor cell formation, progression, and prognosis 8 . full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONThis study reveals that systemic inflammatory markers show a statistically significant correlation with the severity of cervical cytopathology and HPV positivity in a large screening cohort. Our key finding demonstrates a progressive increase in these markers as cervical lesions progress from benign to high grade. Specifically, the NLR emerged as the strongest independently predictive marker for high-grade lesions (HSIL+), with a remarkable specificity of 99.2% at a cutoff value of 4.41.The linear progression of HPV positivity—ranging from 5.2% in the benign group to 100% in high-grade lesions—highlights the critical role HPV performs in the development of cervical cancer. This tendency is consistent with the established understanding that high-risk HPV types promote a chronic inflammatory environment prone to neoplastic transformation 14 . Our results suggest that this inflammation is not limited to the local area, but appears to be systemic, as indicated by elevated hematological indices. The strong correlation between HPV positivity and NLR (r=0.665) suggests that the systemic inflammatory response is linked to viral load or the persistence of high-risk HPV subtypes. This situation is consistent with recent findings regarding the complementary role of HPV status in cytological smear reporting 15 . Additionally, in a study carried out by Tóth et al. involving 395 patients, the NLR was observed to be significantly associated with HPV DNA positivity and p16 expression; the NLR was found to be higher in HPV-positive patients. But its diagnostic performance remained moderate (AUC≈0.61) 16 .In a 2024 study by Qin and Zhang evaluating 324 participants, it was found that although NLR, PLR, and SII levels were significantly higher in patients with cervical lesions, the predictive power of these markers alone was restricted, and their AUC values were relatively low, which indicates that the clinical utility of these markers as triage biomarkers is limited. Compared with other studies, our study achieved an AUC of 0.871 for NLR, which is statistically significantly higher than previously reported values in the literature, including the AUC of 0.569 reported by Qin and Zhang 17 . This inconsistency may be related to our larger sample size (n=2,758) and the inclusion of a wider range of cytological abnormalities in the study.Atlıhan et al. noted that although both NLR and PLR levels tended to increase with the severity of CIN, only NLR showed a statistically significant association, whereas PLR was not an independent predictor 18 . The lower specificity of the PLR may be attributed to the fact that platelet count is influenced by multiple factors. Consequently, the NLR appears to be a more reliable biomarker for cervical lesions. While the PLR was found to be meaningful in the univariate analysis, it likely became insignificant after adjustment due to multicollinearity with the NLR and SII. In contrast, NLR was a significant independent predictor in all models; this confirms its clinical value as a simpler and more reliable parameter compared to PLR or SII.Our findings have significant clinical value. Given the NLR’s high specificity (99.2%) at a cutoff >4.41, this indicator can serve as a meaningful “diagnostic verification” tool in triage procedures. In situations where resources are limited or as a supplement to primary HPV/cytology screening, the NLR can help determine which patients should be referred for colposcopy, potentially reducing unnecessary procedures while ensuring that high-risk patients receive prompt treatment. The availability and cost-effectiveness of complete blood counts enhance the feasibility of incorporating these markers into routine clinical practice 19 .Despite the strengths of this study, certain limitations must also be considered. First, the retrospective nature of this study complicates the identification of a definitive causal relationship between systemic inflammation and the progression of cervical lesions. The small sample sizes in rare high-risk groups (AGC, AIS, SCC/adenocarcinoma) limit the generalizability of the findings. Also, although we have determined optimal threshold values, they were derived from the same data set; therefore, an external validation study in independent cohorts is required to verify their diagnostic performance 17 .
full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONIn conclusion, markers of systemic inflammation are associated with abnormal cervical screening results, but their clinical utility varies. Among these, NLR appears to be a reliable independent predictor of abnormal cytology and high-grade lesions, while PLR lost its significance after adjusting for covariates, and SII did not demonstrate superior performance. While these findings suggest that inflammation may play a role in cervical carcinogenesis and HPV persistence, they indicate that NLR is the most practical biomarker. Given their limited discriminatory ability, however, these markers should be considered complementary rather than primary screening tools. Future multicenter prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONCervical cancer is a type of malignant tumor affecting the female reproductive system; it is the most common gynecological cancer in developing countries and accounts for the fourth most common type of cancer worldwide 1 Global Cancer Statistics (GLOBOCAN 2022) data indicate that 662,301 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2022, and an estimated 348,874 died from the disease 2 . As cancer screening programs have become more widely available, it is known that the rate of diagnosed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) has increased. In contrast, the incidence of advanced-stage cancer has decreased 3 . Early detection plays an important role in the prevention and treatment of cervical cancer 4 . During clinical practice, women who receive abnormal screening results should be evaluated with a colposcopy and biopsy to detect precancerous lesions and cervical cancer 5 .Human papillomavirus infection is a major risk factor associated with the development of cancer and can potentially lead to CIN. This infection is relatively common and affects approximately 90% of people during their lifetime, potentially leading to serious health issues. There are more than 200 genotypes of HPV. While the majority of them are not associated with complications and resolve spontaneously, some types are considered high-risk and can lead to cancer 6,7 .In recent studies, the potential value of hematological markers in the early diagnosis and prognosis of cancers has been recognized. It is considered that inflammatory parameters such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) are correlated with tumor cell formation, progression, and prognosis 8 . The cytokines, vascular endothelial growth factor, and chemokines produced by neutrophils are involved in tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis. In the same way, platelets stimulate tumor cell proliferation and help these cells evade immune control, thereby promoting tumor spread 9 . The is a novel marker of inflammation and a useful biomarker for assessing the prognosis of various cancers; it is calculated using the formula: platelet count × neutrophil count/lymphocyte count 10,11 . Several inflammatory markers in the blood are linked to the formation and development of tumors in various types of cancer 12,13 . In our study, 2,758 patients who had undergone smear tests were retrospectively analyzed to ensure accurate patient assessment, improve screening effectiveness, prevent unnecessary colposcopy and biopsy referrals, and reduce overtreatment to identify more effective alternative biomarkers for predicting cervical lesions and establishing more appropriate clinical criteria for colposcopy. Study population and sampling strategyThe study population consisted of women who presented to our outpatient clinic, had a complete blood count within 1 month, and underwent cervical cytology screening between January 1, 2020, and January 1, 2025. During the study period, a total of 2,758 pap smear tests and blood tests were performed. All women aged 21–65 years who were not pregnant, had no history of treatment for cervical lesions, had a pap smear and/or HPV testing and a blood test within the defined period, and had complete medical records were included. Patients under 21 or over 65 years of age, those with organ failure, people with an active infection or malignant neoplastic diseases, those who had been treated with antibiotics before testing, those taking medication impacting inflammatory markers, and pregnant women were excluded. A total of 82 cases were excluded due to not meeting the inclusion criteria and/or having incomplete data. Research questionsThe study aimed to evaluate effective alternative biomarkers for predicting cervical lesions and to assess their impact on clinical processes in determining the requirement for colposcopy. Data collection and variablesData were retrospectively obtained from the hospital’s Electronic Health Record (EHR) system. The following variables were recorded: age, parity, pap smear and HPV test results, PLR, NLR, and SII values based on the complete blood count results. All data were anonymized before analysis. Definition of exposure and outcome measuresExposure variables were defined as hematological inflammation parameters, including NLR, PLR, and SII, derived from complete blood count measurements obtained within 1 month preceding cervical cancer screening.NLR=neutrophil count/lymphocyte countPLR=platelet count/lymphocyte countSII=(platelet × neutrophil)/lymphocyteWe defined the primary outcome as the presence of an abnormal cervical screening result. Abnormal cytology (≥ASC-US) and/or high-risk HPV positivity were considered to constitute this outcome. Secondary outcomes consisted of the presence of high-grade cytological abnormalities (≥HSIL), evaluation of the relationship between inflammatory indicators and the presence of HPV, and investigation of the performance of hematological inflammation indices in the prediction of abnormal screening results. Follow-upNo follow-up was conducted because of the study’s retrospective design. Handling of missing dataCases with incomplete or missing data were excluded from the study. Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 27. Quantitative variables were expressed as mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum, while qualitative variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. The Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test was used to compare qualitative data, and p<0.01 was considered statistically significant. Ethical considerationsEthical approval was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee (Approval No: 5163; Date: November 11, 2025). The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the ethical standards of the country of origin. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Funding Statement Funding: none. FootnotesFunding: none. DATA AVAILABILITY STATEMENTThe datasets generated and/or analyzed during the current study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. full_text: Radiotherapy (RT) remains a cornerstone in the management of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) across both definitive and multimodality treatment settings. While hypofractionated radiotherapy (HFRT) has become an established standard of care for several solid tumors, including prostate, breast, lung, and rectal cancers, its adoption in HNSCC has been more cautious owing to the complex anatomy of the head and neck region, the proximity of numerous critical organs at risk, and concerns regarding severe late toxicity. However, major advances in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), image guidance, adaptive radiotherapy, and radiobiological understanding have renewed interest in HFRT as a strategy to maintain oncological efficacy while reducing overall treatment time. Additional drivers include the need to optimize healthcare resource utilization, improve access to radiotherapy in low- and middle-income countries, and minimize hospital visits, as highlighted during the COVID-19 pandemic. Recent prospective evidence has further strengthened the rationale for carefully selected hypofractionated approaches in HNSCC. In elderly and frail patients, the phase III ELAN-RT trial has also provided prospective evidence regarding a tailored hypofractionated approach for patients unable to undergo standard treatment. Among head and neck subsites, laryngeal cancer—particularly early-stage glottic carcinoma—represents the most mature clinical model for HFRT and therefore constitutes the principal focus of this review, while evidence from other HNSCC subsites is examined to assess the broader applicability of hypofractionated treatment strategies. This review critically summarizes the radiobiological rationale, current clinical evidence, technological advances, and ongoing challenges surrounding radical HFRT in HNSCC, with particular emphasis on laryngeal cancer, and discusses future directions for its broader implementation in clinical practice. 2Materials and methodsAn electronic literature search was conducted in the PubMed database for English articles published up to May 31,2026. Boolean operators (OR, AND) were used to combine the following search terms: “hypofractionation”, “head and neck cancer”, “radiation therapy”, “modern radiation therapy”, “intensity-modulated radiotherapy”, “IMRT”, “HNC”, “volumetric modulated arc therapy”, “vmat”, “late effects”, “radiation induced toxicity”, “toxicity”, “radical radiotherapy”, “SBRT”, “chemoradiotherapy”, “green radiotherapy”. Two independent reviewers (C.G and O.S.) screened titles and abstracts and performed the final article selection. Any discrepancy was resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (G.C.I.). Thereafter, meeting proceedings (European Society of Medical Oncology – ESMO –, European Society for Radiotherapy & Oncology – ESTRO –, American Society of Clinical Oncology – ASCO – and American Society for Radiation Oncology – ASTRO), trial registries (clinicaltrials.gov), reference lists of published studies, review articles and relevant books were also considered. This review was designed as a narrative review supported by a structured literature search rather than as a systematic or scoping review; therefore, a PRISMA-based study selection process was not prospectively performed and corresponding record counts are not available. The bibliographic search was restricted to PubMed, which should be acknowledged as a methodological limitation. 3.2.5Elderly and frail patientsThe potential role of hypofractionated radiotherapy may be particularly relevant in older and frail patients, a population frequently underrepresented in prospective clinical trials and often unable to tolerate prolonged treatment courses. The ELAN-RT trial specifically addressed this population, enrolling patients aged ≥70 years with stage II–IV unresectable HNSCC who were deemed frail based on geriatric assessment (16). Participants were randomized to standard fractionation (70 Gy in 35 fractions over 7 weeks) or a hypofractionated split-course regimen (55 Gy in 20 fractions), delivered in two 2-week courses separated by a planned 2-week treatment-free interval. The hypofractionated regimen met the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for the primary endpoint of being alive without locoregional disease at 6 months and was associated with numerically lower rates of severe acute toxicity. However, overall survival favored standard fractionation, with a median OS of 18.9 months compared with 13.0 months in the hypofractionated arm (16). Importantly, the experimental regimen should be interpreted as split-course hypofractionation rather than continuous HFRT. The planned treatment interruption is radiobiologically relevant in HNSCC, as it occurs during a period in which accelerated tumor repopulation may become increasingly important, potentially counteracting some of the benefits associated with a shorter fractionation schedule. Whether this contributed to the observed difference in overall survival remains unknown and cannot be established from ELAN-RT (16). These findings should therefore not be extrapolated to fit older patients solely on the basis of chronological age. For carefully selected frail patients unable to tolerate standard continuous radiotherapy, the ELAN-RT regimen may represent a pragmatic alternative (16); however, standard fractionation should remain preferred when clinically feasible. 3Results3.1Radiobiological evidenceRadiobiological modeling and translational research provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying differential responses to fractionation in HNSCC. Using an advanced Monte Carlo simulation model of HNSCC originating from a single cancer stem cell (CSC), Marcu and Marcu demonstrated that hypofractionated radiotherapy may be particularly advantageous in early-stage, well-oxygenated tumors (19). In these tumors, shortening the overall treatment time may mitigate the detrimental effects of accelerated tumor repopulation, a phenomenon largely driven by the CSC compartment. In their model, CSCs represented approximately 5.9% of the pretreatment tumor population and exhibited substantial radioresistance, with a surviving fraction at 2 Gy (SF2) of approximately 77% (19). These assumptions were based on seminal studies identifying CD44+ cells as the tumorigenic subpopulation in HNSCC capable of self-renewal and tumor initiation (20), as well as evidence demonstrating enhanced radioresistance among cancer-initiating cells (21). Conversely, the same modeling studies suggested that advanced tumors characterized by severe hypoxia (oxygen tension<6 mmHg) may derive greater benefit from hyperfractionated approaches (19). In this setting, increased opportunities for reoxygenation and cellular redistribution may partially compensate for hypoxia-induced radioresistance, potentially improving tumor control compared with larger fraction sizes (19). However, these findings derive from theoretical radiobiological modeling and remain hypothesis-generating, requiring clinical validation before they can inform fractionation selection. Beyond direct cytotoxic effects, increasing evidence indicates that fractionation schedules may differentially modulate antitumor immunity. In vitro studies by Wimmer et al. demonstrated that hypofractionated irradiation (5 × 3 Gy) significantly altered the expression of immune checkpoint molecules in HNSCC cell lines regardless of human papilloma virus (HPV) status (22). Hypofractionation induced upregulation of the immunosuppressive molecules programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), PD-L2, and herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM), whereas the co-stimulatory molecule inducible T-cell costimulator ligand (ICOS-L) was selectively increased in HPV-positive cell lines (22). These findings suggest that radiation dose and fractionation may influence the immunological landscape of HNSCC and potentially affect responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Additional support for this concept comes from the work of Frey et al., who demonstrated that hypofractionated radiotherapy can stimulate dendritic-cell activation and promote coordinated recruitment of innate and adaptive immune populations within the tumor microenvironment (23). Collectively, these preclinical observations suggest that hypofractionated regimens may exert biological effects extending beyond tumor cell kill, influencing both CSC dynamics and immune responses. Such findings provide a rationale for further investigation of the interaction between fractionation and antitumor immunity. However, their clinical relevance in HNSCC and their implications for combination with immunotherapy remain to be established.3.2Clinical evidenceThe following section reviews the clinical evidence on HFRT for laryngeal, oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal, and oral cavity cancers. The available data are narratively summarized and critically discussed, while the treatment schedules and key findings of the principal studies are presented in Table 1.Table 1Comparative summary of clinical characteristics and key findings of the main HFRT studies.StudyHypofractionated scheduleCancer typeKey findingsKang et al. 2019 (35)Prospective59.5 Gy to GTV and 47.6 Gy to the remaining larynx/17 fractionsor55 Gy to GTV and 40.7 Gy the remaining larynx/11 fractions• Glottic tumors cT1-T2• One dose level not tolerated due to dose-limiting toxicitySchwartz et al. 2017 (36)Prospective50 Gy/15 fractionsor45 Gy/10 fractionsor42.5 Gy/5 fractions• Glottic tumors cTis-T2• SBRT feasible with acceptable acute toxicityKovarik et al. 2023 (28)Prospective55 Gy/20 fractions vs63–65 Gy/30 fractions• Glottic tumors cT2• No significant differences in DFS, OS and LRFS• Similar toxicityHuang et al. 2020 (43)Retrospective60 Gy/20 fractions• Oropharynx• Acceptable locoregional control and disease control ratesBentzen et al. 2026 (15)Prospective55 Gy/20 fractions vs66 Gy/33 fractions• HNSCC (~51% of the cohort was OPSCC)• Non-inferior to normofractionated RT in terms of locoregional control and late toxicityFranzese et al. 2020 (48)Prospective69.96-54.45 Gy/33 fractions vs 66–54 Gy/30 fractions• HNSCC• No significant late toxicity differences• Higher rate of locoregional progressionMayo et al. 2022 (46)Retrospective50 or 55 Gy/20 fractions• HNSCC• Definitive or postoperative treatment appears safe and well tolerated• No G4 o G5 toxicityLiu et al. 2023 (50)Prospective60 Gy/25 fractions vs69.96 Gy/33 fractions• Nasopharyngeal tumors• No significant differences in PFS or OS• Similar toxicityHNSCC, Head and Neck squamous cell carcinoma; OS, overall survival; DFS, disease free survival; PFS- progression free survival; SBRT, stereotactic body radiotherapy; LRFS, local recurrence free survival; HFRT, hypofractionated radiotherapy; GTV, gross tumor volume.3.2.1LarynxAmong head and neck malignancies, laryngeal cancer represents the most mature clinical model for the application of hypofractionated radiotherapy. In fact, moderate hypofractionation is currently recognized as a standard treatment option for early-stage glottic cancer and is included among the recommended radiotherapy schedules in current NCCN guidelines (24). The radiobiological rationale for hypofractionation in early glottic carcinoma is supported by evidence demonstrating the importance of both fraction size and overall treatment time (OTT). In a seminal analysis of T1–T2 glottic carcinomas, Le et al. reported that local control in T2 disease was significantly influenced by fractionation parameters, with larger fraction sizes (2.25 Gy) and shorter treatment durations (<43 days) associated with improved 5-year local control rates (25). These findings were subsequently corroborated by Yamazaki et al. in a prospective randomized trial of T1N0M0 glottic carcinoma, which demonstrated superior local control with 2.25 Gy fractions compared with conventional 2 Gy fractions, despite the lower total dose delivered in the hypofractionated arm (26). Additional evidence supporting hypofractionation has emerged from large population-based analyses. Using the National Cancer Database, Bledsoe et al. reported a potential overall survival (OS) advantage associated with hypofractionated schedules in early glottic cancer (27). However, given the retrospective registry-based nature of this analysis, the observed survival difference should be interpreted cautiously because of the potential for selection bias and residual confounding. More recently, Kovarik et al. compared 55 Gy in 20 fractions with conventional regimens delivering 63–65 Gy in 30 fractions for T2N0M0 disease and observed comparable oncological outcomes, with no significant differences in survival or recurrence rates (28). Although not statistically significant, a trend toward reduced acute dysphagia was noted in patients receiving hypofractionated treatment (28). Beyond tumor control, functional preservation remains a major therapeutic objective in laryngeal cancer. Prospective evaluations using the Voice Handicap Index (VHI) have demonstrated favorable long-term voice outcomes following hypofractionated radiotherapy for early glottic cancer (29, 30). These findings are consistent with earlier evidence from altered-fractionation studies showing that shortening OTT may improve local control while also improving voice preservation in patients with laryngeal cancer (31). Collectively, these data support the use of moderate hypofractionation as an effective and function-preserving treatment strategy for early-stage glottic carcinoma. In parallel with changes in dose fractionation, contemporary image-guided techniques have enabled investigation of reduced target volumes for early glottic cancer, particularly single-vocal-cord irradiation (SVCI). Initial experiences established the technical feasibility of limiting irradiation to the involved vocal cord, with encouraging local control and potential reductions in the irradiation of adjacent normal tissues (32). Subsequently, Al-Mamgani et al. evaluated image-guided hypofractionated SVCI (58.08 Gy in 16 fractions) in T1a glottic cancer, reporting excellent local control, limited acute toxicity, and favorable patient-reported voice outcomes (30). These findings were subsequently supported in an expanded cohort of 111 patients, in which 5-year local control and laryngectomy-free survival were 97.1% and 98.1%, respectively, although grade 3 late toxicity occurred in 6.5% of evaluable patients (33). Most recently, a prospective randomized phase II trial compared hypofractionated SVCI (58.08 Gy in 16 fractions) with whole-larynx radiotherapy (63 Gy in 28 fractions) in 57 patients with T1aN0 glottic cancer, reporting comparable local control together with superior voice outcomes and a favorable toxicity profile with SVCI (34). These findings support limited-volume hypofractionated irradiation as a promising strategy for carefully selected T1a glottic cancers, although its implementation requires high-quality image guidance and precise target definition, and further prospective validation remains warranted. Building upon the success of moderate hypofractionation, several groups have explored stereotactic body RT (SBRT) as a means of further reducing treatment duration. Early phase I dose-escalation studies highlighted both the promise and the challenges of this approach. Notably, Kang et al. reported premature closure of one treatment arm because of unexpected dose-limiting toxicities, underscoring the narrow therapeutic window of extreme hypofractionation in the larynx and the exquisite sensitivity of endolaryngeal structures to large fraction sizes (35). Subsequent prospective investigations demonstrated more encouraging results. Schwartz et al. and Sher et al. reported promising local control rates with five-fraction SBRT regimens, accompanied by predominantly grade 1–2 acute toxicities, mainly transient hoarseness and mild dysphagia (36, 37). Importantly, long-term functional assessments suggested preservation of voice quality and a low incidence of severe late toxicity when strict target volume definitions and dosimetric constraints were respected (37). More recently, Sanguineti et al. evaluated an ultra-short regimen of 36 Gy delivered in three fractions for T1 glottic carcinoma in a phase I/II trial (38). The study demonstrated excellent local control, favorable functional outcomes, and no grade 3 or higher acute or late toxicities, further supporting the feasibility of carefully selected ultra-hypofractionated approaches. Nevertheless, given the limited clinical experience and the potentially severe consequences of treatment-related toxicity, SBRT for laryngeal cancer should currently remain restricted to prospective clinical trials led by highly specialized centers with extensive expertise in stereotactic radiotherapy, image guidance, and motion management. Beyond radiobiological and resource-related considerations, shorter treatment duration may also influence the positioning of radiotherapy among available curative options. This is particularly relevant in early glottic cancer, where both radiotherapy and transoral surgical approaches are established treatments. By reducing overall treatment time, moderate hypofractionation may lessen a practical disadvantage of conventionally fractionated radiotherapy and improve convenience for appropriately selected patients. Nevertheless, hypofractionation does not alter the underlying oncological and functional considerations informing the choice between radiotherapy and surgery, and treatment selection should remain based on disease characteristics, expected functional outcomes, and patient preferences.In contrast to early-stage disease, evidence supporting hypofractionation in locally advanced laryngeal cancer remains limited. full_text_sections.abstract: Radiotherapy (RT) remains a cornerstone in the management of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) across both definitive and multimodality treatment settings. While hypofractionated radiotherapy (HFRT) has become an established standard of care for several solid tumors, including prostate, breast, lung, and rectal cancers, its adoption in HNSCC has been more cautious owing to the complex anatomy of the head and neck region, the proximity of numerous critical organs at risk, and concerns regarding severe late toxicity. However, major advances in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), image guidance, adaptive radiotherapy, and radiobiological understanding have renewed interest in HFRT as a strategy to maintain oncological efficacy while reducing overall treatment time. Additional drivers include the need to optimize healthcare resource utilization, improve access to radiotherapy in low- and middle-income countries, and minimize hospital visits, as highlighted during the COVID-19 pandemic. Recent prospective evidence has further strengthened the rationale for carefully selected hypofractionated approaches in HNSCC. In elderly and frail patients, the phase III ELAN-RT trial has also provided prospective evidence regarding a tailored hypofractionated approach for patients unable to undergo standard treatment. Among head and neck subsites, laryngeal cancer—particularly early-stage glottic carcinoma—represents the most mature clinical model for HFRT and therefore constitutes the principal focus of this review, while evidence from other HNSCC subsites is examined to assess the broader applicability of hypofractionated treatment strategies. This review critically summarizes the radiobiological rationale, current clinical evidence, technological advances, and ongoing challenges surrounding radical HFRT in HNSCC, with particular emphasis on laryngeal cancer, and discusses future directions for its broader implementation in clinical practice.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Materials and methodsAn electronic literature search was conducted in the PubMed database for English articles published up to May 31,2026. Boolean operators (OR, AND) were used to combine the following search terms: “hypofractionation”, “head and neck cancer”, “radiation therapy”, “modern radiation therapy”, “intensity-modulated radiotherapy”, “IMRT”, “HNC”, “volumetric modulated arc therapy”, “vmat”, “late effects”, “radiation induced toxicity”, “toxicity”, “radical radiotherapy”, “SBRT”, “chemoradiotherapy”, “green radiotherapy”. Two independent reviewers (C.G and O.S.) screened titles and abstracts and performed the final article selection. Any discrepancy was resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (G.C.I.). Thereafter, meeting proceedings (European Society of Medical Oncology – ESMO –, European Society for Radiotherapy & Oncology – ESTRO –, American Society of Clinical Oncology – ASCO – and American Society for Radiation Oncology – ASTRO), trial registries (clinicaltrials.gov), reference lists of published studies, review articles and relevant books were also considered. This review was designed as a narrative review supported by a structured literature search rather than as a systematic or scoping review; therefore, a PRISMA-based study selection process was not prospectively performed and corresponding record counts are not available. The bibliographic search was restricted to PubMed, which should be acknowledged as a methodological limitation. 3.2.5Elderly and frail patientsThe potential role of hypofractionated radiotherapy may be particularly relevant in older and frail patients, a population frequently underrepresented in prospective clinical trials and often unable to tolerate prolonged treatment courses. The ELAN-RT trial specifically addressed this population, enrolling patients aged ≥70 years with stage II–IV unresectable HNSCC who were deemed frail based on geriatric assessment (16). Participants were randomized to standard fractionation (70 Gy in 35 fractions over 7 weeks) or a hypofractionated split-course regimen (55 Gy in 20 fractions), delivered in two 2-week courses separated by a planned 2-week treatment-free interval. The hypofractionated regimen met the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for the primary endpoint of being alive without locoregional disease at 6 months and was associated with numerically lower rates of severe acute toxicity. However, overall survival favored standard fractionation, with a median OS of 18.9 months compared with 13.0 months in the hypofractionated arm (16). Importantly, the experimental regimen should be interpreted as split-course hypofractionation rather than continuous HFRT. The planned treatment interruption is radiobiologically relevant in HNSCC, as it occurs during a period in which accelerated tumor repopulation may become increasingly important, potentially counteracting some of the benefits associated with a shorter fractionation schedule. Whether this contributed to the observed difference in overall survival remains unknown and cannot be established from ELAN-RT (16). These findings should therefore not be extrapolated to fit older patients solely on the basis of chronological age. For carefully selected frail patients unable to tolerate standard continuous radiotherapy, the ELAN-RT regimen may represent a pragmatic alternative (16); however, standard fractionation should remain preferred when clinically feasible.
full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Radiobiological evidenceRadiobiological modeling and translational research provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying differential responses to fractionation in HNSCC. Using an advanced Monte Carlo simulation model of HNSCC originating from a single cancer stem cell (CSC), Marcu and Marcu demonstrated that hypofractionated radiotherapy may be particularly advantageous in early-stage, well-oxygenated tumors (19). In these tumors, shortening the overall treatment time may mitigate the detrimental effects of accelerated tumor repopulation, a phenomenon largely driven by the CSC compartment. In their model, CSCs represented approximately 5.9% of the pretreatment tumor population and exhibited substantial radioresistance, with a surviving fraction at 2 Gy (SF2) of approximately 77% (19). These assumptions were based on seminal studies identifying CD44+ cells as the tumorigenic subpopulation in HNSCC capable of self-renewal and tumor initiation (20), as well as evidence demonstrating enhanced radioresistance among cancer-initiating cells (21). Conversely, the same modeling studies suggested that advanced tumors characterized by severe hypoxia (oxygen tension<6 mmHg) may derive greater benefit from hyperfractionated approaches (19). In this setting, increased opportunities for reoxygenation and cellular redistribution may partially compensate for hypoxia-induced radioresistance, potentially improving tumor control compared with larger fraction sizes (19). However, these findings derive from theoretical radiobiological modeling and remain hypothesis-generating, requiring clinical validation before they can inform fractionation selection. Beyond direct cytotoxic effects, increasing evidence indicates that fractionation schedules may differentially modulate antitumor immunity. In vitro studies by Wimmer et al. demonstrated that hypofractionated irradiation (5 × 3 Gy) significantly altered the expression of immune checkpoint molecules in HNSCC cell lines regardless of human papilloma virus (HPV) status (22). Hypofractionation induced upregulation of the immunosuppressive molecules programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), PD-L2, and herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM), whereas the co-stimulatory molecule inducible T-cell costimulator ligand (ICOS-L) was selectively increased in HPV-positive cell lines (22). These findings suggest that radiation dose and fractionation may influence the immunological landscape of HNSCC and potentially affect responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Additional support for this concept comes from the work of Frey et al., who demonstrated that hypofractionated radiotherapy can stimulate dendritic-cell activation and promote coordinated recruitment of innate and adaptive immune populations within the tumor microenvironment (23). Collectively, these preclinical observations suggest that hypofractionated regimens may exert biological effects extending beyond tumor cell kill, influencing both CSC dynamics and immune responses. Such findings provide a rationale for further investigation of the interaction between fractionation and antitumor immunity. However, their clinical relevance in HNSCC and their implications for combination with immunotherapy remain to be established.3.2Clinical evidenceThe following section reviews the clinical evidence on HFRT for laryngeal, oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal, and oral cavity cancers. In fact, moderate hypofractionation is currently recognized as a standard treatment option for early-stage glottic cancer and is included among the recommended radiotherapy schedules in current NCCN guidelines (24). The radiobiological rationale for hypofractionation in early glottic carcinoma is supported by evidence demonstrating the importance of both fraction size and overall treatment time (OTT). In a seminal analysis of T1–T2 glottic carcinomas, Le et al. reported that local control in T2 disease was significantly influenced by fractionation parameters, with larger fraction sizes (2.25 Gy) and shorter treatment durations (<43 days) associated with improved 5-year local control rates (25). These findings were subsequently corroborated by Yamazaki et al. in a prospective randomized trial of T1N0M0 glottic carcinoma, which demonstrated superior local control with 2.25 Gy fractions compared with conventional 2 Gy fractions, despite the lower total dose delivered in the hypofractionated arm (26). Using the National Cancer Database, Bledsoe et al. reported a potential overall survival (OS) advantage associated with hypofractionated schedules in early glottic cancer (27). However, given the retrospective registry-based nature of this analysis, the observed survival difference should be interpreted cautiously because of the potential for selection bias and residual confounding. More recently, Kovarik et al. compared 55 Gy in 20 fractions with conventional regimens delivering 63–65 Gy in 30 fractions for T2N0M0 disease and observed comparable oncological outcomes, with no significant differences in survival or recurrence rates (28). Although not statistically significant, a trend toward reduced acute dysphagia was noted in patients receiving hypofractionated treatment (28). Beyond tumor control, functional preservation remains a major therapeutic objective in laryngeal cancer. full_text_sections.conclusion: 4ConclusionHypofractionated radiotherapy represents an increasingly investigated strategy for optimizing the delivery of RT in HNSCC. Advances in treatment planning, image guidance, and radiobiological understanding have renewed interest in abbreviated treatment schedules capable of reducing overall treatment time, improving patient convenience, increasing treatment capacity, and potentially lowering healthcare costs while maintaining oncological efficacy in appropriately selected settings. The strength of evidence supporting HFRT, however, varies considerably across head and neck cancer subsites. Among these, laryngeal cancer—particularly early-stage glottic carcinoma—represents the most mature clinical model, with moderate hypofractionation recognized as a standard treatment approach supported by robust long-term efficacy and functional outcome data. In contrast, evidence in other disease sites remains less definitive. Recent randomized data, including the HYPNO (15) trial, have strengthened the evidence for moderate hypofractionation in selected patients with locally advanced HNSCC, while nasopharyngeal and oral cavity carcinomas remain areas of active investigation with limited evidence. In elderly and frail patients, ELAN-RT (16) supports hypofractionated split-course radiotherapy as a potential alternative when standard treatment is not feasible, although the observed overall survival difference underscores the importance of careful patient selection. Beyond logistical advantages, hypofractionation may have biological implications related to shortening overall treatment time and modulation of antitumor immune responses. However, the clinical relevance of these mechanisms remains incompletely defined, and available radiobiological and preclinical findings should not be directly extrapolated to treatment selection or combinations with immunotherapy. Concerns regarding late toxicity, patient selection, target volume definition, and the optimal integration of systemic therapies further emphasize the need for careful evaluation of HFRT within specific clinical contexts. At present, conventional fractionation remains the standard of care for most patients with HNSCC. Future progress will depend on well-designed prospective randomized trials incorporating subsite-specific analyses, standardized toxicity reporting, patient-reported outcomes, functional endpoints, and long-term follow-up. The identification of biological, molecular, and imaging biomarkers capable of guiding individualized fractionation strategies may further help define which patients are most likely to benefit from hypofractionated approaches. Overall, HFRT represents an established treatment option in selected HNSCC settings, most notably early-stage glottic cancer, while its role across other disease subsites and clinical scenarios remains heterogeneous and, in many cases, investigational. Emerging prospective evidence supports continued evaluation of appropriately selected hypofractionated strategies, but broader implementation should remain guided by disease setting, patient selection, treatment technique, and the maturity of the available clinical evidence.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionRadiotherapy (RT) represents a cornerstone in the management of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), playing a central role across virtually all disease stages and treatment settings, either alone or in combination with surgery and systemic therapies (1, 2). Over the last decade, hypofractionated radiotherapy (HFRT) has progressively emerged as a standard treatment approach in several solid malignancies. This paradigm shift has been particularly evident in prostate, breast, lung, and rectal cancers, where shorter treatment schedules have demonstrated oncological outcomes and toxicity profiles comparable to those of conventional fractionation, while simultaneously improving patient convenience, treatment accessibility, and healthcare resource utilization (3–11). The primary objective of these strategies has been to preserve treatment efficacy and safety while substantially reducing overall treatment time (12). In HNSCC, however, the implementation of HFRT has historically been more challenging because of the close proximity of target volumes to multiple radiosensitive organs at risk (OARs) and concerns regarding potentially severe late toxicity from larger doses per fraction. Consequently, the delivery of larger doses per fraction raises concerns regarding the risk of severe and potentially irreversible late toxicities, such as soft-tissue necrosis, dysphagia, aspiration, cranial neuropathies, and xerostomia. Furthermore, the radiobiological characteristics of HNSCC and surrounding normal tissues have traditionally favored conventional fractionation schedules, given the relatively low α/β ratio of late-responding tissues and the associated risk of increased late toxicity with dose escalation per fraction.These concerns are reflected in the substantial burden of treatment-related toxicity historically associated with RT for HNSCC (13, 14). Nevertheless, HFRT remains an area of growing clinical interest, driven by advances in treatment planning, image guidance, intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), adaptive radiotherapy, and improved understanding of radiobiological principles (12, 13). Such technological developments have enhanced dose conformity and OAR sparing, potentially expanding the therapeutic window for hypofractionated approaches. Interest in HFRT has been further stimulated by global disparities in access to radiotherapy. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where radiotherapy resources are often limited and treatment demand exceeds capacity, shorter treatment schedules may significantly improve access to potentially curative therapy. Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the potential advantages of reducing the number of hospital visits without compromising treatment outcomes.
