full_text: Cervical cancer remains a leading malignancy among women globally, with its pathogenesis strongly associated with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Despite the widespread adoption of HPV testing in cervical cancer screening, its suboptimal specificity frequently results in overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Gene methylation, a key epigenetic modification, has emerged as a highly specific biomarker associated with cervical precancerous lesions and carcinogenesis, holding significant promise for enhancing screening precision. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in gene methylation detection for cervical cancer screening, with a focus on the identification of methylation biomarkers, the evolution of detection technologies, and their clinical utility. Furthermore, it addresses the current challenges and limitations in implementing methylation-based assays in routine clinical practice. By offering a systematic overview of the field, this work aims to support the optimization of cervical cancer screening strategies and promote the integration of epigenetic biomarkers into standard clinical workflows. 2.1Limitations of traditional screening methodsTraditional cervical cancer screening methods, including cytology (Pap smear) and human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, have been the cornerstone of cervical cancer prevention programs worldwide. However, these methods exhibit inherent limitations that affect their overall effectiveness and clinical utility. Cytology, which relies heavily on the morphological assessment of cervical cells by pathologists, suffers from moderate sensitivity, generally ranging from approximately 50% to 70%. This sensitivity is particularly inadequate for detecting adenocarcinomas, a subtype of cervical cancer that arises from glandular cells and is often less accessible to cytological sampling. The dependence on the subjective expertise of pathologists introduces variability and potential for missed diagnoses, especially in low-resource settings or where cytological expertise is limited (2).HPV testing, on the other hand, offers superior sensitivity exceeding 90% for detecting high-risk HPV infections associated with cervical neoplasia. Despite this high sensitivity, HPV testing is plagued by low specificity. This is largely due to the high prevalence of transient HPV infections, especially in younger women under 30 years of age, which often resolve spontaneously without progressing to neoplasia. Consequently, a significant proportion of HPV-positive results represent transient infections rather than clinically significant lesions, leading to a high rate of false positives. This low specificity results in unnecessary referrals for colposcopy and potential overtreatment, imposing psychological distress on patients and increasing healthcare costs (6).To mitigate these limitations, combined screening strategies integrating cytology and HPV testing have been adopted. While combined screening improves detection rates of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and invasive cancer, it also escalates the financial burden on healthcare systems and amplifies the psychological impact on patients due to increased follow-up procedures. Moreover, the management of HPV-positive young women remains controversial, as the natural history of HPV infections in this demographic often involves spontaneous clearance, raising concerns about overtreatment and its associated morbidity (6).The limitations of traditional screening methods underscore the need for more precise triage tools that can accurately distinguish between transient HPV infections and lesions with malignant potential. For example, methylation of tumor suppressor genes such as PAX1 and SOX1 has demonstrated higher specificity in detecting high-grade lesions compared to HPV testing alone. Additionally, methylation panels such as FAM19A4/miR124-2 have shown consistent performance across diverse populations and sample types, suggesting their potential utility as triage tests to reduce unnecessary colposcopy referrals.In summary, while cytology and HPV testing remain foundational in cervical cancer screening, their limitations—moderate sensitivity of cytology, low specificity of HPV testing, and the complexities introduced by combined screening—highlight the necessity for novel, more accurate, and cost-effective triage methods. Integration of molecular assays, particularly DNA methylation-based tests, may address these challenges by improving risk stratification, reducing overtreatment, and ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of cervical cancer screening programs. 4.1PCR-based detection methodsPolymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based methods have become pivotal in the detection of DNA methylation alterations associated with cervical cancer, offering a combination of sensitivity, specificity, and practicality that is suitable for clinical application. Among these, methylation-specific PCR (MSP) and its quantitative variant, real-time quantitative MSP (qMSP), are the most widely employed techniques due to their operational simplicity and cost-effectiveness. MSP involves bisulfite treatment of DNA, which converts unmethylated cytosines to uracils while leaving methylated cytosines unchanged, enabling the design of primers specific for methylated or unmethylated sequences. This specificity allows MSP to detect methylation status at particular gene loci with high accuracy. Real-time qMSP enhances this approach by quantifying methylation levels, providing a more nuanced assessment of methylation burden that correlates with disease severity. These methods have been successfully applied to cervical tissue and cervical smear samples, demonstrating robust sensitivity and specificity for detecting high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). For instance, a five-gene methylation panel including FMN2, EDNRB, ZNF671, TBXT, and MOS, validated across diverse populations, achieved sensitivities up to 100% for SCC detection and specificities exceeding 90% in cervical tissue samples, with similarly high performance in cervical smears (28). This underscores the clinical utility of MSP/qMSP as a triage tool following high-risk HPV screening, enabling more precise identification of women requiring further diagnostic intervention or treatment.The advancement of multiplex qMSP assays has further improved throughput and diagnostic efficiency by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple methylation markers. Multiplexing not only conserves sample material but also enhances diagnostic accuracy by combining markers with complementary methylation profiles. A notable example is the multiplex qMSP assay targeting PAX1, SOX1, and ZNF582, which has progressed into clinical trials. These genes exhibit promoter hypermethylation in cervical neoplasia, and their combined analysis improves discrimination between benign, precancerous, and malignant lesions. Clinical studies have demonstrated that such multiplex panels yield high sensitivity and specificity for CIN3+ lesions, with area under the curve (AUC) values of approximately 0.8–0.9, indicating strong diagnostic performance (29). The integration of multiplex qMSP assays into screening algorithms holds promise for reducing unnecessary colposcopies and overtreatment, particularly in resource-limited settings where cytology-based triage may be less feasible.Restriction enzyme-PCR (RE-PCR) represents another PCR-based approach that enhances methylation detection specificity by exploiting methylation-sensitive restriction endonucleases. These enzymes selectively digest unmethylated DNA at specific recognition sites, leaving methylated DNA intact for subsequent PCR amplification. This enzymatic digestion step reduces background from unmethylated sequences, thereby increasing assay specificity. However, RE-PCR requires careful optimization of enzyme digestion conditions to ensure complete cleavage of unmethylated DNA without compromising methylated DNA integrity. The method’s reliance on enzyme efficiency and DNA quality can pose challenges in clinical samples, particularly those with limited or degraded DNA. Despite these limitations, RE-PCR has been applied successfully to cervical cancer methylation studies, providing an alternative or complementary approach to bisulfite-based MSP methods (30). Its utility may be enhanced when combined with quantitative PCR techniques or multiplexing to improve sensitivity and throughput.Overall, PCR-based methylation detection methods offer a balance of sensitivity, specificity, and practicality that supports their clinical translation in cervical cancer screening and triage. MSP and qMSP are particularly well-suited for routine use due to their simplicity and cost-effectiveness, while multiplex qMSP assays improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency by targeting multiple methylation markers simultaneously. RE-PCR adds specificity through enzymatic digestion but requires meticulous optimization. The ongoing validation of methylation marker panels across diverse populations and sample types, including cervical smears, supports the potential of these PCR-based methods to complement or even replace cytology in HPV-positive women, facilitating earlier and more accurate identification of high-risk lesions and reducing unnecessary interventions. Future developments may focus on integrating these assays into automated platforms and combining methylation analysis with other molecular markers to further enhance cervical cancer screening programs worldwide (28, 29, 30). 4.2Sequencing-based detection methodsSequencing-based methods have become pivotal in the detection and quantification of DNA methylation alterations associated with cervical cancer, offering high-resolution, comprehensive profiling capabilities. Among these, bisulfite sequencing PCR (BSP) remains the gold standard for methylation analysis at single-CpG-site resolution. BSP involves the treatment of DNA with sodium bisulfite, which converts unmethylated cytosines to uracils while leaving methylated cytosines unchanged, enabling subsequent sequencing to distinguish methylated from unmethylated cytosines. This method allows for quantitative assessment of methylation levels at individual CpG sites, providing precise epigenetic information critical for understanding gene regulation in cervical carcinogenesis. However, BSP is labor-intensive, technically demanding, and costly, limiting its scalability for large numbers of samples or genome-wide analyses (30). The bisulfite treatment itself can cause DNA degradation, further complicating sample preparation and reducing DNA yield, which is particularly challenging when working with limited clinical specimens (31).To overcome these limitations, next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have been increasingly applied to methylation analysis in cervical cancer. Targeted methylation sequencing enables simultaneous interrogation of hundreds of genes or specific genomic regions of interest, facilitating the discovery and validation of methylation biomarkers for early detection and prognosis. Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), another NGS-based approach, provides an unbiased, base-resolution map of methylation across the entire genome, capturing both known and novel epigenetic alterations. These high-throughput methods have been instrumental in identifying differential methylation patterns associated with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia progression and invasive carcinoma, revealing epigenetic drivers and potential therapeutic targets. For example, genome-wide methylation profiling has uncovered hypermethylation of tumor suppressor genes such as NRG1, whose promoter methylation correlates with decreased expression and cervical cancer progression (32). Moreover, integrated analyses combining methylation data with transcriptomic and immune infiltration profiles have elucidated the complex interplay between epigenetic modifications and the tumor microenvironment, informing immunotherapy strategies (33). Despite their advantages, NGS-based methylation assays require sophisticated bioinformatics pipelines and remain relatively costly, which may limit their routine clinical application in resource-constrained settings.Emerging third-generation sequencing technologies, including single-molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing and nanopore sequencing, offer novel opportunities for direct detection of DNA methylation without the need for bisulfite conversion. SMRT sequencing, developed by Pacific Biosciences, detects methylation by measuring the kinetics of DNA polymerase during sequencing, allowing for the identification of modified bases in native DNA molecules. Similarly, nanopore sequencing, exemplified by Oxford Nanopore Technologies, reads DNA sequences by monitoring changes in electrical current as single DNA strands pass through a nanopore, enabling simultaneous detection of sequence and epigenetic modifications. These approaches reduce DNA damage and loss associated with bisulfite treatment, preserve DNA integrity, and allow for longer read lengths, which facilitate the analysis of methylation patterns in repetitive or complex genomic regions. In cervical cancer research, these technologies hold promise for comprehensive methylation profiling and biomarker discovery with improved accuracy and efficiency. However, challenges remain, including higher error rates compared to short-read sequencing and the need for optimized algorithms to accurately call methylation states. As these technologies mature, they are expected to complement existing methods and enhance the epigenetic characterization of cervical cancer (33).In summary, sequencing-based methylation detection methods have evolved from laborious, locus-specific BSP to high-throughput NGS and direct methylation detection via third-generation sequencing. BSP provides precise quantification at single-CpG resolution but is limited by complexity and cost. NGS approaches enable broad, multiplexed methylation analysis suitable for biomarker discovery and validation, while SMRT and nanopore sequencing offer direct, bisulfite-free methylation detection with potential advantages in DNA preservation and long-read capabilities. Together, these methods contribute to advancing cervical cancer screening by enabling detailed epigenetic profiling, improving early diagnosis, risk stratification, and informing personalized therapeutic interventions. However, third-generation sequencing technologies also face significant challenges in clinical applications. Firstly, their single-base sequencing error rate remains significantly higher than that of short-read sequencing (NGS), which can affect the accuracy of CpG site methylation determination. Secondly, the high sequencing costs and complex bioinformatics analysis algorithms make these technologies difficult to use as a routine options for large-scale primary screening of cervical cancer at this stage. Several studies have systematically compared these sequencing-based methods. For example, Kurdyukov and Bullock (2016) reviewed the strengths and limitations of BSP, NGS, and third-generation sequencing, highlighting trade-offs in resolution, throughput, cost, and DNA integrity (30). More recent comparisons have demonstrated that while NGS offers high multiplexing capacity, third-generation platforms reduce bisulfite-induced bias and enable long-read methylation profiling (31). These comparative analyses inform the choice of method for specific screening or biomarker discovery purposes. 5.1As a triage tool for HPV-positive patientsThe application of DNA methylation detection as a triage tool for HPV-positive women represents a significant advancement in cervical cancer screening, addressing the limitations of HPV testing alone. While high-risk HPV (hrHPV) testing is highly sensitive for identifying women at risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer, it lacks specificity, leading to unnecessary colposcopy referrals and overtreatment. Methylation assays targeting host-cell genes have emerged as effective molecular triage methods to stratify risk among HPV-positive women, thereby optimizing clinical management by identifying those who require immediate colposcopic evaluation and reducing unnecessary procedures in low-risk individuals.Several studies have demonstrated the utility of methylation markers in this context. For instance, a five-gene methylation panel including FMN2, EDNRB, ZNF671, TBXT, and MOS showed high sensitivity and specificity in detecting squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) in cervical smears from diverse populations, including the USA, South Africa, and Vietnam. This panel achieved a sensitivity of 87% and a specificity of 95% for SCC detection, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.925, and 70% sensitivity and 94% specificity for HSIL detection (AUC = 0.884), outperforming HPV testing alone (28). These findings underscore the potential of methylation markers to accurately identify high-risk lesions among HPV-positive women, facilitating timely treatment and reducing unnecessary colposcopy referrals.Among individual methylation markers, PAX1 methylation has been extensively studied and validated as a triage tool. Quantitative methylation-specific PCR assays have shown that PAX1 methylation levels increase with the severity of cervical lesions and that their diagnostic performance is superior to the of HPV testing and cytology. In a study comparing PAX1 methylation with folic acid receptor-mediated diagnosis, ThinPrep cytology, and HPV testing, PAX1 methylation exhibited the highest area under the curve (AUC = 0.902), with sensitivity and specificity of 92.3% and 78.6%, respectively, for invasive cervical cancer detection (10). full_text_sections.abstract: Cervical cancer remains a leading malignancy among women globally, with its pathogenesis strongly associated with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Despite the widespread adoption of HPV testing in cervical cancer screening, its suboptimal specificity frequently results in overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Gene methylation, a key epigenetic modification, has emerged as a highly specific biomarker associated with cervical precancerous lesions and carcinogenesis, holding significant promise for enhancing screening precision. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in gene methylation detection for cervical cancer screening, with a focus on the identification of methylation biomarkers, the evolution of detection technologies, and their clinical utility. Furthermore, it addresses the current challenges and limitations in implementing methylation-based assays in routine clinical practice. By offering a systematic overview of the field, this work aims to support the optimization of cervical cancer screening strategies and promote the integration of epigenetic biomarkers into standard clinical workflows.
full_text_sections.methods: 2.1Limitations of traditional screening methodsTraditional cervical cancer screening methods, including cytology (Pap smear) and human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, have been the cornerstone of cervical cancer prevention programs worldwide. However, these methods exhibit inherent limitations that affect their overall effectiveness and clinical utility. Cytology, which relies heavily on the morphological assessment of cervical cells by pathologists, suffers from moderate sensitivity, generally ranging from approximately 50% to 70%. This sensitivity is particularly inadequate for detecting adenocarcinomas, a subtype of cervical cancer that arises from glandular cells and is often less accessible to cytological sampling. The dependence on the subjective expertise of pathologists introduces variability and potential for missed diagnoses, especially in low-resource settings or where cytological expertise is limited (2).HPV testing, on the other hand, offers superior sensitivity exceeding 90% for detecting high-risk HPV infections associated with cervical neoplasia. Despite this high sensitivity, HPV testing is plagued by low specificity. This is largely due to the high prevalence of transient HPV infections, especially in younger women under 30 years of age, which often resolve spontaneously without progressing to neoplasia. Consequently, a significant proportion of HPV-positive results represent transient infections rather than clinically significant lesions, leading to a high rate of false positives. This low specificity results in unnecessary referrals for colposcopy and potential overtreatment, imposing psychological distress on patients and increasing healthcare costs (6).To mitigate these limitations, combined screening strategies integrating cytology and HPV testing have been adopted. While combined screening improves detection rates of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and invasive cancer, it also escalates the financial burden on healthcare systems and amplifies the psychological impact on patients due to increased follow-up procedures. Moreover, the management of HPV-positive young women remains controversial, as the natural history of HPV infections in this demographic often involves spontaneous clearance, raising concerns about overtreatment and its associated morbidity (6).The limitations of traditional screening methods underscore the need for more precise triage tools that can accurately distinguish between transient HPV infections and lesions with malignant potential. For example, methylation of tumor suppressor genes such as PAX1 and SOX1 has demonstrated higher specificity in detecting high-grade lesions compared to HPV testing alone. Additionally, methylation panels such as FAM19A4/miR124-2 have shown consistent performance across diverse populations and sample types, suggesting their potential utility as triage tests to reduce unnecessary colposcopy referrals.In summary, while cytology and HPV testing remain foundational in cervical cancer screening, their limitations—moderate sensitivity of cytology, low specificity of HPV testing, and the complexities introduced by combined screening—highlight the necessity for novel, more accurate, and cost-effective triage methods. Integration of molecular assays, particularly DNA methylation-based tests, may address these challenges by improving risk stratification, reducing overtreatment, and ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of cervical cancer screening programs. 4.1PCR-based detection methodsPolymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based methods have become pivotal in the detection of DNA methylation alterations associated with cervical cancer, offering a combination of sensitivity, specificity, and practicality that is suitable for clinical application. Among these, methylation-specific PCR (MSP) and its quantitative variant, real-time quantitative MSP (qMSP), are the most widely employed techniques due to their operational simplicity and cost-effectiveness. MSP involves bisulfite treatment of DNA, which converts unmethylated cytosines to uracils while leaving methylated cytosines unchanged, enabling the design of primers specific for methylated or unmethylated sequences. This specificity allows MSP to detect methylation status at particular gene loci with high accuracy. Real-time qMSP enhances this approach by quantifying methylation levels, providing a more nuanced assessment of methylation burden that correlates with disease severity. These methods have been successfully applied to cervical tissue and cervical smear samples, demonstrating robust sensitivity and specificity for detecting high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). For instance, a five-gene methylation panel including FMN2, EDNRB, ZNF671, TBXT, and MOS, validated across diverse populations, achieved sensitivities up to 100% for SCC detection and specificities exceeding 90% in cervical tissue samples, with similarly high performance in cervical smears (28). This underscores the clinical utility of MSP/qMSP as a triage tool following high-risk HPV screening, enabling more precise identification of women requiring further diagnostic intervention or treatment.The advancement of multiplex qMSP assays has further improved throughput and diagnostic efficiency by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple methylation markers. Multiplexing not only conserves sample material but also enhances diagnostic accuracy by combining markers with complementary methylation profiles. A notable example is the multiplex qMSP assay targeting PAX1, SOX1, and ZNF582, which has progressed into clinical trials. These genes exhibit promoter hypermethylation in cervical neoplasia, and their combined analysis improves discrimination between benign, precancerous, and malignant lesions. Clinical studies have demonstrated that such multiplex panels yield high sensitivity and specificity for CIN3+ lesions, with area under the curve (AUC) values of approximately 0.8–0.9, indicating strong diagnostic performance (29). The integration of multiplex qMSP assays into screening algorithms holds promise for reducing unnecessary colposcopies and overtreatment, particularly in resource-limited settings where cytology-based triage may be less feasible.Restriction enzyme-PCR (RE-PCR) represents another PCR-based approach that enhances methylation detection specificity by exploiting methylation-sensitive restriction endonucleases. These enzymes selectively digest unmethylated DNA at specific recognition sites, leaving methylated DNA intact for subsequent PCR amplification. This enzymatic digestion step reduces background from unmethylated sequences, thereby increasing assay specificity. However, RE-PCR requires careful optimization of enzyme digestion conditions to ensure complete cleavage of unmethylated DNA without compromising methylated DNA integrity. The method’s reliance on enzyme efficiency and DNA quality can pose challenges in clinical samples, particularly those with limited or degraded DNA. Despite these limitations, RE-PCR has been applied successfully to cervical cancer methylation studies, providing an alternative or complementary approach to bisulfite-based MSP methods (30). Its utility may be enhanced when combined with quantitative PCR techniques or multiplexing to improve sensitivity and throughput.Overall, PCR-based methylation detection methods offer a balance of sensitivity, specificity, and practicality that supports their clinical translation in cervical cancer screening and triage. MSP and qMSP are particularly well-suited for routine use due to their simplicity and cost-effectiveness, while multiplex qMSP assays improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency by targeting multiple methylation markers simultaneously. RE-PCR adds specificity through enzymatic digestion but requires meticulous optimization. The ongoing validation of methylation marker panels across diverse populations and sample types, inclu…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 10ConclusionThe evolution of gene methylation detection as a novel tool for cervical cancer screening represents a significant advancement in the field of oncology diagnostics. From an expert perspective, this technology addresses critical limitations inherent in traditional screening methods, such as cytology and HPV DNA testing, by offering enhanced specificity, objectivity, and the potential for automation. These attributes collectively contribute to more accurate risk stratification, which is essential for optimizing patient management and reducing unnecessary interventions.The integration of host gene methylation markers, including PAX1 and SOX1, with HPV gene methylation profiles has demonstrated considerable clinical utility. These biomarkers enable effective triage of HPV-positive individuals, thereby refining the screening cascade and focusing resources on those at genuine risk of progression to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or invasive cancer. Moreover, their applicability in self-sampling contexts expands access to screening, particularly in underserved populations, while their role in postoperative surveillance offers a promising avenue for the early detection of residual or recurrent disease. This multifaceted utility underscores the transformative potential of methylation markers in both primary and secondary prevention paradigms.Technological advancements such as quantitative methylation-specific PCR (qMSP), next-generation sequencing (NGS), and digital PCR have been instrumental in translating methylation detection from research settings into clinical practice. These methodologies provide the sensitivity and quantitative precision necessary for reliable biomarker assessment. However, despite these technical strides, challenges remain. Standardization across laboratories is imperative to ensure reproducibility and comparability of results, which is crucial for widespread clinical adoption. Additionally, cost considerations must be addressed to facilitate equitable access, especially in low-resource settings where cervical cancer burden is disproportionately high. Ethical concerns, including informed consent and data privacy related to genetic and epigenetic information, also warrant careful deliberation to maintain patient trust and comply with regulatory frameworks. We must objectively recognize that although DNA methylation detection has shown great potential in laboratory research, there are still three major gaps between the identified biomarkers and their widespread clinical application in the real world: cost control, equipment accessibility, and standardized quality control. Instead of overemphasizing the absolute advantages of the technology itself, we should address its practical challenges within the existing healthcare system. Future research should focus on conducting large-scale, prospective, multicenter clinical trials to generate clinical efficacy data and on performing cost-effectiveness analyses from a health economics perspective.Balancing these diverse research perspectives and findings requires a nuanced approach. While the promise of methylation-based screening is compelling, it is essential to integrate these tools within existing healthcare infrastructures thoughtfully. This includes validating novel biomarkers through large-scale, prospective studies and harmonizing assay protocols to establish clinical guidelines. Furthermore, the incorporation of liquid biopsy techniques offers a minimally invasive alternative that could revolutionize screening and monitoring, enhancing patient compliance and enabling dynamic disease tracking. The convergence of artificial intelligence with methylation data analysis presents another frontier, potentially augmenting diagnostic accuracy through sophisticated pattern recognition and risk prediction models.Future research should prioritize the discovery of new methylation markers with higher sensitivity and specificity, alongside efforts to optimize sample collection and processing methods. The development of multiplexed assays capable of simultaneously evaluating multiple biomarkers could streamline workflows and reduce costs. Importantly, fostering multidisciplinary collaboration among molecular biologists, clinicians, bioinformaticians, and health policy experts will be critical to overcoming existing barriers and accelerating clinical translation.Policy support plays a pivotal role in this endeavor. Investment in infrastructure, reimbursement frameworks, and public health initiatives can facilitate the integration of gene methylation detection into national cervical cancer screening programs. Educational campaigns aimed at healthcare providers and the public are equally vital to promote acceptance and understanding of these novel technologies. Ultimately, the successful implementation of methylation-based screening has the potential to substantially reduce the global burden of cervical cancer by enabling earlier detection, personalized risk assessment, and tailored interventions.In conclusion, gene methylation detection embodies a promising frontier in cervical cancer screening, offering a sophisticated, objective, and scalable approach that complements and enhances existing methodologies. The path forward necessitates a balanced synthesis of technological innovation, rigorous clinical validation, ethical oversight, and policy-driven support. By addressing these multifactorial challenges through coordinated efforts, the medical community can harness the full potential of methylation biomarkers to improve patient outcomes and advance global cervical cancer control.

The primary etiological factor for cervical carcinogenesis is persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV), which initiates a cascade of molecular and cellular events culminating in the development of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and invasive cervical cancer. Effective screening programs are critical for early detection and prevention, substantially reducing both incidence and mortality rates. Traditional cervical cancer screening has relied heavily on cytology-based methods, such as the Papanicolaou (Pap) smear, which, despite its historical success, suffers from limitations including variable sensitivity and the need for repeated testing (2). full_text: AbstractIntroductionPersistent high-risk HPV infection is the principal cause of cervical dysplasia, but variation in disease phenotype may also be associated with differences in the local immune and microbial environment.MethodsWe characterized the cervicovaginal immune microenvironment in relation to HPV status, vaginal community state type (CST), and cytological grade.ResultsHPV-positive samples showed reduced IL-4 and IL-17E/IL-25, while IFN-α2 and IL-3 varied across community state types in a non-monotonic, CST-specific manner: IFN-α2 was relatively elevated in the Lactobacillus gasseri-dominant CST II, and IL-3 was specifically reduced in the Lactobacillus jensenii-dominant CST V. Cytological category was associated with non-monotonic, marker-specific immune variation, with LSIL showing lower IL-4, IFN-γ, IL-17F, PDGF-AB/BB, IL-17E/IL-25, and PDGF-AA levels relative to NILM, while ASC-H showed a distinct rather than uniformly progressive immune profile. CLR-based multi-kingdom analyses identified a restricted set of taxon–cytokine associations after correction of the relative-abundance scale, prespecified prevalence and abundance filtering, and multiple-testing correction. Significant bacterial associations were confined to the genus level, whereas viral associations were observed at the family, genus, and species levels and fungal associations at the family level. Phocaeicola–IL-10 and Rountreeviridae–MIP-1β were the only associations that additionally remained significant after global BH-FDR correction across all taxon–immune-marker tests. Viral and fungal findings were interpreted as exploratory because of substantially lower non-bacterial sequencing depth.DiscussionThese microbial associations provide additional context for the observed immune-marker differences. These findings support further investigation of multi-kingdom host–microbiome immune relationships in HPV-associated cervical abnormalities.Keywords: cervical cytological grade, cervical immune microenvironment, cervicovaginal cytokines, cervicovaginal microbiome, HPV 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study design and participantsThis cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary academic medical center in Astana, Kazakhstan, recruiting non-pregnant women aged 18–46 years with a regular menstrual cycle and an intact uterine cervix through the outpatient gynecology clinic of the National Research Center for Mother and Child Health, University Medical Center. Exclusions included severe chronic or immunocompromising conditions, acute inflammatory disease, recent antibiotic/probiotic/immunosuppressive use, smoking history, IUD use, prior HPV vaccination, or recent invasive gynecological procedures. Participants were included when complete clinical, cytological, HPV, immunological, and metagenomic data were available. The study was approved by the Local Bioethics Committee of the University Medical Centre (protocol No. 5, 23 May 2024) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The source metagenomic cohort comprised 311 participants. Eight participants could not be matched to available immunological data, resulting in 303 participants with integrated clinical, metagenomic, and immunological data. Seven additional participants were excluded from grade-stratified analyses because cytological grade information was unavailable, leaving a final analytical cohort of 296 participants (Supplementary Figure S1). Prior HPV vaccination was an exclusion criterion at recruitment; however, vaccination history for two participants became known only after enrollment and completion of data collection. These participants had already completed the study procedures and were retained in the analytical cohort as a post-enrollment protocol deviation.2.2.Clinical assessment, cytology, and HPV status classificationDemographic and clinical data (age, BMI, menstrual-cycle phase) were collected via standardized questionnaires. Cervical cytology was evaluated using liquid-based preparations and classified according to the 2014 Bethesda System as negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM), atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), or atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H). ASC-H was assigned to specimens showing squamous-cell atypia suspicious for a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, including enlarged nuclei, irregular nuclear membrane contours, uneven chromatin distribution, mildly increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, and atypical parabasal-type squamous cells. These categories were analyzed as distinct cross-sectional cytological groups and were not interpreted as sequential stages of disease progression. Histological confirmation of HSIL was not available for the ASC-H group. HPV status was determined using two complementary approaches. Targeted real-time PCR was performed using the RealBest DNA HPV High Carcinogenic Risk Genotype kit (Vector-Best, Russia), detecting HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59; Ct<35 was considered positive. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was additionally screened for HPV sequences and enabled detection of genotypes outside the targeted PCR panel. Final HPV status was assigned using a union criterion, whereby a participant was classified as HPV-positive if either PCR or metagenomic sequencing detected HPV. In the full sequenced source cohort (n=311), PCR and metagenomic sequencing showed 79.1% overall agreement: 84 samples were positive by both methods, 29 were PCR-positive/MNGS-negative, 36 were PCR-negative/MNGS-positive, and 162 were negative by both methods (Cohen’s κ=0.55). PCR-negative/MNGS-positive cases predominantly reflected HPV genotypes outside the targeted high-risk PCR panel. PCR-detected HPV types were classified as high-risk according to the carcinogenic HPV panel described above. Additional HPV genotypes detected by metagenomic sequencing were retained separately as other HPV types according to their established taxonomic and oncogenic-risk classification. In the source metagenomic cohort (n=311), 84 samples were PCR+/MNGS+, 29 were PCR+/MNGS−, 36 were PCR−/MNGS+, and 162 were PCR−/MNGS−, corresponding to 79.1% overall agreement and Cohen’s κ=0.55. Metagenomic HPV classification was based on HPV taxonomic assignments in the shotgun sequencing dataset. A separate prespecified minimum HPV read-count or genome-coverage threshold was not applied in the original analytical pipeline. Accordingly, PCR/WGS discordance is reported descriptively, and metagenomic HPV-positive cases, particularly those not confirmed by PCR, should be interpreted in the context of this limitation.2.3.Cervical sample collection, DNA extraction, and sequencingCervical samples were collected via sterile swabs and stored at −80 °C. DNA was extracted using the ZymoBIOMICS DNA Miniprep Kit, with negative (nuclease-free water) and positive (ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard) controls. Negative extraction controls were not subjected to shotgun sequencing; therefore, prevalence-based computational contaminant identification using sequenced blanks could not be performed. This limitation was considered explicitly when curating low-abundance and biologically unexpected taxonomic assignments. DNA concentration, purity, and integrity were assessed via Qubit, NanoDrop, and Qsep400, requiring ≥1.0 μg total DNA. Whole-genome shotgun sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (paired-end 150-bp, ~6 Gb/sample). Host reads were removed by alignment to GRCh38 using Bowtie2 v2.5.4. Taxonomic classification used Kraken2 v2.1.3 (PlusPFP database, covering bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other eukaryotes), with Bracken v3.0 refining genus/species-level abundance estimates separately for bacterial, viral, and fungal taxa. Relative kingdom-level contributions were calculated from Kraken2-assigned reads across Bacteria, Viruses, and Fungi for samples in the final analytical cohort. Effective microbial sequencing depth varied substantially among samples. In analyses of the source metagenomic dataset, the median bacterial taxonomic sequencing depth was approximately 3.84 million reads per sample (IQR 3.10–4.87 million; range 0.36–14.04 million). Non-bacterial microbial fractions were substantially lower than the bacterial fraction; in a multi-kingdom subset analysis of the same sequencing resource, median classified counts were approximately 118,233 bacterial reads, 129 fungal reads, and 26 viral reads per sample. These differences in sequencing depth and taxonomic representation were considered when interpreting low-abundance fungal and viral assignments. Because cervicovaginal specimens represent a relatively low-microbial-biomass environment and broad metagenomic reference databases may generate assignments to environmentally or anatomically implausible taxa, additional taxonomic quality control was performed before microbiome–immune association analysis. Taxa were reviewed at the full taxonomic-lineage level, and predefined animal-, plant-, soil-, marine-, rumen-, insect-, and other strongly non-cervicovaginal lineages were excluded. When an implausible genus or higher taxonomic lineage was excluded, all descendant assignments were removed. Species labels containing reference-strain or isolate designations were collapsed to the corresponding biological species where a species-level assignment was supported; unresolved strain- or isolate-level labels were not interpreted as independent species. A complete audit of excluded taxa and taxonomic consolidation is provided in Supplementary Table 3.2.4.Community state type assignmentCervicovaginal bacterial communities were classified into five community state types (CSTs) from species-level relative-abundance profiles. The CST-associated bacterial species with the highest relative abundance within each sample was used to define the dominant community type; no fixed numerical dominance threshold was applied. Samples in which Lactobacillus crispatus, L. gasseri, L. iners, or L. jensenii showed the highest relative abundance were classified as CST I, CST II, CST III, or CST V, respectively. Samples lacking dominance by these Lactobacillus species and characterized by predominance of Gardnerella, Fannyhessea vaginae, Prevotella, Sneathia, and/or other anaerobic taxa were assigned to CST IV. Mixed communities were therefore classified according to the taxon or community pattern with the greatest relative representation. CST was included as a categorical variable in downstream models, with CST I as the reference category. In the final analytical cohort, the CST distribution was CST I (n = 66), CST II (n = 24), CST III (n = 68), CST IV (n = 136), and CST V (n = 9).2.5.Cervicovaginal cytokine, chemokine, and growth-factor profilingCervical swab specimens were immersed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and vortexed to release cervicovaginal material from the swab. The suspensions were incubated on ice for approximately 10 min and subsequently centrifuged at approximately 4000 rpm before collection of the resulting supernatant for immune-marker analysis. The recovered cervical-swab eluate was then analyzed using the MILLIPLEX® Human Cytokine/Chemokine/Growth Factor Panel A magnetic bead assay. Cervicovaginal immune mediators were quantified using the MILLIPLEX® Human Cytokine/Chemokine/Growth Factor Panel A magnetic bead assay (HCYTA-60K-PX38; MilliporeSigma/Merck, Burlington, MA, USA; kit lot 4191809) on a Luminex FLEXMAP 3D® platform, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The panel comprised 37 analytes: EGF, Eotaxin, G-CSF, GM-CSF, IFN-α2, IFN-γ, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-1RA, IL-2, IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-7, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12(p40), IL-12(p70), IL-13, IL-15, IL-17A, IL-17E/IL-25, IL-17F, IL-18, IL-22, IP-10, MCP-1, M-CSF, MIG, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, PDGF-AA, PDGF-AB/BB, TNF-α, TNF-β, and VEGF. Cervicovaginal immune mediators were quantified using the MILLIPLEX® Human Cytokine/Chemokine/Growth Factor Panel A magnetic bead assay (HCYTA-60K-PX38; MilliporeSigma/Merck, Burlington, MA, USA; kit lot 4191809) on a Luminex FLEXMAP 3D® platform, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Concentrations were expressed as pg/mL. Due to limited specimen volume, samples were analyzed in single wells rather than technical duplicates. Assay performance was monitored using the manufacturer-provided Control 1 and Control 2 materials (HCYTA-6060-2; lots A6602–106 and A6602-206), with analyte-specific expected concentration ranges provided by the manufacturer. Manufacturer-reported assay precision for this panel is<15% intra-assay coefficient of variation and<20% inter-assay coefficient of variation. The instrument output additionally contained a parameter labelled “Total Events.” This parameter was generated directly by the Luminex acquisition system and was analyzed separately from individual cytokine concentrations. Because it represents an instrument/acquisition-related parameter rather than a cytokine concentration, it was not interpreted as a direct measure of cumulative immune activation.2.6.Statistical analysis of immune-marker levelsAnalyses were conducted in Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, matplotlib, seaborn). Concentrations were log10-transformed after adding a pseudocount of 1 to reduce right-skewness typical of cytokine concentration data; log10-transformed values approximated normal distributions more closely than raw concentrations, supporting the use of Welch’s t-test and ordinary least-squares regression on transformed values, while the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test was additionally used for unadjusted comparisons involving more than two groups as a distribution-free check. Unadjusted pairwise and two-group comparisons used Welch’s t-test (robust to unequal variances) on log10-transformed values, and unadjusted comparisons involving more than two groups used the Kruskal-Wallis test. Adjusted analyses were performed using ordinary least-squares regression. For HPV status, CST, and HPV type-group analyses, models included the grouping variable together with available covariates (age, BMI, and menstrual phase). For cytological-grade analyses, HPV status was additionally included as a covariate:log10(immune−marker + 1) = β� + β1 × cytological grade + β2 × age + β3 × BMI + β4 × menstrual phase + β5× HPV status + εwith HPV status added as a covariate for the cytological-grade model. Overall associations between each grouping variable and each immune marker were assessed by comparing the full adjusted model with a reduced model omitting the grouping variable using a partial F-test. Reference categories were HPV-negative, NILM, no HPV for HPV type group, and CST I for CST analyses. Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied separately to the overall unadjusted tests, overall adjusted model-comparison tests, and regression coefficient-level tests within each grouping variable; FDR-adjusted p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. For exploratory identification of the group pairs contributing to significant overall associations, pairwise comparisons were performed using Welch’s t-tests on log10-transformed values. Pairwise p-values displayed as brackets in Figures 1, 2 were nominal and uncorrected and were interpreted as exploratory rather than independently multiplicity-controlled inferential tests. Pairwise p-values were additionally adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate procedure within each immune marker and grouping variable; both nominal p-values and FDR-adjusted q-values are displayed in Figures 1, 2. As a prespecified exploratory subgroup analysis, associations between cytological grade and individual immune-marker concentrations were additionally evaluated separately according to HPV status. Among HPV-positive participants, grade-associated immune-marker differences were assessed using the same log10-transformed cytokine data and covariate-adjusted framework described above, with age and BMI included as covariates. Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across the tested immune markers, and markers with FDR-adjusted p<0.05 were retained for visualization in Figure 3. Pairwise comparisons between cytological categories were used for descriptive interpretation of significant overall associations and are shown in the figure. Among HPV-negative participants, no immune marker remained significant after FDR correction; therefore, no corresponding HPV-negative figure was generated. Because only one HPV-negative participant had ASC-H cytology, this category was not considered statistically interpretable within the HPV-negative subgroup.Figure 1Cervicovaginal IFN-α2 and IL-3 levels differ across vaginal community state types. Cervicovaginal concentrations of (A) IFN-α2 and (B) IL-3 were compared across five bacterial community state types (CST I–V). Each point represents one participant, and horizontal bars indicate group medians. Values are shown on a log10 scale after addition of a pseudocount of 1; statistical methods are described in Section 2.6. (B) IL-3 concentrations also varied across CSTs (adjusted P = 0.037), with lower IL-3 levels in CST V compared with CST I (P<0.001), CST II (P = 0.005), CST III (P = 0.006), and CST IV (P = 0.002).Two-panel dot plot showing immune marker levels by CST group. Panel a displays IFN-alpha2 (adjusted p=0.035) values across five CST groups on a log10 scale, with significant differences denoted by brackets and p-values.
