full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractIntroductionPersistent high-risk HPV infection is the principal cause of cervical dysplasia, but variation in disease phenotype may also be associated with differences in the local immune and microbial environment.MethodsWe characterized the cervicovaginal immune microenvironment in relation to HPV status, vaginal community state type (CST), and cytological grade.ResultsHPV-positive samples showed reduced IL-4 and IL-17E/IL-25, while IFN-α2 and IL-3 varied across community state types in a non-monotonic, CST-specific manner: IFN-α2 was relatively elevated in the Lactobacillus gasseri-dominant CST II, and IL-3 was specifically reduced in the Lactobacillus jensenii-dominant CST V. Cytological category was associated with non-monotonic, marker-specific immune variation, with LSIL showing lower IL-4, IFN-γ, IL-17F, PDGF-AB/BB, IL-17E/IL-25, and PDGF-AA levels relative to NILM, while ASC-H showed a distinct rather than uniformly progressive immune profile. CLR-based multi-kingdom analyses identified a restricted set of taxon–cytokine associations after correction of the relative-abundance scale, prespecified prevalence and abundance filtering, and multiple-testing correction. Significant bacterial associations were confined to the genus level, whereas viral associations were observed at the family, genus, and species levels and fungal associations at the family level. Phocaeicola–IL-10 and Rountreeviridae–MIP-1β were the only associations that additionally remained significant after global BH-FDR correction across all taxon–immune-marker tests. Viral and fungal findings were interpreted as exploratory because of substantially lower non-bacterial sequencing depth.DiscussionThese microbial associations provide additional context for the observed immune-marker differences. These findings support further investigation of multi-kingdom host–microbiome immune relationships in HPV-associated cervical abnormalities.Keywords: cervical cytological grade, cervical immune microenvironment, cervicovaginal cytokines, cervicovaginal microbiome, HPV
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study design and participantsThis cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary academic medical center in Astana, Kazakhstan, recruiting non-pregnant women aged 18–46 years with a regular menstrual cycle and an intact uterine cervix through the outpatient gynecology clinic of the National Research Center for Mother and Child Health, University Medical Center. Exclusions included severe chronic or immunocompromising conditions, acute inflammatory disease, recent antibiotic/probiotic/immunosuppressive use, smoking history, IUD use, prior HPV vaccination, or recent invasive gynecological procedures. Participants were included when complete clinical, cytological, HPV, immunological, and metagenomic data were available. The study was approved by the Local Bioethics Committee of the University Medical Centre (protocol No. 5, 23 May 2024) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The source metagenomic cohort comprised 311 participants. Eight participants could not be matched to available immunological data, resulting in 303 participants with integrated clinical, metagenomic, and immunological data. Seven additional participants were excluded from grade-stratified analyses because cytological grade information was unavailable, leaving a final analytical cohort of 296 participants (Supplementary Figure S1). Prior HPV vaccination was an exclusion criterion at recruitment; however, vaccination history for two participants became known only after enrollment and completion of data collection. These participants had already completed the study procedures and were retained in the analytical cohort as a post-enrollment protocol deviation.2.2.Clinical assessment, cytology, and HPV status classificationDemographic and clinical data (age, BMI, menstrual-cycle phase) were collected via standardized questionnaires. Cervical cytology was evaluated using liquid-based preparations and classified according to the 2014 Bethesda System as negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM), atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), or atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H). ASC-H was assigned to specimens showing squamous-cell atypia suspicious for a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, including enlarged nuclei, irregular nuclear membrane contours, uneven chromatin distribution, mildly increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, and atypical parabasal-type squamous cells. These categories were analyzed as distinct cross-sectional cytological groups and were not interpreted as sequential stages of disease progression. Histological confirmation of HSIL was not available for the ASC-H group. HPV status was determined using two complementary approaches. Targeted real-time PCR was performed using the RealBest DNA HPV High Carcinogenic Risk Genotype kit (Vector-Best, Russia), detecting HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59; Ct<35 was considered positive. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was additionally screened for HPV sequences and enabled detection of genotypes outside the targeted PCR panel. Final HPV status was assigned using a union criterion, whereby a participant was classified as HPV-positive if either PCR or metagenomic sequencing detected HPV. In the full sequenced source cohort (n=311), PCR and metagenomic sequencing showed 79.1% overall agreement: 84 samples were positive by both methods, 29 were PCR-positive/MNGS-negative, 36 were PCR-negative/MNGS-positive, and 162 were negative by both methods (Cohen’s κ=0.55). PCR-negative/MNGS-positive cases predominantly reflected HPV genotypes outside the targeted high-risk PCR panel. PCR-detected HPV types were classified as high-risk according to the carcinogenic HPV panel described above. Additional HPV genotypes detected by metagenomic sequencing were retained separately as other HPV types according to their established taxonomic and oncogenic-risk classification. In the source metagenomic cohort (n=311), 84 samples were PCR+/MNGS+, 29 were PCR+/MNGS−, 36 were PCR−/MNGS+, and 162 were PCR−/MNGS−, corresponding to 79.1% overall agreement and Cohen’s κ=0.55. Metagenomic HPV classification was based on HPV taxonomic assignments in the shotgun sequencing dataset. A separate prespecified minimum HPV read-count or genome-coverage threshold was not applied in the original analytical pipeline. Accordingly, PCR/WGS discordance is reported descriptively, and metagenomic HPV-positive cases, particularly those not confirmed by PCR, should be interpreted in the context of this limitation.2.3.Cervical sample collection, DNA extraction, and sequencingCervical samples were collected via sterile swabs and stored at −80 °C. DNA was extracted using the ZymoBIOMICS DNA Miniprep Kit, with negative (nuclease-free water) and positive (ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard) controls. Negative extraction controls were not subjected to shotgun sequencing; therefore, prevalence-based computational contaminant identification using sequenced blanks could not be performed. This limitation was considered explicitly when curating low-abundance and biologically unexpected taxonomic assignments. DNA concentration, purity, and integrity were assessed via Qubit, NanoDrop, and Qsep400, requiring ≥1.0 μg total DNA. Whole-genome shotgun sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (paired-end 150-bp, ~6 Gb/sample). Host reads were removed by alignment to GRCh38 using Bowtie2 v2.5.4. Taxonomic classification used Kraken2 v2.1.3 (PlusPFP database, covering bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other eukaryotes), with Bracken v3.0 refining genus/species-level abundance estimates separately for bacterial, viral, and fungal taxa. Relative kingdom-level contributions were calculated from Kraken2-assigned reads across Bacteria, Viruses, and Fungi for samples in the final analytical cohort. Effective microbial sequencing depth varied substantially among samples. In analyses of the source metagenomic dataset, the median bacterial taxonomic sequencing depth was approximately 3.84 million reads per sample (IQR 3.10–4.87 million; range 0.36–14.04 million). Non-bacterial microbial fractions were substantially lower than the bacterial fraction; in a multi-kingdom subset analysis of the same sequencing resource, median classified counts were approximately 118,233 bacterial reads, 129 fungal reads, and 26 viral reads per sample. These differences in sequencing depth and taxonomic representation were considered when interpreting low-abundance fungal and viral assignments. Because cervicovaginal specimens represent a relatively low-microbial-biomass environment and broad metagenomic reference databases may generate assignments to environmentally or anatomically implausible taxa, additional taxonomic quality control was performed before microbiome–immune association analysis. Taxa were reviewed at the full taxonomic-lineage level, and predefined animal-, plant-, soil-, marine-, rumen-, insect-, and other strongly non-cervicovaginal lineages were excluded. When an implausible genus or higher taxonomic lineage was excluded, all descendant assignments were removed. Species labels containing reference-strain or isolate designations were collapsed to the corresponding biological species where a species-level assignment was supported; unresolved strain- or isolate-level labels were not interpreted as independent species. A complete audit of excluded taxa and taxonomic consolidation is provided in Supplementary Table 3.2.4.Community state type assignmentCervicovaginal bacterial communities were classified into five community state types (CSTs) from species-level relative-abundance profiles. The CST-associated bacterial species with the highest relative abundance within each sample was used to define the dominant community type; no fixed numerical dominance threshold was applied. Samples in which Lactobacillus crispatus, L. gasseri, L. in…
full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Cohort characteristics relevant to immune profilingOf the 311 participants in the source metagenomic cohort, 303 had matched immunological data. Seven of these participants lacked cytological grade information and were excluded from grade-based analyses, resulting in a final analytical cohort of 296 women stratified by cytological grade: NILM (n = 141, 47.6%), ASC-US (n = 70, 23.6%), LSIL (n = 76, 25.7%), and ASC-H (n = 9, 3.0%). Because CST V and ASC-H contained only nine participants each in the final analytical cohort, estimates involving these categories were expected to have reduced precision. Accordingly, regression coefficients and pairwise comparisons involving CST V or ASC-H are reported with 95% confidence intervals and should be interpreted cautiously as exploratory estimates rather than as stable group-specific effects. As cervical cytokine levels can be influenced by HPV status, parity, and microbiome composition, these variables were examined across grade groups prior to immunological analysis (Supplementary Table 1).In the source metagenomic cohort, agreement between targeted PCR and metagenomic HPV detection was 79.1% (84 PCR+/MNGS+, 29 PCR+/MNGS−, 36 PCR−/MNGS+, and 162 PCR−/MNGS−; Cohen’s κ=0.55). PCR+/MNGS− discordance was interpreted as likely reflecting lower HPV abundance below metagenomic detection sensitivity, whereas PCR−/MNGS+ cases largely reflected detection of HPV genotypes not represented in the targeted PCR panel. By targeted PCR, the most frequently detected genotypes were HPV16 (23%), HPV52 (15%), HPV33 (12%), HPV45 (9%), HPV59 (9%), HPV39 (8%), HPV18 (8%), HPV51 (7%), HPV56 (7%), HPV31 (6%), HPV35 (6%), and HPV58 (6%). Multiple infection with two or more genotypes was identified in 42 participants by PCR.HPV status differed markedly by grade (p< 0.001): the proportion of HPV-negative women declined from 70.2% in NILM to 11.1% in ASC-H, while HPV High Risk rose correspondingly from 12.8% to 88.9%, confirming the expected grade–HPV gradient and necessitating HPV status as a covariate in cytokine modeling. History of pregnancy also varied significantly across grades (p = 0.001), though based on a smaller subset of the cohort.Community state type showed no significant association with cytological grade (p = 0.166), despite CST IV being numerically most frequent in ASC-H (55.6%). Age, BMI, age at menarche, menstrual cycle characteristics, parity, sexual history, contraceptive use, comorbidities, ethnicity, education, and marital status were all balanced across grade groups (all p > 0.05), arguing against these factors as major confounders of cytokine measurements in this cohort.Overall, HPV status was the principal source of demographic heterogeneity across cytological grade groups and was accounted for accordingly in the cytokine association analyses below.3.2.Determinants of the cervicovaginal immune microenvironmentTo characterize the local immune environment, cytokine levels were measured in cervicovaginal swab samples.3.2.1.Immunological marker levels by HPV statusComparison of cervicovaginal cytokine levels between HPV-negative and HPV-positive patients revealed significant differences in two key immune markers (Figure 4). IL-4 levels were significantly higher in HPV-negative compared to HPV-positive samples (adjusted P<0.001), with median levels approximately 25 pg/mL versus 15 pg/mL, respectively, suggesting suppression of Th2-associated immune responses upon HPV infection. Similarly, IL-17E/IL-25 levels were significantly higher in HPV-negative individuals (adjusted P = 0.002). These findings demonstrate cross-sectional differences in Th2-associated and epithelial-derived immune mediators according to HPV status.Figure 4Reduced cervicovaginal IL-4 and IL-17E levels in HPV-positive participants. Cervicovaginal concentrations of IL-4 and IL-17E were compared between HPV-negative and HPV-positive participants. Each point represents one participant; filled circles indicate HPV-negative samples and open circles indicate HPV-positive samples. Horizontal bars represent group medians. Values are displayed on a log10 scale after addition of a pseudocount of 1. Overall adjusted p-values were obtained from linear regression models adjusted for age, BMI, and menstrual phase. IL-4 concentrations were significantly lower in HPV-positive participants than in HPV-negative participants (adjusted P<0.001), as were IL-17E concentrations (adjusted P = 0.002).Scatter plot compares IL-4 and IL-17E immune marker levels by HPV status, with log-transformed values plotted for negative (filled circles) and positive (open circles) groups. Statistical significance is indicated as p less than 0.001 for IL-4 and p equals 0.002 for IL-17E.3.2.2.Immunological marker levels by community state typeAnalysis of cervicovaginal cytokine levels across community state types (CST I-V) revealed significant differences in antiviral and hematopoietic immune markers (Figure 1).IFN-α2 levels differed significantly across CSTs (Figure 1A, adjusted P = 0.035), with the pattern driven primarily by relatively elevated levels in CST II rather than by a monotonic decline across CSTs. Significantly higher IFN-α2 concentrations were observed in CST II compared to CST I (P = 0.001, q = 0.013), CST III (P = 0.010, q = 0.049), and CST V (P = 0.019, q = 0.049). An additional difference was observed between CST I and CST IV (P = 0.015, q = 0.049), with CST V exhibiting the lowest median values (~250 pg/mL). Because the highest IFN-α2 levels occurred in CST II and the lowest in CST V - both Lactobacillus-dominant states - this pattern does not support a straightforward, monotonic suppression of type I interferon with increasing community diversity; rather, it reflects CST-specific differences whose biological basis remains to be established.IL-3 levels similarly varied significantly across CSTs (Figure 1B). CST I and CST II maintained comparable median levels (~25–30 pg/mL), whereas CST V demonstrated markedly reduced IL-3 concentrations relative to CST I (P<0.001, q = 0.009), CST II (P = 0.005, q = 0.016), CST III (P = 0.006, q = 0.016) and CST IV (P = 0.002, q = 0.010). Because CST V represents a Lactobacillus jensenii–dominant community rather than a Lactobacillus-depleted, polymicrobial community (CST IV), this reduction in IL-3 - a hematopoietic, myeloid-supportive cytokine - is not attributable to the anaerobe-dominated community type and instead identifies a CST-V-specific signal.Collectively, these findings indicate that cervicovaginal IFN-α2 and IL-3 differ across community state types in a CST-specific manner, with relative elevation of IFN-α2 in CST II and a specific reduction of IL-3 in CST V.3.2.3.Differences in cervicovaginal immune profiles across cytological categoriesThe instrument-reported Total Events parameter differed across cytological categories (adjusted P = 0.006), with higher values observed in ASC-US and LSIL compared with NILM. Because Total Events represents an acquisition-related parameter rather than a cytokine concentration measure, this finding was considered exploratory and was not interpreted as evidence of increased overall immune activation. In contrast, the standardized immune-module scores summarized coordinated patterns across biologically related cytokine and chemokine profiles across cytological grades revealed significant grade-dependent alterations in 13 immune mediators spanning all four functional modules, with all analyses adjusted for age, BMI, menstrual phase, and HPV status. Median scores for all four functional immune modules Growth/epithelial, Inflammatory cytokines, Th17/type-2 response, and Chemokine/myeloid were positive at NILM and lower values in ASCUS, LSIL and ASC-H. The Growth/epithelial module showed the most pronounced and sustained decline, while the Th17/type-2 module showed a distinct ASC-H profile relative to LSIL (Figure 2A).Profiling of the significant immune markers showed a consistent pat…
full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study provides an integrated, multi-kingdom characterization of the cervicovaginal immune microenvironment in relation to HPV status, vaginal community state type, cytological grade, and microbiome composition spanning bacteria, viruses, and fungi. HPV infection and CST group were each associated with attenuation of innate antiviral and Th2-associated signaling. Immune-marker patterns differed non-monotonically across cytological categories, rather than showing a simple ordered gradient from NILM through ASC-H. Microbiome–immune associations were observed across bacterial, viral, and fungal domains, with distinct immune-marker patterns according to microbial kingdom and taxonomic level. The lower IL-4 and IL-17E/IL-25 concentrations observed in HPV-positive participants are consistent with previously reported differences in local Th2-associated and epithelial immune signaling in HPV infection. Experimental studies have described HPV immune-evasion mechanisms, but the present cross-sectional analysis cannot determine whether HPV directly caused the observed cytokine differences (Stanley, 2010; Łaniewski et al., 2018). Even though HPV has established immune-evasion mechanisms in experimental systems, the cross-sectional associations observed in this work cannot determine whether HPV directly caused the lower cytokine levels. The CST-specific differences observed here - relative elevation of IFN-α2 in CST II and reduction of IL-3 in CST V - do not follow a simple monotonic pattern across CST groups. Notably, the lowest IL-3 levels occurred in CST V, a Lactobacillus jensenii-dominant rather than Lactobacillus-depleted community, so these findings cannot be straightforwardly attributed to the polymicrobial CST IV state. They are nonetheless broadly compatible with reports that vaginal community composition modulates local antiviral and myeloid-supportive signaling (Gardella et al., 2022; Tosado-Rodríguez et al., 2023), although the CST-specificity and direction observed here warrant cautious interpretation and replication. Mechanistically, depletion of lactic-acid-producing Lactobacillus spp. removes a key suppressor of bacterial biofilm formation and epithelial Toll-like receptor activation — a systems-level interaction recently formalized in a triad model linking HPV, the cervicovaginal microbiome, and bacterial biofilm dynamics (Nazarova et al., 2026) — a process exemplified by Fannyhessea vaginae, which has been shown to activate TLR2/NF-κB signaling in cervicovaginal epithelial cells and drive pro-inflammatory cytokine output (Łaniewski et al., 2018; Gardella et al., 2022). Reduced type I interferon tone combined with an anaerobe-enriched bacterial community could create a local environment less capable of clearing incident HPV infection, consistent with longitudinal evidence linking taxa such as Gardnerella to impaired HR-HPV clearance and accelerated progression to precancer (Mitra et al., 2020).The grade-dependent immune remodeling observed here a rise in total events alongside a biphasic decline-and-partial-recovery pattern across individual cytokine modules extends previous reports of non-linear immune trajectories in cervical carcinogenesis (Audirac-Chalifour et al., 2016; Łaniewski et al., 2018). The distinct profiles of IL-18, IL-1α, MIP-1β, and Eotaxin across cytological grades reveal non-linear patterns, characterized by lower relative levels in LSIL samples compared to higher levels observed in NILM/ASC-US and partial re-elevation of IL-1α in ASC-H samples. Rather than a uniform continuum, these cross-sectional differences suggest that different cytological categories exhibit distinct local immune microenvironments, with LSIL marked by lower baseline chemokine levels relative to both low-grade atypia (ASC-US) and high-grade lesion categories (ASC-H). Although all ASC-H specimens in this cohort demonstrated cytomorphological abnormalities suspicious for high-grade squamous intraepithelial disease, including nuclear enlargement, irregular nuclear contours, abnormal chromatin distribution, and atypical parabasal-type cells, histological confirmation was not available. This pattern parallels the broader concept, established in invasive cervical cancer, that advanced cervical neoplasia is accompanied by elevated TNF-α, TNF-β, MIP-1α, GM-CSF, and IL-10, suggestive of a shift toward an immunosuppressive, tumor-permissive cytokine milieu (Łaniewski et al., 2018). The lower growth/epithelial module scores observed in LSIL and ASC-H may indicate differences in epithelial-associated signaling across cytological categories; however, epithelial barrier integrity was not directly measured in this study.The exploratory machine-learning analysis provided a multivariable assessment of whether cervicovaginal cytokine profiles contained discriminatory information beyond individual marker comparisons. After repeated nested cross-validation and regularization, the LSIL-versus-NILM classifier showed moderate internal discrimination (AUC 0.70, 95% CI 0.59–0.79), whereas ASCUS-versus-NILM discrimination was essentially at chance level (AUC 0.51, 95% CI 0.38–0.64). Performance for ASC-H versus NILM was also limited and highly uncertain (AUC 0.59, 95% CI 0.34–0.83), reflecting the very small ASC-H subgroup. Although several cytokines, including IFN-γ, M-CSF, IL-1α, IL-17F, IFN-α2, and EGF, showed positive mean permutation importance in the LSIL comparison, confidence intervals for individual feature-importance estimates crossed zero. Consequently, these variables should not be interpreted as stable predictive biomarkers. Rather, the classification results provide hypothesis-generating evidence that multivariate cytokine patterns may distinguish HPV-positive LSIL from NILM within this cohort, a finding that requires replication and external validation before any clinical interpretation. Notably, no cytokine reached FDR-significance for cytological grade among HPV-negative participants, indicating that grade-associated cytokine difference in this cohort is largely restricted to, or at least substantially amplified within, the context of HPV infection. Taken together, these classification analyses suggest that cytokine-based discrimination of cytological grade showed its highest internally cross-validated discrimination for the comparison between HPV-positive NILM and LSIL participants and is constrained both by sample size at the small ASC-H subgroup and by the absence of detectable cytokine remodeling in the HPV-negative population.The restricted, taxon-specific pattern observed in our study is consistent with previous cervicovaginal studies showing that microbial community composition is linked to selective, rather than uniform, changes in local immune mediators. Łaniewski et al. demonstrated that cervicovaginal microbiota composition was associated with distinct immune signatures across HPV infection and cervical carcinogenesis (Łaniewski et al., 2018). while Tosado-Rodríguez et al. found that greater cervicovaginal microbial diversity and dysbiosis were associated with inflammatory and trafficking-related cytokines, including IL-6, MIP-1α, MCP-1, IP-10, and anti-inflammatory IL-10 (Tosado-Rodríguez et al., 2023). More recently, Yonezawa et al. showed that cervicovaginal bacterial community patterns and the abundance of Gardnerella spp. and Fannyhessea vaginae were associated with variation in IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL8, IL-10, and TNF-α, further supporting the concept that specific bacterial configurations correspond to distinct local inflammatory and regulatory profiles (Yonezawa et al., 2026). In this context, our associations of Escherichia with IL-6 and MIP-1β and of Phocaeicola with IL-10 fit a broader cervicovaginal pattern in which individual bacterial taxa or community structures are linked to both pro-inflammatory and immunoregulatory mediators, although the specific Phocaeicola–IL-10 relationship appears to be novel and requires independent…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionThis cross-sectional study identified differences in the cervicovaginal immune microenvironment according to HPV status, bacterial community state type, and cervical cytological category. Compositional microbiome reanalysis identified a limited number of bacterial, viral, and fungal associations with cervicovaginal immune mediators after taxonomic curation and multiple-testing correction. Significant bacterial associations were confined to the genus level, fungal associations to the family level, and viral associations were observed across family, genus, and species levels. Of the associations meeting within-kingdom × taxonomic-level FDR criteria, only Phocaeicola–IL-10 and Rountreeviridae–MIP-1β also remained significant after global correction across all tested taxon–immune-marker pairs. Viral and fungal findings should be considered exploratory given the substantially lower non-bacterial sequencing depth and lack of independent taxon-specific validation. These relationships should be considered hypothesis-generating taxon-cytokine associations rather than evidence of direct microbial regulation of the local immune response. Among HPV-positive participants, internally cross-validated cytokine profiles showed moderate discrimination between LSIL and NILM, whereas discrimination of ASC-US was close to chance and estimates for ASC-H were limited by the small sample size. Overall, these findings provide hypothesis-generating evidence of multi-kingdom microbiome–immune associations in HPV-associated cervical abnormalities and support longitudinal and mechanistic studies to determine their temporal and biological significance.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionPersistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) remains the principal etiological factor in cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and invasive cervical cancer, yet only a minority of HR-HPV infections progress to high-grade dysplasia or malignancy (Mitra et al., 2016; Kyrgiou and Moscicki, 2022). In Kazakhstan, cervical cancer remains a substantial public health burden, underscoring the need for region-specific data on the host and microbial cofactors that shape HPV-related disease trajectories in this population (Rakhmankulova et al., 2026). This discordance between viral exposure and clinical outcome has directed increasing attention toward host- and microenvironment-level cofactors that modulate the natural history of HPV infection, including local mucosal immunity and the composition of the cervicovaginal microbiome (CVM) (Mitra et al., 2020; Kyrgiou and Moscicki, 2022).The CVM is conventionally classified into five community state types (CSTs) on the basis of dominant bacterial taxa, ranging from Lactobacillus crispatus-dominated communities (CST I), associated with mucosal homeostasis and low pH, to polymicrobial, Lactobacillus-depleted communities enriched in strict and facultative anaerobes such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Fannyhessea (Atopobium) vaginae, and Sneathia spp. (CST IV) (Ravel et al., 2011). CST IV and related dysbiotic states have been repeatedly and independently associated with HR-HPV persistence, accelerated progression to high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), and invasive cervical cancer across diverse populations (Gardella et al., 2022; Kyrgiou and Moscicki, 2022; Tosado-Rodríguez et al., 2023). Proposed mechanisms linking dysbiosis to disease progression include loss of the protective lactic-acid barrier, biofilm formation by anaerobic taxa, activation of epithelial Toll-like receptor signaling, and induction of a chronic, low-grade mucosal inflammatory state that favors viral persistence and immune evasion (Łaniewski et al., 2018; Gardella et al., 2022).Cervicovaginal cytokines and chemokines constitute the principal effector layer through which microbial composition is translated into local immunological consequence. Cross-sectional and longitudinal studies have shown that Lactobacillus-dominant CVM is generally associated with a low-inflammatory cytokine profile, whereas dysbiotic, Lactobacillus-depleted states correlate with elevated pro-inflammatory and chemotactic mediators, including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, MIP-1α, and MCP-1 (Łaniewski et al., 2018; Tosado-Rodríguez et al., 2023; Gonçalves-Nobre et al., 2024). Such pro-inflammatory shifts have, in turn, been implicated in promoting epithelial transformation, recruitment of myeloid and Th17 effector populations, and impaired antiviral interferon signaling across stages of cervical disease (Audirac-Chalifour et al., 2016; Łaniewski et al., 2018). However, the majority of this literature has examined the bacterial microbiome and a comparatively narrow cytokine panel in isolation, leaving the broader, multi-domain microbial ecosystem of the female genital tract spanning bacteria, viruses, and fungi and its joint relationship with the local immune milieu considerably less well characterized.Beyond the bacterial compartment, accumulating evidence indicates that non-bacterial constituents of the CVM are not inert bystanders. The cervicovaginal virome, comprising both eukaryotic viruses and bacteriophages, shows compositional shifts that track with genital inflammation and bacterial community structure, suggesting trans-kingdom interactions within the local ecosystem (Kaelin et al., 2022). Similarly, the vaginal mycobiome though quantitatively minor relative to the bacteriome has been associated with cervical disease severity, HPV status, and CST composition, with reduced fungal diversity reported in high-grade lesions and specific taxa such as Candida spp. linked to local inflammatory responses that may facilitate HPV persistence (Usyk et al., 2017; Onywera et al., 2019; Godoy-Vitorino et al., 2026); in a Kazakhstani shotgun metagenomic cohort, Lactobacillus iners dominance was similarly identified as a Candida-permissive niche associated with α-9 HPV genotypes even in cytologically normal women (Kozhakhmetov et al., 2026).Cervical cytological grade itself provides an additional, clinically anchored axis along which immune remodeling can be tracked. Cervical cytological categories provide a clinically relevant framework for examining differences in the local immune microenvironment. Previous studies have reported that progression from normal cytology (NILM) to atypical squamous cells cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H) has been associated with non-linear, module-specific changes in growth/epithelial, inflammatory, Th17/type-2, and chemokine/myeloid cytokine signatures, suggesting a transition from active immune surveillance at early stages toward immune exhaustion and dysregulation at higher grades (Audirac-Chalifour et al., 2016; Łaniewski et al., 2018). full_text: In 2025, the IARC Monographs programme identified two new modifiable potential causes of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, with limited evidence: automotive gasoline and human cytomegalovirus. Previously, for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia only one potential cause was identified (parental tobacco smoking, with limited evidence). The Monographs programme, throughout its history, has identified few other causes for specific childhood cancers. Here, we aim to: i) summarise IARC Monographs classifications relevant for childhood cancer aetiology; ii) describe the evidence that contributed to the recent classifications of automotive gasoline and human cytomegalovirus; and iii) list agents with evidence for an association with childhood cancer that are currently prioritised for an IARC Monographs evaluation in the 2025–2029 period. Several factors have been increasingly identified as potential modifiable causes of childhood cancers. Methodologically, studies have been improved by including assessment of the exposure prior to diagnosis (e.g., use of geocoding methodology or stored neonatal bloodspots) that were instrumental in the automotive gasoline and human cytomegalovirus classifications. Several agents currently prioritised for IARC Monographs evaluation, mainly individual pesticides or air pollution components, present sporadic positive findings for specific childhood cancer subtypes. IARC Monographs evaluation of cannabis smoking is planned for November 2026. Sporadic positive associations for specific childhood cancer subtypes were also reported for cannabis smoking (through parental habits) in case–control studies in the 1990s and early 2000s. Studies informative for cancer hazard identification are likely those able to well define the exposure (e.g., individual pesticides), the window of exposures (e.g., in utero) and the outcome (e.g., avoiding combining childhood cancers). Considerations on exposure assessment methodsThe IARC Monographs evaluation, following the 2019 revision of the Preamble [9], has moved towards a systematic and detailed review of the exposure assessment in human studies considered in the evaluation. This has resulted in the development of a specific workflow, which was followed for the evaluation of automotive gasoline and HCMV [24]. The novelty of these two recent evaluations, with respect to past childhood cancer evaluations, was the availability of studies with pre-diagnostic measurements, which complemented the evidence from traditional interview-based case–control studies.Given the challenge of obtaining pre-diagnostic samples in childhood cancer studies, studies traditionally have relied on parental reporting on past exposure, which may be subject to recall bias [25]. Extensive effort has gone into assessing in utero and childhood exposure at different time points in maternal–child cohort studies, but these tend to be inefficient for rare childhood cancer subtypes. Despite ongoing efforts to pool birth cohorts to study childhood cancer outcomes, such as the International Childhood Cancer Cohort Consortium, the statistical power in cohort studies remains low, especially for rarer childhood cancer subtypes [26].Geographic information systems (GIS)-based studies to assess residential environmental exposure are increasing, and many of the studies of agents currently prioritised for evaluation used in the Monographs also present this type of design (see below and see Table 1). Stored neonatal blood spots are increasingly used to assess biomarkers of environmental exposure [63], such as nicotine, trace elements and persistent organic pollutants [64]. It is important to note, however, that biological-based measurements, especially if taken at a single time point, may still be subject to non-differential exposure misclassification, particularly for agents with short half-lives [25]. Likewise, GIS-based studies might also be affected by exposure misclassification because full residential history is often lacking. Additional non-differential exposure misclassification in GIS-based study could come from modelling uncertainty. It is also important to consider that recall bias might not be a concern for all interview-based studies in case–control studies. For example, reporting of the occupational use of pesticides has not been found to be differential between cases and controls [65]. In the automotive gasoline evaluation, interviewed-based study were not discarded, rather they were evaluated together with residential-based studies [10].Table 1.Environmental agents* prioritised for evaluation by the IARC Monographs programme (2025–2029) with evidence of childhood cancersAgent (priority); previous IARC classificationExposuresChildhood cancerParental habits and occupations Parental tobacco smoking (high); IARC Group 1Widespread globallyThe advisory group noted that new studies that link parental tobacco smoking and childhood cancers have been available since the latest tobacco smoking evaluation [16]. Several recent meta-analyses have highlighted increased risk for maternal smoking and childhood brain tumours [27] or for paternal smoking and childhood ALL [28]. The 1.2 or 1.3-fold risk for pre- and postnatal paternal smoking observed for childhood AML in the pooled analysis of Childhood Leukaemia International Consortium was also highlighted; however, maternal smoking showed associations only in specific ethnic subgroups [29]. In addition, prenatal maternal and paternal smoking were associated with increased risk of neuroblastoma in offspring in a recent meta-analysis [30]. Cannabis smoking; never evaluatedThrough exposure to maternal or parental cannabis smokingThe advisory group mainly highlighted positive associations for testicular germ cell tumours, which are the most common cancers in males 15–35 years of age. As regards childhood cancers, although not specifically cited in the Advisory Group report, reviews, including the California state evaluations [31,32], have highlighted that sporadic positive findings were reported in several case–control studies conducted in the 1990s and early 2000s, mostly by the Children’s Cancer Study Group for: - Childhood acute non-lymphoblastic leukaemia - Childhood astrocytoma - Neuroblastoma. Textile manufacturing industry work; Group 2BMaternal or paternal occupationIn addition to the adult cancer studies highlighted in the IARC Advisory Group report, several studies were identified that explored the associations between parental occupation and childhood cancer in offspring, using either census data or parental interviews. Associations were reported for parental (maternal and/or paternal) textile manufacturing industry work and childhood central nervous system (CNS) tumours [33–35], paternal or maternal contact with textile dust and Ewing sarcoma [36] or childhood cancer tumours other than leukaemia or CNS tumours [37], maternal textile work and childhood acute non-lymphoblastic leukaemia [38] or childhood soft tissue sarcoma [39].Outdoor air pollution and its components Outdoor air pollution (high); IARC Group 1Widespread, especially low- and middle-income countries (LMIC)The IARC Advisory Group reported the available evidence for childhood leukaemia (including subtypes) citing a recent meta-analysis which identified several studies reporting associations between proxies of outdoor air pollution (e.g., traffic density, benzene) and childhood leukaemia, including subtypes (ALL, AML). A stronger risk was found for benzene and AML (RR = 1.84), and other measurements of air pollution were weakly or imprecisely associated [40]. For other childhood cancer subtypes (childhood NHL, childhood CNS tumours, neuroblastoma, other subtypes of childhood cancer), several studies with positive results for air pollution metrics, many also based on geocoding data, are available and identified in a recent scoping review [41]. Ultrafine particles (UFP) (high); never evaluatedComponent of air pollutionOnly a single study that associated UFP and childhood cancer risk was identified by the advisory group. A case–control study in Canada reported an association between UFP exposure in the first trimester, based on residential air pollution exposure modelling, and overall childhood cancer incidence; however, associations weakened when studying specific subtypes [42]. Acetaldehyde (high); acetaldehyde: Group 2B, acetaldehyde associated with consumption of alcoholic beverages: Group 1Component of air pollutionThe advisory group highlighted the sporadic positive associations between early life exposure to acetaldehyde and several childhood cancers. In a single case–control study of retinoblastoma (<6 years of age) in California, acetaldehyde exposure in the first year of life was found to be associated with increased retinoblastoma risk [43]. Based on residential-based modelling exposure, acetaldehyde in air pollution during the third trimester was associated with Wilms tumour in a single case–control study [44]. The occurrence of the CNS primitive neuroectodermal tumour was also associated with prenatal acetaldehyde exposure in a California case–control study [45]. No additional studies were identified. Formaldehyde (high); Group 1Component of air pollutionIn addition to the adult studies highlighted by the AG, formaldehyde found in air pollution during pregnancy, as based on residential-based exposure modelling in a single case–control study, has been positively associated with risk of Wilms tumours in offspring (in younger than 6 years of age) [44]. Small imprecise increased associations were found for childhood leukaemia in a similar case–control study in California [46]. NO2 (high); never evaluatedComponent of air pollutionNo specific study on childhood cancer was highlighted by the Advisory Group on childhood cancer. However, a recent meta-analysis identified nine studies associating NO2 and childhood leukaemia, including subtypes, with some evidence of increased risk in the dose–response analysis for the highest category of exposure, although this was imprecise [40]. Residential NO2 levels were associated with childhood AML in a subsequent study [47]. Few studies explored prenatal windows of exposures, with one study reporting associations for first trimester NO2 exposure and childhood ALL, but not for other windows of exposure [48]. Xylene (medium); Group 3Component of air pollutionThe Advisory Group report that findings for human cancer are only sporadic. Regarding childhood cancers, in a single case–control study in California in children (<6 years of age), meta/para-xylene exposure was associated with all germ cell tumours and yolk sac tumours (<6 years of age), especially for exposure that happened in the second trimester. Orto-xylene exposure in second and third trimester was also associated with increased risk of yolk sac tumour [49]. In a similar case–control study in California focused on retinoblastoma (<6 years of age), average meta/para-xylene exposure in utero was associated with increased risk of retinoblastoma [43]. No other study was identified. Selenium (medium) Group 3Component of air pollution, diet intakeThe Advisory Group report highlighted mixed results for human cancer evidence and reported the challenge of the interpretation of the data in human cancer studies. Childhood cancer studies were not highlighted in the report. For childhood cancer studies, selenium, as a component of air pollution, was analysed in some of the air pollution modelling studies identified for other air pollution components. Some imprecise positive associations were reported for childhood leukaemia. There are also some positive findings for childhood leukaemia in case–control studies with blood measurements of metals, although this is not consistent across all forms of selenium and measurements are taken after diagnosis, raising concern over reverse causation [50]. Carbon tetrachloride (high); Group 2BSolvents, agricultural fumigants, industrial processes (use now restricted), air pollutionThe Advisory Group report cited a single Californian case–control study of neuroblastoma (<6 years of age), carbon tetrachloride exposure in utero (2.5 km buffer) was associated with neuroblastoma risk with a very imprecise 7-fold increase [51]. In addition, parental occupation exposure to carbon tetrachloride, particularly paternal pre-conception exposure, was found to be associated with increased childhood leukaemia and NHL in offspring in the north of England [52]. Of note, the Advisory Group report has highlighted positive and consistent findings for adult NHL.Physical agents Radon-222 and its decay products (high); Group 1Naturally occurring gas. Exposure occurs at residential levels, especially in areas with high concentrations or in indoor subterranean areas.The Advisory Group report highlighted the availability of an increased number of studies with respect to radon evaluation in 2009, on childhood leukaemia [13]. These include several recent meta-analyses with positive results, which merit further evaluation [53].Pesticides Pyrethrin and pyrethroid insecticides (high); Group 3 Note: Several other pyrethrins and pyrethroids have been recommended by the Advisory Group to be evaluated and the recommendation is evaluating single pyrethroid and pyrethrins in a single volume, not the class combined.Insecticide class Use: Worldwide agricultural, veterinary, domestic and public health use (disinfection of buildings, treatment of mosquito nets). Childhood exposure could occur through environment (residence near crop fields), contact with family members occupationally exposed, exposure in residential setting (used in home or gardens).Few available studies were reported by the Advisory Group. Residences near where pyrethroids were sprayed (600 m buffer) was not associated with childhood leukaemia [54]; however, permethrin (see below) was associated. In single studies, parental-reported use of insecticidal shampoo containing pyrethroids was associated with acute childhood leukaemia (ALL and ANLL) [55] and urinary levels (at diagnosis) of pyrethroids insecticides were higher in cases of childhood ALL [56]. Permethrin (high); Group 3Class: pyrethroid pesticide (see above) .Childhood exposure also could occur through the application of shampoo for treatment of head lice and scabies.Few available studies were reported by the Advisory Group. Increased risk was found in the geocoding-based childhood leunkemia study based in California [54], but not in the Californian childhood ALL study using measures of permethrin in household dust [57]. Parental-reported exposure to permethrin was associated with childhood ALL and AML in Brazil [58]. Chlorpyrifos (high); never evaluatedOrganophosphate insecticide still registers in the US but registration was cancelled in the European Union since 2020. Exposure in children occurs through contaminated water and food.No specific childhood cancer study was highlighted by the Advisory Group. In the Californian geocode state-wide case–control study chlorpyrifos was associated with childhood ALL (<6 years of age) in a single pesticide-adjusted model [59]. No other study was identified. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsWhile few modifiable risk factors have been established as causes of childhood cancer, two IARC Monographs evaluations in 2025 established that there is limited evidence that automotive gasoline and HCMV are causes of childhood ALL. This highlights a potentially larger role for environmental factors in the aetiology of childhood cancer than previously appreciated and the need for additional epidemiological data informative for cancer hazard identification.The recent classifications of automotive gasoline and HCMV reflect advancements in childhood cancer aetiological epidemiological research, particularly in studies that are able to obtain pre-diagnostic exposure assessment data through the exploitation of historical residential location data or stored pre-diagnostic biological samples, including neonatal bloodspots.Among the agents prioritised for evaluation by the IARC Monographs programme, with evidence of increased risks for some types of childhood cancers, the data are currently generally restricted to single studies with positive findings.In conclusion, aetiological factors for childhood cancer are increasingly being identified, and epidemiological research in this area has evolved to incorporate novel approaches for pre-diagnostic exposure assessment. These approaches move away from relying solely on interview-based information or biological samples collected at diagnosis, which are subject to recall bias and reverse causality, respectively. Future Monographs evaluations are likely to be informed by studies with pre-diagnostic exposure assessments. Studies conducted in different geographical locations, focusing on specific cancer types, including leukaemia subtypes, and relevant exposure windows, seem likely to be informative.
full_text_sections.other: BackgroundChildhood cancer is rare, yet it remains a leading cause of death in children, despite significant improvement in childhood cancer survival rates [1]. It is also an important public health burden, because childhood cancer survivors are at higher risk of chronic diseases, second primary cancers or financial distress [2].The most common cancer types in children (<15 years old) are leukaemias, with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) being the most common paediatric malignancy, Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and brain tumours, particularly gliomas and embryonal tumours (e.g., medulloblastomas). There are also other cancer types that tend to occur almost exclusively in children, such as Wilms tumour and other embryonal tumours [1,3].The incidence of childhood cancer is slowly and steady increasing worldwide [1]. Such trends cannot be entirely explained by advancements in diagnosis, genetics or physiological factors (e.g., parental age), and it is likely that environmental factors, which change over time, play a role [4].Children can be especially vulnerable to environmental pollutants or biological agents owing to their potentially high exposure (e.g., hand–mouth habits), their developing physiology and longer lifespan to develop long-term health effects [5]. Parental exposure is also a concern in children, owing to potential effects in the pre-conception or pregnancy window [6]. New suspected modifiable causes of childhood cancers are increasingly being reported because of the progress made in the last decade to develop new infrastructure for studying childhood cancer risk factors, including the creation of large consortia and data platforms [7]. However, few environmental or lifestyle causes of childhood cancer have been established or recognised by authoritative public health organisations. Environmental risk factors have been generally downplayed or are less well known compared to genetic factors. In 2025, two IARC Monographs Working Groups classified two agents with limited evidence for childhood ALL: automotive gasoline [10] and human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) [11]. A sufficient determination in human cancer studies can lead to a Group 1 classification. A Group 1 classification can also be reached when combining sufficient evidence in animals and strong evidence from human mechanistic studies [9]. full_text: Lower anogenital tract malignancies comprise anatomically adjacent but biologically heterogeneous epithelial cancers of the cervix, vulva, vagina, anal canal and penis. This narrative and conceptual Review used a transparent literature search to examine how human papillomavirus (HPV) etiology intersects with tumor lineage, somatic alterations, antigen-presentation competence, immune-cell state and spatial organization. Evidence quality is heterogeneous: cervical cancer is supported by the largest genomic, single-cell, spatial and randomized-trial literature, whereas vaginal, vulvar and penile cancers remain constrained by small retrospective cohorts and cross-site extrapolation. HPV-associated tumors retain non-self E6/E7 antigens, but viral transcription does not ensure peptide presentation, dendritic-cell priming or epithelial access by functional T cells. HPV-independent tumors lack constitutive viral antigens yet may generate mutation- or differentiation-derived immunity and checkpoint-restrained myeloid–lymphoid niches. We therefore distinguish etiological status from functional immune phenotype and critically appraise three spatial architectures—an inflamed/epithelial-penetrating pattern, a stromally excluded pattern, and an immune-desert pattern—together with an immunosuppressive functional overlay that may occur in any architecture. Clinical evidence is graded separately from mechanistic inference: immune checkpoint blockade has established roles in defined cervical and anal cancer settings, whereas therapeutic vaccines, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, T-cell receptor-engineered therapies, myeloid or stromal sensitization and artificial-intelligence-guided selection remain investigational or context dependent. A three-tier biomarker framework is proposed, separating routine clinical assays from extended translational profiling and exploratory single-cell, spatial and artificial-intelligence methods. This framework is hypothesis-generating, not a validated treatment-selection algorithm; assay combinations, thresholds and incremental clinical utility require prospective, multicenter and site-stratified validation. 2Review methodologyThis article is a narrative and conceptual Review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus from database inception through 25 July 2026. ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, the US Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency websites were consulted for trial status and jurisdiction-specific regulatory information. Principal concepts combined terms for HPV, p16, E6/E7, HPV-independent disease, cervix, vulva, vagina, anus, penis, squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, tumor immune microenvironment, antigen presentation, HLA, B2M, dendritic cells, macrophages, tertiary lymphoid structures, single-cell RNA sequencing, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, immunometabolism, immune checkpoint inhibition, therapeutic vaccination, adoptive cell therapy, circulating tumor HPV DNA, digital pathology and artificial intelligence.English-language original studies, randomized trials, prospective cohorts, well-annotated retrospective cohorts, pathological classification studies, systematic reviews and authoritative tumor classifications were eligible. Conference abstracts were used only when no full report was available and were explicitly labeled; preprints were not used as core evidence. Regulatory documents were cited only to describe a named jurisdiction and date, not as universal clinical standards. Case reports were excluded unless they supplied unique mechanistic evidence in an exceptionally rare setting.Landmark studies were defined as those establishing an etiological classification, practice-changing randomized result or first direct demonstration of a mechanism. Representative studies were selected to illustrate major anatomical sites, technologies and geographical settings. Confirmatory studies were included when they tested the same biological proposition in an independent cohort or by an orthogonal method. When cohorts overlapped, the largest or most mature report was used for the principal clinical endpoint; related publications were retained only when they supplied distinct molecular or longitudinal analyses. Evidence from other solid tumors was used selectively for general mechanisms such as TGF-β-associated exclusion, extracellular-matrix restriction or metabolic competition and is identified as extrapolative rather than direct lower anogenital evidence.No formal pooled effect estimate or risk-of-bias score was calculated. Instead, claims were graded narratively as: (i) regulatory or guideline-linked indication within a named jurisdiction; (ii) randomized clinical evidence; (iii) prospective disease-specific activity; (iv) prognostic association; (v) computational or spatial association; (vi) functional perturbation; or (vii) unvalidated mechanistic hypothesis. This hierarchy was used to prevent computational ligand–receptor inference or HPV prevalence within a trial population from being interpreted as functional causality or predictive biomarker evidence.The authors independently reviewed the search decisions, evidence appraisal, factual statements, citations, references, clinical data, scientific interpretation, final wording, and visual elements and take full responsibility for the final content. 8Methodological appraisal of single-cell and spatial evidenceSingle-cell and spatial technologies are central to this Review but are also a major source of overinterpretation. Table 3 summarizes representative studies, sample numbers, platforms, validation and limitations. Findings are classified as transcriptional association, computational communication inference, spatial colocalization, protein-level validation, functional perturbation or clinical association.Table 3Methodological appraisal of representative single-cell and spatial studies.Cancer/site (reference)Patients/specimens and treatment statePlatform/materialHPV ascertainmentMain reported findingEvidence levelPrincipal limitationsCervical SCC (22)5 samples for snRNA-seq; 18 spatial samples; treatment context variedsnRNA-seq on frozen tissue; Stereo-seqStudy-specific HPV/pathology annotationLGALS9 and IDO1 spatial programsTranscriptional association and spatial localizationDifferent specimen sets; nuclear transcript bias; cross-sample integrationCervical progression (23)9 scRNA-seq specimens: 2 uninfected normal, 2 HPV-positive normal, 2 HPV-positive HSIL and 3 HPV-positive cervical cancers; plus 2 cervical-cancer spatial specimens. Dataset overlap was not clearly specified.scRNA-seq (GSE208653) plus 10x spatial transcriptomics (GSE208654)Dataset labels: NO_HPV, N_HPV, HSIL_HPV and CA_HPVSPP1+ macrophage expansion; inferred SPP1-CD44 communicationComputational communication inference; spatial associationSmall public-data cohort; only 2 spatial cancers; dataset overlap unclear; no receptor perturbation; stage/batch confoundingHPV-positive versus HPV-negative cervix (24)7 untreated biopsies; scRNA component included 2 HPV+ and 2 HPV− tumors10x scRNA-seq and Visium; fresh biopsyHPV DNA genotyping plus p16Distinct cDC2, T-cell and epithelial-myeloid programs; inferred ANXA1-FPR and MDK-LRP1Small-cohort transcriptional and computational associationPatient n very small; spots contain many cells; no functional perturbationCervical histology comparison (26)8 tumors: 5 SCC and 3 adenocarcinomassnRNA-seqHPV-related cervical cancersHistology-specific malignant and immune statesTranscriptional associationLineage and patient effects; no spatial validationVulvar SCC (47)4 early-stage cases spanning HPV-dependent and independent diseaseSpatial transcriptomicsStudy-specific HPV/p16 classificationDifferent epithelial, collagen and inflammatory programsSpatial associationExtremely small cohort; spot admixture; no single-cell reference or perturbationPenile SCC (53)6 patients; 6 snRNA-seq samples and 4 spatial samples; untreated primary tumorssnRNA-seq and Stereo-seq on frozen tissue2 HPV-associated and 4 HPV-independent patientsLAMC2-high boundary state; inferred laminin-integrin signalingTranscriptional/spatial associationSmall unbalanced groups; inferred interaction; no interventionEvidence categories and priority labels are defined in the main text; author-proposed research tiers are not clinical guidelines.Fresh-tissue dissociation can induce immediate-early and stress-response genes and preferentially lose fragile granulocytes, adipocytes or stromal cells (63, 64). Single-nucleus RNA sequencing enables frozen-tissue analysis and may preserve difficult cell populations, but it captures nuclear rather than whole-cell transcripts and can underrepresent cytoplasmic activation markers. Direct comparisons show that single-cell and single-nucleus workflows have cell-type-specific biases (65). Therefore, apparent differences between studies may reflect preparation rather than biology.Patient number, not cell number, determines biological replication. Differential expression based on thousands of cells from two or three patients can generate artificially small P values if donor effects are ignored. Pseudobulk or mixed-effects analyses are preferable, and pseudoreplication should be explicitly reported (66). Batch correction can remove technical variation but may also erase genuine site or treatment differences. Cell-state annotation depends on selected markers and reference atlases; copy-number inference identifies probable malignant cells but is less reliable in low-aneuploid or normal-like tumors.Ligand–receptor tools infer that a ligand and receptor are expressed in candidate sender and receiver populations. They do not demonstrate secretion, protein binding, receptor activation, directionality or biological necessity. Spatial colocalization strengthens plausibility but remains associative. Orthogonal protein imaging, receptor phosphorylation, ex vivo perturbation, genetic or pharmacological interruption and clinical replication represent progressively stronger evidence. Accordingly, SPP1–CD44, MDK–LRP1 and LAMC2–integrin programs are described here as inferred or associated unless direct perturbation was performed.Spatial transcriptomic platforms vary from multicellular spots to near-cellular or subcellular resolution. Spot admixture can create apparent co-expression between cells that never interact, and deconvolution depends on the accuracy of the reference single-cell dataset (67). Small tissue regions may miss invasive margins, tertiary lymphoid structures or hypoxic cores. Treatment exposure, tissue fixation and primary versus metastatic origin must be recorded. Similar macrophage or fibroblast labels across studies should be considered candidate conserved programs only after harmonized analysis and orthogonal validation. 13Discussion and limitationsThe principal contribution of this Review is to separate etiological origin from functional immune phenotype. HPV association supplies a shared viral-antigen source but does not guarantee transcription, presentation, priming or spatial access. HPV-independent tumors lack constitutive viral antigens but are not necessarily immune silent. This distinction is supported directly by cervical, vulvar and penile observations, although the density and quality of evidence vary markedly by site.The proposed spatial framework deliberately revises the earlier four-architecture model. Inflamed/epithelial-penetrating, stromally excluded and immune-desert states describe spatial organization. “Inflamed but suppressed” is better understood as a functional overlay that can coexist with an inflamed or excluded architecture. This formulation aligns more closely with established solid-tumor models and prevents checkpoint expression or macrophage abundance from being mistaken for a separate topology. The categories remain conceptual; no validated cutoff defines epithelial penetration, exclusion or desert status in these diseases.Several limitations constrain the synthesis. First, cervical cancer dominates the literature and includes more randomized trials and multi-omic datasets than vaginal, vulvar or penile cancer. Cross-site extrapolation was therefore minimized but cannot be eliminated. Second, histological and anatomical heterogeneity is substantial, especially when HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinomas are compared with squamous tumors. Third, many cohorts are retrospective, geographically concentrated and small; immune-compromised populations are incompletely represented despite their high disease burden.Fourth, HPV ascertainment differs across studies. HPV DNA, PCR, DNA in situ hybridization, E6/E7 RNA, p16 and morphology have different analytical meanings, and false-negative mechanisms are not uniformly investigated. Fifth, single-cell and spatial studies frequently include few patients, use different preparation platforms, and are vulnerable to dissociation bias, pseudoreplication, batch effects and spot admixture. Recurrent labels such as SPP1-positive macrophage or LAMC2-high tumor cell may indicate conserved programs, but they may also reflect annotation conventions or technical convergence.Sixth, treatment-related remodeling complicates comparison of untreated primary tissue with post-radiotherapy, recurrent or metastatic specimens. Seventh, the clinical evidence hierarchy is jurisdiction dependent and evolves rapidly; regulatory status was reviewed through 25 July 2026. Finally, the tiered biomarker workflow and AI component are hypothesis-generating. Assay combinations, cutoffs, turnaround time, cost, accessibility and incremental utility are undefined. The framework should not be interpreted as a clinical treatment-selection algorithm.These limitations define a practical research agenda. The decisive next step is not to add every available assay to every patient, but to prospectively test whether one clearly defined bottleneck and its matched measurement improve treatment selection within a specific site and disease setting. 14ConclusionsHPV-associated and HPV-independent lower anogenital tract malignancies begin with different oncogenic and antigenic programs but can converge on the same immune-evasion bottlenecks. HPV association is an evolutionary and etiological descriptor, not a fixed immune phenotype. HPV independence does not imply an immune desert.Immune checkpoint inhibitors have established roles in defined cervical and anal cancer settings, whereas evidence in vulvar, vaginal and penile cancer is more limited. Therapeutic vaccines, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, T-cell receptor-engineered therapies and myeloid, stromal or metabolic sensitization remain investigational or context dependent. Computational ligand–receptor inference and spatial colocalization should not be written as functional causality.The proposed three-tier biomarker framework and spatial architectures are hypothesis-generating research tools. They are not validated clinical classes, and assay combinations and thresholds remain undefined. Prospective, multicenter, site- and lineage-stratified studies must demonstrate analytical validity, clinical validity and incremental utility beyond existing pathological and molecular standards before the framework can influence routine treatment selection. 1IntroductionLower anogenital tract malignancies include invasive epithelial cancers of the uterine cervix, vulva, vagina, anal canal and penis. Their anatomical proximity and shared susceptibility to oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) have encouraged their treatment as a related disease family. That grouping is useful for prevention and for understanding viral oncogenesis, but it can become misleading when it overrides epithelial lineage, precursor lesion, site-specific stroma, lymphatic anatomy and established treatment standards. Cervical squamous cell carcinoma, usual-type endocervical adenocarcinoma, gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma and keratinizing vulvar or penile squamous carcinoma are not biologically interchangeable even when discussed under the same anogenital label (1–4).Persistent infection with a carcinogenic HPV genotype drives almost all conventional cervical cancers and most anal squamous cell carcinomas, but contributes more variably to vaginal, vulvar and penile squamous carcinomas. HPV16 predominates at most non-cervical sites, whereas cervical tumors display a broader genotype distribution. The resulting burden is shaped by vaccination, screening, sex, age, immune status, geography and access to care. People living with HIV and solid-organ transplant recipients have particularly elevated incidences of several HPV-related cancers, illustrating the importance of durable immune surveillance (5, 6).Contemporary pathology increasingly separates HPV-associated from HPV-independent disease. This distinction is most mature in vulvar squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma, where HPV/p16 and p53-informed classifications identify clinically distinct entities (7–9). However, the terms HPV-positive, p16-positive, transcriptionally active HPV and HPV-associated are not synonymous. HPV DNA may be incidental or transcriptionally silent; block-type p16 is an etiological surrogate whose specificity varies by site and histology; and a negative assay can reflect technical failure rather than genuine HPV independence. Etiological assignment therefore requires a site-aware integration of morphology and molecular testing.The immunological consequences of HPV are paradoxical. E6 and E7 are non-self proteins required for maintenance of transformation and are therefore attractive antigens. Yet established cancers have already passed through antiviral and antitumor immune selection. Viral antigenicity may coexist with defective innate sensing, impaired dendritic-cell maturation,…

Recurrent labels such as SPP1-positive macrophage or LAMC2-high tumor cell may indicate conserved programs, but they may also reflect annotation conventions or technical convergence.Sixth, treatment-related remodeling complicates comparison of untreated primary tissue with post-radiotherapy, recurrent or metastatic specimens. Seventh, the clinical evidence hierarchy is jurisdiction dependent and evolves rapidly; regulatory status was reviewed through 25 July 2026. Finally, the tiered biomarker workflow and AI component are hypothesis-generating. Assay combinations, cutoffs, turnaround time, cost, accessibility and incremental utility are undefined. The framework should not be interpreted as a clinical treatment-selection algorithm.These limitations define a practical research agenda. The decisive next step is not to add every available assay to every patient, but to prospectively test whether one clearly defined bottleneck and its matched measurement improve treatment selection within a specific site and disease setting.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 14ConclusionsHPV-associated and HPV-independent lower anogenital tract malignancies begin with different oncogenic and antigenic programs but can converge on the same immune-evasion bottlenecks. HPV association is an evolutionary and etiological descriptor, not a fixed immune phenotype. HPV independence does not imply an immune desert.Immune checkpoint inhibitors have established roles in defined cervical and anal cancer settings, whereas evidence in vulvar, vaginal and penile cancer is more limited. Therapeutic vaccines, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, T-cell receptor-engineered therapies and myeloid, stromal or metabolic sensitization remain investigational or context dependent. Computational ligand–receptor inference and spatial colocalization should not be written as functional causality.The proposed three-tier biomarker framework and spatial architectures are hypothesis-generating research tools. They are not validated clinical classes, and assay combinations and thresholds remain undefined. Prospective, multicenter, site- and lineage-stratified studies must demonstrate analytical validity, clinical validity and incremental utility beyond existing pathological and molecular standards before the framework can influence routine treatment selection.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionLower anogenital tract malignancies include invasive epithelial cancers of the uterine cervix, vulva, vagina, anal canal and penis. Their anatomical proximity and shared susceptibility to oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) have encouraged their treatment as a related disease family. That grouping is useful for prevention and for understanding viral oncogenesis, but it can become misleading when it overrides epithelial lineage, precursor lesion, site-specific stroma, lymphatic anatomy and established treatment standards. Cervical squamous cell carcinoma, usual-type endocervical adenocarcinoma, gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma and keratinizing vulvar or penile squamous carcinoma are not biologically interchangeable even when discussed under the same anogenital label (1–4).Persistent infection with a carcinogenic HPV genotype drives almost all conventional cervical cancers and most anal squamous cell carcinomas, but contributes more variably to vaginal, vulvar and penile squamous carcinomas. HPV16 predominates at most non-cervical sites, whereas cervical tumors display a broader genotype distribution. The resulting burden is shaped by vaccination, screening, sex, age, immune status, geography and access to care. People living with HIV and solid-organ transplant recipients have particularly elevated incidences of several HPV-related cancers, illustrating the importance of durable immune surveillance (5, 6).Contemporary pathology increasingly separates HPV-associated from HPV-independent disease. This distinction is most mature in vulvar squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma, where HPV/p16 and p53-informed classifications identify clinically distinct entities (7–9). However, the terms HPV-positive, p16-positive, transcriptionally active HPV and HPV-associated are not synonymous. HPV DNA may be incidental or transcriptionally silent; block-type p16 is an etiological surrogate whose specificity varies by site and histology; and a negative assay can reflect technical failure rather than genuine HPV independence. Etiological assignment therefore requires a site-aware integration of morphology and molecular testing.The immunological consequences of HPV are paradoxical. E6 and E7 are non-self proteins required for maintenance of transformation and are therefore attractive antigens. Yet established cancers have already passed through antiviral and antitumor immune selection. Viral antigenicity may coexist with defective innate sensing, impaired dendritic-cell maturation, HLA class I loss, regulatory lymphocytes, suppressive macrophages, metabolic stress and fibroblast-rich exclusion (10–13). Conversely, HPV-independent tumors may generate clonal neoantigens or altered differentiation antigens and can contain active, although frequently restrained, immune responses. The shorthand that HPV-associated tumors are uniformly immune-hot and HPV-independent tumors uniformly immune-cold is therefore mechanistically inadequate.This Review has three objectives. First, it defines which histological entities can be compared within a lower anogenital framework and where lineage- or site-specific interpretation must take precedence. Second, it evaluates molecular, single-cell, spatial and clinical evidence according to what each method can actually establish. Third, it proposes a tiered, explicitly hypothesis-generating biomarker framework that separates routine clinical assays from translational and exploratory measurements. Because most direct evidence derives from cervical cancer, that disease is treated as the reference model; conclusions for rarer sites are not inferred automatically from cervical data. 3Scope and site-specific etiological classificationThe comparative framework includes invasive cervical squamous cell carcinoma and usual-type HPV-associated endocervical adenocarcinoma; HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinomas, particularly gastric-type, clear-cell and mesonephric carcinomas; and invasive squamous cell carcinomas of the vulva, vagina, anal canal and penis. Precursor lesions are discussed only when they clarify the route to invasion. Non-epithelial malignancies, neuroendocrine carcinomas, melanoma and sarcoma are outside the main scope. Cross-site comparison is biologically justified when tumors share transcriptionally active high-risk HPV and E6/E7 dependence or when a common immune bottleneck, such as HLA loss, is directly demonstrated. Site- or lineage-specific interpretation takes precedence for cervical adenocarcinoma, chronic-dermatosis-associated vulvar cancer and other tumors whose developmental origin and genomic drivers differ substantially.Etiological classification should begin with morphology and an adequate tumor sample. HPV DNA testing detects viral genomic material but does not prove transcriptional activity. PCR-based assays offer genotype sensitivity but may detect incidental infection and can be affected by DNA quality or limited genotype coverage. DNA in situ hybridization adds localization but is less sensitive at low copy number. E6/E7 RNA in situ hybridization provides cellular localization of transforming transcription and has been analytically compared with PCR, DNA in situ hybridization and p16 immunohistochemistry, but performance still depends on fixation, RNA preservation and assay coverage (14).Block-type p16 immunohistochemistry is a practical surrogate for transforming HPV in cervical squamous carcinoma and many vulvar or penile squamous tumors, but it is not equally specific across sites and histologies. Non-HPV mechanisms can activate p16, and some transcriptionally active HPV tumors may lack classic block staining. p53 immunohistochemistry is not an HPV assay; it is used to identify mutation-pattern abnormalities and is particularly important in HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma. A three-tier biomarker framework is proposed, separating routine clinical assays from extended translational profiling and exploratory single-cell, spatial and artificial-intelligence methods. 2Review methodologyThis article is a narrative and conceptual Review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. Case reports were excluded unless they supplied unique mechanistic evidence in an exceptionally rare setting.Landmark studies were defined as those establishing an etiological classification, practice-changing randomized result or first direct demonstration of a mechanism. Confirmatory studies were included when they tested the same biological proposition in an independent cohort or by an orthogonal method. 8Methodological appraisal of single-cell and spatial evidenceSingle-cell and spatial technologies are central to this Review but are also a major source of overinterpretation.
