full_text: Transparency StatementThe corresponding author (Fábio Ferreira Amorim) affirms that this manuscript provides an honest, accurate, and transparent account of the study being reported; that no important aspects of the study have been omitted; and that there were no discrepancies from the original protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board. We thank the author for the careful and thoughtful reading of our study and for highlighting the clinical relevance of the gaps identified between preventive practices, knowledge, and awareness regarding human papillomavirus (HPV), cervical cancer screening, and HPV vaccination [1]. We particularly appreciate the recognition that, despite substantial knowledge gaps, our findings revealed generally favorable attitudes toward HPV vaccination. The points raised in the Letter to the Editor are constructive and provide an important opportunity to clarify aspects of the study, refine the interpretation of selected findings, and address numerical inconsistencies in the published report.We agree that the apparent contrast between preventive behavior and understanding deserves careful consideration. In our sample, 69.9% of participants reported having previously undergone a Pap smear, whereas 19.9% were classified as having a screening frequency consistent with the recommended protocol in the original analysis. Likewise, although 72.7% reported that they would “certainly” vaccinate their children against HPV, only 18.5% were aware of the association between HPV infection and cervical cancer [1]. These findings illustrate an important distinction between engaging in, or expressing favorable attitudes toward, preventive practices and having a comprehensive understanding of their rationale. We appreciate the author's emphasis on this issue, which is consistent with one of the central messages of our study.Concerning cervical cancer screening adherence, we thank the author for this important observation regarding the denominator used to report adherence. In the original analysis, we calculated the screening adherence estimate of 19.9% (60/302) using the entire study sample as the denominator, consistent with the general approach used for the descriptive percentages in the study. We agree, however, that screening adherence is more appropriately and clinically interpreted when specifically examined among women within the age range targeted by the Brazilian cervical cancer screening recommendations [2]. We therefore performed an additional analysis restricted to women aged 25–64 years. Of the 302 participants, 218 (72.2%) were within this target age range. Among these women, 53 (24.3%) reported a Pap smear frequency consistent with the screening protocol. Thus, when the denominator is restricted to women within the recommended screening age range, the estimated adherence increases from 19.9% in the overall sample to 24.3% (53/218). Importantly, although this age‐restricted analysis provides a more clinically appropriate estimate, adherence remained low, with fewer than one in four women in the recommended screening age range reporting a screening frequency consistent with the protocol. This finding reinforces an important gap between prior cervical cancer screening and adherence to the recommended screening schedule. It highlights the need to strengthen longitudinal follow‐up, patient education, and strategies to promote timely screening within primary health care.Regarding participants' certainty about vaccinating children against HPV, we clarify that this variable was intended to measure stated vaccination intention and, importantly, the degree of certainty regarding that intention, rather than actual parental vaccine uptake. In this context, “I do not know yet” represents a less favorable response in terms of vaccination certainty than “Certainly yes,” because it reflects the absence of a definite intention to vaccinate. We did not collect information on parental or guardian status, number of children, or children's ages in our questionnaire. Therefore, we cannot determine how many participants were mothers or guardians or stratify vaccination intention by parental status. We agree that this aspect may be particularly relevant when interpreting the responses, especially among younger women. The “I do not know yet” response may reflect uncertainty about HPV vaccination itself. However, for some participants, it may also reflect the hypothetical nature of the question among women who did not yet have children. Nevertheless, regardless of parental status, an “I do not know yet” response indicates lower vaccination certainty and a lack of definite intention to vaccinate. It may therefore reflect uncertainty or reduced confidence regarding HPV vaccination and can be considered relevant when identifying opportunities for vaccine education and counseling. However, because parental status, children's ages, and an actual vaccination decision were not assessed, these responses should not, by themselves, be interpreted as definitive evidence of parental vaccine hesitancy. Rather, they indicate a group for whom the importance and benefits of HPV vaccination may not yet be sufficiently established to support a definite positive intention.Concerning the interpretation of FHS/PHC evaluations among younger women, we agree that “I do not know/do not remember” should not be interpreted as equivalent to an explicitly negative response such as “Certainly no.” However, we believe it is important to distinguish these responses from a favorable assessment of FHS/PHC. Our classification was intended to distinguish a definite positive perception from the absence of such a perception. Accordingly, only responses in which participants were able to affirm the assessed attribute were considered favorable, whereas “I do not know/do not remember” appropriately remained outside the positive category. This distinction is particularly relevant considering the study setting. All participants were registered and receiving care at the participating FHS/PHC unit and therefore had an established relationship with primary health care [1]. In this context, being unable to affirm that professionals understood their questions, provided clear responses, allowed sufficient time to discuss their concerns, or offered specific services cannot be assumed to represent a favorable perception of those attributes. Rather, it indicates that a definite positive perception was not established, whether because of uncertainty, limited knowledge of the service, or lack of confidence regarding the attribute being assessed. We acknowledge that younger women may have had less cumulative exposure to FHS/PHC services than older women, which could have contributed to their greater frequency of “I do not know/do not remember” responses. However, because we did not specifically measure frequency and duration of primary care use, we cannot establish this explanation from our data. Importantly, our interpretation does not equate uncertain responses with negative experiences or imply poorer objective quality of care. Rather, it reflects younger participants' more limited ability to provide a definite positive assessment of several FHS/PHC attributes. We believe this distinction accurately reflects both the operational classification used in the study and the population in which these questions were assessed.Regarding healthcare professionals as an information source, we agree that reporting healthcare professionals as an information source is conceptually different from receiving a direct and explicit recommendation for HPV vaccination. Our questionnaire assessed the former but did not specifically evaluate whether a healthcare professional had recommended HPV vaccination, the strength of that recommendation, or the content of the recommendation. Therefore, the absence of an independent association between healthcare professionals as an information source and vaccination certainty should not be interpreted as evidence that professional recommendations are ineffective. The evidence the author cites regarding the importance of physician recommendations is consistent with this distinction and provides useful context for interpreting our findings [2].Concerning television as a source of health information, we agree that the observed association between television and greater certainty about vaccinating children should not be interpreted as a causal effect of television itself. Our cross‐sectional findings demonstrate an association between reporting television as a source of health information and greater vaccination certainty, rather than demonstrating that television inherently increases vaccine confidence. The content, framing, credibility, and context of information conveyed through any communication medium may determine whether that information influences vaccination attitudes favorably or unfavorably. The example the author raised regarding adverse media framing therefore complements rather than contradicts this interpretation [3]. Our findings suggest that television may be an important channel through which health information reaches the population. However, they do not establish that exposure to television per se leads to greater vaccine acceptance. We have therefore interpreted this finding as supporting the potential relevance of mass communication channels for public health communication.Finally, regarding the numerical discrepancies identified by the author, we thank them for carefully pointing them out. After rechecking the analytical dataset, we confirm that the points raised by the author require clarification. First, the 96.4% reported in the Abstract was inadvertently attributed to awareness of the Pap smear. This percentage corresponds to awareness of the cervical cancer prevention examination (291/302), whereas 226/302 participants (74.8%) specifically reported awareness of the Pap smear. Second, we confirm that the four categories of intention to vaccinate children included 300 valid responses rather than 302: 218 (72.7%) answered “Certainly yes,” 26 (8.7%) “Yes, but only if they wish to,” 47 (15.7%) “I do not know yet,” and 9 (3.0%) “No, in any case.” Two responses were missing for this item in the analytical dataset. We acknowledge that the statement in the Statistical Analysis section indicating that no missing data were identified should have been qualified for this specific item. Third, we also confirm an inconsistency in the presentation of the item assessing whether participants would seek FHS/PHC first for a new health issue. After rechecking the analytical dataset and the original statistical results, the correct distribution was 146 (48.3%) “Certainly yes”, 65 (21.5%) “Probably yes”, 65 (21.5%) “Certainly no”, and 26 (8.6%) “I do not know/do not remember”, totaling 302 participants. Among women aged ≤ 22 years, the corresponding counts were 16 (33.3%), 15 (31.3%), 15 (31.3%), and 2 (4.2%), respectively, whereas among women aged ≥ 23 years, they were 130 (51.2%), 50 (19.7%), 50 (19.7%), and 24 (9.4%), respectively. This corrected distribution is also consistent with the final analytical dataset, in which the “Certainly no” and “I do not know/do not remember” categories had been combined into a single negative/uncertain category: 65 + 26 = 91 participants overall, including 15 + 2 = 17 women aged ≤ 22 years and 50 + 24 = 74 women aged ≥ 23 years. Therefore, the discrepancy was restricted to the presentation of the counts and percentages for the “Certainly no” category and did not affect the statistical comparison between age groups. Finally, the author is correct that 39 of 302 participants correspond to 12.9%, rather than 6.0%. The number of participants was correct, but the percentage was a typographical error.We sincerely thank the author for the careful, constructive, and clinically oriented appraisal of our study. The issues raised provided an opportunity not only to identify and correct numerical inconsistencies but also to refine the interpretation of screening adherence, vaccination certainty, and younger women's perceptions of primary healthcare services. We believe that these clarifications improve the accuracy, transparency, and clinical interpretation of our findings. Importantly, they also reinforce a central message of the study: favorable preventive behaviors or intentions may coexist with substantial gaps in knowledge and certainty regarding HPV, cervical cancer, and their prevention, underscoring the continuing importance of effective health education and communication strategies within primary health care [1]. full_text: AbstractBackgroundHuman papillomaviruses (HPVs) utilize specifically modified proteoglycans (PGs) within the basement membrane as attachment factors prior to cell entry and infection. Similarly modified PGs are also found on cancer cells, which enables HPV with tumor-selective binding properties and highlights the potential development of HPV capsid-based anti-cancer therapies. In this study, we sought to investigate cancer-specific gene signatures and genetic factors that give rise to selective binding by HPV capsids.MethodsUsing belzupacap sarotalocan (bel-sar; AU-011), an HPV virus-like drug conjugate (HPV-VDC) currently in clinical trials, we performed a cell binding screen using 115 cancer cell lines from which we performed gene expressions analysis. We developed drug resistant lines to investigate the developmental factors involved in tumor targeting.ResultsWe identified a strong association between drug binding and pathways involved in TGF-β-induced epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT). Furthermore, dose escalation treatments leading to selection of bel-sar resistant HeLa cells resulted in a marked reduction in TGF-β signaling and reversal of EMT, which was associated with a reduction in the synthesis and expression of heparan- and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans.ConclusionOverall, these data suggest that bel-sar binding is strongly dependent on the differential expression and modification of PGs that occurs during the EMT process. As many cancers undergo EMT during progression and invasion, these data provide mechanistic insights underlying the tumor-selective binding ability of HPV-VDCs. (200 words).Keywords: heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG), human papillomavirus, tumor tropism, virus-like particle, virus-like drug conjugate 2.Methods2.1.Cell culture and reagentsAll culture conditions and sources of the cell lines for the binding screen are listed in Supplementary Table 1. HeLa cells and derived clones were also cultured in DMEM + 10% FBS and sub-passaged every 3-4 days to maintain sub-confluency. TGF-β1 (R&D biosystems cat: 7754-BH) was used at 10 ng/mL diluted in DMEM + 10% FBS, unless otherwise stated. SB431542 (Selleckchem cat. S1067) was used at a final concentration of 4 μM and also diluted in DMEM + 10% FBS. Bel-sar was acquired from Aura Biosciences. Heparinase I (HepI; cat. H2519), Heparinase III (HepIII; cat. H8891), and chondroitinase ABC (ChABC; cat. C3667), were all purchased from Millipore-Sigma and reconstituted according to the manufacturer’s recommendations (PBS + 50 mM NaCl + 4 mM CaCl2 + 0.01% BSA).2.2.Bel-sar binding screenAssessment of bel-sar binding capacity across the cell panel was performed as described previously (7). In brief, cell lines were harvested using 10mM EDTA, recovered for 2 hrs in culture media at 37 °C on a nutating rocker and seeded in 96-well round bottom plates at 2x106 cells/mL. Cells were then washed with media, before adding a serial dilution range of bel-sar doses (200 μL each, starting at 25 μg/mL) made in PBS + 2% FBS. Cells were then incubated for 1 hr at 4 °C and washed two times with PBS + 2% FBS to removed unbound particles. Cells were resuspended in 200 μL of phenol-red free DMEM + 10% FBS and to test bel-sar cytotoxicity, 100 μl of each sample was transferred to a black 96-well plate for treatment with 25 J/cm2 near infrared light (NIR) (Modulight ML6700-PDT with MLA Kit). The remaining 100 μL of cells were kept in the dark and served as the baseline control. Cells were allowed to recover for 1 hr at 37 °C followed by Live-Dead Yellow staining (ThermoFisher Scientific cat: L34968) for 20 mins at RT, followed by a PBS + 2% wash and fixation with 4% PFA for 10 mins at RT. Cells were then washed two times with PBS + 2% FBS prior to detection on a FACS Canto II flow cytometer (BD). FlowJo Analysis software was used to analyze the geometric mean fluorescent intensity (GMFI) of the cell-bound bel-sar using the conjugated fluorescent dye and potency was determined using the Live-Dead stain. Using GraphPad Prism to plot these values, binding and potency dose response curves were generated. Area under the dose response curve (AUC) was then calculated using GraphPad prism to generate final binding and potency capacity AUC values from the bel-sar dose range between 0 μg/mL - 7.5 μg/mL.2.3.Gene expression data and bioinformatic analysis of cell binding screenGene expression data for the cell panel was acquired from the Dependency Map Project (https://depmap.org/portal/) which contained RNA sequencing expression (RSEM) values and cell line metadata (originating tumor type, RRIDs, etc.) for all cell lines used in the analysis. Data was analyzed in R, using packages: ggplot2, GSVA, clusterProfiler, DESeq2, msigdb, and pheatmap, among others. Analysis code is available upon request. Gene sets used for GSEA were imported from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDb). GSEA was performed on a pre-ranked gene list, derived from the Spearman correlation coefficient of log10(bel-sar AUC) and variance stabilized transformation (VST) of gene expression RSEM values for each gene. Epithelial and Mesenchymal defining gene sets used for k-means clustering were acquired and used as described previously for determination of EMT intermediate states (22, 30). Gene-gene correlation studies were performed comparing the Pearson correlation coefficient of gene expression for canonical EMT markers and PG/GAG genes (Supplementary Table 2). Hierarchical clustering was then performed and plotted in R to subgroup the genes based on expression similarities.2.4.Bel-sar resistance generationTo create Bel-sar resistant HeLa clones, parental HeLas were split into 4 unique cultures (RxHeLa, RxA, RxB, and RxC) of which RxA, RxB, and RxC were treated 14 times with increasing bel-sar doses (from 0.175 – 15 μg/mL). Treatments were spaced on average 7 days apart to allow time for cell regrowth, with cells split in between treatments as needed. Bel-sar treatment consisted of harvesting each clone with Accutase (Innovative Cell Technologies Inc. cat. AT104) and aliquoting 3x106 cells into 15 mL centrifuge tubes. Cells were then washed with DMEM + 10% FBS and spun to remove supernatant, followed by treatment with the pre-determined bel-sar dose diluted in 3 mL DMEM + 10% FBS. Next, the cells were incubated at 4 °C for 1 hr with intermittent mixing, spun to remove unbound drug, and washed three times with phenol-red free DMEM + 10% FBS. The cells were then resuspended in 3 mL phenol-red free DMEM + 10% FBS and transferred to a 35 mm plate, which was treated with 25 J/cm2 NIR. Treated cell solutions were then placed in new 15 mL tubes, with 3 mL of fresh culture media, and allowed to recover for 1 hr, shaking at 37 °C, prior to replating in new culture dishes for resistance outgrowth. To note, RxHeLas were co-passaged for the duration of the study but were not treated. On even-numbered treatments, 200 μL of the recovered cells were seeded into 96-well plates for bel-sar binding and Live-Dead viability assessment as described above. Additional viability measurements were made at the conclusion of the resistance treatments using CellTiter-Glo 2.0 (Promega cat. G9242) according to manufacturer’s recommendations. After treatments 1, 5, 10, and 14, cell pellets were collected from treated cell plates, and RNA was extracted using an RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen cat. 74104). RNA sequencing was run using a NextSeq 550 instrument on poly A/mRNA enriched samples, and gene expression was analyzed from raw read counts quantified via mapping transcripts to human GENCODE v33 using salmon v1.1.0. Gene expression analysis was performed using R to calculate GSEA and GSVA enrichment scores, as well as generate plots. Analysis scripts are available upon request.2.5.Western blottingTo assess protein expression of canonical EMT markers, cells were harvested using 10 mM EDTA, washed with PBS, and spun to form pellets. Cell pellets were then lysed with RIPA buffer (150 mM NaCl. 1% NP40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, 50 mM Tris base, 1 mM EDTA) for 25 min on ice, followed by spin clarification and protein quantification using Pierce BCA protein assay kit (ThermoFisher Scientific cat. 23227). Lysates were then diluted in RIPA buffer, NuPAGE sample reducing agent and LDS Sample buffers (ThermoFisher Scientific cats. NP0009, NP0007), prior to loading on a NuPAGE 4-12% polyacrylamide gel (ThermoFisher Scientific cat. NP0322). Gels were transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore-Sigma IPVH85R) and then blocked at RT for 1 hr in 5% BSA (Millipore-Sigma 2980-1 kg). Next, blots were incubated with primary antibodies diluted 1:1000 in 5% BSA, unless otherwise indicated, and rotated overnight (O/N) at 4 °C. Antibodies were acquired from Cell Signaling Technology (E-Cadherin #3195; VIM # 5741; SNAIL #3879), Santa Cruz Biotechnology (N-Cadherin sc-59987), and ProteinTech Group (GAPDH-HRP cat. hrp-60004 *diluted 1:5000 in 5% milk). After O/N incubation, the blots were washed 3 times with Tris buffered saline + 0.1% Tween 20 (TBST), and incubated with secondary anti-rabbit or anti-mouse IgG antibodies (Cell Signaling Technology #7074 and #7076, respectively) diluted 1:3000 in 5% BSA for 1 hr. Blots were then washed three times with TBST, and protein bands were detected using Western Lightening ECL detection reagent (Millipore-Sigma NEL105001) on an Amersham Imager 600 (GE). Western blots for the detection of SMAD2 phosphorylation were performed as described above, from cell pellets harvested after 1 hr treatment with 10 ng/mL TGF-β1 using 0.05% trypsin as the detachment reagent. Phospho-SMAD2 and total SMAD2 antibodies were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (cats. #3108 and #3102, respectively).Detection of secreted biglycan and decorin was performed using concentrated conditioned media from the indicated cell cultures. Cells were seeded at 1x106 cells in T75 flasks and grown for 72 hrs prior to conditioned media collection. The collected medias were then spun at 2000 xg for 5 mins to remove any floating cells and transferred to Amicon Ultra-4 30 kDa MW cut-off filters for concentration according to the manufacture’s recommendation. The concentrated supernatants were collected and diluted in PBS to a final volume equivalent to 50-fold concentration. Samples were than diluted in reducing agent and LDS sample buffers for western blot detection as described above. Anti-BGN and DCN antibodies (R&D Biosystems cats. AF2667 and AF143 respectively) were diluted 1:1000 while HRP-conjugated, donkey anti-goat IgG (ThermoFisher Scientific cat. A15999) was diluted 1:10,000, both in 5% BSA.2.6.SMAD binding element luciferase reporter and TGF-β signaling activityThe SBE4-Luc plasmid, (a gift from Bert Vogelstein Addgene plasmid #16495) (31), was co-transfected into our HeLa-derived lines using Lipofectamine 2000 (ThermoFisher Scientific cat. 11668019), with a control pNL1.1.TK[Nluc/TK] (Promega) reporter plasmid at a 100 ng/10 ng ratio. Transfected cells were incubated for 16 hrs at 37 °C, after which the media was replaced. Cells were then treated with 10 ng/mL TGF-β1 and incubated for 24 hrs at 37 °C, before lysis and luciferase detection via the Nano-Glo Dual-luciferase Reporter Assay system (Promega cat. N1521). Luciferase signal was detected using a Synergy H1 plate reader (Biotek) and normalized relative light units (RLUs) were calculated according to the manufacturer’s guidelines, dividing RLU from the SBE4-Luc reporter by the pNL1.1.TK nano-luc signal for each well.To assess the transcriptional effects of TGF-β1 treatment within our isogenic HeLa models, cells were treated with 10 ng/mL TGF-β1 or 4 μM SB431542 for 72 hrs, prior to cell harvest and pelleting. RNA was extracted and sequenced as described above, using a NextSeq2000 instrument. Gene expression differences and analysis was performed in R and plotted using ggplot2 and GraphPad prism.2.7.GAG isolationWhole cells were lysed by physical disruption and brief sonication (30 sec on, 60 sec off for 5 mins on ice). The samples were then suspended in 2 mL 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, containing 2 mM CaCl2 and 1% Triton X-100. To this, pronase (Roche) was added to bring the final concentration up to 0.8 mg/mL, and the tissue was digested with shaking at 50 °C. After 24 hrs a second, 1.6 mg, aliquot of pronase was added and digestion continued for another 24 hrs. Finally, the enzyme was inactivated by heating to 100 °C for 15 mins. The buffer was adjusted to 2 mM MgCl2, benzonase (100 mU) was added, and the sample was incubated for 2 hrs at 37 °C. After inactivation of the enzyme (15 mins, 100 °C) any undigested material was removed by centrifugation for 1 hr at 4000 xg.The supernatant containing whole free GAGs was applied to a DEAE-Sepharose –column (Cytiva, 2 mL free bed volume), washed with ~10 column volumes of loading buffer (20 mL, pH 8 Tris Buffer, 0.1 M NaCl). The sample was passed through the column, reapplied, and the bound GAG was washed with 10CV (20 mL) loading buffer. The sample was then eluted in 3 column volumes of elution buffer (6 mL, pH 8 Tris Buffer, 2 M NaCl). The eluate was collected and lyophilized to dryness. Remaining salts were removed with a commercial PD-10 column (Cytiva), and then re lyophilized before disaccharide analysis.2.8.Disaccharide analysis and GAG quantificationAn aliquot of purified GAG material was selectively digested with either a blend of Bacteroides Heparinases I-III (specific for Heparan/Heparin Sulfate; New England Biolabs), Chondroitinase AC from Flavobacterium heparinum (specific for Chondroitin Sulfate; Sigma), or Chondroitinase B from Flavobacterium heparinum (specific for Dermatan Sulfate; Sigma) in a pH 7.0 Tris-HCl and incubated for 24 hrs at 37 °C. The enzyme was heat-inactived at 100 °C for 5 mins and then centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 30 mins to pellet any protein before introduction to the HPLC.The enzymatic products were then separated with SAX-HPLC (4.6 × 250 mm Waters Spherisorb analytical column with 5 μm particle at 1.0 ml/min flow rate) coupled to fluorescence detection via post-column derivatization using methods previously described (32). The separations of sample disaccharides were compared to the separation of standard disaccharides (Galen Laboratories) for identification and quantification.Cell surface HS and CS was also measured by cell staining with anti-HS 10E4 (Amsbio cat: 370255-1) and anti-CS-56 antibodies (Millipore-Sigma cat: SAB4200696). Cells were harvested with 10 mM EDTA, washed once with DMEM + 10% FBS, blocked with PBS + 10% FBS, and incubated for 1 hr at 4 °C with either antibody, diluted 1:200 in culture media. Next, cells were washed three times with blocking buffer and incubated with secondary anti-mouse IgM-488 antibody (Invitrogen cat: A21042) for 1 hr at 4 °C. Cells were then washed again and fixed with 4% PFA prior to detection on a flow cytometer.2.9.Cell imaging and scratch migration assayTo image morphologic changes across the HeLa clones, 2000 cells were seeded at per well in a 96-well plate, and incubated for 4 hrs at 37 °C. The cells were then left untreated, or treated with TGF-β1 (10 ng/mL) or SB431542 (4 μM) for 72 hrs at 37 °C. Following the treatments, cells were then washed with PBS prior to fixing with 4% PFA for 20 mins at RT. Next, cells were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 mins at RT and stained for 30 mins with HCS CellMask Green stain and Hoechst 33342 (ThermoFisher Scientific cats. H32721 and H3570, respectively), followed by imaging using a 10x objective and a CellVoyager CV8000 high-content microscope (Yokogawa).For the scratch migration assay, HeLa-derived cell lines were seeded at 4000 (RxHeLa) or 6000 (bel-sar resistant clones) cells per well in a 96-well plate and incubated 72 hours until confluent. Scratches were then made across each well, using a p200 pipet tip. Wells were then washed with warm culture media, and incubated for 30 mins at 37 °C. Following this incubation, the plate was transferred to a Cytation7 automated imaging microscope (Biotek), which was kept at 37 °C and 5% CO2 throughout the duration of the experiment. Brightfield images of each well were acquired using a 4x objective every 30 mins for 24 hours. Images were then processed using Gen5 software, and total wound area was calculated for every well and time point. In addition, average velocity measurements were determined for each well, calculated as μm2 per second, for the first 12 hrs of imaging, corresponding to overall cell migration across the wound.2.10.Binding assessments of bel-sar resistant clonesMeasurement of bel-sar binding capacity for the HeLa-derived cell clones was performed as described above (see section entitled Bel-sar binding screen), with the notable exception of bel-sar dilutions occurring in DMEM + 10% FBS. For assessment of bel-sar binding in high serum conditions, bel-sar was first pre-diluted to a final concentration of 2 μg/mL in DMEM containing varying concentrations of FBS, and incubated at RT for 30 mins prior to cell binding assessment. For glycosidase treatments, cells were seeded in a 96-well plate at 50 k/well and pre-treated with the different enzymes diluted in DMEM without FBS to a final concentration of 1 U/mL (HepIII) or 2 U/mL (HepI and ChABC). Enzyme treatments were performed at 37 °C for 1.5 hrs, after which bel-sar was added at a final concentration of 2 μg/mL and binding was assessed via flow cytometry as described above. When indicated, AUC was calculated as area under the GMFI intensity-dose curve, for bel-sar doses 0-10 μg/mL.2.11.Data analysis, graphing, and statisticsData was analyzed and plotted using R (gene expression correlation, volcano plots, hierarchical clustering, heatmaps, and spot density plots) or GraphPad prism (select bar/line plots, and non-linear regression fitting). Unless otherwise stated, data points represent the mean of three independent biological replicat…

full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.HPV-VDC binding correlates with EMT gene expression signaturesTo investigate the broad tumor tropism of HPV-VDCs, we first performed a binding screen of 115 cancer cell lines, originating from 20 different tumor types, with the drug, AU-011 (bel-sar). Bel-sar binding was assessed via direct fluorescent detection of the conjugated dye on cells and quantified as a summed area under the dose range-intensity curve (AUC) (Supplementary Table 1). Overall, bel-sar displayed a remarkably broad binding affinity, strongly interacting to cell line representatives from nearly all tumor types (Figure 1A). Both central nervous system (CNS) and melanoma (labelled as skin) cell lines were strongly represented in the top binding quintile of the panel (Supplementary Figure 1A). As expected, hematopoietic cancers (lymphoid and myeloid), which are known to express very low levels of cell surface PGs (33), were almost completely devoid of binding and heavily enriched in the lowest binding quintile. Of note, the binding capacity of cell lines for bel-sar was strongly predicative of drug-sensitivity (pearson r2 = 0.70), supporting previous work that found cell surface binding is an essential pre-requisite for drug-induced cell killing (7) (Supplementary Figure 1B).Figure 1HPV-VDC binding correlates with gene expression signatures involved in the Epithelial to Mesenchymal Transition. (A) Bel-sar binding capacity of 115 cancer cell lines as measured by calculating area under the dose response curve (AUC) for bel-sar binding geometric mean fluorescence intensity (GMFI). Dashed lines indicate separations of binding quintiles. (B) Top ten positively and negatively enriched gene sets from Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using expression data acquired from the Dependency Map Project (34). (C, D) Gene set variant analysis (GSVA) enrichment scores (ES) of cells in A, sorted by binding quintile for Hallmark_EMT (C) and TGFB_UP (D) gene sets. (E) GSVA enrichment scores (ES) of epithelial- and mesenchymal-derived gene sets for cell lines in A, colored by k-means computed clusters. (F, G) Hallmark_EMT enrichment score (F) and Bel-sar binding of cell lines (log(AUC) (G), *p < 0.05, **p< 0.01, ***p<0.001.Panel A shows a bar chart of area under the curve for bel-sar binding across various cancer cell lines, color-coded by cancer type. Panel B presents a bubble plot listing the top ten most positive and negative gene sets with normalized enrichment scores, indicating upregulated and downregulated pathways. Panel C contains a violin plot comparing hallmark epithelial-mesenchymal transition enrichment score among five binding groups. Panel D provides a violin plot representing TGFB_UP enrichment score by binding group. Panel E displays a scatter plot of mesenchymal versus epithelial enrichment scores, sized and colored by binding group and k-means cluster. Panel F features a violin plot of hallmark EMT enrichment score by k-means cluster. Panel G shows a violin plot of log-transformed AUC values by k-means cluster, with significance bars above groups.Next, we wished to explore the transcriptomic signatures and identify genetic biomarkers which underlie the susceptibility of cancer cell lines for HPV-VDC binding. RNA-seq expression data from the Cancer Dependency Map project (DepMap) (34) were available for all of the cancer cell lines tested and displayed a broad level of transcriptional diversity across the panel (Supplementary Figure 1C). Spearman correlation coefficients comparing binding capacity and gene expression were then used to create a ranked gene list for gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Supplementary Figure 2A). Using more than 10,000 curated gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (35, 36), we identified the HALLMARK_EPITHELIAL_TO_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION gene set (henceforth labeled, Hallmark_EMT) as the most positively enriched gene set associated with bel-sar binding (Figure 1B; Supplementary Figure 2B). Interestingly, a number of ECM-related gene sets were also positively enriched, indicating a preference for cells with large-scale dysregulation of their extracellular environment. To assess how the Hallmark_EMT gene set was presented throughout the cell line panel, an enrichment score was calculated via gene set variant analysis (GSVA) (37) for all 115 cell lines. We found a strong positive association of Hallmark_EMT with bel-sar binding, with the top two binding quintiles displaying very high average enrichment scores (Figure 1C). Additionally, using previously described (24) and curated lists of genes over- or under-expressed during TGF-β induced EMT (TGF-β UP and TGF-β DOWN, respectively), we found a notable enrichment in TGF-β UP genes within our highest binding quintiles with little to no correlation associated with TGF-β DOWN genes (Figure 1D; Supplementary Figure 2C). Together, this suggests that EMT, and more specifically TGF-β-induced EMT, may drive genetic expression patterns that act to enhance the binding of bel-sar to cancer cell lines.To understand how bel-sar binding capacity changes as cells progress through EMT, enrichment scores were generated as described previously (30) for epithelial-defining and mesenchymal-defining genes. These scores were calculated for all 115 cell lines, and k-means clustering was performed to subgroup each cell line into clusters corresponding to different intermediate stages of the EMT process (Figure 1E). To note, cell lines that displayed strong negative enrichment scores for both epithelial and mesenchymal gene lists, were classified as a non-EMT subgroup, which contained nearly all of the hematopoietic-derived cell lines. Bel-sar binding capacity was found to vary based on these defined EMT clusters and was significantly reduced in the more epithelial-like cell lines (clusters 3,4, and 5) compared to the mesenchymal-like cells (clusters 1 and 2), with the non-EMT cluster (cluster 6) having the lowest overall binding capacity (Figure 1G). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionOverall, we have found that HPV-VDC binding to cancer cells is dependent on the cell surface expression of PGs that are upregulated during the process of EMT. Using an extensive panel of diverse cancer cell lines, we identified a strong association between TGF-β-induced EMT and binding with bel-sar. This connection was supported through examination of gene expression correlation approaches, which identified a subset of genes involved in HS and CS biosynthesis that are important for bel-sar binding and whose expression firmly correlated with EMT induced by TGF-β signaling. Additionally, we identified inhibition of TGF-β as a major driving event during the step-wise development of bel-sar resistance in HeLa cells. This loss corresponded with reduced levels of cell surface GAGs, a partial MET phenotype, and the downregulation of key PG/GAG-related genes. Lastly, we found that bel-sar resistance in our HeLa cells originated via both TGF-β dependent and independent processes. The concomitant loss of CS polymerization factors and the overexpression of Class I SLRPs, such as biglycan, work together to repress TGF-β signaling. This repression results in the dysregulation of many other HS and CS biosynthesis enzymes, further perpetuating the observed TGF-β inhibition, and driving overall resistance to bel-sar binding and killing (Figure 6).Figure 6Bel-sar resistance in HeLa cells is driven by inhibition of TGF-β dependent and independent processes. Graphic model for the selection of bel-sar binding-impaired HeLa cell clones. Bel-sar dose escalation selects for cells which have reduced CS/DS expression, which decreases the overall glycosylation of Class I SLRPs, such as BGN, and enhances their TGF-β inhibitory abilities. The resulting inhibition of TGF-β signaling results in a partial mesenchymal to epithelial transition (MET), and a repression of numerous GAG biosynthesis and core proteoglycan genes. This reduction in PG/GAG genes further reduces the bel-sar binding capacity of HeLa cell clones and strengthens the inhibition of TGF-β signaling through the additional loss of glycosylation on SLRPs and HSPG2. Figure was generated using BioRender.Complex pathway diagram illustrating the relationship between Bel-sar selection, impaired proteoglycan (PG) expression, TGF-beta signaling, and gene repression, with specific emphasis on Class I SLRPs, gene expression changes, and key molecular players such as DCN, BGN, and TGF-beta receptor, leading to acquired Bel-sar resistance or mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET).The binding affinity of bel-sar for PGs, or more specifically GAG chains, has been previously documented, and is derived from the main component of the VDC, an HPV virus-like-particle (8). Natural HPV infection occurs at sites of wounds, which expose both the basement membrane and basal epithelial cells to binding by the incoming virus (1, 8). In such wounding environments, the virus is surrounded by a multitude of host cells and factors which are tasked with repairing the epithelial barrier. One important aspect of this wound repair process is the induction of EMT in the surrounding epithelial cells. Platelets, invading immune cells, and adjacent epithelium all release cytokines, such as TGF-β, which induce EMT in the local epithelial cells, and promote cell migration and the overall re-epithelialization of the wound (38). Thus, it is likely that physiological HPV binding occurs in the presence of these EMT-inducing growth factors, and may in fact, have evolved to take advantage of them. In support of this, it has been well-documented that HPV interacts with a variety of extracellular enzymes and growth factors associated with a wounding environment, and that these interactions are required for proper viral entry and infection (39). Further, the influx of serum and platelet factors present in a wound may also determine the specificity of viral binding events. Previous work from our lab has shown that elevated serum or platelet factors effectively block canonical HSPG receptors on the cell surface and promote CSPG-mediated binding of HPV (4). While the potential advantages of CSPG-binding for viral infection remain to be elucidated, this change in receptor binding may result in altered tropism towards certain cell populations more suitable for viral proliferation. Interestingly, we found that all three bel-sar resistant HeLa clones completely lost the ability to bind the HPV-VDC in high serum conditions, and that enzymatic removal of CS chains from these cells had very limited impact on bel-sar binding compared to parental HeLas, even in normal media conditions. Altogether, this suggests that HPV-VDC interactions with cell surface CSPGs are likely important mediators of bel-sar induced cell killing and likely contribute to the enhanced binding observed on mesenchymal-like cancer cells.As a dynamic regulator of EMT progression, TGF-β controls the expression of countless genes, including many well-characterized extracellular PGs (17, 24). Additionally, TGF-β has been shown to influence total GAG content of cells, indicating that underlying GAG biosynthesis may also be under its control (40, 41). There is mounting evidence that the levels of specific GAGs change during the EMT process, with the balance shifting from HS towards increasing CS content (42–44). Despite this, there remains much to be understood regarding the exact alterations that occur in GAG biosynthesis during EMT, as well as the genetic players involved. Here we show, that across a number of genetically diverse cancer cell lines, the expression of many GAG-related enzymes is strongly associated with transcriptional markers of EMT, including TGF-β1. Further, we show that TGF-β treatment in HeLa cells results in the enhancement of many of these GAG genes, including NDST1, EXT1, CHST11, and CHPF2, directly linking TGF-β signaling with the biosynthesis of HS and CS. As these GAGs perform a plethora of important cellular functions, the effects of TGF-β-induced changes in HS/CS expression expand well beyond HPV-VDC binding and likely influence the cellular binding and interactions with structural ECM proteins and cytokines. For example, FGF, Wnt, and IGF-1 all use HSPGs as co-receptors for activation and signaling through their canonical receptors (12, 26). This is of note, as these growth factors have been shown to modulate TGF-β signaling via crosstalk with downstream effectors and can act independently to initiate progression through EMT (20, 45). Thus, these HS-regulated growth factors may also have direct effects on the expression of GAGs and provide examples of how TGF-β independent processes may control the binding of bel-sar and other HPV-VDCs.As mentioned previously, due in part to their pleiotropic growth factor binding abilities, GAGs and PGs have been associated as biomarkers for a number of different cancers (12). As a result of this link, targeting tumor-specific PGs is gaining momentum as a promising area in cancer therapeutics development (8, 46). With the notable exception of a monoclonal antibody that recognizes cancer-restricted CSPG modifications, identifying monoclonal antibodies that directly interact with the cancer-associated GAG chains has been challenging (47). This is due in part to the size and complexity of polysaccharides. GAG chains can extended up to 250 disaccharides in length and typically contain diverse stretches of sulfated and non-sulfated regions (10). It is thought that this linear spacing, as well as overall chain length and the individual array of sulfated sugars, are what determine binding affinity (10). Consequently, antibodies or other similarly-sized molecules, have binding epitopes that are generally too small to decipher these structural differences and are less effective at sampling the true range of cancer-targetable GAG modifications. full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionHuman papillomaviruses (HPVs) are a family of non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses which infect actively dividing basal cells at sites of epithelial wounding (1). HPV particles initially bind secreted heparan sulfate- or chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans located within the exposed basement membrane, before transferring to host cell receptors for viral internalization and transduction (1–4). Interestingly, HPV pseudovirus (PsV) has been shown to selectively bind and infect a variety of cancer cell lines through direct interaction with cell surface proteoglycans (PGs), bypassing the requirement for initial basement membrane interaction (4, 5). As primary, non-cancer-derived, cell cultures are unable to bind HPV PsV, it was proposed that cancer cell lines in particular, express specifically modified PGs which mimic those found within the basement membrane and facilitate viral binding (5, 6). This observation has prompted the development of HPV capsid-based anti-cancer therapies such as belzupacap sarotalocan (bel-sar; AU-011)), which is currently in clinical trials for the treatment of choroidal melanoma and bladder cancer (7, 8).Proteoglycans are cell surface-expressed or secreted glycoproteins which are comprised of a protein core covalently attached to at least one glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chain, such as heparan sulfate (HS), chondroitin sulfate (CS), keratan sulfate (KS), or dermatan sulfate (DS) (9). While all types of PGs are expressed in humans, heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) especially, make up a diverse family of receptor molecules that participate in many important cellular processes, including cell growth, signal transduction, angiogenesis, and adhesion (10–12). HS and CS chain biosynthesis involves a series of semi-overlapping enzymes that regulate initiation, elongation, and sulfation of the growing polysaccharide, which can sometimes reach chain lengths of up to 250 disaccharides (10, 13, 14). Both the length and sulfation pattern of the resulting GAG chain are crucial for the function of PGs, providing binding sites for growth factors (e.g. FGF, VEGF, TGFβ) as well as for extracellular matrix (ECM) components (e.g. collagen, integrins, and fibronectin) (9, 10, 12). Given their vital functions in integrating extracellular cues, it is unsurprising that alterations in the expression and modification of CSPGs and HSPGs have been identified as driving events in cancer development and progression (15, 16). One such driving event relates to the regulatory roles that PGs play during the process of epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) (17). EMT encompasses a variety of global cellular events that occur as cells switch from epithelial to mesenchymal phenotypes, such as changes in gene expression, behavior, and overall morphology (18). During EMT, epithelial cells lose their characteristic tight cell junctions, apical-basal polarity, and overall adhesion to the basement membrane, developing instead a flatter, fibroblast-like morphology with increased migratory and invasive capacity (18, 19). EMT is an essential process for many normal-physiological conditions, including embryonic development, stem cell maintenance, and wound healing (20). However, EMT also occurs in pathogenic settings, such as cancer, where it promotes local metastasis and resistance to therapies (18–21). Both EMT and its reciprocal process, the mesenchymal to epithelial transition (MET), are reversible events, stimulated and enacted by a variety of extracellular cues and effector signaling molecules (18–20). These processes rarely result in complete phenotypic transitions, and instead manifest as a continuum of intermediate states, with cells possessing mixtures of both epithelial and mesenchymal characteristics (18, 22).Many PGs, including members of the syndecan and glypican family of proteins, are notable participants in EMT and found to be upregulated during the transition from epithelial to mesenchymal phenotypes (17). Their functional role in focal adhesion formation and binding to ECM components can directly control cell morphology, cell adhesion, and migration, all key hallmarks of EMT (18, 23). In addition to these contributions, PGs also play a regulatory role throughout the EMT process, via interactions with stromal cytokines such as TGF-β (17). Perhaps the most well-known, and best studied, of the many EMT-inducing growth factors, TGF-β activates SMAD-dependent and SMAD-independent signaling pathways to drive the expression and repression of hundreds of genes (19, 24). Genes induced by TGF-β include important transcription factors SNAIL, SLUG, and TWIST1, which act to repress epithelial genes, such as E-cadherin (CDH1), and stimulate the expression of numerous mesenchymal genes, including N-Cadherin (CDH2), vimentin (VIM) and all three known TGF-β isoforms, ultimately driving EMT (19, 25). In addition to these classic EMT markers, TGF-β has also been found to regulate the expression of cell surface and secreted PGs, laying the framework for many of the phenotypic changes that occur during the EMT process (17). Interestingly, TGF-β activity can be controlled by PGs at a variety of levels. HSPGs act as crucial coreceptors for FGF, IGF-1, and Wnt receptor activation (26). These signaling pathways crosstalk with downstream SMAD and non-SMAD pathways and can modulate TGF-β activity in a context-specific manner (26). Extracellularly, PGs can control the activation of TGF-β from latency and regulate its overall bioavailability. For example, latent TGF-β relies on the presence of secreted PGs (e.g. perlecan, shed syndecans etc.) in the ECM for binding prior to activation by cellular proteases or integrin-mediated processes (27, 28). Additionally, stromal inhibitors such as biglycan (BGN) and decorin (DCN), two small leucine-rich proteoglycan (SLRP) Class I family members, tightly bind and sequester TGF-β, reducing its availability to activate neighboring cells (27, 29). Interestingly, the chondroitin and dermatan sulfate chains present on BGN and DCN, are known to interfere with this TGF-β binding ability. Therefore, in addition to the roles described for the different cell surface and secreted PGs, their associated GAG chains may also provide additional levels of control over TGF-β activity.Despite widespread pre-clinical and clinical evidence for PGs as mediators of oncogenic signaling, less is known about the exact GAG modifications that occur during cancer development and how they contribute to the binding affinity of these pleiotropic receptors. Insights here could provide a better understanding of general tumor biology as well as afford detailed information regarding specific GAG binding motifs which can be therapeutically exploited by proteoglycan-targeted anti-cancer therapies. One such promising therapy, bel-sar, is an HPV-based virus-drug conjugate (VDC) comprised of an HPV-derived virus-like-particle conjugated to a photoactivatable infrared dye. Bel-sar has been shown to directly bind cancer cells via cell surface PG receptors and upon photoactivation, promote immediate reactive oxygen species (ROS)-induced necrotic cell death (7, 8). In this study, we wished to investigate the transcriptional signatures and PG/GAG biomarkers that are responsible for the cancer-selective binding properties of bel-sar. We found that enhanced drug binding is strongly associated with TGF-β-induced EMT expression signatures across a wide array of different cancer cell lines. Additionally, we observed that inhibition of TGF-β signaling is accompanied by a global loss in HS and CS expression and can result in resistance to HPV-VDC treatment in vitro. Overall, this work suggests that PGs and GAGs are dynamically and specifically modified throughout the EMT process, especially as a result of TGF-β signaling. full_text: Abstract Background and objectives Women with autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases (AIIRDs) are more vulnerable to human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and HPV-related cervical cancers, however, the HPV screening and vaccination rate is low. We conducted a real-world single-center, convenience-sample survey to evaluate the awareness and status of HPV vaccination among patients with AIIRDs at a tertiary hospital in China. Methods Female AIIRDs patients aged ≥ 9 years were enrolled between 1 April 2024 and 31 Aug 2024. Eligible participants were recruited via social media invitations and at outpatient clinics and invited to complete a predefined 41-item questionnaire. Demographic characteristics, rheumatic disease history, awareness of HPV infection and vaccination, results of HPV testing, HPV vaccination status and willingness to receive HPV vaccination were analyzed. Stratified comparison was performed between systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients. Results A total of 550 participants with a median age of 34.7 (IQR 29.5–42.0) years completed the questionnaires. The awareness rates of HPV infection and vaccination were 82.4% and 85.8%, respectively. However, only 69.3% of participants recognized the increased risk of cervical cancer associated with HPV, and only 52.0% reported having received cervical cancer screening in the past 5 years. Although 72.5% expressed willingness to receive the HPV vaccine, the reported vaccination rate was only 18.7%. Among the respondents, there were 334 SLE patients and 98 RA patients. Compared to RA patients, SLE patients were younger, reported higher awareness of HPV vaccination, but a lower vaccination rate. Conclusion This study identifies several patient-reported knowledge gaps and perceived obstacles to HPV vaccination among a single-center cohort of Chinese AIIRDs patients, alongside a pronounced disconnect between awareness, willingness, and actual uptake. Larger, multicenter studies are needed to confirm these patterns.
